papers.title: Selective suppression of harmful cyanobacteria in an entire lake with hydrogen peroxide
papers.scale: lab incubations; duplicate lake enclosures (0, 2.5, 5, 8 mg/L); whole Lake Koetshuis, NL (~0.12 km2, max depth 2 m) with untreated Lake Langebosch as reference
papers.dose: 2.0 mg/L H2O2 target (23 mL of 10% stock per m3 via water harrow), once; measured 1.0-2.5 mg/L within 3 h
papers.result: Cyanobacteria fell from 600x10^3 cells/mL the day before to <10x10^3 cells/mL within 10 days (microcystin followed with a 2-day lag) while the untreated reference lake kept rising; numbers stayed low for 7 weeks, then rose to ~200x10^3 cells/mL by end of September. In enclosures, P. agardhii was >98% below control at day 9.
papers.env_effects: H2O2 fell to 0.7 mg/L after 1 day and below detection after 2 days. Enclosures: zooplankton (Daphnia, Diaphanosoma) fell ~35% at 2.5 mg/L and nearly vanished at 5-8 mg/L; green algae showed cell-wall damage at 5-8 mg/L. Whole lake at 2 mg/L: zooplankton stable for 5 weeks, eukaryotic phytoplankton not strongly affected, ammonium spiked after lysis, and transparency did not improve (stayed 45-60 cm).
papers.key_details: Stepwise design: lab incubations (duplicates) showed 1-4 mg/L cut photosynthetic vitality to <30% within 3 h, with ~0.3 mg/L consumed by water-matrix reactions; duplicate lake enclosures at 2.5, 5 and 8 mg/L cut P. agardhii >98% vs control by day 9 but higher doses nearly eliminated zooplankton, so 2 mg/L was chosen for the whole lake. Whole-lake treatment (single lake, unreplicated, one untreated reference lake) collapsed the Planktothrix bloom within 10 days and microcystin followed. Recovery began after ~7 weeks with P. agardhii plus invading Woronichinia naegeliana. Water clarity did not improve despite the collapse.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record's '99% within a few days' is slightly compressed: counts fell from 600x10^3 to <10x10^3 cells/mL within 10 days. Record omitted that enclosure doses >=5 mg/L nearly eliminated zooplankton (and 2.5 mg/L cut it ~35%), that transparency did not improve, and that cyanobacteria returned after 7 weeks. Whole-lake part is n=1 with one reference lake.

reasons.reproducibility: Whole-lake H2O2 dosing with a water harrow needs permits and field equipment.
reasons.effectiveness: Duplicate enclosures cut Planktothrix >98% vs control and the whole lake fell from 600,000 to <10,000 cells/mL against a rising reference lake, lasting 7 weeks.
reasons.cost: Treating a 0.12 km2 lake with field gear costs over $5,000.
reasons.time: The bloom collapsed within about 10 days of the single dose.
reasons.environment: H2O2 was gone in 2 days and lake zooplankton held at 2 mg/L, but enclosures lost ~35% of zooplankton at 2.5 mg/L and ammonium spiked.

papers.title: Termination of a toxic Alexandrium bloom with hydrogen peroxide
papers.scale: whole brackish creek (after lab and canal tests)
papers.dose: 50 mg/L H2O2
papers.result: Vegetative cells and pellicle cysts -99.8% within 48 h; PSP toxins below 15 µg/L; bloom recurred at lower levels the next year.
papers.env_effects: Zooplankton strongly affected; macroinvertebrates and fish minimally.

reasons.reproducibility: Treating a whole brackish creek with a toxic Alexandrium bloom needs permits and field-scale dosing.
reasons.effectiveness: Cells and cysts fell 99.8% in 48 h, though the bloom recurred at lower levels the next year.
reasons.cost: A 50 mg/L dose across a whole creek is well over $5,000.
reasons.time: Result visible within 48 h.
reasons.environment: At 50 mg/L zooplankton were strongly affected, a clear non-target harm.

papers.title: Applicability of Hydrogen Peroxide in Brown Tide Control – Culture and Microcosm Studies
papers.organism: Aureococcus anophagefferens + 11 marine species (Phaeodactylum, T. pseudonana, T. weissflogii, P. micans, Amphidinium, Micromonas, etc.)
papers.scale: cultures + Barnegat Bay seawater microcosms
papers.result: 1.6 mg/L cut Aureococcus chl-a >90% by 24 h (24-h EC50 0.91 mg/L); of the other 11 species only Micromonas was eradicated; at 6.4 mg/L P. micans (11.2%) and T. weissflogii (2.6%) were not significantly inhibited; inhibition fell with cell size.
papers.env_effects: Microcosms: diatoms and greens dipped, then exceeded controls within 72 h; cyanobacteria down about 50%.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Aureococcus anophagefferens + 11 marine species (Phaeodactylum

reasons.reproducibility: Bench cultures and microcosms with purchased Aureococcus and 11 other strains are doable with a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: 1.6 mg/L cut Aureococcus chl-a >90% by 24 h, but most other species were barely touched.
reasons.cost: Twelve purchased cultures plus H2O2 and fluorometry fall around $150-500.
reasons.time: Aureococcus reduction seen within 24 h.
reasons.environment: Diatoms and greens dipped then rebounded within 72 h, but cyanobacteria fell about 50%, a minor non-target effect.

papers.title: Effect of algal growth phase on Aureococcus anophagefferens susceptibility to hydrogen peroxide
papers.scale: cultures at 1.6×10⁶ cells/mL
papers.result: Stationary-phase cells had weaker ROS scavenging and needed 30-40% less H2O2 for 90% removal within 12 h.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.

reasons.reproducibility: Single-species culture dosing at 0.4-1.6 mg/L is simple, but Aureococcus must be bought and grown.
reasons.effectiveness: 90% removal within 12 h at low doses, with a clear growth-phase effect.
reasons.cost: One purchased culture, H2O2 and cell counting is roughly $150-500.
reasons.time: 90% removal inside 12 h.
reasons.environment: Non-target effects not reported; H2O2 itself is short-lived, so scored as short-lived residue.

papers.title: Mitigation of Marine Dinoflagellates Using Hydrogen Peroxide (H2O2) Increases Toxicity towards Epithelial Gill Cells
papers.organism: Alexandrium catenella, Karenia selliformis, Lepidodinium, Prorocentrum micans; RTgill-W1 fish gill cells
papers.scale: cultures at 1000 cells/mL (salinity 25/33) + gill-cell assay
papers.dose: 50-1000 mg/L (ppm) H2O2
papers.result: 50 mg/L (lowest dose tested) killed all 4 dinoflagellates, leaving photosynthetic efficiency at 12% and viability at 6.4%; gill-cell toxicity rose, even with non-toxic P. micans and Lepidodinium.
papers.env_effects: Lysed cells made the water more toxic to fish gill cells (aldehydes from lipid peroxidation proposed); H2O2 alone cytotoxic to gill cells, fading after 24 h below 200 ppm.

reasons.reproducibility: Four dinoflagellate cultures (two toxic) plus a fish gill cell line need a cell-culture lab.
reasons.effectiveness: 50 mg/L killed all four dinoflagellates (viability 6.4%), a strong algal effect even though the paper is flagged negative.
reasons.cost: Algal cultures plus RTgill-W1 cell culture reagents run $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Duration not reported; photosynthesis and viability assays are short-term, scored as ≤3 days.
reasons.environment: Lysed cells made the water more toxic to fish gill cells, and H2O2 itself was cytotoxic.

papers.title: Removal of the red tide dinoflagellate Cochlodinium polykrikoides using chemical disinfectants
papers.scale: 10 mL batch reactors (25 mL flasks), 22 +/- 2 C; C. polykrikoides 0.5-3x10^3 cells/mL; fish 72 h acute tests
papers.dose: H2O2 0.1, 1, 5 and 10 mg/L (O3 0.5-5; MnO4- and NaOCl 0.1-5 mg/L)
papers.duration: minutes to 3 h (cell removal); 72 h (fish LC50)
papers.result: All four oxidants inactivated and lysed C. polykrikoides with efficacy O3 > MnO4- > NaOCl > H2O2; 10 mg/L H2O2 completely inactivated 3x10^3 cells/mL in 3 h. Fish 72-h LC50s were 1.35 (O3, estimated), 0.39 (MnO4-), 1.32 (NaOCl) and 102.61 mg/L (H2O2).
papers.env_effects: O3 and NaOCl formed bromate (probable human carcinogen) via HOBr; MnO4- and H2O2 formed no detectable bromate or significant residual oxidants. Red sea bream showed no mortality at 50 mg/L H2O2 over 72 h; low H2O2 fish toxicity was also confirmed in juvenile starry flounder. Authors judge H2O2 the most practical and safe option.
papers.key_details: Lab batch comparison of four disinfectants against cultured C. polykrikoides at several doses and initial cell densities, with triplicate sampling at each time point and sulfite quenching. Removal rates fell with higher cell density for all oxidants, but less so for H2O2 because its decay was little affected by cells. H2O2 needed higher doses (up to 10 mg/L) to match the others. Fish acute toxicity (probit LC50) showed H2O2 ~75-260x safer than the other oxidants.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record said the effective H2O2 dose was not in the abstract; full text shows complete inactivation of 3x10^3 cells/mL at 10 mg/L in 3 h, with doses tested 0.1-10 mg/L.

reasons.reproducibility: Uses a purchased ichthyotoxic Cochlodinium culture, an ozone generator, bromate analysis and fish LC50 tests.
reasons.effectiveness: 10 mg/L H2O2 completely inactivated 3,000 cells/mL within 3 h with triplicate sampling, though lower doses were weaker and H2O2 was the least potent oxidant.
reasons.cost: Culture, ozone generator, fish and bromate analysis cost $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Inactivation was complete within 3 hours.
reasons.environment: H2O2 left no bromate or residual oxidant and its fish LC50 was 102.6 mg/L, far above the working dose.

papers.title: Treatment of the red tide dinoflagellate Karenia brevis and brevetoxins using USEPA-registered algaecides
papers.scale: lab, natural bloom density (1.79×10⁷ cells/L)
papers.dose: 3 peroxide products; 4.89-7.08 mg/L needed
papers.result: K. brevis needed 4.89-7.08 mg/L of the peroxide products vs 0.31-0.34 mg Cu/L for copper; the most stable product lost 0.467 mg/L per day in natural seawater.
papers.env_effects: Decay faster with salinity, microbes and particles ≥0.2 µm; authors call for pilot studies on marine non-targets.

reasons.reproducibility: Needs K. brevis, a toxic organism, grown at bloom density (1.79e7 cells/L).
reasons.effectiveness: Peroxide products worked only at 4.89-7.08 mg/L, ~20x the copper dose; no percent reduction given.
reasons.cost: Toxic culture plus three commercial products is about $150-500.
reasons.time: Duration not reported; product decay measured per day, scored ≤3 days.
reasons.environment: Decays at 0.467 mg/L/day, but marine non-target effects untested.

papers.title: Evaluation of algaecide effectiveness of five different oxidants applied on harmful phytoplankton
papers.scale: lab; 100 mL subcultures in natural Cadiz Bay seawater + f/2, started at ~10^4 cells/mL (ballast-water context)
papers.dose: dose-response per oxidant; H2O2 EC50 6.67-7.08 mg/L
papers.result: H2O2 gave a moderate growth inhibition sustained over 14 d with similar effect on both species (EC50 6.67-7.08 mg/L); PMS and PAA were stronger but depleted within 24 h, and PDS failed to inhibit growth.
papers.env_effects: H2O2 half-life in the cultures 0.2-0.3 days at 7.5 mg/L.
papers.key_details: Cultured Prymnesium parvum and Heterosigma akashiwo (Spanish isolates) were grown to ~10^4 cells/mL and split into 100 mL subcultures dosed with H2O2, peracetic acid, peroxymonosulfate, peroxydisulfate or hypochlorite, with untreated negative controls. Cell density was tracked by calibrated fluorescence every 2 days and oxidant decay daily for 14 d; EC50s came from integrated growth curves. H2O2 EC50 was 6.67-7.08 mg/L with a sustained effect and similar potency on both species; PMS (EC50 0.40-1.99 mg/L) and PAA (0.32-2.70 mg/L) were stronger but short-lived; PDS had negligible effect. The authors warn that concentration-response readings before day 7 can mislead. Replicate numbers were not stated in the text read.

reasons.reproducibility: Needs purchased ichthyotoxic Prymnesium and Heterosigma cultures and a calibrated fluorometer.
reasons.effectiveness: H2O2 gave only moderate sustained inhibition (EC50 6.7-7.1 mg/L), and replicate numbers were not stated.
reasons.cost: Two cultures, reagents and fluorescence readings cost $150-500.
reasons.time: Effects were tracked over 14 days and the authors warn readings before day 7 mislead.
reasons.environment: H2O2 half-life was 0.2-0.3 days, leaving little residue; non-targets were not tested.

papers.title: Chemical Control of Ichthyotoxic Algal Blooms in Aquaculture: Assessing Algicide Impacts on Cellular Motility and Bloom Suppression
papers.organism: Prymnesium parvum, Heterosigma akashiwo, Fibrocapsa japonica
papers.scale: cultures (f/2, f/20)
papers.dose: dose-response
papers.result: 24-h EC50: 3.35 (P. parvum), 6.01 (H. akashiwo), 7.86 (F. japonica) mg/L; motility and mean squared displacement fell at sublethal doses.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.

reasons.reproducibility: Three purchased ichthyotoxic cultures with motility tracking need a microscope camera but are sponsor-doable.
reasons.effectiveness: 24-h EC50s of 3.35-7.86 mg/L vary by species; no large percent reduction stated.
reasons.cost: Three cultures plus video microscopy is about $150-500.
reasons.time: 24-h endpoint.
reasons.environment: Non-target effects not reported; H2O2 is short-lived.

papers.title: Combating Toxic Blooms of Prymnesium parvum: Hydrogen Peroxide Influence on the Haptophyte, Other Phytoplankton Taxa, and Concentrations of Prymnesins Under Experimental Conditions
papers.scale: four 40 L tanks of Gliwice Canal bloom water (one control + one tank per dose, no replication), continuous light
papers.dose: 14, 28, 42 mg/L H2O2 nominal, single dose
papers.duration: 12 d stage 1 + 15 d stage 2 (after 15 L re-inoculation with bloom water)
papers.result: P. parvum fell 98.6%, 98.8% and 99.0% within 24 h at 14, 28 and 42 mg/L, with no living cells by day 3 and no recovery through day 12; after re-inoculation with bloom water P. parvum in the 14 and 28 mg/L tanks rose above the control.
papers.env_effects: Total phytoplankton biomass dropped 83%, 84% and 81% in 24 h; filamentous cyanobacteria (Planktothrix agardhii, Pseudanabaena limnetica) disappeared, green algae then dominated (~80% in T1). H2O2 was below 1 mg/L by day 3. Prymnesins decomposed rather than being released abruptly; a shift toward PRM 990 and higher per-cell toxin after re-inoculation.
papers.key_details: Water from a P. parvum bloom in the Gliwice Canal (Poland, April 2023) was split into four 40 L tanks: a control and single doses of 14, 28 and 42 mg/L H2O2; each treatment is a single unreplicated tank. P. parvum declined 98.6-99.0% within 24 h and no living cells remained by day 3 in any treated tank; total phytoplankton biomass fell 81-84% in 24 h. H2O2 dropped to about 3, <10 and 30 mg/L after 24 h and was undetectable after day 3. On day 12, 15 L of each tank was replaced with fresh bloom water (4.6 x 10^7 cells/L): P. parvum in T1 and T2 then exceeded the control, while T3 tracked the control. Prymnesins were degraded along with the cells, but the regrown population had a more toxic profile.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record's duration was 'Not reported'; the lab setting was actually 40 L tanks of natural canal bloom water with no replication, and the 14 mg/L dose already gave 98.6% kill in 24 h.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Prymnesium parvum + phytoplankton community

reasons.reproducibility: 40 L tanks of natural toxic Prymnesium bloom water need access to a bloom and toxin analysis.
reasons.effectiveness: P. parvum fell 98.6-99.0% in 24 h, but each dose was one unreplicated tank and after re-inoculation it regrew above the control.
reasons.cost: H2O2 is cheap, but tanks and prymnesin analysis bring it to $150-500.
reasons.time: The kill was visible within 24 hours.
reasons.environment: Total phytoplankton fell 81-84% and regrown P. parvum had a more toxic profile, although H2O2 vanished by day 3.

papers.title: An effective algaecide for the targeted destruction of Karenia brevis
papers.scale: lab; 500 mL K. brevis cultures (~26,000 cells/mL) and 30 mL settling columns with PAC + CaO2 (~4,500 cells/mL)
papers.dose: CaO2 10, 30, 50 mg/L (30 mg/L releases about 8 mg/L H2O2; 10 mg/L about 2.8 mg/L), with polyaluminum chloride
papers.duration: 72 h (cells lysed within 3 h at 50 mg/L)
papers.result: 30 and 50 mg/L CaO2 killed K. brevis with no recovery, and with PAC removed >98% of cells from the water column in 72 h vs control; 10 mg/L gave ~80% removal at 24 h followed by partial recovery.
papers.env_effects: CaO2 alone cut PbTx-2 by 90% and PbTx-3 by 80% at 24 h vs control; PAC alone did not degrade toxins, and PAC+CaO2 degraded them less than CaO2 alone. Off-target effects were not tested.
papers.key_details: Lab study with cultured K. brevis (CCMP 2281 at Tulane; CCMP 2228 at Mote). CaO2 converted about 82% to H2O2 in seawater. In 500 mL cultures, 10 mg/L CaO2 cut cells at first but they recovered by 48 h while the control grew 81%; 30 and 50 mg/L caused lasting loss of viability and falling Fv/Fm. Combined with PAC flocculation in 30 mL columns, 30-50 mg/L removed >98% of cells vs control in 72 h, while PAC alone removed 76% in 24 h but the column was repopulated by 72 h. Toxin data are described by the authors as preliminary; replication was not clearly stated in the text read, and no non-target organisms were tested despite the 'minimal off-target impact' claim.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Abstract-based record gave no removal percentage or toxin numbers; the 10 mg/L dose failed (recovery by 48 h), and the 'targeted, minimal off-target' claim is untested.

reasons.reproducibility: Handles brevetoxin-producing Karenia brevis cultures with CaO2 and PAC flocculant.
reasons.effectiveness: 30-50 mg/L CaO2 with PAC removed >98% of cells vs control in 72 h, but 10 mg/L failed with regrowth by 48 h and replication was not clearly stated.
reasons.cost: Culture, CaO2, PAC and PAM measurements cost about $150-500.
reasons.time: Cells lysed within 3 hours at 50 mg/L.
reasons.environment: CaO2 cut brevetoxins 80-90%, but aluminium flocculant settles as residue, pH rises and off-target effects were never tested.

papers.title: Hydrogen peroxide lifetimes in south Florida coastal and offshore waters
papers.scale: South Florida coastal and offshore water
papers.dose: natural H2O2
papers.result: First-order decay of natural H2O2; half-life <10 h in coastal water, >120 h open ocean; decay mostly biological (organisms <1 µm).
papers.env_effects: n/a (fate study).
papers.study_note: natural H2O2 decay rates in seawater

reasons.reproducibility: Ship-based sampling of coastal and offshore water is field-scale.
reasons.effectiveness: A fate study of natural H2O2; no algae were treated.
reasons.cost: Field cruises and H2O2 assays are $500-5,000 or more.
reasons.time: Coastal half-life <10 h is measured within hours.
reasons.environment: Nothing was added; it measures natural H2O2 decay.

papers.title: The effects of hydrogen peroxide on mortality, escape response, and oxygen consumption of Calanus spp.
papers.scale: lab, 1 h pulses
papers.dose: 8.5, 17, 85, 170 mg/L H2O2 (plus 340 and 1700 mg/L in a preliminary test); 1h-LC50 214.1 (CV) / 48.3 adult in Table 2 (48.6 in abstract); 25h-LC50 77.1 / 30.6 mg/L; 25h-LC10 10.9 (CV) / 11.6 (adult) mg/L
papers.result: Total mortality after a 1 h pulse + 24 h recovery was 30% (CV) and 14% (adults) at 17 mg/L, 34% and 89% at 85 mg/L, and 92% and 100% at 170 mg/L; none at 8.5 mg/L, but escape performance was already impaired at 8.5 and 17 mg/L and absent at 85 mg/L.
papers.env_effects: Non-target harm; authors warn 'safe' values underestimate harm.
papers.key_details: Wild Calanus spp. (copepodite V and adult females) from Austevoll, Norway were given 1 h H2O2 exposures then 24 h recovery; the mortality test was run in triplicate (Table 1 N = 324 copepodite V and 327 adults), with no control mortality. Mortality rose steeply with dose: 0% at 8.5 mg/L, 14-30% at 17 mg/L, up to 100% at 170 mg/L. The 25h-LC10 was about 11 mg/L for both stages, i.e. within the 14 mg/L-plus range used on HABs. Escape distance fell 1.4 mm per 10 mg/L and oxygen consumption fell with dose. Context is salmon-lice treatment (1700 mg/L), so the doses and pulse design are not a HAB treatment.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Adult 1h-LC50 is 48.3 in the paper's Table 2 but 48.6 in the abstract (the record used 48.6). The 25h-LC10 of ~11 mg/L is the more relevant non-target threshold for HAB dosing.

reasons.reproducibility: Needs wild-caught Calanus copepods and chilled seawater.
reasons.effectiveness: Non-target copepod toxicity study; no algae were treated.
reasons.cost: Copepod collection and seawater setup cost about $150-500.
reasons.time: Mortality was read 25 hours after a 1 h pulse.
reasons.environment: 25 h LC10 was ~11 mg/L, within HAB dosing range, and escape responses were impaired even at 8.5 mg/L.

papers.title: Gill damage and delayed mortality of Northern shrimp (Pandalus borealis) after short time exposure to anti-parasitic veterinary medicine containing hydrogen peroxide
papers.scale: lab flow-through tanks, 6.8 C; Exp 1-2: 6 replicate tanks x 10 shrimp per treatment; Exp 3: 4 tanks x 6 shrimp
papers.dose: PARAMOVE H2O2 at 0.15, 1.5, 15 mg/L
papers.duration: 1-2 h pulses (once, or on 3 consecutive days); 2-12 d recovery
papers.result: Three 2 h pulses of 15 mg/L killed 46% after the third pulse and 80% two days later; three pulses of 1.5 mg/L killed 33%; a single 2 h pulse of 15 mg/L killed 50% with deaths starting on day 3; 0.15 mg/L caused no deaths.
papers.env_effects: Gill swelling, haemocyte infiltration, fusion and necrosis after a single 1 h pulse of 1.5 or 15 mg/L; feeding 66% below control 12 days after three 1.5 mg/L pulses.
papers.key_details: Female Northern shrimp in a continuous-flow seawater system were given PARAMOVE (H2O2 anti-sea-lice product) pulses with clean-water recovery. Exp 1-2 used 6 replicate tanks of 10 shrimp; Exp 3 used 4 tanks of 6 shrimp; no control mortality in any experiment. Mortality was delayed: none immediately after pulses, then 80% for 3 x 15 mg/L, 33% for 3 x 1.5 mg/L and 50% for one 2 h 15 mg/L pulse (one-pulse differences at lower doses not significant). Gills were progressively damaged at 1.5 and 15 mg/L, and feeding stayed depressed through 12 d of recovery. Delayed effects mean short-term toxicity tests underestimate harm.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record omitted the 80% mortality after three 15 mg/L pulses and the sublethal effects (gill necrosis, feeding -66%) at 1.5 mg/L, a dose far below HAB treatment doses.

reasons.reproducibility: Needs Northern shrimp in a chilled (6.8 C) flow-through seawater system.
reasons.effectiveness: Non-target shrimp toxicity study; no algae were treated.
reasons.cost: A chilled flow-through system with replicate tanks costs $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Deaths began on day 3 and reached 80% two days after the third pulse.
reasons.environment: Three 2 h pulses of 15 mg/L killed 80% and 1.5 mg/L caused gill necrosis and 66% lower feeding.

papers.title: The Acute and Delayed Mortality of the Northern Krill (Meganyctiphanes norvegica) When Exposed to Hydrogen Peroxide
papers.venue: Bulletin of Environmental Contamination and Toxicology
papers.scale: lab, 1 h exposure
papers.dose: 1.7, 8.5, 17, 170, 850 and 1700 mg/L H2O2 for 1 h (0.1-100% of the 1700 mg/L salmon-delousing dose)
papers.duration: 1 h exposure, then 48 h post-exposure in clean seawater (checks at 6, 24, 48 h)
papers.result: 1 h at 170 mg/L killed 100% of krill; acute 1h-LC50 32.5 mg/L (16.8-48.2), falling to 14.11 mg/L at 6 h, 4.92 mg/L at 24 h and 0.86 mg/L at 48 h post-exposure.
papers.env_effects: Non-target delayed mortality; 48 h post-exposure LC50 0.86 mg/L after only a 1 h pulse. No mortality at 1.7 mg/L or in controls. Authors call krill the most sensitive species tested so far.
papers.key_details: Wild Meganyctiphanes norvegica caught by light trap in Norway, exposed for 1 h to six H2O2 concentrations in 500 mL glassware at 8 C, then moved to clean seawater. 140 krill: 7 groups (incl. control) x 4 replicates x 5 krill. LC50s from probit GLM. Acute 1h-LC50 32.5 mg/L; delayed LC50 fell to 0.86 mg/L at 48 h. Context is salmon-lice bath treatment (1500-2100 mg/L), not HAB treatment, but the 48 h LC50 is below common HAB H2O2 doses.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record gave only the acute LC50; the delayed 48 h LC50 (0.86 mg/L) is ~38x lower and is the key number.

reasons.reproducibility: Needs light-trapped wild krill held at 8 C.
reasons.effectiveness: Non-target krill toxicity study; no algae were treated.
reasons.cost: Collection gear and cold seawater setup cost about $150-500.
reasons.time: Mortality was read 6-48 h after a 1 h exposure.
reasons.environment: The 48 h delayed LC50 was 0.86 mg/L after a 1 h pulse, below common HAB doses.

papers.title: Acute Toxicological Response of Daphnia and Moina to Hydrogen Peroxide
papers.organism: Daphnia carinata (s.l.) and Moina sp. clonal cultures, Western Australia (non-target zooplankton)
papers.scale: lab acute tests in 1.2 um filtered lake water with food, 21 C, n=3 per concentration
papers.dose: Moina 14 concentrations 0-12,500 mg/L; Daphnia 16 concentrations 0-12,500 mg/L
papers.result: 48-h LC50 (probit) 5.6 mg/L for Daphnia (95% CI 5-6.3) and 2 mg/L for Moina (linear regression 5.7 and 1.9); NOAEC 3 and 1.5 mg/L. Complete mortality at >=3 mg/L for Moina and >=12.5 mg/L for Daphnia within 48 h.
papers.env_effects: Non-target lethal levels near cyanobacterial treatment doses.
papers.key_details: Acute 48 h exposures of 20 adults per species acclimated in filtered lake water, fed Desmodesmus, under low light to limit H2O2 breakdown, with three replicates per concentration; survival checked 10 times over 48 h. Moina reached 100% mortality within 12 h at >=6 mg/L; Daphnia needed >40 mg/L for 100% mortality within 12 h. Mean survival time was significantly longer in Daphnia at >=2 mg/L (Kaplan-Meier). Moina's NOAEC-LC50 gap is very small, so any effect already means high mortality. Context is waste stabilisation ponds; food was added, which may alter toxicity compared with standard tests.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Minor: Moina LC50 is 2 mg/L (probit) / 1.9 mg/L (regression). Complete Moina mortality occurred at doses as low as 3 mg/L, within the range used for cyanobacteria treatment.

reasons.reproducibility: Daphnia and Moina acute tests in filtered lake water are standard school-friendly bioassays.
reasons.effectiveness: Non-target zooplankton toxicity study; algae were only food.
reasons.cost: Daphnia, H2O2 and glassware cost about $50-150.
reasons.time: 48 h tests.
reasons.environment: Moina LC50 was 2 mg/L with complete mortality at 3 mg/L, inside the cyanobacteria treatment range.

papers.title: The Effects of Sodium Percarbonate Generated Free Oxygen on Daphnia—Implications for the Management of Harmful Algal Blooms
papers.organism: Daphnia in a natural plankton sample (non-target)
papers.scale: lab microcosms: ten 1 L containers of lake water (3 controls, one container per SP dose), 1944 zooplankton counted (1610 Daphnia)
papers.dose: sodium percarbonate 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 mg/L (1.4-16.6 mg/L H2O2)
papers.result: Daphnia survival was 97.9% in controls, fell slightly at 5-10 mg/L SP, dropped ~50 percentage points between 20 and 30 mg/L SP (5.5-8.3 mg/L H2O2), was 3% at 40 mg/L SP (11.1 mg/L H2O2), 1.1% at 50 and 0% at 60 mg/L SP (16.6 mg/L H2O2).
papers.env_effects: Non-target harm above the safe level.
papers.key_details: Surface water from a shallow Polish lake (phytoplankton dominated by cryptophytes and chlorophytes; cyanobacteria ~3%) was split into ten 1 L containers: three controls and single, unreplicated containers at 5-60 mg/L sodium percarbonate. Survival was counted after 24 h; percarbonate concentration and Daphnia survival were strongly inversely correlated (Spearman r = -0.976). The authors recommend keeping doses below 10 mg/L SP (2.8 mg/L H2O2) to protect zooplankton. Algal effects were not measured, and the design has no replication of treatments.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record says large Daphnia died more; the paper found no significant size difference in survival (0.2-2.0 mm), only a suggestion that larger ones may be more vulnerable. Duration (24 h) was missing.

reasons.reproducibility: Sodium percarbonate, lake water and 1 L containers with Daphnia counts are common school materials.
reasons.effectiveness: Algal effects were not measured; only Daphnia survival.
reasons.cost: Percarbonate and containers cost under $50 with a school microscope.
reasons.time: 24 hour exposure.
reasons.environment: Daphnia survival fell ~50 points at 5.5-8.3 mg/L H2O2 and to 3% at 11 mg/L, doses used on blooms.

papers.title: Sensitivity of phytoplankton, zooplankton and macroinvertebrates to hydrogen peroxide treatments of cyanobacterial blooms
papers.scale: 24-h lab tests on 26 taxa (species sensitivity distribution) + two whole-lake H2O2 treatments of Lake Oosterduinse Meer (June and August 2018)
papers.dose: lab graded; lake treatment 1 mean 1.13 mg/L (0.2-2.7 mg/L for 5.5 h), treatment 2 mean 2.19 mg/L (1.7-3.7 mg/L for at least 13 h)
papers.result: Cyanobacteria were most sensitive (24-h EC50 1.39 mg/L for Planktothrix to 3.49 mg/L for Anabaena; green algae ~20x higher, 27.7-74.4 mg/L). The first lake treatment cut cyanobacterial biovolume 85.1% in two days with little non-target effect; the second, stronger and longer, collapsed Dolichospermum by 96.8% but also rotifers by 82.0%.
papers.env_effects: Second lake treatment: 82.0% collapse of rotifers and fewer small cladocerans. Authors' dose classes: <=2 mg/L mild (no non-target effects); 2-4 mg/L harms rotifers and small cladocerans; 4-10 mg/L harms many zooplankton and some macroinvertebrates; 10-100 mg/L suppresses most zooplankton and other eukaryotic phytoplankton.
papers.key_details: 24-h toxicity tests on 3 cyanobacteria, 6 green algae, 8 zooplankton and 9 macroinvertebrate taxa (controls kept >=90% yield or survival) fed a species sensitivity distribution, which was then checked against two treatments of the same Dutch lake. Treatment 1 (mean 1.13 mg/L, gone after 6.5 h; predicted 8 +/- 5% of species affected) cut an Aphanizomenon-dominated bloom by 85.1% of cyanobacterial biovolume in two days without significant effects on most eukaryotic phytoplankton. Treatment 2 (mean 2.19 mg/L, lasting >=13 h; 14 +/- 2% of species affected) collapsed Dolichospermum flos-aquae by 96.8% but also caused an 82.0% rotifer collapse. The SSD predictions matched the lake responses. Only one lake, two treatments, before/after comparison with no control lake.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record listed setting 'lab'; the paper includes two whole-lake field treatments with measured cyanobacterial reductions (85.1%) and a rotifer collapse (82.0%).

reasons.reproducibility: Combines 24 h tests on 26 cultured taxa with two whole-lake H2O2 treatments.
reasons.effectiveness: The lake treatments cut cyanobacterial biovolume 85.1% and 96.8% within days, matching lab EC50s, but only one lake with before/after comparison and no control lake.
reasons.cost: Whole-lake dosing plus 26 cultures costs over $5,000.
reasons.time: Cyanobacteria fell within two days.
reasons.environment: At <=2 mg/L non-target effects were small, but the second treatment collapsed rotifers by 82%.

papers.title: Combatting cyanobacteria with hydrogen peroxide: a laboratory study on the consequences for phytoplankton community and diversity
papers.scale: bottles at 3 densities
papers.result: Dense water degraded all H2O2 within 24 h except at 50 mg/L (6.3 mg/L left); in diluted water 2.5 mg/L removed the cyanobacterial signal.
papers.env_effects: Greens and diatoms left intact in diluted water.

reasons.reproducibility: Bottles of lake water dosed with 2.5-50 mg/L H2O2 is simple bench work.
reasons.effectiveness: Diluted water: 2.5 mg/L removed the cyanobacterial signal; dense water consumed H2O2 within 24 h, so mixed by density.
reasons.cost: Lake water, H2O2 and a fluorometer loan about $50-150.
reasons.time: 24-h endpoint.
reasons.environment: Greens and diatoms left intact in diluted water; H2O2 degraded within 24 h.

papers.title: Combined Exposure to Hydrogen Peroxide and LightSelective Effects on Cyanobacteria, Green Algae, and Diatoms
papers.organism: Microcystis aeruginosa PCC 7806, green alga Pseudokirchneriella subcapitata, diatom Navicula seminulum
papers.scale: lab cultures, 27 C, irradiance 0-500 umol/m2/s
papers.dose: H2O2 concentration series (0.6 and 2.5 mg/L for decay tests)
papers.result: EC50 (photosynthetic yield) for Microcystis fell from 6.63 mg/L in the dark to 1.13 at 10, 0.45 at 40 and 0.27 mg/L at 500 umol/m2/s; the green alga (4.05-21.26 mg/L) and diatom (12.19-71.26 mg/L) were roughly 10-60x less sensitive.
papers.env_effects: At 500 umol/m2/s, 2.5 mg/L H2O2 fell to <4% within 3 h (half-life ~0.6 h without algae); Microcystis and Navicula cells degraded it in the dark (half-life 1.6 h). Preadaptation to high light did not reduce sensitivity.
papers.key_details: Short-term (3 h) lab tests of H2O2 toxicity to one cyanobacterium, one green alga and one diatom at five irradiances, with photosynthetic yield (Fv/Fm, PAM fluorometry) as the endpoint and logistic dose-response fits. Light strongly increased toxicity, most for Microcystis (about 20x lower EC50 at 500 umol/m2/s than dark; 5x even at 10 umol/m2/s). Endpoint is photosynthetic inhibition, not cell death or growth. Duplicate measurements for decay tests; high light alone reduced control Fv/Fm by 20-55%.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record said green alga and diatom were 'about 10x less sensitive'; at 500 umol/m2/s they were ~15x (green alga) and ~58x (diatom) less sensitive. Duration (3 h) and the Fv/Fm endpoint were missing.

reasons.reproducibility: Three purchased cultures and a PAM fluorometer under controlled light are doable with a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: Microcystis EC50 fell to 0.27 mg/L at high light, but the endpoint is 3 h photosynthetic yield, not cell death or growth.
reasons.cost: A PAM fluorometer puts the cost at $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Three-hour exposures.
reasons.environment: H2O2 fell to <4% within 3 h in light and the green alga and diatom were 15-58x less sensitive.

papers.title: Comparative assessment of algaecide performance on freshwater phytoplankton: Understanding differential sensitivities to frame cyanobacteria management
papers.organism: 12 freshwater strains: cyanobacteria (Synechococcus, Microcystis aeruginosa, Dolichospermum flosaquae), chlorophytes, diatoms, mixotrophs (Cryptomonas, Dinobryon, Prymnesium parvum)
papers.scale: lab; 30 mL cultures in 55 mL tubes, triplicates
papers.dose: H2O2 and CuSO4.5H2O at 0, 0.5, 2.5, 5, 10, 20 mg/L
papers.result: Mean H2O2 EC50 was 2.18 mg/L for mixotrophs, 4.38 for cyanobacteria, 18.7 for diatoms and 93.26 for chlorophytes (CuSO4 lower for all but chlorophytes); H2O2 is not selective, since mixotrophs and some diatoms were as sensitive as cyanobacteria.
papers.env_effects: Diatoms and mixotrophs nearly as sensitive as cyanobacteria.
papers.key_details: Twelve culture-collection strains in four divisions were exposed in triplicate to six concentrations (0-20 mg/L) of H2O2 or copper sulfate, with photosynthetic yield (Phyto-PAM) giving 48-h EC50s. H2O2 EC50s: Dolichospermum 1.25, Microcystis 4.74, Synechococcus 7.15 mg/L; Cryptomonas 1.80, P. parvum 4.4 mg/L; Navicula 7.8, Cyclotella 11.8 mg/L; chlorophytes 30.14-166.57 mg/L. Copper was more potent than H2O2 in every division except chlorophytes. The authors conclude that H2O2 and CuSO4 give comparable outcomes and that H2O2's selectivity for cyanobacteria is debatable. Monocultures in culture media, not natural communities.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Duration (48 h) and the dose range were missing; the ranking in the record matches.

reasons.reproducibility: Twelve culture-collection strains and a Phyto-PAM are specialist but sponsor-feasible.
reasons.effectiveness: Cyanobacterial EC50s were 1.25-7.15 mg/L on photosynthetic yield only, and copper beat H2O2 in most divisions.
reasons.cost: Twelve strains plus Phyto-PAM access cost $500-5,000.
reasons.time: 48 hour tests.
reasons.environment: H2O2 was not selective: mixotrophs and diatoms were nearly as sensitive as cyanobacteria.

papers.title: Calcium peroxide (CaO2) granules enclosed in fabrics as an alternative H2O2 delivery system to combat Microcystis sp.
papers.scale: bench; 200 mL surface water (Kouris dam) spiked with cultured Microcystis to 8000 RFU; CaO2 granules in 4 fabric types
papers.dose: 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 g/L CaO2 granules (loose or enclosed in fabric)
papers.result: 2.0 g/L CaO2 in fabric types B and C cut phycocyanin fluorescence 87.5-91% and quantum yield 77.8-82.5% by 48 h; lower doses mostly recovered (QY), fabric A barely worked. Granules released up to 12 mg/L H2O2 by 24 h, but residual H2O2 during treatment stayed <0.5 mg/L.
papers.env_effects: Loose granules raised pH above 11; fabric-enclosed systems kept pH at or below ~10 (starting pH 9.5). Toxin release not measured during treatment. No non-target organisms tested.
papers.key_details: Lab bench study, all runs in triplicate at 20 C with continuous light. Artificial bloom: cultured Microcystis added to dam water to Ft 8000 RFU (intracellular MC-RR 4.66 ug/L, MC-YR 1.45 ug/L). Treatments 0-2.0 g/L CaO2 enclosed in fabric types A-C vs no-fabric; control = 0 g/L. Endpoint is fluorescence (Ft) and PSII quantum yield, not cell counts. Only 2.0 g/L (types B, C) and 1 g/L type C gave lasting suppression.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record effect_pct was null; full text gives 87.5-91% Ft reduction at 48 h. Record's pH note ('not in abstract') now filled: loose granules pushed pH >11.

reasons.reproducibility: CaO2 granules in fabric bags in 200 mL dam water with Microcystis are simple bench work.
reasons.effectiveness: 2 g/L CaO2 in fabrics B and C cut phycocyanin fluorescence 87.5-91% in triplicate, but lower doses mostly recovered and the endpoint is fluorescence, not counts.
reasons.cost: CaO2, fabric and a culture cost about $50-150 plus fluorometer access.
reasons.time: Effects were clear by 48 hours.
reasons.environment: Fabric enclosure is retrievable and kept pH <=10 (loose granules >11); toxins and non-targets were not measured.

papers.title: Algaecide-Releasing Buoys for Sustained Harmful Algal Bloom Control
papers.scale: lab microcosm: six 1 L beakers of Lake Erie water diluted to 2.0-2.5 ug/L Chl-a (3 with a 20 mL buoy, 3 controls), 10% daily water exchange
papers.dose: small buoy with 1 cm gel loaded with diluted Oximycin P5 (6 g/L H2O2), targeting ~1 mg/L H2O2 in the beaker
papers.result: Buoy release cut Chl-a to 0.07 ug/L after 14 d, about 5% of the control average, with significant reductions at all time points except days 1 and 3; the effect grew over time.
papers.env_effects: 16S rRNA: cyanobacteria fell from ~9% of the bacterial community to 0.24% (day 7) and 1.8% (day 14) vs 1.9% and 5.9% in controls. Biofouling of the buoys needs further work; non-target organisms were not assessed.
papers.key_details: Reusable PVC buoys release a commercial H2O2 algaecide through a polyacrylate hydrogel disk; release followed first-order kinetics set by gel thickness, area and internal concentration, lasting more than a month. The only biological test was a 14-day microcosm: three 1 L beakers with the smallest buoy vs three untreated beakers of Lake Erie water diluted to an early-bloom level (2.0-2.5 ug/L Chl-a), with 10% daily lake-water replacement. Treated Chl-a fell to 0.07 ug/L at day 14, ~5% of the control, significant at all times except days 1 and 3. The starting bloom was deliberately minor (prevention scenario), and medium and large buoys were not tested on algae.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record gave no number; the full text reports Chl-a at ~5% of control after 14 d, but only in 1 L beakers at a very low starting Chl-a (2.0-2.5 ug/L), not a real bloom.

reasons.reproducibility: Building PVC buoys with a hydrogel disk and commercial H2O2 algaecide in 1 L beakers is feasible with a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: Chl-a fell to ~5% of control after 14 d with 3 vs 3 beakers, but at a very low starting chlorophyll (2-2.5 ug/L), not a real bloom.
reasons.cost: Buoy materials, algaecide and lake water cost $150-500.
reasons.time: Significant reductions appeared after day 3 and grew through day 14.
reasons.environment: Sustained H2O2 release cut cyanobacteria, but non-target organisms were not assessed.

papers.title: The Efficacy of Hydrogen Peroxide in Mitigating Cyanobacterial Blooms and Altering Microbial Communities across Four Lakes in NY, USA | Repeated hydrogen peroxide dosing briefly reduces cyanobacterial blooms and microcystin while increasing fecal bacteria indicators in a eutrophic pond (doi:10.1016/j.jes.2021.11.031)
papers.organism: Cyanobacteria (Planktothrix, Microcystis, Dolichospermum, Cylindrospermopsis, Aphanizomenon) in bloom water from four Long Island lakes/ponds
papers.freshwater_or_marine: freshwater (one brackish site, Georgica Pond 0-20 PSU)
papers.scale: 4 L bottles of field bloom water, incubated outdoors; 11 experiments, 4 water bodies
papers.dose: 4 mg/L H2O2, single dose
papers.result: Cyanobacteria fell significantly in 10 of 11 experiments, from on average 85% to 29% of the phytoplankton; cyanobacterial Chl-a was 43-99.8% below controls (e.g. Mill Pond 93-99%, Roth Pond 82%, Lake Agawam 43-52%, one Agawam run not significant).
papers.env_effects: Green algae rose in 6 of 8 experiments (up to 400% above control); heterotrophic bacteria fell 44%; Actinobacteria, Planctomycetes, Verrucomicrobia strongly reduced. Planktothrix most sensitive, Cylindrospermopsis most resistant; Microcystis share of cyanobacteria rose in one run. No fecal-bacteria or whole-pond data in this paper.
papers.key_details: Bottle incubations: each experiment had an unamended control and a 4 mg/L H2O2 treatment, 3 replicate 4 L bottles each, incubated 4-7 d in an outdoor flow-through table. 8 first-round experiments by FluoroProbe; 3 detailed experiments added microscopy, flow cytometry and 16S sequencing. Initial cyanobacterial Chl-a 45-394 ug/L; treatment brought levels below the 25 ug/L NYSDEC threshold only in some runs. Authors conclude H2O2 reduces but does not eliminate cyanobacteria in high-biomass water. The abstract's '4 ug/L' is a typo for 4 mg/L.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record conflated this bottle study with a different Gobler pond-dosing paper: this paper has no whole-pond treatment, no 8 mg/L dose, no 2-week rebound and no fecal-indicator bacteria. Setting should be bottle/mesocosm, not field. effect_pct 82 is a median-ish headline (range 43-99.8%).
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Long Island lake/pond cyanobacteria

reasons.reproducibility: 4 L bottles of bloom water dosed with 4 mg/L H2O2 are simple, but need bloom access and a FluoroProbe.
reasons.effectiveness: Cyanobacteria fell significantly in 10 of 11 triplicated experiments, 43-99.8% below controls, though high-biomass water often stayed above thresholds.
reasons.cost: FluoroProbe and sequencing put it at $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Bottles were incubated 4-7 days.
reasons.environment: Green algae rose up to 400% and heterotrophic bacteria fell 44%; H2O2 itself leaves no residue.

papers.title: Hydrogen peroxide treatment promotes chlorophytes over toxic cyanobacteria in a hyper-eutrophic aquaculture pond
papers.scale: lab EC50 tests on 4 cyanobacteria + twelve 1500 L limnocorrals in a 1.5 ha hyper-eutrophic catfish pond (Auburn, AL, May 2017), 3 replicates per dose (one enclosure lost)
papers.dose: 0, 1.3, 6.7, 20 mg/L H2O2, single application
papers.result: 6.7 and 20 mg/L gave rapid, sustained cuts in Microcystis and phycocyanin, with day-7 cyanobacterial biovolume 16.4 and 1.5 million um3/mL vs 202.8 million in controls (Table 2); 1.3 mg/L cut Planktothrix but not Microcystis, and chlorophyll a recovered to control levels in all treatments by day 7.
papers.env_effects: Chlorophytes increased. Extracellular microcystin rose 1 day after treatment then fell to control levels by day 7; intracellular microcystin stayed low at 6.7 and 20 mg/L. Zooplankton were significantly suppressed only at 20 mg/L; 6.7 mg/L was similar to control.
papers.key_details: Lab EC50s were ~0.41 mg/L for three filamentous cyanobacteria vs 5.06 mg/L for Microcystis. In the field, twelve 1500 L enclosures of a Planktothrix/Microcystis bloom were dosed once with 0, 1.3, 6.7 or 20 mg/L H2O2 (triplicates; one enclosure damaged) and sampled over 7 days. Phycocyanin stayed very low at 6.7 and 20 mg/L but recovered at 1.3 mg/L; chlorophyll a recovered everywhere by day 7 as chlorophytes replaced cyanobacteria. Day-7 cyanobacterial biovolume at 6.7 mg/L was 91.9% below control (computed from Table 2 means; 99.3% at 20 mg/L). Zooplankton were harmed only at 20 mg/L.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: The 'field' work was 1500 L enclosures (mesocosm) inside the pond, not a whole-pond treatment; the record gave no reduction figure. effect_pct 91.9 is computed from Table 2, not stated by the authors.

reasons.reproducibility: 1500 L limnocorrals in a hyper-eutrophic catfish pond need field access.
reasons.effectiveness: 6.7 mg/L cut cyanobacterial biovolume 91.9% vs controls at day 7 in triplicate enclosures, though total chlorophyll recovered as chlorophytes replaced them.
reasons.cost: Twelve limnocorrals and analyses cost $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Cuts were rapid and read over 7 days.
reasons.environment: Extracellular microcystin briefly rose and zooplankton were harmed at 20 mg/L but not 6.7 mg/L.

papers.title: Microcystis bloom control using hydrogen peroxide and floating sodium percarbonate algaecide Lake Guard Oxy in Florida
papers.scale: 400 m2 semi-enclosed area below Franklin Lock (S-79), Caloosahatchee River, FL; Lake Guard Oxy spread over 2,023 m2
papers.dose: Liquid: 12 L of 3% H2O2 sprayed, nominal 20 mg/L over top 10 cm (measured peak 73.7 mg/L at 0 min, 4.3 mg/L at 1 h). Lake Guard Oxy (sodium percarbonate): 65 kg on day 2 and day 7 (label max; measured 37.3 mg/L peak at 15 min, 12.6 mg/L at 1 h)
papers.duration: 14 days; 3 treatments (day 0 liquid, days 2 and 7 granules)
papers.result: Short-term: liquid H2O2 vs LGOxy cut cyanobacterial 16S share 79% vs 46%, Chl-a 81% vs 90%, Microcystis colony density 91% vs 97%; effects did not persist beyond ~1 day to a week and the bloom was not eliminated by day 14 (Chl-a still 447 ug/L).
papers.env_effects: H2O2 back to background within 24 h. Alligators, manatees, birds and fish seen in the area with no mortalities in 14 d (visual only). Total microcystin peaked at 35.6 ug/L on day 2; nitrogen-fixation gene expression in diazotrophs rose after LGOxy. Water exchange with the river undid treatments.
papers.key_details: Single-site field trial in a flowing, tidally influenced river; no replicated treatment plots. A reference site outside the treatment area was sampled only on days 0, 1 and 14. H2O2, nutrients, Chl-a, microcystin (ELISA), colony counts, 16S amplicons and transcriptomics measured; triplicate samples from 3 points. Treatment scheme was opportunistic (two organizations working at the same site). Measured H2O2 differed strongly from nominal dose.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record swapped the two Chl-a numbers: liquid H2O2 gave -81% and the percarbonate granules (LGOxy) gave -90%, not the reverse. Doses were given in the paper (nominal 20 mg/L liquid; 65 kg LGOxy per application), not 'not given'.

reasons.reproducibility: Spraying H2O2 and spreading 65 kg of percarbonate in a tidal river needs permits and field crews.
reasons.effectiveness: Chl-a fell 81-90% short-term, but effects faded within a day to a week, the bloom persisted (447 ug/L at day 14) and there were no replicated plots.
reasons.cost: Products, boat work and transcriptomics cost $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Reductions were visible within hours to a day.
reasons.environment: H2O2 was gone within 24 h and no wildlife deaths were seen, but microcystin peaked at 35.6 ug/L.

papers.title: Effects of peroxide-based compounds on growth and toxicity of Microcystis aeruginosa
papers.scale: lab; 200 mL cultures in 300 mL flasks; 5 products (liquid H2O2, CaO2, Lake Guard Oxy, Phycomycin SCP, Oximycin P5)
papers.dose: 0, 1, 3, 5, 10, 20 mg H2O2-equivalent/L (series 1); 0, 1, 3, 10 mg/L (series 2 and 3)
papers.duration: 9 days (series 1, 150 ug/L Chl-a) and 15 days (series 2 and 3, 300 and 600 ug/L Chl-a)
papers.result: At 150 ug/L Chl-a, Oximycin P5, Phycomycin SCP and liquid H2O2 kept Chl-a undetectable at 1 mg/L, CaO2 and Lake Guard Oxy needed 3 mg/L; at 600 ug/L, CaO2 and Lake Guard Oxy let Chl-a recover at 3 mg/L while the others did not; all products worked at 10 mg/L with no recovery.
papers.env_effects: Extracellular microcystin rose after 1 day in all treatments, then fell below control by day 9. CaO2 raised pH in a dose-dependent way. No non-target organisms tested.
papers.key_details: Three lab series with triplicate flasks per product x dose, at 20 C, 100 umol photons m-2 s-1, 16:8 light. Chl-a and PSII efficiency by PHYTO-PAM; H2O2 by test strips; intra/extracellular microcystins by LC-MS/MS (series 1). Biomass yield analysed by two-way ANOVA (OECD 201 approach). A co-author works for SePRO, which makes two of the tested products.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record duration 'Not reported' -> 9 and 15 days. Record omitted that Chl-a was driven to zero (effective 100%) at >=3 mg/L for most products, and the transient extracellular-toxin rise.

reasons.reproducibility: Microcystis flask cultures dosed with five commercial peroxide products, read by PHYTO-PAM, need a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: At >=3 mg/L most products drove Chl-a to undetectable with no recovery, in triplicate at three biomass levels vs controls.
reasons.cost: Cultures, products and PAM access cost $150-500 (LC-MS toxins extra).
reasons.time: Declines appeared within days in the 9-15 day series.
reasons.environment: Extracellular microcystin rose after 1 day before falling, and CaO2 raised pH.

papers.title: Mitigation of Karenia brevis Cells and Brevetoxins Using Curcumin, a Natural Supplement
papers.scale: 1.5 L beakers and 10 L aquaria; 13 experiments
papers.dose: 0.1-40 mg/L curcumin (turmeric extract >95% curcuminoids)
papers.result: 5 mg/L: -89% cells at 24 h and -60% toxin; 0.1-2 mg/L no different from each other; 30-40 mg/L >90% reduction by 4 h.
papers.env_effects: pH, salinity, temperature and DO stable except the ethanol experiment (DO fell to 1.55 mg/L by 48 h, bacterial bloom); nutrients unchanged; water turned yellow to dark orange.

reasons.reproducibility: Uses toxic K. brevis in beakers and 10 L aquaria; turmeric extract is common but the organism needs a sponsor lab.
reasons.effectiveness: 5 mg/L cut cells 89% at 24 h and toxin 60%; 0.1-2 mg/L did little.
reasons.cost: Culture, curcumin and toxin assay about $150-500.
reasons.time: 89% reduction at 24 h; >90% by 4 h at 30-40 mg/L.
reasons.environment: Water chemistry stable except the ethanol run (DO to 1.55 mg/L); water turned orange.

papers.title: Lessons learned from mesocosm experiments with curcumin: Pilot studies of a harmful algal bloom mitigation technique
papers.organism: Karenia brevis; hard clams, sea urchins, blue crabs
papers.scale: 1,400 L fiberglass mesocosms at the Mote RTMTDI facility, Sarasota FL (6 tanks in March 2022, 12 in January 2024; 3 curcumin-treated tanks each year), cultured K. brevis
papers.dose: 5 mg/L curcumin
papers.duration: up to 72 h (both runs cut short by bacterial blooms, K. brevis crashes and hypoxia at 48-72 h)
papers.result: 2022: cells -86% at 24 h and -99% at 48 h, total brevetoxins -65% and -74%; 2024: cells only -32% at 24 h and -47% at 48 h, toxins -46% and -7%; no measured effects on clams, urchins or crabs within 72 h.
papers.env_effects: No measured impacts on hard clams, sea urchins or blue crabs within 72 h (2024 run; 4 clams, 4 urchins, 3 crabs per tank). Bacterial blooms and hypoxia (<2 mg/L) appeared in all groups including controls, attributed to a facility-wide problem.
papers.key_details: Two pilot runs in 1,400 L mesocosms dosed with 5 mg/L curcumin, three treated tanks per run; only 2024 had curcumin-only and seawater controls. Changes were measured relative to each tank's time-0 value and compared with Karenia controls (Kruskal-Wallis). In 2022 cells fell 86.34% at 24 h (control +18.52%) and 99.22% at 48 h (control +70.79%); in 2024 the reduction was significant only at 6 h (-27.35%) and reached just 47% at 48 h, with toxin reduction fluctuating (-5.39% to -45.66%) and ending at -7.56%. Both runs were cut short by bacterial blooms, Karenia control crashes to 0 cells/L and hypoxia; affected tanks were discarded, and one 2024 treated tank crashed, leaving n = 2 at 48 h. The authors frame the study as lessons learned about mesocosm methods; the year-to-year inconsistency and small n make the efficacy estimate weak.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Abstract-based record said percentages were not given and implied consistent drops; the full text shows a 99% cell cut in 2022 but only 47% (and 7% toxin) in 2024, with runs compromised by bacterial blooms and hypoxia.

reasons.reproducibility: 1,400 L mesocosms with toxic K. brevis and live clams, urchins and crabs.
reasons.effectiveness: 5 mg/L cut cells 99% at 48 h in 2022 but only 47% in 2024 (toxins -7% at the end), with n = 2-3 tanks and runs compromised by bacterial blooms, control crashes and hypoxia.
reasons.cost: Two runs of 1,400 L mesocosms at a marine lab with cultured K. brevis and animals exceed $5,000.
reasons.time: Drop within 24 h.
reasons.environment: No measured effects on clams, urchins or crabs within 72 h (2024 run); hypoxia appeared in all groups including controls.

papers.title: Inhibition of five natural products from Chinese herbs on the growth of Chattonella marina
papers.scale: 100 mL flasks with 50 mL culture; initial 4.4 x 10^6 cells/L; n=3
papers.dose: each of 5 compounds at 10 mg/L (curcumin dissolved in ethanol; ethanol solvent control); gramine further at 0.32-3 mg/L
papers.result: At 10 mg/L curcumin was the second-strongest inhibitor of C. marina, with an inhibitory rate similar to gramine at 72 h, but it was dropped from further study because it turned the medium yellow. Gramine LC50 was 1.12, 0.77, 0.58 and 0.51 mg/L at 24, 48, 72 and 96 h.
papers.env_effects: Curcumin turned the culture medium yellow, which the authors flag as a potential adverse impact on the aquatic environment.
papers.key_details: Batch cultures of C. marina in f/2 at 20 °C, 12:12 h light; five Chinese-herb compounds (evodiamine, 4-methoxysalicylaldehyde, gramine, esculin hydrate, curcumin) each added at 10 mg/L, with ethanol/acetone solvent controls, n=3, cell counts by hemocytometer at 24/48/72 h. Gramine had the highest inhibitory rate, curcumin a similar one; evodiamine gave 40% at 72 h and the other two little inhibition. Only gramine was studied further (Fv/Fm, Chl a, SOD/CAT, MDA); 3 mg/L gramine gave 80% inhibition within 150 min. The curcumin inhibition percentage is shown only in Fig. 1 and is not stated numerically in the text.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: The 80% at 10 mg/L (72 h) figure for curcumin comes from a secondary citation; the paper's text gives no number for curcumin (Fig. 1 only), just 'similar inhibitory rate as gramine'. The 96 h LC50 0.51 mg/L is gramine's, not curcumin's; curcumin had no dose-response work.

reasons.reproducibility: Purchased Chattonella culture with 10 mg/L compounds is sponsor-doable.
reasons.effectiveness: Curcumin at 10 mg/L was only described as 'similar inhibitory rate as gramine' at 72 h (Fig. 1, no number); the 80% figure is secondary and there was no dose-response work (n = 3).
reasons.cost: Culture and five compounds about $150-500.
reasons.time: 72-h endpoint.
reasons.environment: Curcumin coloured the water; other non-target effects not reported.

papers.title: Targeting Florida red tide: Curcumin inhibits Karenia brevis thioredoxin reductase
papers.organism: Recombinant Karenia brevis thioredoxin reductase (KbTrxR, expressed in E. coli)
papers.scale: in vitro enzyme assay
papers.dose: TrxR assay
papers.result: Curcumin inhibited KbTrxR in a time-dependent way: IC50 fell from 111.0 uM to 3.0 uM after 60 min pre-incubation (~20x more potent than PbTx-2); inhibition also seen with H2O2 as substrate; covalent adduct at Cys53.
papers.env_effects: n/a (mechanism).
papers.key_details: Purely in vitro enzyme study on synthetic recombinant KbTrxR; no live K. brevis cells were treated. DTNB-reduction and H2O2-reduction assays run in triplicate; IC50 by nonlinear regression. LC-MS/MS located the curcumin adduct at N-terminal Cys53. Authors cite prior work that 0.1-5 mg/L curcumin reduces K. brevis 2-89% in 24 h, and note enzyme IC50 is not comparable with whole-cell toxicity.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record's 3.0 uM IC50 is only after 60 min pre-incubation; without it the IC50 was 111.0 uM. Enzyme was recombinant, not from cells.
papers.study_note: enzyme (thioredoxin reductase) inhibition assay, no cell outcome

reasons.reproducibility: Requires expressing recombinant KbTrxR in E. coli, enzyme kinetics and LC-MS/MS adduct mapping.
reasons.effectiveness: Enzyme-only study: IC50 111 uM without pre-incubation, 3.0 uM after 60 min; no live algae treated.
reasons.cost: Recombinant protein expression and LC-MS/MS put it at $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Enzyme assay results within hours.
reasons.environment: Mechanism study; nothing released to the environment.

papers.title: Inhibition of Diarrheal Shellfish Toxins Accumulation in the Mussel Perna viridis by Curcumin and Underlying Mechanisms
papers.organism: mussel Perna viridis fed Prorocentrum lima
papers.scale: lab; mussels in 6 L seawater; digestive glands of 6 mussels pooled per sample, n = 3 samples per group
papers.dose: Prorocentrum lima 2 x 10^6 cells/L; curcumin 0, 1, 5, 10, 20, 50 umol/L (step I); 20 umol/L (step II)
papers.result: Curcumin at 10 and 20 umol/L significantly lowered DST (okadaic acid-eq) in the digestive gland vs no curcumin (p<0.05), with more DST found in the water instead; gill DST unchanged. Curcumin reduced P. lima-induced digestive-gland damage.
papers.env_effects: Curcumin alone (20 uM) caused no visible digestive-gland damage in mussels. Curcumin was dissolved in NaOH; solvent given to controls. Does not reduce the algae; it is a shellfish-detox approach.
papers.key_details: Two-step lab design with Perna viridis (8-10 cm) fed Tetraselmis plus toxic P. lima (CCMP 2579). Step I: curcumin dose series, DST by ELISA at 48 h. Step II: 4 groups (control, curcumin, P. lima, P. lima + curcumin at 20 uM), sampled at 12 and 48 h for DST, qPCR (AhR, HR96, CYP3A4) and histology. Pooled samples give only n = 3 per group; % reductions are shown only in figures. Mechanism proposed: curcumin blocks toxin-induced transcription of AhR/HR96/CYP3A4.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record dose/duration 'not in abstract' -> 1-50 uM curcumin, 48 h. Effective doses were 10-20 uM (~3.7-7.4 mg/L). Toxin appears to be moved to the water, not destroyed.
papers.study_note: curcumin reduces DST accumulation in mussels; no bloom reduction

reasons.reproducibility: Needs mussels fed toxic Prorocentrum lima and toxin analysis.
reasons.effectiveness: Measures DST in mussel glands (lower at 10-20 uM curcumin), not reduction of P. lima; toxin moved to the water rather than being destroyed.
reasons.cost: Mussels, a toxic P. lima culture, ELISA, qPCR and histology run $500-5,000.
reasons.time: DST differences were measured at 12 and 48 h.
reasons.environment: 20 uM curcumin caused no visible gland damage, but toxin shifted into the surrounding water and NaOH solvent was used.

papers.title: The Chemistry of Curcumin: From Extraction to Therapeutic Agent
papers.scale: review
papers.dose: n/a
papers.result: λmax 410-430 nm; pKa1 7.5-8.5 (anion absorbs at 467 nm); logP ~3; 90% of µM solutions degrade in 30 min; much faster fading in sunlight.
papers.env_effects: Breakdown products vanillin, ferulic acid and small phenols.

reasons.reproducibility: A chemistry review; no experiment to repeat.
reasons.effectiveness: Review of curcumin chemistry; no algal reduction.
reasons.cost: No experiment cost; reading only.
reasons.time: Degradation in 30 min is the headline timescale.
reasons.environment: Breaks down fast to vanillin, ferulic acid and small phenols; short-lived residue.

papers.title: Stability of curcumin in buffer solutions and characterization of its degradation products
papers.venue: Journal of Pharmaceutical and Biomedical Analysis
papers.scale: 0.1 M phosphate buffer, 37 °C
papers.result: About 90% decomposed within 30 min at pH 7.2; faster at neutral-basic pH; serum proteins slow it (~50% left at 8 h).
papers.env_effects: Breakdown products vanillin, ferulic acid.

reasons.reproducibility: Curcumin in phosphate buffer with a spectrophotometer is simple school chemistry.
reasons.effectiveness: Stability study; no algae treated.
reasons.cost: Curcumin, buffer and spectrophotometer use about $50-150.
reasons.time: 90% decomposed within 30 min.
reasons.environment: Degrades to vanillin and ferulic acid quickly; minimal residue.

papers.title: Physical and Chemical Stability of Curcumin in Aqueous Solutions and Emulsions: Impact of pH, Temperature, and Molecular Environment
papers.venue: Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry
papers.scale: 40 µM curcumin in 10 mM phosphate buffer (pH 2.0-8.0) in a cuvette; MCT oil-in-water emulsions (30 wt% oil, Tween 80, 0.285 mg/mL curcumin, pH 3.0-8.0)
papers.dose: n/a
papers.duration: buffer solutions: minutes to 60 min at 37 °C; emulsions: 31 days at 37 °C (plus other temperatures)
papers.result: In buffer at pH ≥7.0 curcumin degraded rapidly in the first 7 min (initial rates 92, 135 and 125 cm-1/min at pH 7.0, 7.4, 8.0), while at pH <7 it crystallized (10-50 µm crystals). In MCT emulsions 85-95% remained after 31 days at acidic pH but only 53-62% at pH ≥7.0.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.
papers.key_details: Spectrophotometric (433 nm) degradation and turbidity (600 nm) assays of 40 µM curcumin (added from a DMSO stock) in phosphate buffers at 37 °C, with and without stirring; emulsion storage over 31 days at several pH values and temperatures. Stirring promoted crystallization and aggregation of crystals in acidic solutions; alkaline solutions stayed clear but faded fast. Oil solubility of pure curcumin in MCT was 2.90 mg/g; in bulk MCT at 55 °C for 31 days there was no significant loss, so degradation happens at the oil-water interface. Water solubility of curcumin is cited as 11 ng/mL. Caveat for HAB use: seawater pH (~8) is the regime where free curcumin degrades within minutes.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record is broadly correct. Retention after 31 days at 37 °C was 53-62% for pH 7.0-8.0 (the per-pH 62/60/53 split is from Fig. 3B, not stated in text). Crystals formed at pH 3, 5 and 7, not only below pH 7.
papers.study_note: curcumin stability vs pH and emulsions

reasons.reproducibility: 40 uM curcumin in phosphate buffers read at 433/600 nm needs only a spectrophotometer and common chemicals; emulsions add MCT oil and Tween 80.
reasons.effectiveness: Stability study; no algae treated.
reasons.cost: Oils, emulsifier and curcumin about $50-150.
reasons.time: Buffer degradation shows within 7 min at pH >= 7, but the emulsion arm ran 31 days.
reasons.environment: Not reported; relevant finding is that free curcumin degrades within minutes at seawater pH ~8.

papers.title: Influence of vehicle properties and excipients on hydrolytic and photochemical stability of curcumin in preparations containing Pluronics: Studies of curcumin and curcuminoids XLVIII
papers.scale: Pluronic preparations
papers.result: Hydrolysis faster at pH 8.0-8.8 and in carbonate buffer; ethanol lowered stability; photochemical half-life 'in the minutes range'.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.

reasons.reproducibility: Pluronic preparations and photostability tests need a spectrophotometer and light source.
reasons.effectiveness: Stability study; no algae treated.
reasons.cost: Pluronic and curcumin about $50-150.
reasons.time: Photochemical half-life in minutes.
reasons.environment: Not reported; Pluronic carrier is an added polymer.

papers.title: Studies of curcumin and curcuminoids. XXVII. Cyclodextrin complexation: solubility, chemical and photochemical stability
papers.scale: aqueous buffer solutions with six cyclodextrins (HPαCD, HPβCD, HPγCD, RMβCD, SBβCD, HTAβCD), mostly 5% w/v; xenon-lamp photolysis; n=3
papers.dose: cyclodextrin 1-5%; hydrolysis tested at pH 8.0, complexation at pH 5
papers.duration: minutes (photolysis, hydrolysis of free curcumin) to days (complexed curcumin)
papers.result: Complexation raised curcumin's water solubility about 10^4-fold at pH 5 and dramatically improved hydrolytic stability at alkaline pH (free curcumin half-life a few minutes above pH 7; 5% HPβCD complex half-life 19.8 days at pH 5). Photostability fell: photolysis half-lives were 20.4-46.2 min in 5% cyclodextrins versus 70.7 min in ethanol-buffer and 133.3 min in methanol.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.
papers.key_details: Phase-solubility and kinetic study of curcumin with six neutral or charged cyclodextrins at room temperature. RMβCD and HPγCD gave the highest affinity, cationic HTAβCD the lowest; neutral cyclodextrins protected against hydrolysis better than charged ones. The most stable pH 8 sample (5% HPβCD) degraded at 0.035 per day at pH 5 (half-life 19.8 d, n=3). Photodegradation followed first-order kinetics and was faster in every cyclodextrin than in organic solvent systems. No algae or organisms tested.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Solubility gain is 'approximately 10^4', not '≥10^4'.

reasons.reproducibility: Cyclodextrin complexation and photostability need analytical chemistry support.
reasons.effectiveness: Stability study; no algae treated.
reasons.cost: Cyclodextrins and analysis about $150-500.
reasons.time: Photolysis half-lives were 20-46 min, but complexed curcumin's hydrolysis half-life (19.8 d) needs weeks of tracking.
reasons.environment: Not reported; cyclodextrin carrier added.

papers.title: On the photobehaviour of curcumin in biocompatible hosts: The role of H-abstraction in the photodegradation and photosensitization
papers.venue: Journal of Photochemistry and Photobiology B: Biology
papers.scale: curcumin in Pluronic micelles, microemulsions and zein nanoparticles; steady-state photolysis (anaerobic, visible light), 1O2 luminescence, laser flash photolysis; dioxane as reference solvent
papers.dose: n/a
papers.result: No singlet oxygen was detected from curcumin in any host (only in dioxane); the triplet of the diketo form abstracts hydrogen from the host, giving ketyl radicals that react with O2 to form peroxyl radicals. The authors argue curcumin is a poor photosensitizer and its phototoxicity is probably radical-mediated, not 1O2-mediated.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.
papers.key_details: Spectroscopic study of curcumin encapsulated in three biocompatible hosts, which shifted its keto-enol equilibrium towards the diketo form. Photolysis was run anaerobically under visible light and 1O2 phosphorescence was measured in each host and in dioxane. A clear 1O2 signal appeared in dioxane but none in any host, partly because the triplet lifetime in the hosts is too short for oxygen quenching to compete. The authors note curcumin absorbs only blue light, has ISC/1O2 quantum yields of ca. 0.1 at most in organic solvents, reacts readily with 1O2 and is poorly water-soluble. No organisms tested.

reasons.reproducibility: Laser flash photolysis is research-grade equipment.
reasons.effectiveness: Photochemistry study; no algae treated.
reasons.cost: Laser flash photolysis setup over $5,000.
reasons.time: Photophysics measured in microseconds to minutes.
reasons.environment: Not reported; forms peroxyl radicals, short-lived.

papers.title: Back to the roots: photodynamic inactivation of bacteria based on water-soluble curcumin bound to polyvinylpyrrolidone as a photosensitizer
papers.scale: lab photodynamic inactivation
papers.dose: 5-50 µM PVP-curcumin + 435 nm light, 33.8 J/cm²
papers.result: 5 µM (≈1.8 mg/L) gave >6 log10 kill of S. aureus; 50 µM for 15-25 min eradicated it; longer pre-incubation was less phototoxic.
papers.env_effects: E. coli needed CaCl2 to open the cell wall.
papers.study_note: photodynamic dose on bacteria, not algae

reasons.reproducibility: Bacterial photodynamic inactivation with 435 nm light needs a microbiology lab.
reasons.effectiveness: Targets bacteria (>6 log S. aureus kill), not algae.
reasons.cost: PVP-curcumin, light source and culture about $150-500.
reasons.time: Results within minutes of illumination.
reasons.environment: Non-target (algal) effects not reported; curcumin photodegrades.

papers.title: Curcumin Affects Development of Zebrafish Embryo
papers.scale: lab
papers.dose: 5, 7.5, 10, 12.5, 15 uM curcumin (DMSO stock)
papers.duration: 24 h LD50; embryos followed daily to hatching, larvae exposed from 3 d old
papers.result: 24 h LD50 7.5 uM for embryos and 5 uM for larvae; 15 uM killed all embryos within 2 d and 10 uM killed all larvae; embryos at >=5 uM developed bent/hooked tails, spinal curvature, pericardial edema, retarded yolk resorption.
papers.env_effects: Lethal below the 5 mg/L algal dose.
papers.key_details: Zebrafish embryos (from 30 min post-fertilization) and 3-day-old larvae exposed in 6-well plates, 10 embryos per well; 30 animals x 4 replicates per concentration. Survival judged by heartbeat. Resveratrol, quercetin and rutin up to 100 uM had no effect. Curcumin decomposed in water over 2-3 d, which the authors used to explain survival differences. No DMSO-only solvent control is described.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record essentially correct; adds that teratogenic effects began at 5 uM and no solvent control is reported.

reasons.reproducibility: Zebrafish embryo tests need an animal facility and approval.
reasons.effectiveness: Non-target study; algal reduction not measured.
reasons.cost: Zebrafish embryos about $150-500.
reasons.environment: 24 h LD50 7.5 uM (embryos) and 5 uM (larvae), ~1.8-2.8 mg/L, below the 5 mg/L algal dose, with tail and spinal deformities from 5 uM (no solvent control reported).

papers.title: Environmental safety and mode of action of a novel curcumin-based photolarvicide
papers.organism: Aedes aegypti larvae (target); Daphnia magna, Danio rerio (zebrafish) and Pseudokirchneriella subcapitata feeding (non-target)
papers.scale: lab; 3 formulations
papers.dose: three formulations: curcumin in 1% DMSO/99% ethanol (1.5 mg/mL stock), or 1% curcumin in 99% sucrose or 99% D-mannitol (w/w); non-target tests up to 100 mg/L; larvae 0.45-5.4 mg/L
papers.duration: Daphnia 24-48 h (acute), 6 h (sub-lethal); zebrafish 48 h; larvae up to 8 h natural sunlight
papers.result: The ethanol+DMSO formulation gave a zebrafish LC50 of 5.9 mg/L (2.55-13.6) and its solvents killed >10% of Daphnia in the solvent control; the sucrose and D-mannitol formulations were practically non-toxic to Daphnia and zebrafish even at 100 mg/L. Sugar formulations killed 100% of Aedes larvae at 0.45, 1.8 and 5.4 mg/L after 8 h of sunlight.
papers.env_effects: Daphnia at 50 mg/L showed a 59% rise in ROS; at 50 mg/L of the D-mannitol formulation algal growth in the Daphnia feeding test was 117% of control; curcumin adhered to Daphnia bodies and guts at 100 mg/L. Solvent carrier was more toxic than curcumin.
papers.key_details: Tested a curcumin photolarvicide in three carriers on non-target D. magna (OECD 202, in dark and 16:8 light, n=35 for sub-lethal assays) and zebrafish (10 fish per replicate, n=20), plus target Aedes aegypti larvae in natural sunlight. The ethanol+DMSO formulation was judged unfeasible for field use and not tested on larvae. Sugar-carrier formulations showed no acute toxicity to Daphnia at 100 mg/L and were non-toxic to fish, while killing all larvae at 0.45 mg/L and above within 8 h of sunlight; larvae were lethargic after 1 h. Larval CAT and GSH changes were measured for the D-mannitol formulation. No harmful algae were tested; relevant to curcumin as an outdoor photosensitizer's non-target safety.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record omits the target organism (Aedes aegypti larvae) and the 100 mg/L no-effect level of the sugar formulations; 'Duration: Not reported' is wrong (24-48 h acute tests, 8 h sunlight larval tests).
papers.study_note: Daphnia and zebrafish toxicity of formulations

reasons.reproducibility: Daphnia and zebrafish tests on three formulations; sponsor needed for fish.
reasons.effectiveness: Non-target study; algal reduction not measured.
reasons.cost: Daphnia, zebrafish and formulations about $150-500.
reasons.time: Acute tests ran 24-48 h and larval tests 8 h of sunlight.
reasons.environment: Sugar-carrier formulations were practically non-toxic to Daphnia and zebrafish at 100 mg/L, but the ethanol+DMSO form had a fish LC50 of 5.9 mg/L and Daphnia ROS rose 59% at 50 mg/L.

papers.title: Environmentally Safe Photodynamic Control of Aedes aegypti Using Sunlight-Activated Synthetic Curcumin: Photodegradation, Aquatic Ecotoxicity, and Field Trial
papers.scale: lab + simulated field
papers.dose: 4.6 mg/L with sucrose, sunlight
papers.result: LT50 3 d in sunlight and no toxicity in the dark; cited LC50-3h 2.2-20 mg/L and LC50-24h 0.04 mg/L in sun.
papers.env_effects: Animal toxicity is light-gated; photoproduct toxicity only predicted (ECOSAR), not measured.

reasons.reproducibility: Aedes larvae in sunlight with curcumin-sucrose is sponsor-doable with insect handling.
reasons.effectiveness: Targets mosquito larvae, not algae.
reasons.cost: Synthetic curcumin and larvae about $150-500.
reasons.time: 21-d trial with LT50 of 3 d.
reasons.environment: Light-gated animal toxicity (24-h LC50 0.04 mg/L in sun); photoproduct toxicity only predicted.

papers.title: Biocompatibility Study of Curcumin-Loaded Pluronic F127 Nanoformulation (NanoCUR) against the Embryonic Development of Zebrafish (Danio rerio)
papers.scale: lab
papers.dose: native curcumin 1-100 uM vs NanoCUR (Pluronic F127) 1-100 uM; Pluronic F127 alone to 2% w/v
papers.result: Native curcumin LC50 fell from 8.077 uM at 24 hpf to 6.302 uM at 96 hpf; NanoCUR LC50 was >100 uM through 72 hpf and 28.4 uM at 96 hpf; 10 uM native curcumin left 41% survival at 24 hpf and 20% at 72 hpf; >30 uM killed 100% by 24 hpf.
papers.env_effects: Native curcumin toxic to zebrafish embryos at ~6 uM (~2.3 mg/L); nano-encapsulation cut toxicity ~4.5x at 96 h; carrier alone non-toxic.
papers.key_details: Zebrafish embryo toxicity test comparing native curcumin, curcumin-loaded Pluronic F127 micelles and the carrier alone; endpoints survival, hatching, heart rate, malformations (yolk-sac edema, scoliosis) and ROS. At least three independent experiments. 1 uM native curcumin gave 100% survival. Drug-delivery context, not HAB treatment.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record had no numbers; full text gives native curcumin 96 h LC50 6.302 uM vs 28.4 uM for NanoCUR.

reasons.reproducibility: Zebrafish embryo tests with Pluronic nanoformulation need animal facility.
reasons.effectiveness: Non-target study; algal reduction not measured.
reasons.cost: Embryos and Pluronic about $150-500.
reasons.time: Embryo toxicity was read at 24-96 h post-fertilization.
reasons.environment: Native curcumin 96 h LC50 was 6.3 uM (~2.3 mg/L), below the 5 mg/L algal dose; Pluronic encapsulation raised it to 28.4 uM.

papers.title: The effectiveness of five natural products against three species of harmful algae
papers.organism: Chattonella marina, Alexandrium tamarense, Karenia mikimotoi
papers.scale: 100 mL beakers with 50 mL culture; f/2, 20 °C, 12:12 h light; initial ~5-6, 3-4 and 7-8 x 10^6 cells/L (C. marina, A. tamarense, K. mikimotoi)
papers.dose: screen: ε-polylysine, berberine, stachydrine, betaine, chitosan each at 50 mg/L; LC50 series; berberine 10-30 mg/L short-term; 4 and 8 mg/L for TEM
papers.result: At 50 mg/L only berberine inhibited K. mikimotoi (IR nearly 100% in 24 h; LC50-120h 3.1 mg/L), ε-polylysine was best on C. marina (70.9% at 120 h; LC50-120h 29.2 mg/L), and betaine and stachydrine were best on A. tamarense (LC50-120h 17.8 and 20.0 mg/L). Chitosan's apparent effect matched its acetic-acid control.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.
papers.key_details: Screen of five natural products (no curcumin) against three marine HAB species with water and acetic-acid controls; cell counts at 24-120 h; means ± SD with t-tests (replicate number not stated in text). Selectivity was strong: berberine LC50-120h was 3.1 mg/L on K. mikimotoi but 71.9 mg/L on C. marina and 58.5 mg/L on A. tamarense. Berberine at 30 mg/L inhibited K. mikimotoi within 120 min; at 10 mg/L IR was ≤40% and at 20 mg/L nearly 60% in 120 min. TEM showed organelle dissolution at 4 mg/L and membrane rupture at 8 mg/L within 12 h. No non-target toxicity tests were done, though the authors call berberine environmentally safe.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Dose was reported (50 mg/L screen), not missing. The paper contains no curcumin. Nearly 100% K. mikimotoi inhibition by berberine at 50 mg/L in 24 h was omitted.
papers.study_note: plant-compound comparator tested on algae (berberine/chitosan, curcumin not reported)

reasons.reproducibility: 50 mL beaker screens with purchased cultures and hemocytometer counts are sponsor-doable, though A. tamarense is a toxin producer.
reasons.effectiveness: Berberine gave ~100% inhibition of K. mikimotoi in 24 h at 50 mg/L (LC50 3.1 mg/L) but was weak on the other two species (LC50 58-72 mg/L); replication not stated and no curcumin tested.
reasons.cost: Three cultures and five compounds about $150-500.
reasons.time: 120-h (5-day) test.
reasons.environment: Non-target effects not reported.

papers.title: Comparing effects of berberine on the growth and photosynthetic activities of Microcystis aeruginosa and Chlorella pyrenoidosa
papers.scale: lab cultures in BG11, triplicates, 12:12 light-dark vs constant dark
papers.dose: 4 mg/L berberine (growth tests); 24 h-EC50 on M. aeruginosa 0.47 mg/L
papers.result: Under light-dark, 4 mg/L berberine drove M. aeruginosa cell density to zero by day 6, with Fv/Fm and ETR near zero after 1 day; it had no effect in constant darkness and no effect on Chlorella pyrenoidosa in either condition.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.
papers.key_details: Lab monocultures of Microcystis aeruginosa and Chlorella pyrenoidosa were exposed to 4 mg/L berberine (an allelochemical) in triplicate for 9 days under 12:12 light-dark or constant dark, with untreated controls. In light, M. aeruginosa density fell to zero by day 6 and Fv/Fm dropped to 0.04 within 10 h; in darkness there was no algicidal effect. The 24 h-EC50 for M. aeruginosa was 0.47 mg/L, which cut true photosynthesis (131.20 to 107.82 umol O2/mg Chl a/h) but not dark respiration. C. pyrenoidosa growth and photosynthesis were unaffected. Single strains in culture medium; no natural community, toxin or non-target animal data.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record listed dose and duration as 'Not reported'; the paper used 4 mg/L for 9 days (EC50 0.47 mg/L) and reached complete Microcystis elimination by day 6.

reasons.reproducibility: Berberine at 4 mg/L on Microcystis and Chlorella cultures with cell counts is a simple bench protocol with a purchased culture.
reasons.effectiveness: 4 mg/L berberine drove M. aeruginosa to zero by day 6 in triplicate vs untreated controls (light-dark), with no effect in constant dark; single strain.
reasons.cost: Two cultures, berberine, PAM fluorometry about $150-500.
reasons.time: Fv/Fm collapsed within a day and cells were gone by day 6.
