reasons.environment: Chlorella pyrenoidosa was unaffected; no toxin or animal data.

papers.title: Effect of environmental factors on allelopathic inhibition of Microcystis aeruginosa by berberine
papers.scale: lab
papers.dose: berberine 0.001% w/v (10 mg/L)
papers.result: Strongest when light and temperature favoured growth; 'hardly' algicidal in darkness.
papers.env_effects: Raised extracellular microcystin by lysing cells.

reasons.reproducibility: Microcystis with 10 mg/L berberine under varied conditions is sponsor-doable.
reasons.effectiveness: Strong only when light and temperature favoured growth; 'hardly' algicidal in dark.
reasons.cost: Culture and berberine about $150-500.
reasons.time: Duration not reported; scored 4-7 days.
reasons.environment: Raised extracellular microcystin by lysing cells.

papers.title: Physiological and Molecular Response of Prorocentrum minimum to Tannic Acid: An Experimental Study to Evaluate the Feasibility of Using Tannic Acid in Controling the Red Tide in a Eutrophic Coastal Water
papers.venue: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
papers.scale: lab
papers.dose: tannic acid 0.5, 2.5, 5, 10 mg/L
papers.result: Growth normal below 2.5 mg/L and slowed above it; 10 mg/L halted photosynthesis; Hsp70/Hsp90 up 10-27× at 48 h.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.
papers.study_note: plant-compound comparator tested on algae (tannic acid)

reasons.reproducibility: Prorocentrum minimum culture with tannic acid is sponsor-doable; gene expression needs qPCR.
reasons.effectiveness: Slowed growth only above 2.5 mg/L; 10 mg/L halted photosynthesis.
reasons.cost: Culture, tannic acid, qPCR about $150-500.
reasons.time: 7-d test.
reasons.environment: Non-target effects not reported; tannic acid is a natural polyphenol.

papers.title: Effects of Dihydroartemisinin and Artemether on the Growth, Chlorophyll Fluorescence, and Extracellular Alkaline Phosphatase Activity of the Cyanobacterium Microcystis aeruginosa
papers.scale: lab
papers.dose: dihydroartemisinin 6, 12, 24 mg/L; artemether results reported at 6 mg/L
papers.result: After 120 h, growth inhibition peaked at 16.67%, 35.94% and 42.17% for 6, 12 and 24 mg/L dihydroartemisinin and 55.72% for 6 mg/L artemether; with artemether Fv/Fm, PhiPSII, ETR and rETRmax fell to 0.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.
papers.key_details: Axenic lab culture of Microcystis aeruginosa in 300 mL BG11, treated vs untreated controls, three replicates. Measured cell density (0-120 h), chlorophyll a, protein, MDA, alkaline phosphatase and chlorophyll fluorescence. Partial growth inhibition only (max ~56%). Compounds are artemisinin derivatives, not curcumin.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: This paper is about dihydroartemisinin and artemether, not curcumin; it probably belongs in a different method bucket. Effect_pct can be set to 55.72 (artemether) or 42.17 (dihydroartemisinin).
papers.study_note: plant-compound comparator tested on algae (artemisinin derivatives)

reasons.reproducibility: Microcystis with artemisinin derivatives is sponsor-doable.
reasons.effectiveness: Partial inhibition only: 17-42% for dihydroartemisinin (6-24 mg/L) and 56% for 6 mg/L artemether at 120 h in triplicate; compounds are not curcumin.
reasons.cost: Culture and compounds about $150-500.
reasons.time: 120-h (5-day) test.
reasons.environment: Non-target effects not reported.

papers.title: Growth, physiological responses and microcystin-production/-release dynamics of Microcystis aeruginosa exposed to various luteolin doses
papers.scale: 250 mL flasks with 100 mL BG11, initial 4 x 10^5 cells/mL, 25 °C, 12:12 h; triplicate
papers.dose: luteolin (DMSO stock) 0.5-32 mg/L range-finding; then 3.25, 6.5 and 13 mg/L (0.5x, 1x, 2x IC50)
papers.result: IC50 was stable at 6.342-6.810 mg/L from day 8 to 14 (about 6.5 mg/L). Growth inhibition in the mid-late stage held at 38-60%, 52-62% and 70-78% for 3.25, 6.5 and 13 mg/L, and extracellular microcystin fell 5.26-78.35% below control, more at higher doses.
papers.env_effects: Extracellular microcystin decreased at all doses versus control (26.13-61.93% day 4, 5.26-74.21% day 8, 42.99-78.35% day 14); MC-release percentage stayed below 10% early on.
papers.key_details: Toxigenic M. aeruginosa FACHB-915 was exposed to luteolin in BG11 for 14 d with triplicate exposure and control flasks; IC50 was estimated by probit regression on days 8 and 14. At each dose inhibition rose until about day 4-6 then plateaued or fell slightly as cells upregulated CAT and GSH (late-stage stimulation 2.58x and 2.36x). Chlorophyll a was stimulated early (1.21-2.25x on day 4) then inhibited. The IC50 is higher than the 1.85 mg/L reported for a non-toxigenic strain (FACHB-469). Single strain, lab only, DMSO carrier.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record implies inhibition fell late; the text says it plateaued or dropped only slightly, holding 38-78% by dose. Record says 'Not reported' for microcystin effects, but extracellular MC fell 5-78% versus control.

reasons.reproducibility: Microcystis with luteolin and enzyme assays is sponsor-doable.
reasons.effectiveness: Luteolin held 38-60%, 52-62% and 70-78% inhibition at 3.25, 6.5 and 13 mg/L over 14 d in triplicate; inhibition plateaued rather than collapsing.
reasons.cost: Culture, luteolin, enzyme kits about $150-500.
reasons.time: 14-d test.
reasons.environment: Extracellular microcystin fell 5-78% vs control; DMSO carrier; no non-target organisms tested.

papers.title: Long-term suppression of Microcystis aeruginosa by tannic acid: Risks of microcystin pollution and proteomic mechanisms
papers.scale: lab, long-term

reasons.cost: Culture plus proteomics/toxin ELISA $150-500.
reasons.time: ≥15-d test.

papers.title: Effects of low concentration of gallic acid on the growth and microcystin production of Microcystis aeruginosa
papers.scale: 160 mL BG11 cultures, initial 7 x 10^5 cells/mL, 25 °C, 10:14 h light, shaken 120 rpm; triplicate
papers.duration: about 32 d, sampled every 4 d (transcriptomics at day 32)
papers.result: Gallic acid inhibited growth at ≥1 µg/L (maximum inhibition 73.79% at 10,000 µg/L) but stimulated it at ≤0.1 µg/L (maximum promotion 45.28% at 0.1 µg/L; growth rate 1.09x and maximum density 1.16x control). At 0.1 µg/L microcystin synthesis rose 1.85x and total MCs reached 1.23 mg/L (+54.73%).
papers.env_effects: At 0.1 µg/L, total microcystins +54.73% (1.23 mg/L), intracellular MC per cell 1.77 times higher than control, and the ecological risk quotient was 0.3, about 30x control (moderate risk). At 10,000 µg/L intracellular MC per cell was lower than control.
papers.key_details: Triplicate BG11 cultures of toxigenic M. aeruginosa exposed to eight gallic acid levels spanning 7 orders of magnitude, with cell density, Chl a, ATP, ROS, SYTOX viability, intra- and extracellular MCs and transcriptomics (0.1 and 10,000 µg/L at day 32). The response was hormetic: inhibition at ≥1 µg/L, stimulation at ≤0.1 µg/L, with the inhibitory effect no longer significant above 10 µg/L per the authors' model and peak promotion at 0.18 µg/L. On day 9 the 0.1 µg/L group was 15.5% denser than control; Chl a per cell peaked at +152.85% (day 17). MC-synthesis genes were upregulated at low dose. Caveat: a single strain in lab culture; the authors warn that dilution and degradation of an applied allelochemical can leave stimulating residues.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: The 1.09x is the growth-rate ratio; the text's headline promotion is 45.28% at 0.1 µg/L (max density 1.16x), so effect_pct -9 understates the stimulation. Duration (~32 d) was reported. High doses did inhibit (73.79% at 10 mg/L).
papers.study_note: plant-compound comparator tested on algae (gallic acid)

reasons.reproducibility: Microcystis with gallic acid dilution series is sponsor-doable.
reasons.effectiveness: Hormetic: up to 74% inhibition at 10 mg/L, but <=0.1 ug/L boosted growth up to 45% (opposite effect), and inhibition was not significant above 10 ug/L in the authors' model.
reasons.cost: Culture and toxin ELISA about $150-500.
reasons.time: Density differences appeared by day 9 of a ~32-day run.
reasons.environment: At 0.1 ug/L total microcystins rose 55% (1.23 mg/L) with a risk quotient ~30x control, so diluted residues can worsen toxicity.

papers.title: Mitigation of harmful algal bloom (Margalefidinium polykrikoides) intensity and toxicity via aeration processes
papers.scale: lab flasks: 150 mL (shaking) or 500 mL cultures in 1 L Erlenmeyer flasks; field bloom water 500 mL flasks in a flow-through outdoor table
papers.dose: macrobubbles via air stone at 25 mL/min (low) or 300 mL/min (high), continuous; nanobubbles (~100 nm) generated 2 h in 500 L (Moleaer XTB 200), ± ozone; orbital shaking 240 rpm (est. epsilon ~8 x 10^-2 m2 s-3)
papers.duration: lab ~10-15 d; bloom-water experiments 24 h (Old Fort Pond) and 2 d (Meetinghouse Creek)
papers.result: High-rate macrobubbles cut M. polykrikoides 21-58% (CPSB-1G) and 34-63% (CP1) vs unaerated controls, and 78% at day 10 in the screening test; high-level treatment gave 0% larval fish mortality vs 100% in controls within 1.5 h. In bloom water, cells were 1477 vs 2022 cells/mL in controls after 24 h (Old Fort Pond) and 29-55% in 2 d (Meetinghouse Creek).
papers.env_effects: In Meetinghouse Creek bloom water, Polykrikos sp. and Prorocentrum cordatum increased under macrobubbling while M. polykrikoides fell.
papers.key_details: Screening test (strain CPSB-1G, 4 replicates, 500 cells/mL) compared orbital shaking at 240 rpm, nanobubbles with and without ozone, and macrobubbles at 300 mL/min; by day 10 macrobubbles were 78% below control and 72% below both nanobubble treatments. In two-level tests (25 vs 300 mL/min, n=4), high-rate bubbling cut CPSB-1G 21-58% and CP1 34-63% vs unaerated controls; Fv/Fm dropped under both rates. Larval M. beryllina had 0% mortality in high-level bubbling vs 100% in the positive control within 1.5 h; C. variegatus survival was 100% under both bubbling rates. In bloom water (n=3), Old Fort Pond cells went from 2000 to 1477 +/- 94 (high) vs 2022 +/- 14 (control) cells/mL in 24 h; at Meetinghouse Creek, M. polykrikoides fell 55% (low) and 29% (high) by day 2. Orbital shaking also significantly reduced growth (days 6-12). Caveat: small flasks with bubbling fitted to 0.5 L volumes; no scale-up tested.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: The record's '>60%' is from the highlights; the reported ranges are 21-58% (CPSB-1G) and 34-63% (CP1) for high-level bubbling, 78% at day 10 in screening. Flow rates (25 and 300 mL/min) and durations are given. The field arm was bloom water in flasks, not in-situ aeration. In one bloom test the low rate beat the high rate (55% vs 29%).
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Margalefidinium polykrikoides (culture + bloom water)

reasons.reproducibility: Aquarium air stones in 0.5 L flasks are simple, but it needs a purchased ichthyotoxic M. polykrikoides culture and larval fish for the toxicity arm.
reasons.effectiveness: High-rate bubbling cut cells 21-63% vs unaerated controls (n=4; 78% in screening at day 10), but bloom water gave only 26-55% and the low rate beat the high rate once.
reasons.cost: Air pumps and stones are cheap, but Margalefidinium cultures, media and fish put it at roughly $150-500.
reasons.time: Bloom-water reductions showed within 1-2 days, while culture differences built over ~10 days.
reasons.environment: Only air is added, but in Meetinghouse Creek water bubbling let Polykrikos and the HAB Prorocentrum cordatum increase.

papers.title: Quantified small-scale turbulence inhibits a red tide dinoflagellate, Gonyaulax polyedra Stein

papers.result: Zero growth at γ ≈ 8 s⁻¹, negative growth above 8, no effect below 2 s⁻¹ (via Gibson & Thomas 1995).
papers.env_effects: Not reported.

papers.title: Effects of turbulence intermittency on growth inhibition of a red tide dinoflagellate, Gonyaulax polyedra Stein
papers.scale: Couette

papers.result: 0.25-2.5 h/day gave negative growth; 5 min/day had no effect; the daily-mean γ needed for zero growth fell to <0.09 s⁻¹ with intermittency.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.

reasons.reproducibility: Needs a Couette device run in daily pulses at ~9 s^-1, which is specialist equipment.
reasons.effectiveness: 0.25-2.5 h/day of shear gave negative growth, but 5 min/day had no effect and no percent reduction is reported.
reasons.cost: Couette apparatus plus culture puts it at roughly $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Daily pulses over an unreported total period, so scored as 1-3 weeks.
reasons.environment: Only water motion is applied; nothing is added.

papers.title: EFFECTS OF SMALL‐SCALE TURBULENCE ON PHOTOSYNTHESIS, PIGMENTATION, CELL DIVISION, AND CELL SIZE IN THE MARINE DINOFLAGELLATE GOMAULAX POLYEDRA (DINOPHYCEAE) 1
papers.scale: rotating bottles + Couette
papers.dose: up to 26.6 s⁻¹
papers.result: Photosynthesis was less sensitive than growth; photosynthesis per cell and respiration rose.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.

reasons.effectiveness: Reports physiology (photosynthesis less sensitive than growth, respiration up) rather than a quantified cell reduction.
reasons.cost: Rotating bottles, culture and pigment analysis likely $150-500.

papers.title: EFFECTS OF TURBULENCE ON THE MARINE DINOFLAGELLATE GYMNODINIUM NELSONII 1
papers.scale: flasks, orbital shaker 100 rpm
papers.dose: shaking at 100 rpm
papers.result: Division stopped, cell volume up to 1.5× and DNA/RNA per cell up to 10×; after a 10-day shake division resumed at ~2/3 the control rate; >20 d gave total death.

reasons.effectiveness: Shaking stopped division entirely and >20 d gave total death, but after 10 d cells resumed at ~2/3 the control rate.

papers.title: Species‐specific physiological response of dinoflagellates to quantified small‐scale turbulence 1
papers.organism: Alexandrium minutum, Prorocentrum triestinum, Gymnodinium sp.
papers.scale: flasks, orbital shaker 100 rpm
papers.dose: ε ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁴ m² s⁻³
papers.result: Shaking cut net growth rate to 33% of still controls in A. minutum (0.108 vs 0.328 d⁻¹) and to 28% in P. triestinum (0.136 vs 0.485 d⁻¹), i.e. roughly two-thirds lower; small Gymnodinium sp. was not significantly affected. Cell volume rose up to 1.4x/2.5x and DNA per cell 1.8x/5.3x; swimming speed halved; cells recovered in still water.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.
papers.key_details: Lab flask experiments at 20°C, orbital shaker at 100 rpm (bulk ε ≈ 2 cm² s⁻³, measured by acoustic Doppler velocimeter), comparing still controls with flasks shaken during exponential growth, then returned to still conditions. Replication was two flasks per treatment once shaking began (six before). Table 3 gives turbulent/still growth ratios (T/S) of 33% (A. minutum, p = 0.009) and 28% (P. triestinum, p = 0.003); after shaking stopped, growth recovered to 62% and 46% of control rates. Gymnodinium sp. T/S was 79-99%, not significant. Response was species-specific with no clear link to taxonomy or morphology; shaker turbulence is far above typical ocean levels.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record reads the abstract's '33% and 28%' as reductions; Table 3 shows these are turbulent/still growth-rate ratios, so growth was reduced by about 67% and 72%.

reasons.reproducibility: Needs an orbital shaker plus toxic Alexandrium minutum and two other dinoflagellate cultures, with ADV turbulence calibration.
reasons.effectiveness: Shaking cut growth ~67% (A. minutum) and ~72% (P. triestinum) vs still controls, but n=2 flasks, no effect on Gymnodinium, and growth recovered once shaking stopped.
reasons.cost: An orbital shaker and three dinoflagellate cultures put it around $150-500 if a shaker is borrowed.
reasons.time: Growth-rate differences appeared over a few days of exponential growth.
reasons.environment: Shaking adds nothing to the water.

papers.title: CELL CYCLE AND CELL MORTALITY OF ALEXANDRIUM MINUTUM (DINOPHYCEAE) UNDER SMALL‐SCALE TURBULENCE CONDITIONS 1
papers.scale: 4 flasks: 2 shaken (orbital shaker, 120 rpm, 30 mm displacement) vs 2 still controls
papers.dose: ε = 27 cm² s⁻³ (2.7 × 10⁻³ W kg⁻¹), orbital shaker
papers.duration: Continuous shaking from day 7 to day 21 (~14 d)
papers.result: Shaken cultures grew at 0.52 ± 0.06 d⁻¹ vs 0.69 ± 0.11 d⁻¹ still (75% of control); final abundance (days 16-21) 27,852 vs 54,333 cells mL⁻¹ (~51% of still). Immediate transient G2/M arrest; mortality signals only after >4 d.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.
papers.key_details: Synchronised A. minutum cultures; on day 7 two flasks were randomly shaken and two kept still (n = 2 flasks per treatment). Turbulence came from an orbital shaker at 120 rpm, ε = 27 cm² s⁻³. Shaken exponential growth rate was 0.52 ± 0.06 d⁻¹ vs 0.69 ± 0.11 d⁻¹ in still cultures (P = 0.005), and final cell abundance was ~51% of the still cultures (27,852 ± 3,461 vs 54,333 ± 14,917 cells mL⁻¹). After 48 h of shaking, G2/M lasted ~75% longer and S phase was ~19% shorter. Mortality was estimated only qualitatively (Coulter size fractions of broken thecae); the authors state no rates could be estimated.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: The record gave ε ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁴; the paper states ε = 27 cm² s⁻³ = 2.7 × 10⁻³ W kg⁻¹. The record also left out the growth and abundance reductions (75% of the still growth rate; ~51% of final cells).

reasons.reproducibility: Requires a toxic Alexandrium minutum culture, an orbital shaker and flow cytometry for the cell-cycle work.
reasons.effectiveness: Final abundance was ~51% of still cultures and growth 75% of control (P=0.005), a moderate effect with only n=2 flasks and no measurable mortality rate.
reasons.cost: Flow cytometry and cell-cycle analysis push repetition of the full study into the $500-5,000 range.
reasons.time: Shaking ran from day 7 to 21 and the abundance gap was read at days 16-21, i.e. about two weeks.
reasons.environment: Mechanical shaking adds no material.

papers.title: Modulation of ecdysal cyst and toxin dynamics of two Alexandrium (Dinophyceae) species under small-scale turbulence
papers.scale: Culture flasks, n = 2 per treatment; orbital shaker (high ε) and orbital grid system (low ε), 5 experiments
papers.duration: Shaking for 4 d (exponential or stationary phase) or continuously ('Always', ~16-17 d, days 4/5 to 21)
papers.result: At high ε, continuously shaken A. minutum grew at 0.19 ± 0.02 vs 0.25 ± 0.01 d⁻¹ and ended at 55.4% of control cell numbers; A. catenella ended at 24.7% and 21.6% of control (two experiments). Low ε (grids) did not suppress growth (A. minutum 127% of control).
papers.env_effects: Ecdysal cyst production was inhibited during shaking and recovered when shaking stopped. Cellular GTX(1+4) toxin was lower under long shaking, e.g. A. catenella 109.2 vs 169.7 fmol cell⁻¹.
papers.key_details: Two Alexandrium species were exposed to ε = 0.4 cm² s⁻³ (orbital grids) or 27 cm² s⁻³ (orbital shaker), for 4 d in exponential or stationary phase or continuously, against still controls (n = 2 flasks per treatment). Continuous shaking at high ε cut A. minutum growth from 0.25 to 0.19 d⁻¹ and final abundance to 55.4% of control (4,690 vs 8,458 cells mL⁻¹). A. catenella final abundance was 24.7% and 21.6% of control, with growth rate not markedly changed. Four-day shaking gave only 86.5-96.3% of control abundance. Low-ε grids favoured growth (A. minutum 127% of control), with cells escaping to calmer layers.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: The record reads the abstract's 'ca. 55.4%' and 'ca. 23%' as reductions. Table 1 shows them as the share of control that remained (%T/S): A. minutum was ~45% lower and A. catenella ~75-78% lower (24.7%/21.6% of control). The record understates the A. catenella effect by a factor of about 3.

reasons.reproducibility: Two toxic Alexandrium species plus an orbital grid system and shaker make this specialist work needing a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: Continuous high-epsilon shaking left A. catenella at 22-25% and A. minutum at 55% of control (n=2), but 4-day shaking gave only 4-14% and low turbulence raised A. minutum 27%.
reasons.cost: Shaker, cultures and media cost roughly $150-500; the grid system and toxin analysis would add more.
reasons.time: The strong effects needed continuous shaking for ~16-17 days.
reasons.environment: Nothing is added; shaking also lowered cellular GTX toxin.

papers.title: EFFECTS OF SMALL‐SCALE TURBULENCE ON NET GROWTH RATE AND SIZE OF TEN SPECIES OF MARINE DINOFLAGELLATES 1
papers.scale: 20 L polycarbonate tanks (24 x 10 x 100 cm, filled to 80 cm), turbulence from a pair of vertically oscillating 2.5 cm rods, calibrated with an acoustic Doppler velocimeter
papers.dose: high epsilon ~10^-4 m2 s-3, low epsilon ~10^-8 m2 s-3, unstirred control; continuous mixing
papers.duration: 1-2 weeks continuous mixing after a 1-day unmixed acclimation
papers.result: High turbulence cut net growth of Ceratium fusus ~25-50% and drove C. tripos and Pyrocystis noctiluca to net mortality (growth <0); four species (A. catenella, A. tamarense, Gyrodinium sp., P. fusiformis) were essentially unaffected; A. fundyense, G. catenatum and L. polyedrum grew ~30-40% faster. Low turbulence (10^-8) had no significant effect on any species.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.
papers.key_details: Ten dinoflagellate species (30-500 um) were grown in three 20 L tanks: high turbulence, low turbulence and an unstirred control, with treatments rotated among tanks. Most species were run in duplicate experiments (C. tripos in three, across two clones); cells were counted about every other day and net growth taken from log-linear regressions. Growth was inhibited in 3 species (C. fusus, C. tripos, P. noctiluca; the last two with net mortality), unchanged in 4 (A. catenella fell ~15% in one of two runs only) and raised ~30-40% in 3 (A. fundyense 0.38 to 0.53 and 0.37 to 0.50 div/d; L. polyedrum 0.33 to 0.53 and 0.33 to 0.49 div/d; G. catenatum significant in one of two runs). L. polyedrum cells were smaller under high turbulence. Caveat: the HAB taxa most relevant to mitigation (Alexandrium, Lingulodinium, Gymnodinium catenatum) grew faster or were unaffected.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: The record says 1 species slower and 2 'no increase'; the full text reports 3 species inhibited (C. fusus slower; C. tripos and P. noctiluca net mortality under high turbulence), 4 unaffected and 3 faster.

reasons.reproducibility: 20 L tanks with motor-driven oscillating rods calibrated by acoustic Doppler velocimeter and ten dinoflagellate cultures need a custom rig.
reasons.effectiveness: Only 3 of 10 species were inhibited; the HAB taxa Alexandrium, Lingulodinium and G. catenatum were unaffected or grew 30-40% faster.
reasons.cost: Building the rod rig and buying ten cultures lands in the $500-5,000 range.
reasons.time: Growth rates were fitted over 1-2 weeks of continuous mixing.
reasons.environment: Mixing adds no material.

papers.title: Effect of growth conditions on flow‐induced inhibition of population growth of a red‐tide dinoflagellate
papers.scale: Couette + shaken flasks
papers.dose: τ = 0.004 Pa, 1 h/day
papers.result: Growth cut was larger when flow was given in the last hour of dark, under low light, and in late-exponential cultures.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.

reasons.reproducibility: Needs a Couette device delivering a set stress (0.004 Pa, 1 h/day), which is specialist gear.
reasons.effectiveness: Growth cut depended on light, timing and growth phase; no percent reduction given, so moderate and conditional.
reasons.cost: Couette apparatus puts the cost at $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Runs lasted 5-8 d, so mostly 4-7 days.
reasons.environment: Only flow is applied; nothing is added.

papers.title: MECHANISMS OF FLUID SHEAR‐INDUCED INHIBITION OF POPULATION GROWTH IN A RED‐TIDE DINOFLAGELLATE 1
papers.scale: isolated cells in 0.5 mL multiwell plates (shaken) and larger cultures in Couette-flow chambers and shaken flasks
papers.dose: Couette laminar shear 0.004, 0.010 or 0.019 N m-2 for 1 to 24 h/day; unquantified shaking
papers.result: At 0.004 N m-2, 1 h/day cut net growth 25.9 +/- 3.9% and 2-24 h/day ~50% (49.9 +/- 3.0%), entirely through fewer divisions; at 0.010-0.019 N m-2, 1 h/day cut growth 44.8 +/- 4.4% and continuous 0.019 N m-2 61.9 +/- 8.2%, with added mortality; shaken flasks gave 66.5 +/- 2.9%.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.
papers.key_details: Lingulodinium polyedrum was tested three ways: shaken isolated cells tracked individually, Couette chambers at quantified shear, and shaken flasks; division frequency came from flow-cytometric DNA per cell. In isolated cells, percent dividing fell with daily shaking duration (F3,12 = 16.38, P = 0.0002) while mortality was unrelated to shaking. At the lowest shear, growth loss matched lower division; at higher shear and in shaken flasks, net growth fell below division estimates, showing shear-induced mortality. In a late-exponential culture at 0.004 N m-2 continuous, 23.6% of cells were disrupted (dead) vs 0.4% in controls. Caveat: statistics used within-experiment replicates, not replicated treatments, and a single shaker table was used for the isolated-cell tests.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: The record's 'Duration: Not reported' can be filled: shear was applied 1-24 h/day over multi-day runs. Growth-inhibition magnitudes (26-67%) were missing from the record.

reasons.reproducibility: Couette-flow chambers, multiwell tracking of isolated cells and flow-cytometric DNA analysis are specialist equipment.
reasons.effectiveness: Shear cut L. polyedrum net growth 26-67%, with added mortality at higher shear, but statistics rested on within-experiment replicates and one shaker table.
reasons.cost: Couette chambers and flow cytometry push costs to $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Growth inhibition was measured over multi-day runs with daily 1-24 h shear.
reasons.environment: Shear adds no material.

papers.title: Effect of fully characterized unsteady flow on population growth of the dinoflagellate Lingulodinium polyedrum
papers.scale: Couette flow chambers, 170 mL culture each; 12 chambers per paired experiment (4 still controls + 4 per flow treatment)
papers.dose: Steady shear 1.8-8 s⁻¹ vs oscillatory (unsteady) flow, average absolute shear 1.8-4 s⁻¹ (max 6.4-6.7 s⁻¹), periods 60-600 s
papers.duration: Daily flow exposure 5 min to 2 h (standard 2 h/d, starting 2 h before end of night phase), over multi-day growth experiments
papers.result: At average absolute shear 4 s⁻¹ for 2 h/d, unsteady flow gave 93.5% ± 35.4% growth inhibition vs 46.5% ± 26.7% for steady flow (p = 0.014); at 1.8 s⁻¹ the two were similar (45% vs 43%). Even 5 min/d of unsteady flow gave 11% inhibition, rising with duration.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.
papers.key_details: Lab study of one L. polyedrum strain in oscillatory Couette chambers with analytically characterised shear. Paired design: each experiment had 4 still controls run simultaneously with two flow treatments of 4 chambers; still-control net growth was 0.14 ± 0.03 d⁻¹ (n = 57 chambers). Unsteady flow at 4 s⁻¹ average absolute shear nearly stopped net growth (93.5% inhibition over periods 60-300 s), 50% more than steady 4 s⁻¹, and was not different from steady 8 s⁻¹. Oscillation period (60-600 s) and flow-direction reversal did not matter; inhibition rose with daily exposure from 11% at 5 min. Effect is growth inhibition (not cell kill) and the difference between steady and unsteady shrank at lower shear.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record gives 'mean |γ| 4 s⁻¹' but omits the headline numbers (93.5% vs 46.5% inhibition) and that the unsteady-vs-steady difference vanishes at 1.8 s⁻¹. Duration '5-120 min' is daily exposure, not total experiment length.

reasons.reproducibility: Needs purpose-built oscillatory Couette chambers with analytically characterised shear.
reasons.effectiveness: Unsteady flow at 4 s-1 gave 93.5% growth inhibition vs 46.5% steady (4 replicate chambers plus 4 paired still controls), though variance was large (+/-35%) and the difference vanished at 1.8 s-1.
reasons.cost: Twelve custom Couette chambers and drives cost $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Inhibition showed in multi-day growth experiments with 2 h/day flow.
reasons.environment: Flow adds no material.

papers.title: Net growth of the bloom-forming dinoflagellate Heterocapsa triquetra and pH: why turbulence matters
papers.scale: Eight 2 L Plexiglas containers with oscillating grids (4 replicates per level in Expt 1)
papers.dose: Four turbulence levels, ε = 0.0001, 0.005, 0.05 and 1 cm² s⁻³ (10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁴ m² s⁻³)
papers.result: Net growth was ~0.42 d⁻¹ at all turbulence levels while pH < 8.9; once densities exceeded 3 × 10⁴ cells/mL, growth was 0.17 d⁻¹ at the highest turbulence vs 0.07 d⁻¹ at the lowest (p = 0.006), because turbulence lowered pH via CO2 exchange. Turbulence did not suppress this dinoflagellate.
papers.env_effects: Turbulence relieves CO2 limitation and holds pH down, which can help algae.
papers.key_details: Lab batch cultures of Heterocapsa triquetra (clone K-0481) in f/2 at 15°C, grids at 4 turbulence levels spanning calm to storm conditions, 10 d. Expt 1 compared T1 vs T4 (4 replicates); Expt 2 compared T1-T3. No growth difference among levels for Days 0-5 (p = 0.914 and 0.909). At high density, T4 (0.17 d⁻¹) and T3 (0.13 d⁻¹) grew faster than T1/T2 (0.07 d⁻¹); pH was lower at high turbulence (p = 0.041). Cell volume (~3000 µm³) unaffected. Turbulence helped rather than hindered the bloom-former at high pH.

reasons.reproducibility: 2 L grid-stirred containers with one purchased Heterocapsa culture are doable with a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: Turbulence did not suppress H. triquetra; at high density it grew faster (0.17 vs 0.07 per day) because mixing lowered pH.
reasons.cost: A culture, grid stirrers and f/2 medium cost roughly $150-500.
reasons.time: Differences appeared only late in the 10-day runs at high cell density.
reasons.environment: Turbulence adds nothing, though it relieved CO2 limitation for the alga.

papers.title: Role of turbulence in Dinophysis spp. growth, feeding, and toxin leakage in culture
papers.organism: Dinophysis acuminata, D. ovum, D. caudata
papers.scale: lab cultures
papers.result: Slower growth in 2 species, faster in D. caudata.
papers.env_effects: More intracellular toxin (D. acuminata) and toxin leakage (D. ovum).

reasons.reproducibility: Dinophysis must be fed Mesodinium prey in a three-species culture chain and produces DSP toxins.
reasons.effectiveness: Mixed: turbulence slowed 2 species but sped up D. caudata.
reasons.cost: Three linked cultures plus toxin analysis is $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Duration not reported, so scored conservatively at 1-3 weeks.
reasons.environment: Turbulence raised toxin content in D. acuminata and caused toxin leakage from D. ovum.

papers.title: Effects of turbulence on plankton: an overview of experimental evidence and some theoretical considerations
papers.scale: review of lab data
papers.dose: many
papers.result: In a meta-analysis of normalized rates, growth was generally reduced by turbulence; dinoflagellates showed the strongest response (rate_x = -0.91 - 0.31 log ε, R = 0.55; bulk 121% decrease in normalized growth rate) and made up 53% of negative-effect cases.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.
papers.key_details: Review and re-analysis of published lab data on small-scale turbulence effects on plankton growth, ingestion and energy expenditure, normalized as rate_x. Dinoflagellates (20-200 µm) showed the clearest negative growth response, with a bulk 121% decrease in normalized growth rate. Without dinoflagellates the growth-rate cloud was slightly positive and not distinguishable from 0. Ingestion rates mostly increased, especially below 10 cm² s⁻³. Many experiments used ε far above oceanic levels.

reasons.reproducibility: The typical reviewed experiment is a shaker or grid culture test with purchased phytoplankton, doable with a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: Across published lab data growth generally fell under turbulence, strongly for dinoflagellates but not distinguishable from zero for other groups, often at unrealistic epsilon.
reasons.cost: A typical shaker/grid culture experiment costs $150-500.
reasons.time: Typical lab turbulence experiments run one to two weeks.
reasons.environment: Turbulence adds no material.

papers.title: Combined effects of nutrients and small-scale turbulence in a microcosm experiment. I. Dynamics and size distribution of osmotrophic plankton
papers.organism: Natural NW Mediterranean coastal plankton (phytoplankton and bacteria), <150 µm
papers.scale: Twelve 15 L microcosms (6 turbulent, 6 still), 2 replicates per nutrient treatment (control, N-surplus N:P 160, Redfield N:P 16)
papers.dose: Oscillating grids, ε = 0.055 cm² s⁻³ (5.5 × 10⁻⁶ m² s⁻³)
papers.result: With nutrients added, turbulence raised total chl a (turbulent NP peaked at 19.0 ± 1.1 µg/L vs still maximum 4.2 ± 0.2 µg/L) and the >10 µm (diatom) fraction; without nutrients turbulence had no effect. Turbulence increased, not reduced, phytoplankton.
papers.env_effects: Diatoms favoured by turbulence.
papers.key_details: Coastal water from Masnou (Catalan coast) enclosed March 1998 in 15 L microcosms at 15°C for 8 d. Design: 3 nutrient conditions x still/turbulent, 2 replicate microcosms each (no replicates for TN and TNP on Day 8). In N and NP treatments turbulent chl a was significantly higher than still from Day 2 (p < 0.001); turbulent N reached 10.2 µg/L, still N peaked at 3.7 ± 2.5 µg/L. Bacterial abundance did not differ between still and turbulent. Turbulence shifted the community to larger cells and diatoms; small replication (n = 2).
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record does not state that turbulence roughly quadrupled chlorophyll in nutrient-enriched microcosms (i.e. mixing enhanced growth).

reasons.reproducibility: 15 L microcosms of natural coastal water with oscillating grids need a built rig but no special organisms.
reasons.effectiveness: Turbulence raised chlorophyll about fourfold with nutrients (19.0 vs 4.2 ug/L) and had no effect without them, the opposite of control.
reasons.cost: Twelve microcosms with grids and nutrient analyses cost roughly $150-500.
reasons.time: Turbulent chlorophyll exceeded still controls from day 2 of the 8-day run.
reasons.environment: Nothing is added, but mixing shifted the community toward larger cells and diatoms.

papers.title: Effects of small-scale turbulence on the growth of two diatoms of different size in a phosphorus-limited medium
papers.scale: 2.5 L polycarbonate bottles, 2 still and 2 turbulent per species (n=2), two independent experiments
papers.dose: orbital shaker at 130 rpm; epsilon ~10 cm2 s-3 (ADV-estimated) vs still
papers.result: Turbulence raised Coscinodiscus growth (0.37 to 0.42 and 0.27 to 0.32 d-1; final 33 vs 55 and 22 vs 38 cells/mL) and slightly lowered T. pseudonana growth (1.74 to 1.52 and 1.69 to 1.35 d-1).
papers.env_effects: Not reported.
papers.key_details: Batch cultures of the small diatom Thalassiosira pseudonana (~6 um) and the large Coscinodiscus sp. (~109 um) were grown in P-limited medium (1 uM P, N/P 88.2) at 22 C with duplicate still and turbulent bottles, in two experiments. Turbulence increased Coscinodiscus growth rate and final density in both experiments and slightly reduced T. pseudonana growth. Results were compared with a nutrient-uptake (Sherwood number) model; Sh under turbulence was 1.17 for T. pseudonana and 2.94 for Coscinodiscus. Caveats: n=2 bottles per treatment, non-axenic cultures, Coscinodiscus growth computed from total shells including empty ones.

reasons.reproducibility: 2.5 L bottles on an orbital shaker with two purchased diatom cultures are doable with a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: Turbulence raised Coscinodiscus growth and density and only slightly lowered T. pseudonana growth, with n=2 bottles.
reasons.cost: Shaker access plus two cultures and P-limited medium cost about $150-500.
reasons.time: Each experiment ran about 5 days.
reasons.environment: Shaking adds nothing.

papers.title: The effects of turbulence on the growth of three different diatom species
papers.organism: Thalassiosira pseudonana, Skeletonema costatum, Phaeodactylum tricornutum
papers.scale: orbital shaker 0-180 rpm
papers.result: T. pseudonana final density 33.5 → 46-58 × 10⁵ mL⁻¹ (up); Skeletonema up but inhibited at 180 rpm after day 7; Phaeodactylum ~no difference.
papers.env_effects: Diatoms helped or unaffected.

reasons.reproducibility: Orbital shaker at 0-180 rpm with easy, non-toxic diatom cultures is a clear bench protocol.
reasons.effectiveness: Negative result: T. pseudonana rose from 33.5 to 46-58 x10^5 cells/mL; only Skeletonema was inhibited at 180 rpm after day 7.
reasons.cost: Three cheap diatom cultures and a borrowed shaker are about $50-150.
reasons.time: 11-day experiment, so 1-3 weeks.
reasons.environment: Only shaking is applied; nothing is added.

papers.title: Effects of agitation on the microalgae Phaeodactylum tricornutum and Porphyridium cruentum
papers.scale: 5 L baffled stirred-tank photobioreactor (BioFlo III), continuous culture at dilution rate 0.0139 h-1, aerated 1.5 L/min
papers.dose: stepwise impeller speed 150-550 rpm (P. tricornutum; tip speed 0.68 to >1.56 m/s) and up to 650 rpm (P. cruentum); Pluronic F68 0.01-0.10% w/v
papers.result: Steady-state biomass rose with agitation up to 350 rpm (1.56 m/s tip speed) for P. tricornutum and 550 rpm (2.45 m/s) for P. cruentum, then fell; P. cruentum washed out at 650 rpm. Damage came from small bubbles rupturing at the surface, and Pluronic F68 protected cells in a dose-dependent way.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.
papers.key_details: Continuous monocultures of Phaeodactylum tricornutum and Porphyridium cruentum were run in a 5 L stirred photobioreactor with agitation raised stepwise; damage was inferred from falls in steady-state biomass at constant dilution rate. pH was held at 7.7 by CO2 injection, and kLa rose with agitation, so CO2 limitation did not explain the decline. Below the threshold, more agitation raised biomass through better light-dark cycling. The authors note that the net biomass data cannot separate growth and death effects, so relative shear sensitivity of the two species is not firmly established. This is a bioprocess study, not HAB control.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: The P. cruentum damage threshold (between 2.45 and 2.89 m/s tip speed) was missing from the record, and agitation below the threshold increased biomass.

reasons.reproducibility: Continuous culture in a 5 L BioFlo III stirred photobioreactor with CO2 pH control is bioprocess equipment.
reasons.effectiveness: Agitation raised biomass up to a threshold and only damaged cells above very high tip speeds (>1.56-2.45 m/s), in non-HAB production strains.
reasons.cost: A controlled stirred-tank photobioreactor costs well over $5,000.
reasons.time: Stepwise steady states at a dilution rate of 0.0139 per hour (~3-day residence) need weeks to months.
reasons.environment: Agitation adds no material; Pluronic F68 was only a protective additive.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic stress and lethal events in sparged microalgae cultures
papers.organism: Dunaliella tertiolecta, Chlamydomonas reinhardtii wild type and cell-wall-lacking mutant (non-HAB production strains)
papers.scale: Lab bubble columns (continuous and batch) plus a pilot-plant bubble column
papers.dose: superficial gas velocity up to 0.085 m/s
papers.result: No cell damage in D. tertiolecta or wild-type C. reinhardtii up to superficial gas velocities of 0.076 and 0.085 m/s; the wall-less mutant died at 0.46 ± 0.08 h⁻¹ (0.076 m/s) and 1.01 ± 0.29 h⁻¹ (0.085 m/s). Varying sparger nozzles gave D. tertiolecta death of 0.047 ± 0.016 h⁻¹ at high gas entrance velocity, implicating the sparger rather than bubble bursting.
papers.env_effects: Rising bubbles harmless to walled cells.
papers.key_details: Photobioreactor engineering study, not a bloom-control test. Superficial gas velocity alone did not kill walled cells; the cell wall protected against hydrodynamic shear. In a pilot-plant column at up to 0.026 m/s with low gas entrance velocities, D. tertiolecta showed no damage. Authors conclude gas entrance velocity at the sparger is the likely main cause of cell death. Relevance to HAB mitigation is indirect: bubbling is unlikely to kill walled algae except at the nozzle.

reasons.reproducibility: Bubbling Dunaliella or Chlamydomonas in a lab bubble column is simple with cheap cultures.
reasons.effectiveness: Bubbling up to 0.085 m/s did not kill walled cells; only a wall-less mutant died, so aeration is ineffective against walled algae.
reasons.cost: A column, aquarium air supply and cultures cost about $50-150.
reasons.time: Death rates were measured per hour.
reasons.environment: Air bubbling adds nothing.

papers.title: The Sensitivity of the Dinoflagellate Crypthecodinium cohnii to Transient Hydrodynamic Forces and Cell‐Bubble Interactions
papers.scale: microfluidic contraction + bubbles
papers.dose: microfluidic flow contraction at 10-90 mL/min (weighted EDR up to ~5.8 x 10^7 W/m3), 1-3 passes; bubbles from a 30-gauge needle (~5 mm) or sintered-glass sparger (~1 mm)
papers.duration: single transient passes (1-3) through the contraction device
papers.result: No lysis (LDH and counts) at any flow up to 5.8 x 10^7 W/m3, but motility fell from 87% to 24% after one pass and 2% after three at 90 mL/min from loss of the longitudinal flagellum, which regrew during static recovery. Small bubbles cut motility (~20% loss vs ~4% for large bubbles) and enriched cells in foam up to 1.80x.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.
papers.key_details: Crypthecodinium cohnii (a heterotrophic DHA-producing dinoflagellate) at 3.5 x 10^6 cells/mL was pumped through a microfluidic contraction whose energy dissipation rate was estimated by CFD. Lysis was measured by LDH release and cell counts; none was significant. Motility after 1, 2 and 3 passes at 90 mL/min was 24, 6 and 2% vs 87% initially; at 50 mL/min it was 70, 67 and 62%. Cells attached to bubble films and were trapped in foam Plateau borders; Pluronic F-68 reduced film attachment but not trapping. Caveat: bioprocess study on a non-HAB species; effects are sublethal and reversible.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Flagellar loss and motility decline were reversible (flagella regrew during static recovery), a detail missing from the record.

reasons.reproducibility: Needs a microfluidic contraction device with CFD-estimated dissipation rates and LDH assays.
reasons.effectiveness: No lysis at any flow; motility loss from flagellar shedding was reversible, in a non-HAB heterotrophic dinoflagellate.
reasons.cost: Microfluidic fabrication, pumps and assays exceed what a school can obtain cheaply.
reasons.time: Effects were measured after single passes lasting seconds.
reasons.environment: Only flow is applied.

papers.title: Effects of shear stress on the microalgae Chaetoceros muelleri
papers.scale: Couette shear cylinders (rheometer-calibrated), laminar flow, medium thickened with locust bean gum (0, 0.3, 0.5%)
papers.dose: 0-500 rpm (shear rate up to 1,079 s⁻¹; shear stress up to 19.4 Pa)
papers.duration: 1 h exposure at 4 °C; time series 1-120 min at 100 rpm
papers.result: Viability threshold τ = 1-1.3 Pa, above which viability drops to 52-66%; effect within 1 min.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.
papers.key_details: Early-stationary C. muelleri was sheared in Couette cylinders, with viscosity raised by locust bean gum so flow stayed laminar. Viability was scored by FDA staining, and all exposures were run in triplicate. Shear stress up to 1 Pa had no effect; above 1.3 Pa viability dropped sharply to 52-66%. Most of the effect happened within 1 min, with a secondary effect up to 8 min. This is a bioreactor-engineering study, not a bloom-control test.

reasons.reproducibility: Needs rheometer-calibrated Couette cylinders and FDA viability staining.
reasons.effectiveness: Above 1.3 Pa viability fell to 52-66% in triplicate, a moderate effect on a non-HAB diatom at shear far above field levels.
reasons.cost: A rheometer or precision Couette cylinder costs more than $5,000.
reasons.time: Most of the viability loss occurred within 1 minute.
reasons.environment: Shear adds no material (locust bean gum was only a lab thickener).

papers.title: Controlling spring Dinoflagellate blooms in a stratified drinking water reservoir via artificial mixing: Effects, mechanisms, and operational thresholds
papers.organism: spring dinoflagellate bloom dominated by Peridiniopsis sp. (also Chlorophyta e.g. Closterium, Bacillariophyta e.g. Cyclotella)
papers.scale: Lijiahe Reservoir, Xi'an, China (2.18 km2, max depth 80 m, 5.7 x 10^7 m3); eight water-lifting aerators installed 2007; sampled at 2 sites
papers.dose: 8 water-lifting aerators (diffusers 5 m above sediment; aeration <20 m3/h, lifting flow 20-50 m3/h each)
papers.duration: 2 weeks of operation (April 9-22, 2021); monitoring March 6 - May 5, 2021
papers.result: Within two weeks of mixing, surface dinoflagellate density fell 97.8% (S1) and 96.8% (S2) from pre-mixing peaks of 2.2 x 10^7 and 1.1 x 10^7 cells/L to <5.0 x 10^5 cells/L; total phytoplankton fell 97.1% and 95.5%, and Chl-a stayed <10 ug/L.
papers.env_effects: Community shifted from large motile taxa (dinoflagellates, Closterium) to small non-motile diatoms (Cyclotella, reduced only 70.0-84.0%); surface water temperature fell below 10 C and stratification weakened (dT 6.8 to 2.3 C at S1).
papers.key_details: Before-during-after field study of one spring bloom (2021) in a eutrophic, stratified drinking-water reservoir: 8 water-lifting aerators ran for two weeks at bloom onset, with weekly to twice-weekly profiles at two sites near the aerators. Pre-mixing surface peaks reached 2.4 x 10^7 cells/L total phytoplankton (Chl-a 438.8 ug/L) at S1. Reductions compare surface densities during mixing with the pre-mixing surface peak, so part of the drop is vertical redistribution (dilution through the water column), which the authors note alongside cell decay. RDA identified water temperature, Zmix, Zeu/Zmix and TP as the main drivers (69.9% of variance for taxonomic groups). Caveats: no unmixed control site or year, a single event, and the two sites were both inside the aerator zone.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: The record's -95.5 to -97.1% are total phytoplankton surface reductions; dinoflagellates specifically fell 96.8-97.8%. The record's effect_pct 95.5 is the total-phytoplankton figure at S2.

reasons.reproducibility: Eight water-lifting aerators in a 57 million m3 drinking-water reservoir are industrial field infrastructure.
reasons.effectiveness: Surface dinoflagellates fell 96.8-97.8%, but there was no unmixed control, a single event, and part of the drop is dilution through the water column.
reasons.cost: Reservoir aerators and compressors cost far more than $5,000.
reasons.time: The reduction appeared within the two weeks of operation.
reasons.environment: Only air is added, but the water cooled, stratification broke and the community shifted to small diatoms.

papers.title: Artificial mixing to control cyanobacterial blooms: a review
papers.scale: lakes and reservoirs
papers.dose: bubble plumes
papers.result: Table 1 lists 13 lake/reservoir mixing applications: reduced cyanobacteria in several (e.g. Lake Brooker, Solomon Dam, Nieuwe Meer, Dalbang, Bleiloch), no effect in others (East Sidney, Chaffey, Sheldon; Lake Yogo 0/?; North Pine -/0). Mixing shifts dominance to greens and diatoms when it is deep and entrains cells, but chl-a per m² often rises.
papers.env_effects: Chl-a per m² often rises.
papers.key_details: Narrative review of artificial mixing (mostly aeration/bubble plumes) aimed at cyanobacteria. The authors tabulate 13 lake/reservoir applications (Table 1). Mixing lowered surface temperature (e.g. Nieuwe Meer 23.4 → 19.1 °C), raised hypolimnetic O2 and often lowered surface pH by 0.5-1 unit. Chaffey Reservoir SRP release from sediment fell ~80%, but Gächter and Wehrli found 10 years of mixing did not stop sediment anoxia or internal P cycling. Standing crop (chl-a per m²) often increased as nutrients were entrained. The authors conclude mixing can shift composition away from cyanobacteria but external nutrient reduction should stay the main focus.

reasons.reproducibility: The reviewed interventions are whole-lake bubble-plume systems.
reasons.effectiveness: Of 13 applications several reduced cyanobacteria but others had no effect, and chlorophyll per m2 often rose.
reasons.cost: Lake-scale aeration costs far more than $5,000.
reasons.time: Lake mixing outcomes are judged over seasons to years.
reasons.environment: Air only, but mixing can entrain nutrients and did not stop sediment anoxia or internal P cycling in one 10-year case.

papers.title: Effect of Artificial Circulation on the Removal Kinetics of Cyanobacteria in a Hypereutrophic Shallow Lake
papers.scale: Santo Anastácio Lake, Fortaleza, Brazil (tropical, ~0.3 hm³, max depth 3.8 m, hypereutrophic); single point-source bubble diffuser at 1.5 m depth, samples inside plume (x = 0) vs outside (x = 2 m)
papers.dose: Air flow rates Q = 1.9, 3.8, 5.7 and 7.6 NL/s (7.5 kW compressor; diffuser with 160 × 1 mm holes)
papers.duration: 120 min per aeration test (November 2014; pre-aeration survey November 2013)
papers.result: After each 120-min test, depth-averaged chl-a was 5-20% lower inside the bubble plume than outside, the gap growing with air flow; first-order net reduction rates scaled with plume hydrodynamics/ε and tracked pheophytin-a production, indicating cell death.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.
papers.key_details: Field test in a shallow hypereutrophic Brazilian lake: a pre-aeration survey (Nov 2013) characterised natural variability, then four aeration tests at different air flows (Nov 2014), with repeat tests at 3.8 and 5.7 NL/s on 11 Nov 2014. Samples every 5-30 min at several depths and distances; the 'control' is water 2 m from the plume, where plume velocity was negligible (no separate control lake). In one test chl-a rose both inside and outside the plume (slower inside); in the other three it fell in both, faster inside. First-order fits had r > 0.97. Local, short-term effect only; whole-lake effect is extrapolated by simulation, not measured.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record lacks the magnitude (chl-a 5-20% lower inside vs outside plume after 120 min), the air flow rates (1.9-7.6 NL/s) and duration (120-min tests); the effect is local to the plume, not lake-wide.

reasons.reproducibility: A 7.5 kW compressor and bubble diffuser in a hypereutrophic lake is field-scale work.
reasons.effectiveness: Chlorophyll was only 5-20% lower inside the plume than 2 m outside after 120 min, with no control lake and chl-a rising in one of four tests.
reasons.cost: Compressor, diffuser and field sampling cost over $5,000.
reasons.time: Each test lasted 120 minutes.
reasons.environment: Only air is added, but killing cyanobacteria (pheophytin rise) may release cell-bound toxins.

papers.title: Effectiveness of ozone nanobubble treatments on high biomass cyanobacterial blooms: A mesocosm experiment and field trial
papers.scale: 2,000 L mesocosm + embayment
papers.dose: O2 nanobubbles vs ozone nanobubbles
papers.result: Ozone nanobubbles -98-99% chl-a; oxygen-only nanobubbles had no effect; embayment trial no effect.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.

reasons.reproducibility: 2,000 L mesocosms, an ozone nanobubble generator and an embayment trial are field-scale.
reasons.effectiveness: Ozone nanobubbles cut chl-a 98-99% in mesocosms, but oxygen-only nanobubbles did nothing and the embayment trial had no effect.
reasons.cost: Nanobubble/ozone generators and mesocosms exceed $5,000.
reasons.time: Duration not reported, so scored conservatively at 1-3 months.
reasons.environment: Ozone is a short-lived oxidant; non-target effects not reported.

papers.title: Artificially generated turbulence: a review of phycological nanocosm, microcosm, and mesocosm experiments
papers.scale: Review of 102 publications on lab turbulence cosms (grid 32, shaker 19, Couette 18, aeration 11, other 21 studies)
papers.dose: n/a
papers.result: Report ε; most lab cosms are too small for large eddies; acrylic can leach toxins under UV.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.
papers.key_details: Methods review of how lab studies generate and quantify turbulence for phytoplankton (102 publications). Grid-generated turbulence dominates (32 studies, 29 quantified). Couette cylinders (18) are usually quantified as shear rate, not ε. Shaker tables (19) and aeration (11) are often unquantified. Most cosms hold <1 m³, which limits the largest eddies. Dinoflagellates were the most studied group because of their HAB relevance. Read from the authors' accepted manuscript.

reasons.reproducibility: The typical reviewed cosm is a grid, shaker or Couette experiment under 1 m3, doable with a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: This methods review of 102 studies gives no pooled algal reduction, only how turbulence is generated and quantified.
reasons.cost: A typical lab turbulence cosm costs $150-500.
reasons.time: Typical reviewed experiments run one to two weeks.
reasons.environment: Turbulence adds nothing, though the authors warn acrylic cosms can leach toxins under UV.

papers.title: Artificial mixing prevents nuisance blooms of the cyanobacterium Microcystis in Lake Nieuwe Meer, the Netherlands
papers.authors: Visser PM, Ibelings BW, van der Veer B, Koedood J, Mur LR
papers.scale: Whole lake: Lake Nieuwe Meer, Amsterdam (1.32 km², 18 × 10⁶ m³, mean depth 18 m, max 30 m); two compressors (55 kW and 30 kW) feeding seven perforated aeration tubes, 13 m³/min air in total
papers.dose: Deep bubble-plume mixing, continuous April-October 1993; intermittent in spring 1994 and near-continuous July-September 1994
papers.duration: 2 mixed years vs 2 preceding control years
papers.result: Microcystis colonies per litre and per m2 were lower than in the two control years and hardly any scums occurred; community shifted to flagellates, greens and diatoms. Volumetric chlorophyll fell but depth-integrated chlorophyll (per m2) increased; intermittent mixing cut energy costs 75% while still preventing stratification.
papers.env_effects: Stratification removed, homogeneous temperature and oxygen; no oxygen problems reported. Intermittent spring mixing cut energy use by 75% in April-June 1994 (whole-season 1994 energy 27% of 1993). Depth-integrated chlorophyll (per m²) increased with mixing.
papers.key_details: Whole-lake before-after comparison: two mixed years (1993, 1994) against two preceding unmixed control years (1990, 1991), no separate control lake. Microcystis colonies per litre and per m² were lower in mixed years and hardly any nuisance scums occurred, while the community shifted to flagellates, greens and diatoms. Volumetric chlorophyll fell but areal (m⁻²) chlorophyll and peak areal content rose, so total phytoplankton was not reduced, only redistributed and shifted away from cyanobacteria. Colony buoyancy showed Microcystis escaped entrainment at some distance from the plumes. Works because the lake is deep (mixing depth >> euphotic depth).
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Full text notes total depth-integrated phytoplankton biomass increased under mixing; benefit is a species shift away from Microcystis, not less algae overall.

reasons.reproducibility: Whole-lake deep bubble-plume mixing with 55 kW and 30 kW compressors in an 18 million m3 lake.
reasons.effectiveness: Microcystis colonies and scums dropped in 2 mixed years vs 2 prior years (no control lake), but depth-integrated chlorophyll rose, so algae were shifted rather than reduced.
reasons.cost: Compressors, aeration tubes and power cost far more than $5,000.
reasons.time: Outcome compared across whole summer seasons.
reasons.environment: Air only; stratification removed without oxygen problems, but total areal phytoplankton increased.

papers.title: Artificial mixing to reduce growth of the blue-green alga Microcystis in Lake Nieuwe Meer, Amsterdam: an evaluation of 7 years of experience
papers.authors: Jungo E, Visser PM, Stroom J, Mur LR
papers.scale: Lake Nieuwe Meer, 1.3 km2, max depth 30 m, TP 500 mg/m3
papers.dose: Bubble-plume installation, 85 kW installed compressor power, summer operation
papers.result: Microcystis mass up to 20 times lower than before mixing and no scums; shift to flagellates, greens and diatoms. Total phosphorus and nitrogen unchanged; chlorophyll-a lower by dilution but transparency did not improve.
papers.env_effects: Surface ~2 °C cooler; oxygen >5 mg/L throughout, widening fish habitat; 85 kW continuous energy use.

reasons.reproducibility: Bubble-plume installation in a 1.3 km2, 30 m deep lake with 85 kW compressors.
reasons.effectiveness: Microcystis biomass up to 20x lower (effect_pct 95) with no scums, consistent over 7 years against pre-mixing years.
reasons.cost: 85 kW continuous compressor installation, far over $5,000.
reasons.time: Seven-year evaluation.
reasons.environment: Nothing added, oxygen >5 mg/L throughout widened fish habitat; cost is continuous 85 kW energy use and ~2 C cooler surface.

papers.title: Changes in turbulent mixing shift competition for light between phytoplankton species
papers.authors: Huisman J, Sharples J, Stroom JM, Visser PM, Kardinaal WEA, Verspagen JMH, et al.
papers.organism: Microcystis vs diatoms and green algae
papers.scale: Lake Nieuwe Meer, Amsterdam (1.3 km2, mean depth 18 m, max depth 30 m, hypertrophic); 3 sampling stations
papers.dose: Air bubbling from seven perforated air tubes laid just above the sediment (running since 1993); turbulent diffusivity measured with SCAMP microstructure profiler
papers.duration: Mixing switched off 19 July - 7 August 2002 and back on, turbulence measured under both regimes; model simulations
papers.result: Mean turbulent diffusivity was 0.17 cm2/s with mixing off and 5.1 cm2/s with mixing on (t test P < 0.0001); the model puts the Microcystis-vs-diatoms/greens switch at D of about 3.4 cm2/s, so artificial mixing moves the lake into the diatom/green-dominated regime. The observed replacement of Microcystis by diatoms and greens is cited from earlier work (Visser et al. 1996a), not new counts.
papers.env_effects: Community composition shift; mechanism is light competition, not cell damage.
papers.key_details: Huisman et al. 2004 parameterised a light-competition model for Microcystis versus lumped diatoms and greens in Lake Nieuwe Meer. Mixing was switched off for about 3 weeks in July-August 2002: the lake stratified within 10 days (thermocline ~5 m) and phytoplankton concentrated in the top 2.5 m. Diffusivity averaged 0.17 cm2/s (N = 105) off vs 5.1 cm2/s (N = 110) on. The model predicts Microcystis surface blooms above 5 x 10^6 cells/mL under weak mixing and diatom/green dominance under intense mixing, with the boundary at D of about 3.4 cm2/s for 18 m depth. No new Microcystis biomass reduction figure is given; it is a mechanism and model-validation paper.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record says 'multi-year lake experiment'; the new field work is a ~3-week mixing switch-off in summer 2002 plus modelling. The species shift itself is taken from earlier Nieuwe Meer studies.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Microcystis vs diatoms and green algae

reasons.reproducibility: Lake-scale aeration switching plus a SCAMP microstructure profiler.
reasons.effectiveness: No new Microcystis reduction was measured; the paper validates a light-competition model and cites the species shift from earlier work.
reasons.cost: Lake aeration and a microstructure profiler cost far more than $5,000.
reasons.time: The field switch-off lasted about 3 weeks, with stratification within 10 days.
reasons.environment: Air only; the mechanism is light competition, not cell damage.

papers.title: Controlling the Growth of Microcystis Using Surged Artificial Aeration
papers.scale: Tegeler See, Berlin (4 km2, max depth 16 m, mean depth 6 m); 15 Limnox hypolimnetic aerators at 12-16 m depth (installed 1980)
papers.dose: Continuous summer aeration (1989, 1990), no aeration (1992), surge aeration events after stable stratification (1993, 1994); mixing tracked with the Lake number
papers.result: Continuous aeration did not affect Microcystis population dynamics in 1989 and 1990, even with Lake numbers below 1, and favoured Microcystis over Ceratium. Surge aeration events in 1993 and 1994 were each followed by a Microcystis decline and delayed its growth, although a stock persisted into September; no percentage reduction is given.
papers.env_effects: Surge aeration had no noticeable effect on the distribution of total inorganic nitrogen or total phosphorus. TP was also falling year on year from external remediation (>50 ug/L in 1989-92 to 30-40 ug/L in 1994), a confounder. Continuous aeration suppressed Ceratium.
papers.key_details: Single-lake, multi-year observational comparison of aerator operating schemes, with no control lake and no replication within years. Evidence is qualitative from time series of Microcystis and Ceratium biomass against Lake number (figure only, no tabulated numbers). Microcystis formed very large colonies (up to tennis-ball size) and adapted to continuous mixing. The author concludes surge aeration after prolonged stability hinders slow-growing Microcystis, while continuous aeration strengthens it against Ceratium. Declining phosphorus over 1993-94 confounds the surge-year comparison.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record implies a clean 3-scheme test; in fact the aerated years were 1989-90, non-aerated 1992 and surge 1993-94, while TP fell over the same period, so the surge effect is confounded and unquantified.

reasons.reproducibility: Fifteen hypolimnetic aerators in a 4 km2 lake over five years.
reasons.effectiveness: Continuous aeration did not affect and even favoured Microcystis; surge-aeration declines were qualitative and confounded by falling phosphorus.
reasons.cost: Lake aerators cost far more than $5,000.
reasons.time: Comparisons span five study years.
reasons.environment: Air only, with no noticeable effect on nitrogen or phosphorus distribution.

papers.title: The long-term effect of artificial destratification on phytoplankton species composition in a subtropical reservoir
papers.authors: Antenucci JP, Ghadouani A, Burford MA, Romero JR
papers.scale: North Pine Dam (Lake Samsonvale), Brisbane: volume 2x10^8 m3, surface area 19.7 km2, supplies ~30% of Brisbane's water
papers.dose: Bubble-plume destratifier installed 1995: compressor pumping 200 L/s of air through a 90 mm pipe with 33 hole clusters ~17 m apart; runs mid-September to end of April
papers.duration: Phytoplankton record from 1983 (weekly to 1998, then fortnightly); temperature/DO compared 1978-94 vs 1998-2002; chlorophyll trends 1984-2002
papers.result: After destratification most taxa increased significantly at the dam wall: Cylindrospermopsis rose from 5584 to 9372 cells/mL and Microcystis from 313 to 1829 cells/mL (randomised intervention analysis, P < 0.025). Only the rate of eutrophication slowed: the chlorophyll a increase fell from 0.74 to 0.49 ug/L per year (~30%).
papers.env_effects: Thermocline gradient fell from 1 to 0.2 degC/m; the low-DO (<1 mg/L) period shrank from 7 to 3 months and its vertical extent from 15 to <2 m above the bottom. The destratifier's horizontal influence was limited, and upstream sites stayed more stratified.
papers.key_details: Before-after design at one reservoir with no control reservoir; intervention effects tested by randomised intervention analysis on surface cell counts (sample sizes about 77-507 before and 46-220 after per genus). Significant increases after destratification for cyanobacteria (Anabaena, Cylindrospermopsis, Microcystis, Planktolyngbya, Pseudanabaena), several chlorophytes and diatoms. Chlorophyll a kept rising, but more slowly (0.74 to 0.49 ug/L per year for the full record). Sampling methods changed after 1997, and retention time varies from 1 month to 3 years, which confounds before-after comparisons.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record correctly flags a negative result but gives no numbers; the full text shows the dominant toxic cyanobacteria increased (Cylindrospermopsis +68%, Microcystis ~5.8x in mean cells/mL), so effect_pct should be negative (-68 for Cylindrospermopsis).

reasons.reproducibility: A reservoir-scale destratifier pumping 200 L/s of air in a 2 x 10^8 m3 water supply.
reasons.effectiveness: Cylindrospermopsis rose 68% and Microcystis ~5.8x after destratification; only the rate of chlorophyll increase slowed.
reasons.cost: A reservoir destratifier costs far more than $5,000.
reasons.time: Before-after comparison over decades of monitoring.
reasons.environment: Oxygen improved, but toxic cyanobacteria increased at the dam wall.

papers.title: A comparison of phytoplankton community assemblages in artificially and naturally mixed subtropical water reservoirs
papers.scale: North Pine Reservoir (21.8 km², destratification system since 1995) vs unmixed Somerset (42.1 km²) and Wivenhoe (107.5 km²); 4-5 sites each, fortnightly
papers.dose: Destratification unit operated in wet summer months
papers.result: All three reservoirs stayed cyanobacteria-dominated (same three genera = 75-80% of abundance). Colonial species were lower in the mixed reservoir, but C. raciborskii and Planktolyngbya peaked earlier, and mixing may favour species that store low phosphate such as C. raciborskii.
papers.env_effects: Surface phosphate near detection limit in mixed reservoir; possible selection for Cylindrospermopsis.
papers.key_details: Observational comparison of one artificially destratified reservoir with two adjacent unmixed reservoirs in SE Queensland. Phytoplankton was sampled fortnightly at 4-5 sites per reservoir, 1997-2003; nutrients were sampled monthly at the wall site. There was no treated-reservoir replication and no before-mixing baseline, since mixing began in 1995. Total phytoplankton density did not differ significantly among the three reservoirs (P > 0.05), and all three were cyanobacteria-dominated. Species composition at the wall site differed in North Pine (ANOSIM P < 0.01). Surface phosphate in North Pine sat near the detection limit (0.06 µM) and did not correlate with algal density there.

reasons.reproducibility: Compares whole reservoirs with and without an installed destratification system.
reasons.effectiveness: All three reservoirs stayed cyanobacteria-dominated with no difference in total density; colonial species were lower but Cylindrospermopsis peaked earlier.
reasons.cost: Reservoir destratification costs far more than $5,000.
reasons.time: Based on six years of fortnightly monitoring.
reasons.environment: Low surface phosphate under mixing may select for Cylindrospermopsis.

papers.title: Understanding the role of induced mixing for management of nuisance algal blooms in an urbanized reservoir
papers.scale: Ford Lake, Michigan (reservoir); managed hypolimnetic withdrawal
papers.dose: Selective hypolimnetic discharge through dam flood gates, target ~300,000 m³/d (sized to sediment oxygen demand of 0.67 g O2/m²/d), applied adaptively when DO declined
papers.result: With selective hypolimnetic withdrawal in 2008-2011, maximum gaps between deep-mixing events were 10-18 d, the hypolimnion stayed mostly oxic and no nuisance cyanobacterial blooms occurred; in drought year 2012 (no withdrawal) the lake stayed stratified 35 d, sediments released P, and an Aphanizomenon bloom followed a cold-front mixing event.
papers.env_effects: Hypolimnetic oxygenation; depends on upstream water availability.
papers.key_details: Observational before/after-style field study in Ford Lake, Michigan (17.4 × 10⁶ m³ hydroelectric reservoir), June-August 2008-2012, with YSI temperature (6 depths), DO (3 depths) and one chlorophyll fluorescence sensor at 3 m logged every 30 min, plus weekly P sampling. No separate control lake; 2012 (drought, no withdrawal) serves as an unplanned contrast year, n = 1. Convective cooling, not wind, dominated mixing energy (KEstir < 1 J/m²/h 99.4% of the time). In August 2012 lake TP export exceeded river input by 11.3 µg/L (SE 3.7, n = 5), about 164 kg P for the month. Even 300,000 m³/d did not guarantee deep mixing in 2010-2011 around the solstice. Blooms were tracked by fluorescence and microscopy, not quantified as a % reduction.

reasons.reproducibility: Managed hypolimnetic withdrawal through hydroelectric dam gates in a 17 million m3 reservoir.
reasons.effectiveness: No nuisance blooms in 4 withdrawal summers vs an Aphanizomenon bloom in the one drought year without it, but n=1 contrast year and no % reduction.
reasons.cost: Dam operation and continuous sensor arrays cost far more than $5,000.
reasons.time: Evaluated over five summers.
reasons.environment: Keeps the hypolimnion oxic, but it releases deep water downstream and depends on upstream flow.

papers.title: Controlling Eutrophication via Surface Aerators in Irregular-Shaped Urban Ponds
papers.authors: Hao A, Kobayashi S, Xia D, Mi Q, Yan N, Su M, et al.
papers.scale: Two urban ponds in Wenzhou, China: ZS pond (5 surge aerators, 1.5 kg O2 kW⁻¹ h⁻¹, 500 rpm, installed late 2018) and MA pond (9 aerators, 18 sites)
papers.dose: Surface aerators
papers.duration: ZS: one June survey before (2018) vs one after (2019); MA: 10 surveys Mar 2018 - Mar 2019, two years after installation
papers.result: DO rose 1.8 to 8.1 mg/L and TP fell 1.6 to 0.4 mg/L and no cyano-blooms occurred, but Microcystis still dominated and chlorophyll-a rose from 29 to 51 µg/L while transparency fell 81 to 27 cm. Authors conclude aeration can promote algal growth.
papers.env_effects: Better oxygen, less sediment P release; higher chlorophyll and lower clarity.
papers.key_details: Uncontrolled before/after design in ZS pond: a single June 2018 survey vs a single June 2019 survey, with no reference pond. After aeration, DO rose from 1.8 ± 0.4 to 8.1 ± 1.2 mg/L and TP fell from 1.64 to 0.44 mg/L. Chl-a still rose from 29 to 51 µg/L, and Microcystis dominated in both years. MA pond was only surveyed after installation: 10 monthly visits at 18 sites, with DO always >5.7 mg/L, TP 0.03-0.07 mg/L, green algae and diatoms dominant and no blooms. Chl-a was higher on the north side, where aerator coverage differed.

reasons.reproducibility: Surface aerators installed in urban ponds by the city, evaluated by surveys.
reasons.effectiveness: Chlorophyll rose from 29 to 51 ug/L and Microcystis still dominated after aeration, in an uncontrolled one-survey before/after comparison.
reasons.cost: Several surge aerators cost roughly $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Before and after surveys were a year apart.
reasons.environment: Oxygen rose (1.8 to 8.1 mg/L) and TP fell, with no added material, though clarity dropped.

papers.title: Water-lifting aerator reduces algal growth in stratified drinking water reservoir: Novel insights into algal metabolic profiling and engineering applications
papers.authors: Zhang H, Yan M, Huang T, Huang X, Yang S, Li N
papers.organism: Field: mixed reservoir phytoplankton dominated by Bacillariophyta and Chlorophyta (cyanobacteria at most 7.58% relative abundance); lab: Microcystis aeruginosa
papers.scale: Lijiahe drinking-water reservoir (China) plus lab hydrodynamic simulation
papers.dose: Eight water-lifting aerators at full load, ~30 m3/h air each, 24 h/day; lab analogue: 6 or 25 degC, light or dark
papers.duration: Field: operated 29 July - 12 October 2019, sampled 28 July, 25 August and 17 October; lab: 72 h (sampled 0-72 h)
papers.result: Surface algal density fell by more than 90% during aerator operation and kept falling after shutdown, with chlorophyll a and photosynthetic yield (mean Fv/Fm 0.435 to 0.074) also falling. In the lab, M. aeruginosa declined only under 6 degC dark (max drop 1.04 x 10^5 cells/mL, 37.08 ug/L chl a).
papers.env_effects: Lower surface water temperature, more uniform vertical profiles of algae, temperature, pH and DO. The cyanobacteria share rose slightly after operation (max 7.58% at 30 m).
papers.key_details: Field study at Lijiahe Reservoir (Xi'an, China) with one before, one during and one after sampling date at 7 depths (0-bottom), triplicate analyses (n = 3), and no control reservoir or site. The '>90%' surface density decrease is confounded by season (July to October) and by mixing moving cells to depth rather than removing them. The lab arm simulated surface (25 degC light) vs bottom (6 degC dark) conditions for M. aeruginosa; growth stopped and cells, dehydrogenase, ATP and photosynthesis fell under cold dark conditions. The reservoir community was mostly diatoms and green algae, not Microcystis.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record implies a Microcystis bloom was controlled in the field; the field phytoplankton was diatom/green dominated (cyanobacteria <=7.58%) and Microcystis was only a lab culture. The full text gives a >90% surface density reduction (unreplicated, seasonally confounded); lab cultures ran 72 h, not 48 h.

reasons.reproducibility: The field arm used eight reservoir aerators; only the 72 h lab Microcystis arm is repeatable at school.
reasons.effectiveness: Surface algae fell >90%, but with one sampling date per phase, no control, seasonal confounding and cells moved to depth; the lab analogue only declined in cold dark.
reasons.cost: Reservoir aerators cost far more than $5,000.
reasons.time: Field operation ran about 2.5 months (July-October).
reasons.environment: Only air is added; profiles became uniform and the cyanobacteria share rose slightly.

papers.title: Management strategies for a eutrophic water supply reservoir - San Roque, Argentina
papers.authors: Antenucci JP, Alexander R, Romero JR, Imberger J
papers.scale: San Roque reservoir, DYRESM-CAEDYM 1-D model
papers.dose: Bubble-plume diffusers and surface impellers with draft tubes, alone and combined
papers.result: The best simulated design combined a deep and a shallow diffuser: the deep one breaks the seasonal thermocline to limit sediment nutrient release and anoxia, the shallow one deepens surface-layer mixing. No numeric reduction in the abstract.
papers.env_effects: Predicted reduction in anoxia and sediment nutrient release.
papers.study_note: hydrodynamic design simulation; no algal numbers

reasons.reproducibility: A 1-D DYRESM-CAEDYM model run needs specialist software and reservoir forcing data, hard but possible with a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: Simulation only, and no numeric algae reduction is given in the abstract.
reasons.cost: Not reported; model licence and data access scored conservatively.
reasons.time: Simulated seasons can be run within days once the model is set up.
reasons.environment: Predicted lower anoxia and sediment nutrient release with nothing added.

papers.title: Artificial destratification options for reservoir management
papers.authors: Chaaya F, Miller BM, Gordos MA, Tamburic B, Felder S
papers.scale: Global review of 138 bubble-plume and mechanical-mixer systems in 114 reservoirs
papers.dose: Air flow per reservoir volume ('volumetric destratification coefficient')
papers.result: Of 59 bubble-plume cases reporting cyanobacteria, 37% reduced them, 12% partly, 34% had no effect and 17% increased them; where thermal destratification succeeded, 63% reported full or partial reduction, and where it failed all 6 cases saw no reduction or an increase. Mechanical mixers: of 12 cases, 5 successful, 2 partial, 3 no improvement, 2 net negative.
papers.env_effects: Successful destratification raised DO and lowered Mn and Fe; cold-water pollution mitigated.
papers.key_details: Global literature review of 138 destratification systems (84% bubble plume, 16% mechanical mixers) in 114 reservoirs, scored against success criteria for thermal, DO, nutrient/metal and cyanobacteria outcomes. Cyanobacteria outcomes were far more variable than thermal or DO outcomes. Reservoirs >100,000 ML had only 30% full/partial success vs 53% in smaller ones; >15 m deep 54% vs 47% for shallower. Cyanobacteria success tracked the volumetric destratification coefficient (air flow per volume); all 5 successful mechanical-mixer cases used draft tubes. Caveat: case reports are heterogeneous and success categories are qualitative, not % biomass change.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record says reduction was 'mixed'; full text quantifies it: only 37% of 59 bubble-plume cases fully succeeded and 17% made cyanobacteria worse.

reasons.reproducibility: The 138 reviewed systems are reservoir-scale bubble plumes and mixers.
reasons.effectiveness: Only 37% of 59 bubble-plume cases fully reduced cyanobacteria, 34% had no effect and 17% made them worse.
reasons.cost: Reservoir destratification costs far more than $5,000.
reasons.time: Outcomes are judged over seasons to years.
reasons.environment: Successful destratification raised DO and lowered Mn and Fe; air only.

papers.title: A critical review on operation and performance of source water control strategies for cyanobacterial blooms: Part II-mechanical and biological control methods
papers.authors: Kibuye FA, Zamyadi A, Wert EC
papers.scale: Review of artificial mixing, hypolimnetic aeration, dredging, sonication, biological methods in drinking-water sources
papers.dose: n/a
papers.result: Optimised mixing and hypolimnetic oxygenation raised DO, cut internal nutrient loading and reduced ions, but benefits were often offset by continued external nutrient inputs and were derailed by organic sedimentation or low Fe/P sediments. Sonication field findings were contradictory.
papers.env_effects: Artificial mixing: resuspension of sediment nutrients/ions, sedimentation of organic matter, warming of the water column may impact cold-water habitats; ineffective in shallow, large-surface-area waters; may need continuous operation.
papers.key_details: Narrative review of mechanical (artificial mixing, hypolimnetic oxygenation/aeration, dredging, sonication) and biological (biomanipulation, macrophytes, barley straw) cyanobacteria controls in drinking-water sources, with tables of field and pilot studies. Artificial mixing is credited with DO increase, suppressed release of P, Fe, Mn and NH3, and cyanobacterial control via light limitation and sedimentation, with benefits up to 7 years under continuous operation; hypolimnetic oxygenation 10-23 years. Main conclusion: all these methods give temporary relief and are commonly derailed by continued external nutrient inputs, so external loading must be controlled first. Sonication lacks field-scale validation. No pooled effect size.

reasons.reproducibility: Reviewed methods are reservoir-scale mixing, oxygenation and dredging.
reasons.effectiveness: Mixing and oxygenation gave only temporary relief, often derailed by continued external nutrient inputs; no pooled effect size.
reasons.cost: Source-water engineering costs far more than $5,000.
reasons.time: Benefits are reported over years of continuous operation.
reasons.environment: Mixing can resuspend sediment nutrients, warm cold-water habitat and needs continuous operation.

papers.title: Mitigation of harmful algal blooms caused by Alexandrium catenella and reduction in saxitoxin accumulation in bivalves using cultivable seaweeds
papers.organism: Saccharina latissima, Ulva, Chondrus → Alexandrium catenella
papers.scale: 250 mL flasks; field bottles; 300 L mesocosm
papers.dose: 0.7-3.8 g/L FW; mesocosm 1 g/L
papers.result: -17-74% at 2-3 d and -42-96% at ~1 wk; in 300 L mesocosms kelp -73% in 48 h and Ulva -54% in 96 h.
