papers.env_effects: Mesocosm total chlorophyll did not fall (other algae replaced the target); Ulva pushed pH to 9.0-9.5 (sometimes >10), kelp stayed 8.1-8.9; mussel STX 71.8 vs 93.5 µg/100 g.

reasons.reproducibility: Flasks are simple, but it uses PSP-toxic Alexandrium catenella, 300 L mesocosms and mussel saxitoxin assays.
reasons.effectiveness: -17-74% at 2-3 d and -42-96% at ~1 wk; kelp gave -73% in 48 h in mesocosms, though total chlorophyll did not fall.
reasons.cost: Mesocosms and saxitoxin analysis put it at $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Kelp gave -73% within 48 h.
reasons.environment: Seaweed is retrievable, but Ulva pushed pH to 9.0-9.5 (sometimes >10) and other algae replaced the target.

papers.title: Cultivable seaweeds eliminate the lethal effects of the harmful alga, Margalefidinium polykrikoides, on early life stage fish
papers.organism: Ulva, Gracilaria, Chondrus, Grateloupia → Margalefidinium polykrikoides; larval fish
papers.scale: well plates (fish); 300 L mesocosm
papers.dose: Ulva 0.17-0.2 g/L
papers.result: No cell reduction until day 5, then -68%, -90% and -92% on days 5-7; fish survival extended, with protection needing close contact.
papers.env_effects: DMSP alone reduced toxicity to fish; live seaweed beat frozen.

reasons.reproducibility: Needs ichthyotoxic Margalefidinium, larval fish in well plates and 300 L mesocosms.
reasons.effectiveness: -68%, -90% and -92% on days 5-7, but no reduction at all before day 5.
reasons.cost: Culture, fish and Ulva at 0.17-0.2 g/L are roughly $150-500 at bench scale.
reasons.time: Reductions appeared on days 5-7.
reasons.environment: Live seaweed is retrievable and protected fish; no non-target harm reported.

papers.title: Inhibition of cosmopolitan toxic diatom, Pseudo‐nitzschia, by seaweeds
papers.scale: 250 mL flasks; field bloom bottles
papers.dose: 0.5-3 g/L FW
papers.result: -13-47% at 24-48 h and -74-94% at ≥72 h; bloom water kelp 2 g/L -69 to -81%, 1 g/L n.s.; Gracilaria no effect.
papers.env_effects: Diatoms lost photosynthetic efficiency and paled.

reasons.reproducibility: 250 mL flasks with kelp/Ulva are simple, but Pseudo-nitzschia is a domoic-acid diatom bought from a culture centre.
reasons.effectiveness: -74-94% at >=72 h and -69 to -81% in bloom water with 2 g/L kelp, but Gracilaria and 1 g/L kelp had no significant effect.
reasons.cost: Culture plus seaweed and flasks is roughly $150-500.
reasons.time: Large reductions at >=72 h (about 3 days).
reasons.environment: Seaweed is retrievable; only target diatoms were reported affected.

papers.title: The green macroalga, Ulva lactuca, inhibits the growth of seven common harmful algal bloom species via allelopathy
papers.scale: lab; field brown-tide bottles
papers.dose: fresh thalli ≈45-725 mg/L DW
papers.result: -24% (P. minimum), -38% (Karlodinium), -50% (K. brevis) at 72 h; extracts lysed Karlodinium and K. brevis after 5 d.
papers.env_effects: Heat-stable allelochemicals.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Ulva lactuca → 7 HAB species

reasons.reproducibility: Fresh Ulva in flasks is easy, but the targets include toxic K. brevis and Karlodinium bought as cultures.
reasons.effectiveness: Only -24% to -50% at 72 h across species, though extracts lysed two species after 5 d.
reasons.cost: Several cultures plus seaweed are roughly $150-500.
reasons.time: Effects measured at 72 h.
reasons.environment: Seaweed is retrievable; allelochemicals are heat-stable but no non-target harm reported.

papers.title: Comparative studies on the allelopathic effects of two different strains of Ulva pertusa on Heterosigma akashiwo and Alexandrium tamarense
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Marine Biology and Ecology
papers.organism: Ulva pertusa (2 strains) → Heterosigma akashiwo, Alexandrium tamarense
papers.scale: 100 mL flasks with 40 mL f/2; axenic cultures; triplicate
papers.dose: fresh tissue 0.625-10 g-wet/L; dry powder 0.15-2.4 g-dry/L; isolation co-culture 2.5 g-wet/L
papers.duration: 10 d coexistence; short-term lysis assays in hours
papers.result: Fresh-tissue EC50 0.3 (nonsexual) / 0.6 (sexual strain) g-wet/L for H. akashiwo and 2.0 / 2.5 g-wet/L for A. tamarense; 5-10 g-wet/L killed all H. akashiwo within 2 days, but A. tamarense was never killed. Culture filtrate did not significantly inhibit either species.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.
papers.key_details: Axenic lab co-cultures of two Ulva pertusa strains (sexual and nonsexual) with H. akashiwo or A. tamarense in 40 mL f/2, n=3, t-tests; nutrients topped up to rule out competition. H. akashiwo growth was lowered at all fresh-tissue doses and all cells died within 2 d at 5 and 10 g-wet/L; A. tamarense was inhibited only above 1.25 g-wet/L with no lethal effect even at 10 g-wet/L. Dry powder EC50s were 0.4/1.0 g-dry/L (H. akashiwo) and 0.6/0.8 g-dry/L (A. tamarense); low powder doses sometimes stimulated growth (H. akashiwo at 0.6 g-dry/L sexual strain; A. tamarense day 6-7 at 0.15 g-dry/L), and survivors revived after day 4-6. Filtrate (initial or semi-continuous) had no significant effect, while physically separated (isolation) co-culture at 2.5 g-wet/L still killed H. akashiwo, suggesting labile allelochemicals needing continuous release. Lysis LT50 for H. akashiwo was 3.0-7.0 h.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record lists only the A. tamarense EC50; the much lower H. akashiwo EC50 (0.3-0.6 g-wet/L) and complete kill of H. akashiwo at 5-10 g-wet/L were missing. Low powder doses could stimulate growth.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Ulva pertusa (2 strains) → Heterosigma akashiwo

reasons.reproducibility: Axenic Heterosigma and Alexandrium cultures co-cultured with collected Ulva need a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: Ulva killed all H. akashiwo at 5-10 g-wet/L (n=3) but never killed A. tamarense, filtrate had no effect and low powder doses stimulated growth.
reasons.cost: Two cultures, f/2 medium and Ulva cost about $150-500.
reasons.time: H. akashiwo died within 2 days (lysis LT50 3-7 h).
reasons.environment: Living Ulva is retrievable, though grams per litre of seaweed are needed.

papers.title: Allelopathic interactions between the macroalga Ulva pertusa and eight microalgal species
papers.organism: Ulva pertusa → 8 microalgae incl. Skeletonema, Nitzschia, Chaetoceros, A. tamarense
papers.scale: 100 mL flasks with 40 mL f/2; axenic; triplicate batch, nutrient-replete semi-continuous and isolated co-cultures
papers.dose: 12.5 g-wet/L fresh U. pertusa; filtrate from 80 g-wet/L
papers.result: Batch co-culture killed H. akashiwo and S. costatum (100%) and cut the other six species 42-84% (A. tamarense 70%); in nutrient-replete semi-continuous culture reductions were 28-90% (A. tamarense 52%). Culture filtrate inhibited only Chroomonas placoidea.
papers.env_effects: Nutrient-replete cultures (NO3 >= 780 umol/L, PO4 >= 36 umol/L) still showed inhibition, ruling out nutrient competition; pH 8.7 +/- 0.3. Some microalgae reduced Ulva growth by 20-30%.
papers.key_details: Axenic lab study: Ulva pertusa (12.5 g-wet/L) co-cultured with eight microalgae in batch, nutrient-replete semi-continuous, and isolated (separated) co-cultures, n=3 each. Percent growth reduction at end (batch/semi-continuous/isolated): H. akashiwo and S. costatum 100/100/100; A. tamarense 70/52/56; Nitzschia 59/28/21; Chaetoceros 42/70/74; Isochrysis 84/90/88; Chroomonas 76/60/67; Tetraselmis 63/60/56. Filtrate (80 g-wet/L, 3 d) inhibited only Chroomonas, so continuous contact/release is needed. Microalgae in turn changed Ulva growth (+16% with H. akashiwo, -20 to -30% with Tetraselmis, Nitzschia, Chaetoceros).
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record said per-species diatom numbers were not retrieved; full table gives them (Skeletonema 100%, Nitzschia 59%, Chaetoceros 42% in batch). The ~70% A. tamarense figure is the batch value; semi-continuous nutrient-replete value is 52%.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Ulva pertusa → 8 microalgae incl. Skeletonema

reasons.reproducibility: Eight axenic microalgal cultures with fresh Ulva in flasks is sponsor-level work.
reasons.effectiveness: Ulva killed H. akashiwo and Skeletonema 100% and cut others 21-90% in triplicate, including nutrient-replete tests that rule out competition.
reasons.cost: Eight cultures and media cost $150-500.
reasons.time: Experiments ran about 11 days.
reasons.environment: Living Ulva is removable; nutrients stayed replete.

papers.title: Allelopathic growth inhibition of Prorocentrum micans (Dinophyta) by Ulva pertusa and Ulva linza (Chlorophyta) in laboratory cultures
papers.organism: Ulva pertusa, U. linza → Prorocentrum micans
papers.scale: lab
papers.dose: 0.625-10 g/L FW; powder 0.15-2.4 g/L DW
papers.result: Fresh Ulva tissue above 0.625 g/L and dry powder above 0.15 g/L significantly cut P. micans growth; 10 g/L fresh tissue and 2.4 g/L powder killed the cultures (EC50 fresh 1.8 and 2.3 g/L; powder 0.7 and 0.8 g/L). Aqueous and methanol extracts inhibited, other solvents did not; a single filtrate dose had no effect but semi-continuous addition did.
papers.env_effects: P. micans did not affect the seaweed; active compounds polar.
papers.key_details: Lab flasks in f/2 at 20°C with an axenic P. micans strain and antibiotic-treated Ulva collected during a Qingdao bloom (May 2003); n = 4 replicates per treatment with untreated controls. Fresh-tissue doses 0.625-10 g/L and powder 0.15-2.4 g/L; at 2.4 g/L powder cultures died completely within 4 days. Methanol extract EC50 was 0.015 ppt (U. pertusa) and 0.017 ppt (U. linza); aqueous extract inhibited above 0.1 ppt over 6 d. P. micans had no effect on Ulva growth in 20-day co-culture. Doses are high (grams of seaweed per litre) relative to open water.

reasons.reproducibility: Collected Ulva and one P. micans culture in f/2 flasks are simple bench work.
reasons.effectiveness: Ulva tissue and powder cut growth dose-dependently in 4 replicates and 10 g/L fresh or 2.4 g/L powder killed the cultures.
reasons.cost: One culture plus free seaweed costs about $50-150.
reasons.time: Powder at 2.4 g/L killed cultures within 4 days.
reasons.environment: Seaweed is natural and removable, though powder adds organic matter at high doses.

papers.title: Effects of macroalgae Ulva pertusa (Chlorophyta) and Gracilaria lemaneiformis (Rhodophyta) on growth of four species of bloom-forming dinoflagellates
papers.scale: 250 mL flasks, 150 mL f/2-enriched seawater; n=3
papers.dose: 3.4 g/L FW
papers.result: U. pertusa thalli killed all P. donghaiense, S. trochoidea and A. tamarense within 144 h (LT50 37.9, 63.6, 59.8 h) and cut A. carterae 34%; G. lemaneiformis killed P. donghaiense (LT50 138.6 h) and cut S. trochoidea 79%, A. tamarense 24%, A. carterae 20%.
papers.env_effects: Filtrates were inconsistent: U. pertusa filtrate stimulated A. carterae +78% and G. lemaneiformis filtrate stimulated A. tamarense +33%. G. lemaneiformis exhausted N and P (3.6 and 0.32 umol/L left), so its effect was partly nutrient competition (relieved by daily f/2); U. pertusa left N and P well above limiting.
papers.key_details: Lab batch co-cultures (n=3, one-way ANOVA) of fresh U. pertusa or G. lemaneiformis thalli (0.5 g FW in 150 mL) with four dinoflagellates at 1.0x10^4 cells/mL (A. tamarense 0.4x10^4). U. pertusa was algicidal to three species (all cells dead within 144 h); G. lemaneiformis was lethal only to P. donghaiense. Culture filtrates gave species-specific inhibition or stimulation (Table 1). Nutrient tests showed G. lemaneiformis' effect on P. donghaiense was largely nutrient depletion (alleviated by daily f/2), while NaHCO3 addition did not relieve U. pertusa inhibition, pointing to allelopathy.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record's G. lemaneiformis results and its nutrient-competition caveat were missing; 'filtrate inhibited 5-27%' refers only to U. pertusa filtrate on three species. The stimulation of A. carterae (+78%) was by U. pertusa filtrate, not a general filtrate effect.

reasons.reproducibility: Four dinoflagellate cultures (including toxic Alexandrium) with collected seaweed need a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: Ulva killed three of four dinoflagellates within 144 h in triplicate; Gracilaria mostly acted through nutrient depletion.
reasons.cost: Four cultures and media cost $150-500.
reasons.time: LT50s were 38-64 h and all cells were dead within 6 days.
reasons.environment: Living thalli are retrievable; filtrates stimulated some species.

papers.title: Allelopathic effects of Ulva lactuca on selected species of harmful bloom-forming microalgae in laboratory cultures
papers.scale: lab
papers.dose: 0.8 g/L FW
papers.result: -48% A. tamarense; filtrate inhibited only for the first 2 d, then growth recovered; powder EC50 0.19 g/L DW (3 d).
papers.env_effects: Not reported.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Ulva lactuca → HAB microalgae

reasons.reproducibility: Ulva co-culture with purchased HAB cultures including toxic A. tamarense.
reasons.effectiveness: -48% A. tamarense at 0.8 g/L; filtrate worked only for 2 d before recovery.
reasons.cost: Cultures plus seaweed are roughly $150-500.
reasons.time: 12-day co-culture (powder EC50 at 3 d).
reasons.environment: Not reported; live seaweed is retrievable.

papers.title: Algicidal activity of polyunsaturated fatty acids derived from Ulva fasciata and U. pertusa (Ulvaceae, Chlorophyta) on phytoplankton
papers.organism: Ulva fasciata, U. pertusa → 10+ red-tide species
papers.scale: 24-well plates, 4 h assays
papers.dose: powder 1.5 g/L DW; fresh tissue 50 g/L
papers.result: Powder 4 h LC50 0.40-0.70 g/L DW against Heterosigma; fresh tissue at 50 g/L killed only 1.6-6.6% in 4 h; PUFAs 2% of peak left at 48 h.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.

reasons.reproducibility: 4-hour assays in 24-well plates with dried Ulva powder and a Heterosigma culture are simple bench work.
reasons.effectiveness: Powder LC50 0.40-0.70 g/L DW, but fresh tissue at 50 g/L killed only 1.6-6.6% in 4 h.
reasons.cost: One culture, well plates and seaweed are about $50-150.
reasons.time: Results within 4 hours.
reasons.environment: Dried powder cannot be retrieved, though its PUFAs fell to 2% of peak by 48 h (short-lived).

papers.title: Effects of two species of macroalgae—Ulva pertusa and Gracilaria lemaneiformis—on growth of Heterosigma akashiwo (Raphidophyceae)
papers.organism: Ulva pertusa, Gracilaria lemaneiformis → Heterosigma akashiwo
papers.scale: lab co-cultures, n=3
papers.dose: fresh thalli 0.34-3.4 g FW/L; filtrate from 4-40 g FW/L; water-soluble extract 0.5-4.0 mL; dry powder
papers.result: U. pertusa fresh thalli, extract and powder (3.4 g/L) killed all H. akashiwo within 120 h (LT50 45.9, 71.7, 66.7 h); fresh thalli killed all cells at >=0.68 g FW/L but only cut numbers ~53% at 0.34 g FW/L. G. lemaneiformis thalli killed all cells at 3.4 g/L (LT50 132.1 h) but stimulated growth ~56% at 0.34 g/L.
papers.env_effects: Ulva co-culture left NO3 470 and PO4 177.2 umol/L (not limiting); Gracilaria exhausted them to ~11.2 and 4.35 umol/L, and daily f/2 relieved its inhibition. Low doses stimulated H. akashiwo: 0.5 mL Ulva extract +72%, 0.34 g/L Gracilaria +56%, Gracilaria dry powder increased growth.
papers.key_details: Lab co-cultures (n=3, ANOVA) of H. akashiwo (1-25x10^4 cells/mL) with fresh thalli, culture filtrate, water-soluble extract or dry powder of U. pertusa or G. lemaneiformis over 72-216 h. U. pertusa was strongly algicidal and dose-dependent (LT50 83.0, 57.9, 35.9 h at 0.68, 1.7, 3.4 g FW/L); filtrate from 40 g/L killed cells within 72 h but filtrates from 4-20 g/L acted only after 72 h, and 3.4 g/L filtrate cut cells to ~52% of control by 216 h. G. lemaneiformis acted mostly via nutrient depletion. Low doses of both algae stimulated the target (hormesis).
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record had duration 'Not reported' (72-216 h) and no doses; it omitted that low doses stimulated H. akashiwo (+56% to +72%) and that Ulva needs >=0.68 g FW/L for complete kill.

reasons.reproducibility: One Heterosigma culture with fresh Ulva or Gracilaria is straightforward bench work.
reasons.effectiveness: Ulva >=0.68 g FW/L killed all H. akashiwo in triplicate, but 0.34 g/L cut only ~53% and low Gracilaria or extract doses stimulated growth 56-72%.
reasons.cost: One culture plus collected seaweed costs about $50-150.
reasons.time: LT50s were 36-83 h and all cells died within 5 days.
reasons.environment: Living seaweed is removable; Gracilaria depleted nutrients.

papers.title: The ability of the red macroalga, Porphyra purpurea (Rhodophyceae) to inhibit the proliferation of seven common harmful microalgae
papers.scale: lab cultures (n=3); 48 h field bottle incubations with Long Island brown-tide water; larval fish bioassay
papers.dose: fresh thalli 20 and 180 mg dry wt/L (P. multiseries 80 and 320); field 1.0 and 9.0 mg dry wt/L; extracts equivalent to 180 mg dry wt/L
papers.duration: 120 h lab (72 h for P. multiseries); 48 h field
papers.result: At 180 mg dry wt/L fresh P. purpurea cut A. anophagefferens >97% (also at 20 mg/L), C. marina 64%, P. multiseries 63%, K. veneficum 49%, K. brevis 44%, C. polykrikoides 30%, P. minimum 20% over 5 d. In natural brown-tide water 9.0 mg dry wt/L cut A. anophagefferens only 21-44% in 48 h (13-28% in 2010).
papers.env_effects: No mortality or abnormal behaviour in 1-week-old sheepshead minnows over 120 h at 900 mg dry wt/L thalli or 180 mg/L extract. Residual nitrate >1,000 uM and phosphate >70 uM, so inhibition was not nutrient limitation.
papers.key_details: Lab co-cultures (triplicate, two-way ANOVA) of fresh Porphyra purpurea thalli at two doses with seven HAB species for 5 d; inhibition was dose- and time-dependent with a synergistic interaction. Sensitivity order: A. anophagefferens > C. marina > K. veneficum > P. multiseries > K. brevis > C. polykrikoides > P. minimum. Extract of fresh thalli (180 mg dry wt/L equivalent) completely eliminated growth of A. anophagefferens, K. brevis, K. veneficum and C. polykrikoides and was more potent than extract of dried powder. P. purpurea was more potent than Ulva lactuca against A. anophagefferens and similar for five other species. Three 48 h field incubations with brown-tide water gave modest reductions (13-44%) only at the higher dose; nutrient addition had no effect.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record dose was a placeholder ('mg/L') and duration 'Not reported'; actual doses 20-180 mg dry wt/L and 5 d. Record said extracts of fresh or dried tissue were 'equal or stronger' than thalli; full text shows fresh-thallus extract was clearly more potent than dried-powder extract. Field-water effect (13-44%) was much weaker than lab effect.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Porphyra purpurea → 7 HAB species

reasons.reproducibility: Seven HAB cultures, brown-tide field water and a larval fish bioassay need a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: Lab thalli cut A. anophagefferens >97% but other species only 20-64%, and in natural brown-tide water only 13-44%.
reasons.cost: Several HAB cultures and fish cost $150-500.
reasons.time: Lab tests ran 5 days and field bottles 48 h.
reasons.environment: No sheepshead minnow mortality at 900 mg dry wt/L and inhibition was not nutrient competition.

papers.title: Inhibition of marine coastal bloom-forming phytoplankton by commercially cultivated Gracilaria lemaneiformis (Rhodophyta)
papers.organism: Gracilaria lemaneiformis -> Dunaliella salina, Prorocentrum micans, Skeletonema costatum, Scrippsiella trochoidea, Chaetoceros curvisetus, Platymonas subcordiformis, natural assemblage incl. Phaeocystis globosa
papers.scale: 40 mL lab; 1 L in situ bottles (Zhuhai); 50 L and 1000 L mesocosms (Nan'ao Island); field survey 2010 and 2012
papers.dose: lab 1.25-25 g FW/L; bottles 10 and 40 g/L; 50 L mesocosm 1.0-6.0 g wet wt/L; 1000 L mesocosm 3 and 6 kg (3.0 and 6.0 g wet wt/L)
papers.duration: lab ~7 d; bottles 3 d; mesocosms 10 d
papers.result: In lab, >1.25 g/L inhibited 4 of 6 species and >12.5 g/L stopped growth completely; bloom-water bottles with P. globosa fell 75-88% vs control in 3 d, 50 L mesocosms 70-82% by day 8, and the 1000 L mesocosm Skeletonema bloom peak was about an order of magnitude lower (3.78x10^6 and 1.33x10^6 vs 3.88x10^7 cells/L).
papers.env_effects: In the 1000 L mesocosm phytoplankton in treatments exceeded control by day 10 after the control bloom crashed; species richness was higher with Gracilaria. Field: phytoplankton abundance lower in farmed areas before harvest; difference vanished after harvest (correlational).
papers.key_details: Multi-scale study, all at least triplicate. Lab: G. lemaneiformis (0-25 g FW/L) significantly inhibited D. salina, P. micans, S. costatum and S. trochoidea above 1.25 g/L, with no effect on C. curvisetus or P. subcordiformis; a natural assemblage died within 2 days above 12.5 g/L. In situ 1 L bottles with P. globosa bloom water (~30x10^3 cells/mL): 22-38% inhibition at 1 d rising to 75-88% at 3 d at 10-40 g/L. 50 L mesocosm: 1-6 g wet wt/L all inhibited, gap growing from <20% (day 2) to 70-82% (day 8). 1000 L mesocosm: bloom peak one order of magnitude lower, but treatments overtook control after day 8. Field 2012: significantly lower abundance in cultivation area before harvest, no difference after harvest (t-tests, 3 vs 3 stations).
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record species list was partly wrong (no Phaeocystis in lab tests; lab species were D. salina, P. micans, S. costatum, S. trochoidea, C. curvisetus, P. subcordiformis) and setting labelled 'field' though core evidence is lab and mesocosm. Quantitative mesocosm results (70-88% reduction) were missing; 1000 L treatments exceeded control at day 10.

reasons.reproducibility: Lab and bottle tests are doable, but the study also used 50 L and 1000 L mesocosms with kilograms of farmed Gracilaria.
reasons.effectiveness: Bloom-water bottles fell 75-88% and 50 L mesocosms 70-82% vs controls in triplicate, though the 1000 L treatment overtook the control after day 8.
reasons.cost: Mesocosms and kilograms of seaweed cost $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Bottle reductions reached 75-88% by day 3, mesocosms by day 8.
reasons.environment: Living seaweed is harvestable and species richness was higher with Gracilaria.

papers.title: Allelopathic interactions between the HAB dinoflagellate Ostreopsis cf. ovata and macroalgae
papers.organism: Ulva rigida, Dictyota, Rhodymenia → Ostreopsis cf. ovata
papers.scale: 500 mL, pH held at 8
papers.dose: 2 g/L FW; powder 0.4-1.6 g/L DW
papers.result: Ulva co-culture ended 94% below the inoculum (LT50 12 d); powder -17-37%; filtrate stimulated growth.
papers.env_effects: Ulva drew down DIN, PO4 unchanged; target cells formed cysts.

reasons.reproducibility: Simple 500 mL co-culture, but Ostreopsis makes palytoxin-like toxins and pH must be held at 8.
reasons.effectiveness: Ulva co-culture ended 94% below the inoculum, but powder gave only -17-37% and filtrate stimulated growth.
reasons.cost: Culture, seaweeds and pH control are roughly $150-500.
reasons.time: LT50 of 12 d over a 20-day run.
reasons.environment: Seaweed is retrievable; Ulva drew down DIN and target cells formed cysts.

papers.title: New insights on the species-specific allelopathic interactions between macrophytes and marine HAB dinoflagellates
papers.organism: Ulva rigida, 2 seagrasses → Ostreopsis, Prorocentrum lima, Coolia, Alexandrium pacificum
papers.scale: 200 mL
papers.dose: 0.4-5 g/L FW
papers.result: Growth rates -35-62% in benthic species; A. pacificum all dead by day 6 at ≥0.8 g/L (EC50 <0.4 g/L FW); Fv/Fm fell 13-15%.
papers.env_effects: pH, DO and nutrients not different from controls.

reasons.reproducibility: 200 mL co-cultures are simple, but targets include toxic Ostreopsis, P. lima and A. pacificum.
reasons.effectiveness: Growth rates fell 35-62% in benthic species and A. pacificum all died by day 6 at >=0.8 g/L.
reasons.cost: Four cultures plus seaweed are roughly $150-500.
reasons.time: A. pacificum was all dead by day 6.
reasons.environment: pH, DO and nutrients did not differ from controls; seaweed is retrievable.

papers.title: Inhibition of harmful algal blooms caused by Aureococcus anophagefferens (Pelagophyceae) using native (Gracilaria tikvahiae) and invasive (Dasysiphonia japonica) red seaweeds from North America
papers.scale: 250 mL; field bottles
papers.result: Dose-dependent reductions in nearly all lab runs, needing ≥0.75-1 g/L and ≥72 h at low nutrients; field bottles 24 h: Dasysiphonia 3 g/L -30%, Gracilaria n.s.
papers.env_effects: pH 9.0 alone inhibited Aureococcus; pH 8.00-8.50 did not.

reasons.reproducibility: 250 mL flasks with local Gracilaria and an Aureococcus culture (no human toxin) are school-feasible.
reasons.effectiveness: Lab reductions needed >=0.75-1 g/L and >=72 h; in field bottles only Dasysiphonia at 3 g/L gave -30% and Gracilaria was not significant.
reasons.cost: One culture plus seaweed is about $50-150.
reasons.time: Reductions at 72 h.
reasons.environment: pH 9.0 alone inhibited Aureococcus, so part of the effect is a pH side-effect, and Dasysiphonia is invasive.

papers.title: Mechanism of the allelopathic effect of macroalgae Gracilaria bailiniae on Nitzschia closterium
papers.organism: Gracilaria bailiniae → Nitzschia closterium (fouling benthic diatom)
papers.scale: Lab flask co-cultures, n = 3 replicates per concentration
papers.dose: Four concentrations each of fresh thalli (GFT) and aqueous extract (GAE); allelochemicals citrate, hydroxyethanesulfonic (isethionic) acid, taurine
papers.result: Fresh thalli suppressed N. closterium at all concentrations by day 4 (IC50-4d 0.667 × 10⁻³ g/mL, i.e. 0.667 g/L); aqueous extract inhibited above 1 × 10⁻³ g/mL (IC50-4d 3.889 × 10⁻³ g/mL). Hydroxyethanesulfonic acid damaged PSII.
papers.env_effects: Cells shrank and plasmolysed; photosystem II damaged.
papers.key_details: Lab co-culture of an antibiotic-treated commercial N. closterium strain with G. bailiniae thalli collected from Fengjia Bay (Hainan), 22°C, salinity 30, 10 d, controls without seaweed, n = 3. Inhibition was dose-dependent with a significant concentration x time interaction (P < 0.01); the lowest extract dose (1 × 10⁻³ g/mL) was not inhibitory by day 10. Metabolomics identified citrate, hydroxyethanesulfonic acid and taurine as main intracellular compounds; HA damaged PSII (OEC, reaction centres). Target is a fouling diatom in seaweed aquaculture, not a toxic HAB species.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record duration '4 d' is the IC50 time point; experiments ran 10 d. Target is a benthic fouling diatom, not a bloom-forming HAB.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Gracilaria bailiniae → Nitzschia closterium (diatom)

reasons.reproducibility: The co-culture is simple, but the mechanism work used metabolomics and PSII analysis.
reasons.effectiveness: Fresh thalli inhibited the fouling diatom dose-dependently (IC50 0.667 g/L at day 4, n=3), but the lowest extract dose was ineffective and the target is not a HAB.
reasons.cost: Culture and seaweed are cheap; PSII and metabolomic work bring it to $150-500.
reasons.time: IC50 was read on day 4.
reasons.environment: Living seaweed is removable, though it releases taurine and isethionic acid.

papers.title: Kelp (Saccharina latissima) Mitigates Coastal Ocean Acidification and Increases the Growth of North Atlantic Bivalves in Lab Experiments and on an Oyster Farm
papers.scale: lab; oyster farm kelp lines
papers.dose: 0.3-1 g/L; field kelp lines
papers.result: pH 7.44 → 7.74 / 8.01 / 8.42 at 0.3 / 0.7 / 1 g/L kelp; +0.15 pH inside field kelp lines.
papers.env_effects: Kelp raised pH ~0.3-0.4 per day in a closed vessel, to ~8.8 by day 7.
papers.study_note: kelp raises pH; no HAB endpoint

reasons.reproducibility: The lab part is simple, but the headline trial uses kelp lines on an oyster farm.
reasons.effectiveness: Measures pH (7.44 to 8.42 at 1 g/L), not any reduction of HAB cells.
reasons.cost: Kelp lines and farm monitoring are $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Field trial ran one month.
reasons.environment: Kelp raised pH (+0.15 in field), a co-benefit against acidification, and is harvested.

papers.title: Use of sugar kelp aquaculture in Long Island Sound and the Bronx River Estuary for nutrient extraction
papers.organism: Saccharina latissima (sugar kelp) cultivation; nutrient bioextraction (no algae target)
papers.scale: Two 50 m longlines per site at WLIS (Fairfield, CT) and CLIS (Branford, CT) and at the Bronx River Estuary mouth; N removal extrapolated to a hypothetical farm with 1.5 m longline spacing
papers.dose: Kelp seedstrings outplanted on longlines at 0.5 and 1.0 m depth
papers.duration: 2012-2013 winter-spring growing season (outplant late 2012 to harvest ~May-June 2013)
papers.result: Estimated N removal up to 180 (BRE), 67 (WLIS) and 38 (CLIS) kg N/ha and C 1350/1800/1100 kg C/ha per season in a hypothetical farm; yield did not differ significantly among sites (p = 0.072), CLIS 62-69% of the others.
papers.env_effects: Nitrogen removal co-benefit.
papers.key_details: Field cultivation trial of native sugar kelp at three sites differing in temperature, salinity and nutrients (BRE >> WLIS ~ CLIS for DIN). Yield (kg FW per m longline) showed no depth effect (0.5 vs 1.0 m) and no significant site effect. N and C removal per hectare were extrapolated from tissue content and yield to a hypothetical 1.5 m-spaced farm; potential N-credit value up to $1600/ha (BRE). No phytoplankton, chlorophyll or HAB outcome was measured, so this is nutrient extraction only, one season, no replication across years.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Per-hectare removals are model extrapolations to a hypothetical farm, not measured farm-scale removal; no HAB/algae endpoint.
papers.study_note: kelp nitrogen extraction; no HAB endpoint

reasons.reproducibility: Kelp longline farming at three Long Island Sound sites needs boats and permits.
reasons.effectiveness: No phytoplankton or HAB outcome was measured; only nutrient extraction.
reasons.cost: Longline farms cost over $5,000.
reasons.time: One winter-spring growing season.
reasons.environment: Kelp removes nitrogen and carbon, with no added material.

papers.title: Allelopathy in macroalgae: Ecological principles, research opportunities and pitfalls reviewed
papers.scale: review
papers.dose: n/a
papers.result: Lists confounders (nutrients, shading, contact, pH, bacteria); recommends a plastic mimic control; few studies held pH constant.
papers.env_effects: Ulva intestinalis pushes rock pools above pH 10.

reasons.reproducibility: The typical reviewed experiment is a simple seaweed-microalga co-culture in flasks.
reasons.effectiveness: Lists confounders (nutrients, shading, pH, bacteria) and notes few studies held pH constant, so reported effects are hard to trust.
reasons.cost: A typical co-culture study is about $50-150.
reasons.time: Typical reviewed co-cultures last several days to ~2 weeks.
reasons.environment: Seaweed is retrievable, but Ulva can push pH above 10.

papers.title: Rebuilding A Collapsed Bivalve Population, Restoring Seagrass Meadows, and Eradicating Harmful Algal Blooms In A Temperate Lagoon Using Spawner Sanctuaries
papers.organism: hard clam → brown tide (Aureococcus), total chl
papers.scale: Shinnecock Bay NY, 64 plots of ~1,850 m²
papers.dose: 3.2 M adult clams at ~27/m²
papers.result: Bay filtration time fell from ≤3 months to 10 days; brown tide <10⁴ cells/mL in 2018-21 vs 0.3-1.9×10⁶ in 2007-16 (correlational).
papers.env_effects: Clam densities rose 18× and harvests 16×; chl a fell significantly in the western bay.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: hard clam → brown tide (Aureococcus)

reasons.reproducibility: Whole-bay restoration of 3.2 M adult clams across 64 plots of ~1,850 m2 in Shinnecock Bay needs permits and a restoration program.
reasons.effectiveness: Brown tide fell from 0.3-1.9x10^6 to <10^4 cells/mL and filtration time from ~3 months to 10 days, a large drop but correlational with no concurrent control.
reasons.cost: Buying and planting 3.2 million adult clams costs far over $5,000.
reasons.time: Effects emerged over 2012-2019 with surveys to 2021, i.e. years.
reasons.environment: Only native clams added; clams rose 18x, harvests 16x and chl a fell, with no non-target harm reported.

papers.title: Effect of the northern quahog Mercenaria mercenaria on the development of blooms of the brown tide alga Aureococcus anophagefferens
papers.scale: 300 L mesocosms, Peconic Bays water
papers.dose: several clam densities
papers.result: No-clam tanks passed 600,000 cells/mL; tanks with many clams were 100× lower; clearing ~40% of tank volume per day was enough.
papers.env_effects: No rise in total biomass and no species shift.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: hard clam → Aureococcus + natural phytoplankton

reasons.reproducibility: 300 L mesocosms of Peconic Bay water with live clams need a sponsor with tank space and a cell counter.
reasons.effectiveness: High-clam tanks held Aureococcus ~100x lower than no-clam tanks (>600,000 cells/mL), a large controlled effect.
reasons.cost: A few hundred litres of tank plus a few dozen hard clams is roughly $150-500.
reasons.time: Differences appeared within the 8-9 day run; clearing ~40% of volume per day acts within days.
reasons.environment: Only native clams added and retrievable; no rise in total biomass or species shift reported.

papers.title: Facilitation of seagrass Zostera marina productivity by suspension-feeding bivalves
papers.organism: hard clam, oyster, mussel → natural phytoplankton
papers.scale: mesocosms with eelgrass
papers.dose: 'environmentally realistic' densities
papers.result: Chl a significantly lower with bivalves (p<0.05).
papers.env_effects: Light penetration higher; eelgrass leaf growth +48 ± 9.3% at the highest bivalve density.

reasons.reproducibility: Mesocosms with eelgrass and three bivalve species need outdoor tanks and sourced seagrass, doable with a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: Chl a significantly lower with bivalves (p<0.05) but no magnitude reported and not HAB-specific.
reasons.cost: Tanks, eelgrass and bivalves at realistic densities likely $150-500.
reasons.time: Duration not reported; eelgrass growth endpoints imply weeks to months, scored conservatively.
reasons.environment: Native bivalves only; light and eelgrass growth rose (+48%); no harm reported.

papers.title: Application of filtration rate models to field populations of bivalves: an assessment using experimental mesocosms
papers.scale: 13 m³ MERL mesocosms (Narragansett Bay)
papers.dose: 16 clams/m²
papers.result: Gross sedimentation +58% with clams; models using natural-seston rates fit, while maximum lab rates overestimated sedimentation by up to 10×.
papers.env_effects: Extra sedimentation: 32% clam assimilation, 47% benthic respiration, 21% permanent biodeposits.

reasons.reproducibility: 13 m3 MERL mesocosms at Narragansett Bay are specialized facilities a school cannot reproduce.
reasons.effectiveness: Measured +58% sedimentation, not an algal reduction; shows lab rates overestimate field removal by up to 10x.
reasons.cost: Large mesocosm facility operation exceeds $5,000.
reasons.time: Duration not reported; sedimentation budgets of this kind run weeks to months, scored conservatively.
reasons.environment: Native clams only, but 21% of extra sediment became permanent biodeposits; no harm reported.

papers.title: Efficiency of particle retention and filtration rate in 6 species of Northeast American bivalves
papers.organism: 6 NE American bivalves incl. hard clam and oyster
papers.dose: size series
papers.result: Clam retains 100% of particles >4 µm, oyster 100% >5-6 µm and 50% at 2 µm; coefficient a in F=aW^b is 1.24 (clam) vs ~6.x (oyster; abstract digits partly unreadable).
papers.env_effects: Not reported.

reasons.reproducibility: Lab particle-retention measurement with bivalves and a particle counter is a standard bench method, doable at school with a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: Clams retain 100% of particles >4 um and oysters 100% >5-6 um, but no bloom reduction measured and abstract digits partly unreadable.
reasons.cost: Six bivalve species plus tanks roughly $50-150 if a particle counter is borrowed.
reasons.time: Filtration rates are measured in hours.
reasons.environment: Nothing added to natural water; not reported otherwise.

papers.title: Comparison of feeding and biodeposition of three bivalves at different food levels
papers.organism: mussel, oyster, hard clam → food suspensions
papers.scale: lab flow-through
papers.dose: food gradient
papers.result: Feeding ranked clam < oyster < mussel at every food level; clam % removal fell at high food.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.
papers.study_note: feeding and biodeposition across food levels

reasons.reproducibility: Lab flow-through feeding with three common bivalves is a bench protocol a sponsor could supervise.
reasons.effectiveness: Ranks feeding clam < oyster < mussel with clam removal falling at high food; no HAB reduction measured.
reasons.cost: Bivalves, pumps and algal food roughly $50-150.
reasons.time: Feeding and biodeposition measured over hours.
reasons.environment: Nothing added; not reported, but a lab feeding study has no release.

papers.title: Bivalve Filter Feeding: Variability and Limits of the Aquaculture Biofilter
papers.venue: Shellfish Aquaculture and the Environment, pp. 81-124
papers.scale: meta-analysis of >60 studies
papers.dose: n/a
papers.result: Oyster median clearance 3.00 L g⁻¹ h⁻¹ (as reported), 1.09 L ind⁻¹ h⁻¹ at 60 mm; most studies deplete <30% of particles.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.

reasons.reproducibility: Meta-analysis of >60 studies; the typical experiment is lab/field clearance measurement needing specialist gear.
reasons.effectiveness: Most studies deplete <30% of particles, a weak removal effect.
reasons.cost: Typical clearance-rate study with animals and counters ~$150-500.
reasons.time: Summarized aquaculture-biofilter effects are seasonal; review scored at weeks to months.
reasons.environment: Filter feeders add nothing; no harm reported.

papers.title: On measurement of filtration rate in bivalves-the stony road to reliable data: review and interpretation | The estimation of filtering rate from the clearance of suspensions (doi:10.1007/BF00355716)
papers.venue: Mar Ecol Prog Ser (Riisgård 2001); Mar Biol 2:356 (Coughlan 1969)
papers.scale: review / method
papers.dose: n/a
papers.result: Conflicting clearance data come partly from misused methods; Coughlan 1969 gives the control-corrected exponential clearance formula (via Cranford 2011, de Silva 2023).
papers.env_effects: Not reported.

reasons.reproducibility: Method review; the typical clearance experiment (beaker, bivalve, cell counts, Coughlan formula) is doable with a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: No algal reduction reported; review of measurement methods only.
reasons.cost: A clearance-rate setup is ~$50-150.
reasons.time: Clearance runs take hours.
reasons.environment: Nothing added in clearance tests; not reported.

papers.title: Effects of the harmful alga Margalefidinium (aka Cochlodinium) polykrikoides on clearance rates of the hard clam, Mercenaria mercenaria
papers.organism: hard clam (10-20 mm) → Margalefidinium, Rhodomonas, Gymnodinium aureolum
papers.scale: 250 mL beakers, 1 clam each, ~21 °C, salinity ~32
papers.dose: 1 clam/beaker; 250-3,000 cells/mL
papers.result: Clams cleared the HAB at ≤1,000 cells/mL but clearance ≈0 at ≥1,500 cells/mL; non-harmful G. aureolum was cleared as fast as Rhodomonas.
papers.env_effects: No change in opening or closing behaviour.

reasons.reproducibility: 250 mL beakers with one 10-20 mm clam and cell counts over 1 h is a simple school bench protocol (culture purchase aside).
reasons.effectiveness: Clams cleared Margalefidinium at <=1,000 cells/mL but clearance was ~0 at >=1,500 cells/mL, i.e. fails at bloom densities.
reasons.cost: Small seed clams and beakers are under $50 beyond the cultures.
reasons.time: Result visible in 1 h.
reasons.environment: Clams only; no change in valve behaviour, nothing added.

papers.title: DIVERSE FEEDING RESPONSES OF FIVE SPECIES OF BIVALVE MOLLUSC WHEN EXPOSED TO THREE SPECIES OF HARMFUL ALGAE
papers.organism: Mytilus edulis, Crassostrea virginica, Mya arenaria, Mercenaria mercenaria, Argopecten irradians -> Alexandrium fundyense, Prorocentrum minimum, Heterosigma akashiwo vs Rhodomonas sp.
papers.scale: lab containers, NOAA Milford CT, May-Oct 2005
papers.dose: HAB cultures
papers.duration: 1 h clearance-rate incubations; 4 h behaviour and biodeposit observations
papers.result: Clearance of HAB cells was either equal to or higher than clearance of Rhodomonas in every mixed-diet combination (no rejection of HAB cells); e.g. quahogs and scallops cleared A. fundyense faster than Rhodomonas, oysters cleared P. minimum faster. H. akashiwo clearance could not be measured because the cells swarmed and aggregated.
papers.env_effects: Intact, undigested (possibly viable) HAB cells and temporary cysts of A. fundyense appeared in feces/pseudofeces of most species; oysters stayed mostly closed during 4 h exposures and produced no biodeposits with H. akashiwo; quahogs partly closed with A. fundyense.
papers.key_details: Lab feeding study with five bivalve species exposed for 1 h to A. fundyense or P. minimum alone, Rhodomonas alone, or a mix, with empty-shell and no-shell controls (no algal loss in controls); ANOVA with LSD post hoc. Clearance rates were species- and alga-specific; the presence of Rhodomonas did not change clearance of HAB cells. H. akashiwo concentrations rose in no-shell controls due to swarming, so its clearance was not quantified. Biodeposits from most bivalves contained many intact HAB cells and A. fundyense temporary cysts, implying possible repackaging rather than destruction of HAB cells.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record's 'HAB cells mostly retained preferentially' is overstated: clearance of HAB vs Rhodomonas was either not different or higher for HAB. H. akashiwo clearance was not measurable. Oysters were mostly closed with all three HABs (not only Heterosigma).
papers.study_note: bivalve feeding responses to HAB species

reasons.reproducibility: Five bivalve species and toxic Alexandrium, Prorocentrum and Heterosigma cultures need a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: Bivalves cleared HAB cells as fast as or faster than Rhodomonas, but many cells came out intact and possibly viable in biodeposits and oysters stayed mostly closed.
reasons.cost: Bivalves and three HAB cultures cost $150-500.
reasons.time: 1 h clearance incubations.
reasons.environment: Viable HAB cells and Alexandrium temporary cysts were repackaged in feces and pseudofeces.

papers.title: Clearance rates and toxin accumulation by North Atlantic bivalves during harmful algal blooms caused by the dinoflagellate, Dinophysis acuminata, in NY, USA, estuaries
papers.organism: oyster, hard clam, mussel → Dinophysis acuminata
papers.scale: 60-min clearance tests in 1 L stirred beakers of whole bloom water (10 bivalves per species, 3 bivalve-free control beakers) at Cold Spring Harbor and Jockey Creek, plus field-deployed bivalves at 3 NY sites (2021-2022)
papers.dose: blooms 10²-10⁵ cells/L
papers.duration: 60 min clearance trials; toxins tracked for ~6 weeks in deployed bivalves
papers.result: Clearance on D. acuminata: oyster 1.69, mussel 0.46, clam 0.41 L h⁻¹ g⁻¹.
papers.env_effects: M. edulis DST loads (265 ng OA + DTX1 per g) exceeded the FDA closure guideline (160 ng/g) for three weeks in 2022; oysters accumulated the most PTX2; toxins persisted ~6 weeks.
papers.key_details: Bivalves starved 24 h were placed individually in 1 L beakers of raw Dinophysis bloom water (10 per species, 3 control beakers without bivalves) and cleared for 60 min, with Chl-a and Dinophysis counts at 0 and 60 min. All species cleared D. acuminata faster than Chl-a; oysters (1.69 +/- 1.34 L/h/g) were significantly faster than mussels (0.46 +/- 0.32) and hard clams (0.41 +/- 0.24). Separately deployed bivalves plus wild ribbed mussels accumulated DSTs and pectenotoxins, with blue mussels over the FDA guideline for three weeks. The study measures grazing and toxin risk, not bloom reduction.
papers.study_note: clearance and toxin accumulation on Dinophysis

reasons.reproducibility: The 1 L beaker clearance test is simple, but it needs Dinophysis bloom water, field deployments and toxin LC-MS.
reasons.effectiveness: Measures clearance rates (oysters 1.69 L/h/g) only, not any reduction of the bloom.
reasons.cost: Toxin analysis and deployments cost $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Clearance was measured in 60 min trials.
reasons.environment: Blue mussels exceeded the FDA DST guideline for three weeks and toxins persisted ~6 weeks.

papers.title: Temporal Variability in Phytoplankton Removal by a Commercial, Suspended Eastern Oyster Nursery and Effects on Local Plankton Dynamics
papers.scale: commercial FLUPSY (4 units x 10 upweller silos), East Creek off Great Peconic Bay, NY
papers.dose: nursery stocking
papers.result: Median weight-specific clearance 0.95 L/h/g during active growth (12 Jun-21 Jul); chlorophyll a removal across the FLUPSY had a season median of 6.45% (15.38% in the growth period, 24-h max 40%). Whole-FLUPSY clearance (median 3.64x10^5 L/h) would need ~18 days to clear the 1.6x10^5 m3 embayment, so no large impact on local phytoplankton.
papers.env_effects: Cochlodinium polykrikoides (~100 cells/mL from 22 Jul) coincided with unstable, low feeding, no growth and higher oyster mortality; a Peridinium quinquecorne bloom (1,460 cells/mL) coincided with pseudofeces release in early June. Negative removal values (biodeposit release) occurred; diel clearance lows (0.32 and 0.45 L/h/g) coincided with lowest and highest DO/pH.
papers.key_details: Field monitoring of inflow/outflow of a commercial oyster-seed FLUPSY at 15-min resolution through summer 2010. Environmental variables explained 58% of day-to-day feeding variability (multiple regression); clearance rose with O2 saturation up to 150%. Diel clearance peaked at 2.21 L/h/g (21:30) and bottomed at 0.32 L/h/g (07:40). Percent chlorophyll removal was highly variable, with a season median of 6.45% and negative values when biodeposits were released. Authors conclude the FLUPSY could not meaningfully reduce embayment phytoplankton because of replenishment by growth and exchange.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record lacked the percent chlorophyll removal numbers (median 6.45%, growth-period 15.38%, max 40%) and the 18-day embayment clearance estimate.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: oyster seed → natural phytoplankton

reasons.reproducibility: Monitors a commercial oyster FLUPSY in an estuary.
reasons.effectiveness: Median chlorophyll removal across the nursery was 6.45%, sometimes negative, and too small to affect the embayment.
reasons.cost: A commercial FLUPSY costs well over $5,000.
reasons.time: Data spanned a four-month season.
reasons.environment: Oysters released biodeposits (negative removal) and died more during a Cochlodinium bloom.

papers.title: Feeding reduction, reproductive failure, and mortality in Mytilus edulis during the 1985 'brown tide' in Narragansett Bay, Rhode Island
papers.scale: Narragansett Bay field + lab
papers.dose: 1985 bloom ~10⁶ cells/mL
papers.result: Clearance normal below 2.5×10⁵ bloom particles/mL and reduced above 5×10⁵.
papers.env_effects: 30-100% mussel mortality along the bay, with complete reproductive failure.
papers.study_note: mussel feeding reduction during brown tide

reasons.reproducibility: Observation of the 1985 Narragansett Bay brown tide cannot be repeated on demand.
reasons.effectiveness: Negative: clearance fell above 5x10^5 cells/mL, so mussels did not control the ~10^6 cells/mL bloom.
reasons.cost: Bay-wide field survey far exceeds $5,000.
reasons.time: Over the course of a season-long bloom.
reasons.environment: 30-100% mussel mortality and complete reproductive failure.

papers.title: Uptake kinetics of paralytic shellfish toxins from the dinoflagellate Alexandrium fundyense in the mussel Mytilus edulis
papers.organism: mussel → Alexandrium fundyense vs Thalassiosira weissflogii
papers.scale: lab
papers.dose: 256 cells/mL
papers.result: Clearance on Alexandrium ~48% lower than on the diatom; toxin passed the 80 µg STXeq/100 g limit in <1 h; 79% of ingested toxin kept.
papers.env_effects: No mussel mortality over 17 d; animals became toxic.

reasons.reproducibility: Lab mussel feeding with a toxic Alexandrium culture needs purchased toxic cultures and toxin assays.
reasons.effectiveness: Clearance on Alexandrium ~48% lower than on the diatom; grazing weakened on the HAB.
reasons.cost: Toxic cultures and PST analysis ~$150-500 excluding assay lab.
reasons.time: Ran 17 d; toxicity passed the limit in <1 h, but the removal question spans weeks.
reasons.environment: Mussels kept 79% of ingested toxin and became unsafe to eat; no mortality.

papers.title: Influence of dinoflagellate cell toxicity on uptake and loss of paralytic shellfish toxins in the northern quahog Mercenaria mercenaria
papers.organism: hard clam → two Alexandrium isolates (+ T. weissflogii)
papers.scale: lab
papers.dose: two isolates, with/without diatom
papers.result: Clams ate the high-toxicity strain only with diatom added; tissues exceeded the closure level 'by several orders of magnitude'.
papers.env_effects: Toxin depurated over 3-6 weeks.
papers.study_note: PST uptake and loss in clams

reasons.reproducibility: Lab clams fed two Alexandrium isolates need toxic cultures and toxin analysis.
reasons.effectiveness: Clams ate the high-toxicity strain only when diatom was added; little removal of the HAB itself.
reasons.cost: Cultures, clams and toxin testing ~$150-500.
reasons.time: ~2 weeks uptake.
reasons.environment: Tissues exceeded closure level by several orders of magnitude, with 3-6 week depuration.

papers.title: Experimental and Histological Studies of Four Life-History Stages of the Eastern Oyster, Crassostrea virginica, Exposed to a Cultured Strain of the Dinoflagellate Prorocentrum minimum
papers.scale: lab
papers.dose: P. minimum diet
papers.result: Juvenile oysters filtered P. minimum but rejected most as pseudofeces for ~2 weeks before digesting it.
papers.env_effects: Larvae grew poorly on P. minimum.

reasons.reproducibility: Oyster life stages with a Prorocentrum culture plus histology needs sponsor lab access.
reasons.effectiveness: Juveniles rejected most P. minimum as pseudofeces for ~2 weeks; little effective removal.
reasons.cost: Oyster seed, cultures and histology ~$150-500.
reasons.time: Effects over weeks.
reasons.environment: Larvae grew poorly on P. minimum, a minor non-target effect on the oysters.

papers.title: Hepatotoxic shellfish poisoning: Accumulation of microcystins in Eastern oysters (Crassostrea virginica) and Asian clams (Corbicula fluminea) exposed to wild and cultured populations of the harmful cyanobacteria, Microcystis
papers.scale: lab 1 L beakers: cultured Microcystis LE-3 (10^6 cells/mL) for 3 d and Lake Agawam NY bloom water (cyanobacteria 118 and 71 ug Chl-a/L; microcystin 38 and 29 ug/L) for 4 d
papers.dose: 10^6 cells/mL cultured Microcystis (single and double cells) vs colonial bloom water
papers.result: On cultured Microcystis, clam tissue microcystin fell from 3668 ng/g at 24 h to 719 ng/g at 72 h as clearance dropped, while oyster tissue rose to 4905 ng/g at 72 h with steady clearance; on colonial bloom water accumulation was only up to 2 ng/g.
papers.env_effects: Both bivalves exceeded the California guidance value (10 ng/g) by orders of magnitude on cultured cells; oysters did not depurate over 3-4 days and are the likelier vector of hepatotoxic shellfish poisoning.
papers.key_details: Lab clearance, particle-selection and toxin-accumulation experiments with Asian clams (Corbicula fluminea) and eastern oysters using toxic Microcystis culture (Lake Erie LE-3) and bloom water from Lake Agawam, NY. Clams cleared Microcystis faster than a green alga in culture, but in bloom water both bivalves cleared more slowly and clams selected green algae over cyanobacteria. Clams accumulated microcystin rapidly (3668 ng/g at 24 h) and then depurated to 719 ng/g by 72 h while clearance fell; oysters kept a steady ~0.11 L/h clearance and rose to 4905 ng/g by 72 h. On colonial bloom water accumulation stayed at or below 2 ng/g. The focus is shellfish safety, not bloom control.
papers.study_note: microcystin uptake in oysters and clams

reasons.reproducibility: Oysters, Asian clams and a toxic Microcystis culture in 1 L beakers need a sponsor and toxin assays.
reasons.effectiveness: Clams cleared cultured Microcystis but in bloom water both bivalves cleared slowly and clams selected green algae over cyanobacteria.
reasons.cost: Bivalves, culture and microcystin assays cost $150-500.
reasons.time: Toxin accumulation was measurable at 24 h in 3-4 day trials.
reasons.environment: Oysters accumulated up to 4905 ng/g microcystin, orders of magnitude over guidance, without depurating.

papers.title: Seston Removal by Natural and Constructed Intertidal Eastern Oyster (Crassostrea virginica) Reefs: A Comparison with Previous Laboratory Studies, and the Value of in situ Methods
papers.organism: intertidal oyster reefs (Crassostrea virginica dominant; hard clams on one reef; few ribbed mussels) -> chl a
papers.scale: 8 intertidal reefs (5 constructed, 3 natural), coastal South Carolina; flow lengths 5-18 m
papers.dose: natural reefs
papers.duration: 0.3-1.3 h measurement runs, May 2005 and June 2006
papers.result: In situ fluorometry showed chl a removal from -9.8% to 27.9% (lab pumped samples -9.3% to 40.7%) across reefs; overall means 12.9% (in situ) and 13.6% (lab).
papers.env_effects: One natural reef showed higher chl a downstream from wind-driven sediment resuspension. Bare planted shell with no live oysters removed no chl a.
papers.key_details: Upstream-downstream in situ fluorometry plus pumped water samples over 8 intertidal South Carolina reefs in shallow water (26-42 cm depth, flow 2.2-13.5 cm/s), bivalve densities 217-2831 per m2. Removal averaged ~13% across reefs; two older reefs removed 15.1% and 23.0%, one young reef 21.8%, and two reefs <5%. A bare-shell control showed no physical removal. Predicted removal matched measured (11.7% vs 12.9%) only when Powell et al. 'low gear' individual feeding rates were used; lab-derived rates overpredict. Each run was a single short time series per reef (no replicate reefs per treatment).
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record gave only the range; the overall mean removal (12.9% in situ, 13.6% lab) and the finding that lab-derived clearance rates overpredict field removal were missing.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: oyster reefs → chl a

reasons.reproducibility: Upstream-downstream fluorometry over eight intertidal oyster reefs is field work.
reasons.effectiveness: Reefs removed a mean of 12.9% of chlorophyll, ranging from -9.8% to 27.9%, with one short run per reef.
reasons.cost: Field fluorometers and reef access cost over $5,000.
reasons.time: Measurement runs lasted 0.3-1.3 h.
reasons.environment: Natural reefs add nothing and bare shell removed no chlorophyll.

papers.title: Can oyster restoration reverse cultural eutrophication in Chesapeake Bay?
papers.scale: Chesapeake Bay eutrophication model
papers.dose: 10× oyster biomass
papers.result: Summer surface chl fell only about 1 mg/m³.
papers.env_effects: Deep DO +0.25 g/m³; SAV +20%; oysters a supplement to, not a substitute for, nutrient cuts.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: oysters → Chesapeake Bay phytoplankton

reasons.reproducibility: Model study; running a published eutrophication model is possible on a computer, though this Chesapeake model is specialist.
reasons.effectiveness: Even 10x oyster biomass cut summer surface chl by only ~1 mg/m3.
reasons.cost: Model runs cost nothing beyond a computer.
reasons.time: Effect is a summer-season outcome of multi-year restoration.
reasons.environment: Oysters add nothing; deep DO +0.25 g/m3 and SAV +20%.

papers.title: Denitrification and nutrient assimilation on a restored oyster reef
papers.scale: restored reef, Choptank River MD
papers.dose: 131 oysters/m²
papers.result: NH4⁺, SRP and O2 fluxes ≥10× the control in every season; denitrification 0.3-1.6 mmol N m⁻² h⁻¹.
papers.env_effects: Ammonium and phosphate release ≥10× control.

reasons.reproducibility: Seasonal flux measurements on a restored reef in the Choptank River need field cores and nutrient analysis.
reasons.effectiveness: Measured nutrient fluxes, not algae; no algal reduction reported.
reasons.cost: Reef restoration and flux campaign exceed $5,000.
reasons.time: All seasons measured.
reasons.environment: Ammonium and phosphate release >=10x control, which can fuel algae.

papers.title: Role of Shellfish Aquaculture in the Reduction of Eutrophication in an Urban Estuary
papers.scale: Long Island Sound models
papers.dose: current vs expanded aquaculture
papers.result: System-scale model: oyster aquaculture removes 1.31% (current) and 2.68% (expanded, 1,340 t N/yr) of annual N inputs to Long Island Sound; modelled Chl reduction by filtration averaged 1.3% (current) and 2.1% (expanded), max 5.3% in one box; farm-scale model showed 0.3% Chl drop.
papers.env_effects: N-removal valued at $8.5M (current) to $470M (max expanded) per year in avoided costs. Optimistic all-lease estimate incl. denitrification: 10-30% of N inputs.
papers.key_details: Modelling study (EcoWin/EWN system model, FARM local model, ASSETS eutrophication index) for Connecticut oyster leases in Long Island Sound, plus avoided-cost valuation. No field manipulation. Oysters cleared 0.95x (current) to 2.08x (expanded) the cultivated-box volume per year. Model overestimates Chl because it lacks zooplankton grazers. Clams, NY leases and denitrification excluded from the base numbers.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record lacked the chlorophyll outcome: filtration lowered modelled Chl only 1.3-2.1% on average, the relevant bloom-control number.

reasons.reproducibility: Running the FARM and EcoWin ecosystem models requires specialist modelling software and data.
reasons.effectiveness: Modelled chlorophyll fell only 1.3-2.1% on average (0.3% farm-scale).
reasons.cost: A modelling study can be repeated with free or web tools.
reasons.time: Model outcomes are annual.
reasons.environment: Oyster aquaculture removes nitrogen with no added material.

papers.title: Benthic Filter Feeding: A Natural Eutrophication Control
papers.scale: South San Francisco Bay
papers.dose: n/a
papers.result: Control works when the benthic water-recycling time ≈ the phytoplankton growth time constant; favoured by shallow water and dense small animals.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.

reasons.reproducibility: Theoretical model comparing recycling and growth timescales is reproducible with a spreadsheet.
reasons.effectiveness: Theory only: gives conditions for control, no measured algal reduction.
reasons.cost: Free to repeat.
reasons.time: No experimental time; the control acts over ecosystem timescales, scored conservatively.
reasons.environment: Natural benthos, nothing added; not reported.

papers.title: Assessment of filtration capacity of different bivalve species suitable for integrated multi-trophic aquaculture (IMTA) systems vis-à-vis waste valorization for sustainable environment
papers.organism: blood clam Tegillarca granosa, oyster Crassostrea madrasensis, green mussel Perna viridis feeding on Thalassiosira sp. (microcosm) and shrimp-farm wastewater (mesocosm)
papers.scale: 9 x 5 L microcosms (1 bivalve per 2 L) and 9 x 300 L tanks with 50 L shrimp wastewater (2 bivalves per 50 L)
papers.dose: 1 animal per 2 L
papers.result: Plankton removal 94% (clam) / 87.1% (oyster) / 77.0% (mussel); species not significantly different.
papers.env_effects: Mesocosm: similar clearance of ammonia, nitrite, phosphate, BOD, TDS across species; oysters removed more COD and TSS; total bacteria lowest with green mussels.
papers.key_details: Lab study from Kakinada, India, 5 days, each species in triplicate (3 species x 3 = 9 units in each setting). Plankton counted daily (Sedgewick-Rafter) and Chl-a measured; filtration and clearance rates calculated. Plankton filtration efficiency 94% (clam), 87.1% (oyster), 77.0% (mussel), not significantly different. There is no bivalve-free control, so settling or die-off of Thalassiosira is not separated from filtration.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record correct on numbers; key caveat missing: no no-bivalve control, so the 77-94% removals are not controlled.
papers.study_note: culture plankton removal in tanks; clearance comparison

reasons.reproducibility: Bivalves in 5 L microcosms with a Thalassiosira culture and counting chamber are simple.
reasons.effectiveness: Removal was 77-94% in triplicate, but with no bivalve-free control, settling or die-off cannot be separated from filtration.
reasons.cost: Bivalves, culture and a counting chamber cost about $50-150.
reasons.time: 5 day experiment.
reasons.environment: Bivalves are retrievable and also cleared nutrients and wastewater solids.

papers.title: Effect of yellow loess on clearance rate in seven species of benthic, filter-feeding invertebrates
papers.scale: lab
papers.dose: 0.01-10 g/L loess
papers.result: Oyster clearance unaffected until 1.0 g/L loess; mussels affected at 1-10 g/L; scallop clearance down at 0.01 g/L.
papers.env_effects: Not reported.
papers.study_note: clay: loess effect on bivalve clearance (dup of clay-10)

reasons.reproducibility: Lab clearance with Rhodomonas plus yellow loess clay is bench-scale but uses seven invertebrate species.
reasons.effectiveness: Tests clay interference with filtration, not algal removal; scallop clearance fell at 0.01 g/L.
reasons.cost: Seven species, culture and loess ~$150-500.
reasons.time: Clearance measured in hours.
reasons.environment: Loess clay suppressed scallop and mussel clearance at 0.01-10 g/L, a non-target effect.

papers.title: Mitigation of harmful algal blooms using modified clays: Theory, mechanisms, and applications
papers.authors: Zhiming Yu, Xiuxian Song, Xihua Cao, Yang Liu
papers.scale: Review of lab and field use; China field applications
papers.dose: Modified clays 4-10 t/km2
papers.result: Surface-modified clays remove HAB cells with efficiencies up to hundreds of times those of natural clays at 4-10 t/km2; the most widely used field HAB mitigation method in China.
papers.env_effects: Authors conclude lab and field results show modified clay improves water quality and has no negative effects on aquatic ecosystems; the clay settles to the seabed and is not retrieved.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Various marine HAB species (dinoflagellates

reasons.reproducibility: Typical reviewed lab work needs surface-modified clays that must be prepared or sourced with a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: Modified clays remove HAB cells far better than natural clay and are widely used in China, but no percent is given.
reasons.cost: Lab-scale modified clay trials are roughly $150-500.
reasons.time: Flocculation removes cells within hours.
reasons.environment: Clay is applied at 4-10 t/km^2, settles to the seabed and is never retrieved, despite the authors' no-harm claim.

papers.title: Controlling Harmful Algal Blooms Through Clay Flocculation1
papers.authors: Mario R. Sengco, Donald Mark Anderson
papers.organism: Karenia brevis, Heterosigma akashiwo, Pfiesteria piscicida, Aureococcus anophagefferens, Cochlodinium
papers.scale: Review of lab, mesocosm, field-enclosure and flume work; field use in Japan and Korea
papers.dose: Lab/mesocosm 0.10-4 g/L clay (0.25-0.5 g/L in the scaled tests), some with PAC; field: Japan montmorillonite/kaolinite 1.3-400 g/m2 (200 g/m2 near fish pens); South Korea 1996 ~60,000 t yellow loess over 260 km2 at 400 g/m2
papers.result: Scale-up table: K. brevis removal 97% in lab (0.5 g/L) and 90% in settling columns (0.25 g/L); Heterocapsa triquetra 85% (Texas mesocosms), 68% (Florida mesocosms), and 100%, 89% and 41% in a flume at 3, 10 and 20 cm/s (0.25 g/L). In Korea, C. polykrikoides removal was calculated at 90-99% to 2 m depth and fisheries losses fell from $100 million to $1 million in the first year.
papers.env_effects: Turbidity returned near background within ~4 h. Phosphatic clay with or without PAC was not lethal to four benthic species (amphipods, sheepshead minnow, grass shrimp) in 4-28 d tests, and settled clay/K. brevis flocs were no more toxic than K. brevis alone. Juvenile hard clams: no mortality, no growth effect when flocs settled, but ~90% lower shell and tissue growth when clay stayed resuspended at 0.25 g/L for two weeks. PAC made settled flocs more erodible. Extracellular brevetoxins were removed by up to 70%; cell mortality rose with clay dose and time in the settled layer.
papers.key_details: Symposium review (Sengco & Anderson) summarizing US lab, mesocosm, limnocorral and flume work plus Japanese and Korean field use. Removal efficiency fell as scale and flow increased (97% lab to 68% in Florida mesocosms and 41% in a 20 cm/s flume). Korean field removal numbers (90-99%) and the $100M to $1M loss reduction are secondhand reports without controls. Benthic tests found no acute toxicity from clay itself, but prolonged resuspension cut clam growth ~90%. Several cited results were unpublished or in press at the time.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record's '>80% removal' hides the drop with scale and flow (68% in Florida mesocosms, 41% in the fastest flume) and omits the ~90% clam growth reduction under resuspended clay.

reasons.reproducibility: Typical reviewed test is a jar/settling-column test with natural clay, but the target cultures (K. brevis, Heterosigma) are purchased, toxin-producing organisms needing a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: Removal was 97% in lab and 90% in settling columns but fell with scale and flow (68% Florida mesocosms, 41% in a 20 cm/s flume); Korean 90-99% field figures are uncontrolled secondhand reports.
reasons.cost: Clay is cheap, but two HAB cultures plus media and a fluorometer or counting setup run about $150-500.
reasons.time: Clay flocculation works within hours.
reasons.environment: Clay persists on the bottom and cell mortality and benthic impacts were studied as concerns.

papers.title: Removal of red- and brown-tide cells using clay flocculation. I. Laboratory culture experiments with Gymnodinium breve and Aureococcus anophagefferens
papers.authors: MR Sengco, A Li, Kimberly I. Tugend, D. M. Kulis, D. M. Anderson
papers.scale: Triplicate borosilicate test tubes; 25 US clays + Korean loess
papers.dose: 0.03-0.25 g/L clay; 5 ppm PAC
papers.duration: 2.5 h removal tests under quiescent conditions; viability/recovery followed over days
papers.result: Twelve clays removed >90% of G. breve at 0.25 g/L (phosphatic clay up to 80% at 0.04 g/L), but no clay exceeded 40% removal of A. anophagefferens at 0.25 g/L unless dispersed through the culture (80%); alum, PAC and organic flocculants alone removed only 30-50%.
papers.env_effects: G. breve fully recovered at clay <0.03 g/L (growth delayed 24 h); mortality up to 100% with no recovery at ≥0.50 g/L; mortality near zero after 2.5 h contact but rose significantly after 12 h.
papers.key_details: Lab screening of 26 clays against G. breve (CCMP 718) and A. anophagefferens (BP3B) in triplicate tubes, removal measured by in vivo fluorescence after 2.5 h versus clay-free controls corrected for sinking. Twelve clays (mostly montmorillonite, bentonite, Florida phosphatic clay) removed >90% of G. breve at 0.25 g/L; IMC-P2 phosphatic clay reached 80% at 0.04 g/L. No clay removed >40% of A. anophagefferens at 0.25 g/L unless dispersed through the culture (then 80%). Alum, PAC and organic flocculants alone removed only 30-50%, but 5 ppm PAC cut the clay needed for G. breve by an order of magnitude. Removed cells can survive and regrow at low loadings, so removal is not always kill.

reasons.reproducibility: Culture-tube screening of clays is simple, but G. breve is a brevetoxin producer.
reasons.effectiveness: Twelve of 26 clays removed >90% of G. breve at 0.25 g/L in triplicate vs sinking-corrected controls, but no clay beat 40% on Aureococcus unless dispersed, and cells can regrow at low loadings.
reasons.cost: Clays are cheap, but two CCMP cultures and in vivo fluorescence measurement put it at about $150-500.
reasons.time: Removal within hours.
reasons.environment: Clay persists and low doses may just move live cells to the bottom where they regrow.

papers.title: Exposure of blue crab (Callinectes sapidus) to modified clay treatment of Karenia brevis as a bloom control strategy
papers.authors: Victoria M. Devillier, Emily R. Hall, Donald Mark Anderson, Kristy A. Lewis
papers.scale: 48 adult blue crabs in individual 20 L static tanks; 4 treatments (seawater, clay only, K. brevis only, clay-treated K. brevis), n = 12 tanks per treatment
papers.dose: Modified Clay II (PAC-modified) 0.5 g/L, sprayed on the surface (authors note 0.1 g/L already removes cells); K. brevis 1 × 10⁶ cells/L; re-dosed on day 4 after a full water change
papers.result: Clay cut K. brevis cells in the water column by 95% at 24 h and 98% at 48 h, but total brevetoxin in the water did not differ from untreated K. brevis tanks. Crab deaths were 2 (seawater), 1 (clay), 1 (K. brevis), 0 (clay + K. brevis), with no significant differences in survival or reflexes.
papers.env_effects: Clay dropped tank pH to 7.25 vs 7.86 in seawater on day 1, recovering within 72 h. Water-column brevetoxin was not reduced by clay. No detectable effect on adult crab survival or reflexes, though K. brevis alone killed only 1 of 12 crabs, so power to detect harm or benefit was low.
papers.key_details: Randomised tank experiment: 48 adult blue crabs, one per 20 L static tank, 12 tanks per treatment. Clay (Modified Clay II, 0.5 g/L) and K. brevis (10⁶ cells/L) were dosed twice, on days 0 and 4, over 8 days. Cell removal was 95% at 24 h and 98% at 48 h (removal efficiency vs untreated 93% at 24 h). Total water-column brevetoxins did not differ between clay-treated and untreated K. brevis tanks at any time (GLM p > 0.05). Only 4 of 48 crabs died, none in the first 48 h, and survival (Cox model) and reflexes did not differ. Clay lowered pH for ~72 h.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: The record left out that clay did not reduce dissolved/total brevetoxin in the water and caused a transient pH drop (7.25 vs 7.86). It also missed that the untreated K. brevis arm barely harmed crabs (1/12 died), so the 'no harm' result has low power.

reasons.reproducibility: Needs 48 adult blue crabs in tanks, PAC-modified clay and toxic K. brevis.
reasons.effectiveness: Randomised tanks (n = 12 per treatment) showed 95% cell removal at 24 h and 98% at 48 h vs untreated K. brevis, though settled cells were not shown dead.
reasons.cost: Crabs, tanks and cultures are $500-5,000.
reasons.time: 95% removal at 24 h.
reasons.environment: Clay dropped pH to 7.25 vs 7.86 for ~72 h and did not lower water-column brevetoxin; no crab harm was detected, but K. brevis alone killed only 1 of 12 crabs, so power was low, and clay stays in sediment.

papers.title: Mesocosm study of PAC-modified clay effects on Karenia brevis cells and toxins, chemical dynamics, and benthic invertebrate physiology
papers.authors: Victoria M. Devillier, Emily R. Hall, Vince Lovko, Richard H. Pierce, Donald Mark Anderson, Kristy A. Lewis
papers.organism: Karenia brevis; blue crab, sea urchin, hard clam
papers.scale: Twelve 1400 L indoor mesocosm tanks (Mote Marine Lab, Sarasota, April 2022), 4 treatments x 3 tanks: seawater only, MC II only, K. brevis only, K. brevis + MC II; each tank with 12 hard clams, 6 sea urchins, 2 blue crabs
papers.dose: MC II (PAC-modified kaolinite) 0.2 g/L vs 1e6 cells/L
papers.result: Cell removal was 57% after 8 h and 95% after 48 h; some brevetoxin analogs (BTx-3, BTx-B5) were higher in treated tanks and in the floc.
papers.env_effects: Dissolved P significantly lower in MC II tanks after 2 h; DIC and alkalinity reduced, pCO2 higher (MC II only) at 2 h; turbidity back to control by 48 h. No lethal or sublethal differences in clams, urchins or crabs vs untreated K. brevis within 72 h. Some brevetoxin analogs (BTx-3, BTx-B5) higher in treated water and floc.
papers.key_details: Randomised mesocosm experiment: K. brevis (CCMP 2228) at 1 × 10⁶ cells/L sprayed with MC II (PAC-modified kaolinite) slurry at 0.2 g/L, with wavemaker circulation (~26 cm/s), static (no recirculation) for 72 h, n = 3 tanks per treatment. Cell removal was 57% at 8 h and 95% at 48 h, slightly lower than earlier lab work; authors suggest flow (>10 cm/s) reduces particle-collision removal. BTx-1 and BTx-2 were higher in untreated water at 24-48 h, but toxin removal was less than expected. Animal endpoints (mortality, physiology) showed no MC II effect over 72 h; longer exposure not tested.

reasons.reproducibility: 1,400 L mesocosms with a Sarasota Bay benthic community are far beyond school scale.
reasons.effectiveness: 0.2 g/L MC II removed 57% at 8 h and 95% at 48 h in triplicate 1,400 L tanks against untreated K. brevis controls.
reasons.cost: Mesocosms and toxin/chemistry analyses exceed $5,000.
reasons.time: 95% removal at 48 h.
reasons.environment: No benthic harm in 72 h, but carbonate chemistry shifted, some brevetoxin analogs rose and clay persists.

papers.title: Degradation of paralytic shellfish toxins during flocculation of Alexandrium pacificum by an oxidized modified clay: A laboratory experiment
papers.authors: Weijia Song, Xiuxian Song, Hui‐Hui Shen, Yu Ding, Ruihong Cheng, Zhiming Yu
papers.scale: 1 L glass cylinders, 2000 cells/mL A. pacificum (strain ATHK), 4 treatments + control in triplicate
papers.dose: PMPS-MC (kaolin:potassium peroxymonosulfate 20:1 by mass) at 5 and 10 mg/L expressed as PMPS content; PMPS alone at 5 and 10 mg/L as comparison
papers.result: PMPS-MC removed >95% of cells from the water column within 3 h and kept it low for 48 h; extracellular PSTs fell below detection within 15 min and total toxin content fell 56-73% within 15 min. Over 70% of cells turned into pellicle cysts within 3 h.
papers.env_effects: Viable cells in the flocculated sediment continued to secrete toxins; clay transformed toxins to less toxic analogues.
papers.key_details: Lab cylinder experiment (triplicate) comparing oxidant PMPS alone with PMPS-modified kaolin at 5 and 10 mg/L PMPS, sampled at 0, 15 min, 3, 9, 24 and 48 h against an untreated control. Water-column removal exceeded 95% at 3 h for both PMPS-MC doses; PMPS alone removed slightly less and low-dose PMPS let the water-column density rise again within 48 h. Toxin profile shifted from GTX1/4 toward less toxic GTX2/3 and C1/2. Caveat: many treated cells formed pellicle cysts and some viable cells in the floc kept releasing toxin, so removal is not complete kill.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record dose '10 mg/L' is the PMPS (oxidant) content, not the clay loading; with the 20:1 kaolin:PMPS ratio the clay itself is about 20 times higher. Record omits the >95% cell removal and the pellicle-cyst formation.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Alexandrium pacificum (paralytic shellfish toxins)

reasons.reproducibility: Needs PSP-toxic Alexandrium, a custom oxidized modified clay and toxin analysis.
reasons.effectiveness: PMPS-modified kaolin removed >95% of A. pacificum from the water column within 3 h in triplicate vs control, but >70% of cells turned into pellicle cysts and some viable cells in the floc kept releasing toxin.
reasons.cost: Kaolin and Oxone-type PMPS are cheap, but a toxic Alexandrium culture and PST analysis put it at $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Toxin cut within 15 minutes.
reasons.environment: Toxins shifted to less toxic analogues, but viable cells and cysts in the settled floc kept secreting toxin and the clay (about 20x the stated PMPS dose) stays in sediment.

papers.title: Removal of cyanobacterial blooms in Taihu Lake using local soils. I. Equilibrium and kinetic screening on the flocculation of Microcystis aeruginosa using commercially available clays and minerals
papers.authors: Gang Pan, Mingming Zhang, Hao Chen, Hua Zou, Hai Yan
papers.scale: Jar flocculation tests; 26 clays/minerals; cultured M. aeruginosa (FACHB) resuspended in 0.5% NaCl at 4.86 × 10⁹ cells/L
papers.dose: 0.2-0.7 g/L clay
papers.result: At 0.7 g/L, Type I materials (sepiolite, talc, ferric oxide, kaolinite) had Q8h > 90% with t50 < 15 min; 14 Type III clays had Q8h < 50% (no practical value). At 0.2 g/L all materials fell below 60% except sepiolite (~97%).
papers.env_effects: Not assessed in the abstract; the clay-algae floc is left in the lake sediment.
papers.key_details: Lab screening of 26 commercially available clays and minerals (<90 µm) against a lab culture of M. aeruginosa, removal tracked by chlorophyll a over 8 h, when curves reached equilibrium. Table 2 lists 8-h removal at 0.7 g/L: talc 97.6%, ferric oxide 96.5%, sepiolite I 96.3%, ferroferric oxide 95.0%, kaolinite 93.9%, argillaceous rocks 92.6%, down to ~29% for pumice/scoria; Ca-bentonite only 34.7%. Sepiolite's performance at low dose was attributed to netting and bridging. Cells were harvested and resuspended in saline, not natural lake water, and replication is not stated in the sections read.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record's '4 of 26 removed >90%' follows the abstract's Type I grouping; Table 2 actually shows 6 materials above 90% at 0.7 g/L (incl. ferroferric oxide 95.0% and argillaceous rocks 92.6%), grouped also by removal rate.

reasons.reproducibility: Jar tests with commercial clays and a Microcystis culture are a clear bench protocol.
reasons.effectiveness: At 0.7 g/L six materials (talc 97.6%, kaolinite 93.9%, etc.) topped 90% in 8 h, but at 0.2 g/L only sepiolite did, 14 clays were <50%, cells were in saline not lake water and replication is not stated.
reasons.cost: Clays and a culture are about $50-150.
reasons.time: 8-hour tests.
reasons.environment: Clay-algae floc is left in the sediment; effects not assessed.

papers.title: ‘Floc and Sink’ Technique Removes Cyanobacteria and Microcystins from Tropical Reservoir Water
papers.authors: Renan Silva Arruda, Natália Pessoa Noyma, Leonardo de Magalhães, Marcella Coelho Berjante Mesquita, Éryka Costa de Almeida, Ernani Pinto et al.
papers.scale: Test tubes and 1 L cylinders with tropical reservoir bloom water
papers.dose: PAC (best dose 3 mg/L) + lanthanum-modified bentonite and/or local red soil
papers.result: PAC plus ballast removed 97 +/- 1.8% of chlorophyll-a from the top of the water column (20-60x lower than controls), 4.3-7.5x more biomass than other treatments; PAC alone did not sink the biomass.
papers.env_effects: PAC alone raised extracellular microcystin 3.5-6x; with ballast the bottom layer had extracellular MC up to 8x above controls, so toxin moves to the sediment layer; PAC lowered pH and PSII efficiency.

reasons.reproducibility: Test tubes and 1 L cylinders are simple, but it needs bloom water, PAC and lanthanum-modified bentonite.
reasons.effectiveness: PAC plus ballast removed 97 +/- 1.8% of chlorophyll-a, 20-60x lower than controls.
reasons.cost: PAC and lanthanum bentonite plus bloom sampling are roughly $150-500.
reasons.time: Results in 2 hours.
reasons.environment: PAC raised extracellular microcystin 3.5-6x, bottom-layer toxin rose up to 8x, and lanthanum persists.

papers.title: Post-ecological effect and risk assessment of using modified clay in harmful algal bloom mitigation: An attempt based on the responses of zooplankton Brachionus plicatilis and bivalve Mytilus edulis
