papers.authors: Sai Cao, Zhengyu Liu, Bin Zhou, Yongshun Jiang, Mengxue Xu, You Wang
papers.organism: Karenia mikimotoi; rotifer Brachionus plicatilis; blue mussel Mytilus edulis
papers.scale: Removal test in triplicate colorimetric tubes; rotifer test in 24-well plates (10 larvae/well, triplicate, 4 groups); mussel test in 14 L tanks, 30 M. edulis per concentration, one tank per treatment
papers.dose: PAC-modified kaolin 0.1 g/L for removal and rotifer tests; 0, 0.1, 0.5 and 1.0 g/L for mussels (0.1 g/L stated as the field application concentration)
papers.duration: 2 h settling for removal; rotifer life-table over days (~180 h); mussel exposure with clay held in suspension
papers.result: Modified clay at 0.1 g/L removed 81% of K. mikimotoi with little impact on rotifers or mussels.
papers.env_effects: Rotifers: clay-treated Karenia supernatant did not worsen Karenia-induced growth/reproduction effects within 2 h and survival/reproduction improved by 2 d. Mussels: gill and digestive-gland damage, and changes in filtration rate, digestive enzymes, condition index and mortality at 0.5 and 1.0 g/L; little impact at 0.1 g/L.
papers.key_details: Removal of K. mikimotoi (1.5 × 10⁵ cells/mL) by 0.1 g/L PAC-modified clay was 81 ± 2.3% after 2 h standing (triplicate). Rotifer groups were control, clay-only supernatant, Karenia, and clay-treated Karenia supernatant. The mussel system contained clay and mussels only (no Karenia) at 0-1.0 g/L, with one 10 L tank of 30 mussels per concentration, so tank-level replication is n = 1. AOP and integrated biomarker analyses flagged risk only at 0.5 and 1.0 g/L. Rotifers in the clay-only group began dying earlier (78 h) than controls (122 h).
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Mussel experiment did not include K. mikimotoi and had one tank per dose (pseudoreplication); 'little impact' applies to 0.1 g/L only.

reasons.reproducibility: Needs toxic K. mikimotoi, rotifers, mussels and tissue histology.
reasons.effectiveness: 0.1 g/L PAC-modified clay removed 81 ± 2.3% of K. mikimotoi in 2 h (triplicate), a single species and short settling test.
reasons.cost: Organisms and histology are $500-5,000.
reasons.time: The 81% removal was measured after 2 h of settling.
reasons.environment: Little mussel impact at 0.1 g/L, but gill and digestive-gland damage at 0.5-1.0 g/L (one tank per dose), and clay-only rotifers died earlier (78 h vs 122 h).

papers.title: Effect of yellow loess on clearance rate in seven species of benthic, filter-feeding invertebrates
papers.authors: Sandra E. Shumway, Dana M. Frank, Lisa M Ewart, J. Evan Ward
papers.organism: Filter feeders: Crassostrea virginica, C. gigas, Mytilus edulis, M. trossulus, Argopecten irradians, Crepidula fornicata, Obelia hydroid
papers.scale: Lab clearance (depletion) trials at UConn Avery Point (1999), Friday Harbor WA (2000) and Southampton NY (2000); Rhodomonas lens 2.5 × 10⁴ cells/mL as food; hydroid polyp opening by video (20 polyps per treatment)
papers.dose: Yellow loess 0.01, 0.1, 1 and 10 g/L
papers.result: All species were negatively affected. Bay scallops were most sensitive (significant clearance drop at 10 mg/L, 1 g/L and 10 g/L; 100 mg/L not significant, p = 0.076); Obelia polyps closed longer from 10 mg/L; mussels, both oysters and Crepidula were affected only at ≥1 g/L.
papers.env_effects: Direct non-target harm: loess significantly impairs feeding of benthic filter-feeding shellfish (scallops most sensitive) and hydroid behaviour.
papers.key_details: Seven benthic suspension feeders were exposed to five loess concentrations (0.01-10 g/L) at 14-18°C and 28-32 ppt, with algae-only controls; pure loess suspensions caused little to no feeding, so Rhodomonas was added. Analysed with one-way ANOVA and Dunnett tests (nested ANOVA for hydroids). Pseudofaeces were seen in all bivalves at ≥0.01 g/L but not quantified. Authors conclude clay use against HABs 'should be approached with extreme caution'. Short-term feeding trials only; no growth or mortality endpoints and no HAB cells present.
papers.study_note: loess effects on bivalve clearance rates; no algal endpoint

reasons.reproducibility: Clearance-rate trials with loess, shellfish and Rhodomonas food are doable with a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: Does not measure HAB removal at all; it tests clay harm to filter feeders.
reasons.cost: Several shellfish species plus loess are roughly $150-500.
reasons.time: Short-term feeding trials give results the same day.
reasons.environment: Loess cut scallop clearance even at 0.01 g/L; authors urge 'extreme caution'.

papers.title: Application of clay minerals to remove extracellular ichthyotoxins produced by the dinoflagellates Karlodinium veneficum and Karenia mikimotoi
papers.scale: Rainbow trout gill cell line (RTgill-W1) assay
papers.dose: Loess, zeolite 0-0.5 g/L; PAC 0-0.1 g/L; PAC-modified clays 0-0.25 g/L; bentonites
papers.result: Korean loess, zeolite, PAC and PAC-modified clays did not significantly reduce ichthyotoxicity, whereas high-swelling bentonites removed 100% of toxicity at 0.1 g/L.
papers.env_effects: Efficacy is highly clay- and species-specific; the commonly used loess and PAC-modified clays failed to detoxify.
papers.study_note: clay removal of HAB ichthyotoxicity; toxin endpoint only

reasons.reproducibility: Needs a rainbow-trout gill cell line (RTgill-W1) and ichthyotoxic cultures.
reasons.effectiveness: Loess, zeolite, PAC and PAC-clays did not reduce toxicity; only high-swelling bentonite removed 100% at 0.1 g/L.
reasons.cost: Cell-line culture and assays are $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Assay-scale results within a day.
reasons.environment: Bentonite clay persists; efficacy and side-effects are clay-specific.

papers.title: Toxic Alexandrium Treatment in Western Australia: Investigating the Efficacy of Modified Nano Clay
papers.authors: Cherono Sheilah Kwambai, Houda Ennaceri, Alan John Lymbery, Damian W. Laird, Jeffrey J. Cosgrove, Navid Reza Moheimani
papers.scale: Review of lab studies and management options (Western Australia focus)
papers.dose: Modified clays roughly 0.1-2 g/L in reviewed studies
papers.result: Reviewed lab trials report ~75-99% removal of Alexandrium with PAC-modified kaolinite depending on dose (0.2-1 g/L), but the authors note limited scalability to blooms spanning hundreds of km2.
papers.env_effects: Reviewed data show cyst formation rose with clay concentration (17.9-24.6%) while germination fell; recommends coupling treatment with monitoring rather than relying on it.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Alexandrium spp. (paralytic shellfish toxins)

reasons.reproducibility: Typical reviewed trials use toxic Alexandrium with PAC-modified kaolinite.
reasons.effectiveness: Lab trials report ~75-99% removal at 0.2-1 g/L, but authors doubt scaling to blooms of hundreds of km^2.
reasons.cost: A lab trial with modified clay is roughly $150-500.
reasons.time: Duration not reported; scored conservatively at 4-7 days.
reasons.environment: Cyst formation rose to 17.9-24.6% with clay dose (seeding future blooms), and clay persists.

papers.title: Controlling eutrophication by combined bloom precipitation and sediment phosphorus inactivation
papers.organism: Aphanizomenon flos-aquae (lake); Microcystis aeruginosa scum from pond De Ploeg (lab)
papers.scale: Lab: 18 tubes of 100 mL, triplicates; whole lake: Lake Rauwbraken (NL), 4 ha, max depth 15 m, stratifying, groundwater-fed with no in/outflow
papers.dose: Lab: PAC 0, 2.2, 4.4 mg Al/L with or without 390 mg/L La-modified bentonite; lake: 2 t PAC + 18 t Phoslock over 21-23 April 2008
papers.duration: Lab 2 h; lake monitored April 2008 through 2013
papers.result: 'Floc and Lock' sank the bloom; mean chlorophyll-a fell from 19.5 to 3.7 ug/L and TP from 169 to 14 ug/L, keeping the lake oligo-mesotrophic through 2013.
papers.env_effects: Adds aluminium and lanthanum clay permanently to the sediment; in the lab neither PAC nor Phoslock alone sank buoyant Microcystis.
papers.key_details: Lab test on Microcystis scum (~845 µg chl-a/L): after 2 h, PAC alone at 2.2 mg Al/L and LMB alone did not sink the buoyant cells (4.4 mg Al/L helped somewhat), but PAC + LMB together moved chlorophyll to the tube bottoms (significant PAC, LMB and interaction effects). Whole-lake 'Flock & Lock' in April 2008 sank a developing Aphanizomenon bloom; mean chl-a fell from 19.5 (±36.5) µg/L in the two years before to 3.7 (±4.5) µg/L after, and TP from 169 (±126) to 14 (±15) µg/L. The lake stayed oligo-mesotrophic through 2013. Single small, isolated, groundwater-fed lake with no control lake; the lake had a 4-month swimming ban in 2007.

reasons.reproducibility: Whole-lake treatment with 2 t PAC and 18 t Phoslock needs permits and industrial application.
reasons.effectiveness: Chl-a fell from 19.5 to 3.7 ug/L (81%) and stayed low to 2013, but it is one lake without a control lake.
reasons.cost: Tonnes of PAC and Phoslock cost far above $5,000.
reasons.time: Evaluated over 2008-2013.
reasons.environment: Aluminium and lanthanum clay are left permanently in the sediment.

papers.title: Management of eutrophication in Lake De Kuil (The Netherlands) using combined flocculant – Lanthanum modified bentonite treatment
papers.authors: Guido Waajen, Frank Van Oosterhout, Grant Douglas, Miquel Lürling
papers.scale: Whole lake, Lake De Kuil (NL): 6.7 ha, mean depth 4 m, max 9 m, 268,000 m³, residence time 3.7 y
papers.dose: 4.38 t FeCl3 (3 m³) over 6.7 ha, buffered with 200 kg Ca(OH)2; LMB 13.65 t spread over 6.7 ha plus 27.85 t injected over 2.2 ha deeper than 6.4 m; May 2009
papers.result: Mean summer chlorophyll-a fell from 16 to 6 ug/L and TP from 0.05 to 0.02 mg/L; bathing standards were met for six summers and macrophyte cover tripled.
papers.env_effects: Secchi rose from 1.5 m to 5 m immediately after treatment; macrophyte cover tripled 2009-2011. Sediment P release fell from 5.2 (2009) to 0.4 mg P/m²/d (2010) but increased in later years, risking reversion.
papers.key_details: Before-after whole-lake study with long-term monitoring (1992-2008 vs 2009-2014), no reference lake. Iron(III) chloride was used instead of PAC because an aluminium permit was refused. Mean summer TP fell from 0.05 to 0.02 mg/L, chlorophyll a from 16 to 6 µg/L and Secchi rose from 2.31 to 3.12 m; bathing-water requirements were met six summers in a row. A Planktothrix rubescens bloom occurred in winter 2010/2011, but summer cyanobacteria biomass was lower than before treatment. Success relied on external P loading being near the critical load; rising sediment P release in later years limits longevity.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Cyanobacteria incl. Planktothrix rubescens

reasons.reproducibility: Whole-lake iron chloride plus lanthanum bentonite treatment of a 6.7 ha lake.
reasons.effectiveness: Summer chl a fell 16 to 6 ug/L and bathing standards were met six summers, but there was no reference lake, a winter Planktothrix bloom occurred and sediment P release crept back up.
reasons.cost: Whole-lake dosing exceeds $5,000.
reasons.time: Evaluated over six years.
reasons.environment: Adds iron and lanthanum permanently to sediment.

papers.title: Eutrophication management in surface waters using lanthanum modified bentonite: A review
papers.authors: Diego Copetti, Karin Finsterle, Laura Marziali, Fabrizio Stefani, Gianni Tartari, Grant Douglas et al.
papers.scale: ~200 treated water bodies worldwide; lab, mesocosm and whole-lake
papers.dose: Lanthanum-modified bentonite (LMB)
papers.result: LMB strongly binds phosphate (SRP cut >98% in 7-d core batch tests and 87-98% in 48-h water tests). Field and mesocosm results vary: e.g. Lake Varese mesocosm bottom-water TP 0.11 → 0.04 mg/L, but one 58-day trial showed treated TP (median 0.58 mg/L) not substantially different from control (0.69 mg/L). Efficacy is reduced by humic substances and pH > 9.
papers.env_effects: La generally below acute toxicity thresholds except in low-alkalinity waters; La accumulation, suspended solids and effects on sediment organisms unresolved; use in saline waters needs careful risk evaluation (La release).
papers.key_details: Narrative review (author accepted manuscript) of LMB/Phoslock in ~200 water bodies. Lab batch tests showed >98% SRP reduction in 7 days and 87-98% in 48 h. Mesocosms gave 94-100% SRP and 83-96% TP reductions over up to 73 days. Field outcomes varied: the Lake Varese mesocosm showed >80% TP/SRP reduction vs the untreated site over 11 months, but another 58-day study found no substantial TP difference from controls. Direct cyanobacteria or chlorophyll outcomes are reported only sparsely, e.g. no scums or algaecide needed in one lake in 2013. Much of the evidence is industry grey literature.

reasons.reproducibility: Typical reviewed use is whole-lake LMB dosing across ~200 water bodies.
reasons.effectiveness: LMB cut SRP >98% in lab and 83-96% TP in mesocosms, but algal outcomes are sparse, one 58-day trial showed no TP difference from control, and much evidence is industry grey literature.
reasons.cost: Whole-lake LMB dosing exceeds $5,000.
reasons.time: Lake responses take seasons to years.
reasons.environment: Lanthanum accumulates, with risk in low-alkalinity and saline waters.

papers.title: Longevity and effectiveness of aluminum addition to reduce sediment phosphorus release and restore lake water quality
papers.authors: Brian Huser, Sara Egemose, Harvey H. Harper, Michael Hupfer, Henning Skovgaard Jensen, Keith M. Pilgrim et al.
papers.scale: Synthesis of 114 alum-treated lakes
papers.dose: Aluminium salts (varied doses)
papers.result: Across 114 Al-treated lakes, short-term epilimnetic TP fell from 0.101 to 0.036 mg/L and chl-a from 42.7 to 16.3 µg/L, with Secchi rising 1.6 → 2.4 m. TP-based longevity averaged 11 years (Secchi 9.7 and chl-a 8.8 years); stratified lakes lasted longer than polymictic ones, and Al dose explained 47% of longevity variation.
papers.env_effects: Adds aluminium to sediments; benthic-feeding fish in shallow lakes appear to shorten effectiveness.
papers.key_details: Multi-lake synthesis of 114 lakes (Denmark, Germany, Sweden, US) treated with Al salts, comparing ≥2 years of pre-treatment growing-season data with post-treatment data. Longevity was defined as years with ≥50% improvement in TP or chl-a, or a Secchi increase. Paired tests: TP 0.101 → 0.036 mg/L, chl-a 42.7 → 16.3 µg/L (~62% lower), Secchi 1.6 → 2.4 m. Longevity averaged 11 years for TP (15 using modelled values) and 8.8 years for chl-a. Stratified lakes averaged 15 years observed (21 modelled) vs 4.6-5.7 years for polymictic lakes. Dose, watershed:lake area and Osgood index explained 47%, 32% and 3% of longevity variance. There were no untreated control lakes.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: The record gave no algal outcome (effect_pct null). The full text reports the chl-a drop of 42.7 → 16.3 µg/L (~62%) and a chl-a longevity of 8.8 years.
papers.study_note: P-inactivation longevity; TP only, no algal endpoint

reasons.reproducibility: Synthesis of 114 whole-lake alum treatments.
reasons.effectiveness: Across 114 lakes chl a fell 42.7 to 16.3 ug/L (~62%) with benefits lasting ~8.8 years, but there were no untreated control lakes and polymictic lakes lasted only 4.6-5.7 years.
reasons.cost: Whole-lake alum costs far above $5,000.
reasons.time: Outcomes span years.
reasons.environment: Adds aluminium to sediments.

papers.title: A meta-analysis of water quality and aquatic macrophyte responses in 18 lakes treated with lanthanum modified bentonite (Phoslock®)
papers.authors: Bryan M. Spears, Eleanor B. Mackay, Said Yasseri, Iain Gunn, Kate E. Waters, Christopher Andrews et al.
papers.scale: Meta-analysis of 18 treated lakes
papers.dose: La-bentonite 1.4-6.7 t/ha
papers.result: Median TP fell 0.08 → 0.03 mg/L and SRP 0.019 → 0.005 mg/L in the 24 months after La-bentonite. Median annual chl-a barely changed (10.1 → 10.0 µg/L; the drop was significant only in Z-scores), spring chl-a fell 14.0 → 6.2 µg/L, and the summer 75th percentile fell 119 → 74 µg/L.
papers.env_effects: Macrophyte recovery and clarity improved; responses highly site-specific.
papers.key_details: Before-after meta-analysis of 18 lakes treated with La-bentonite (1.4-6.7 t/ha), comparing the 24 months before and after first application. There were no untreated control lakes: TP, chl-a and Secchi data came from 15 lakes, SRP from 14, macrophyte species from 6 and colonisation depth from 4. TP and SRP fell significantly. Median annual chl-a was essentially unchanged (10.1 → 10.0 µg/L), with the largest relative response in spring (14.0 → 6.2 µg/L). The 75th-percentile shifts (summer chl-a 119 → 74 µg/L, Secchi 398 → 506 cm) were not formally tested. Macrophyte species rose from a median of 5.5 to 7.0.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: The record's effect_pct of 37.8 came from the summer 75th-percentile chl-a (119 → 74 µg/L), which the paper says was not tested statistically. The median annual chl-a change was only 10.1 → 10.0 µg/L (~1%), significant only after Z-score transformation, so the record overstates the algal response.

reasons.reproducibility: Meta-analysis of 18 whole-lake Phoslock treatments at 1.4-6.7 t/ha.
reasons.effectiveness: Despite TP falling 0.08 to 0.03 mg/L, median annual chl a was essentially unchanged (10.1 to 10.0 ug/L); only spring chl a fell (14.0 to 6.2) and there were no control lakes.
reasons.cost: Whole-lake dosing exceeds $5,000.
reasons.time: 24-month pre/post comparisons.
reasons.environment: Lanthanum clay persists in sediment, though macrophyte diversity rose.

papers.title: Lake responses following lanthanum-modified bentonite clay (Phoslock®) application: An analysis of water column lanthanum data from 16 case study lakes
papers.authors: Bryan M. Spears, Miquel Lürling, Said Yasseri, Ana Teresa Castro, Max M. Gibbs, Sebastian Meis et al.
papers.scale: 16 case-study lakes
papers.dose: Phoslock (La-modified bentonite) applications
papers.result: Post-application surface total La peaked at 0.026-2.30 mg/L and filterable La at 0.002-0.14 mg/L, returning toward baseline in 3-12 months.
papers.env_effects: Surface filterable La exceeded the Ceriodaphnia dubia EC50 (0.08 mg/L) in Loch Flemington during application and in a Niedersachsen lake for 2 months afterwards, falling to 0.001-0.002 mg/L by month 6. In at least two lakes FLa never returned below the <0.001 mg/L baseline during monitoring. Modelled La³⁺ was <0.0004 mg/L at alkalinity >0.8 mEq/L but up to 0.12 mg/L in very low-alkalinity lakes.
papers.key_details: Analysis of water-column lanthanum in 16 lakes treated with Phoslock, monitored up to 60 months after application; pre-application TLa and FLa were <0.001 mg/L everywhere. Maximum post-application surface TLa was 0.026-2.30 mg/L and FLa 0.002-0.14 mg/L. Generalised additive models showed 2nd-order decay, reaching an end-point 3-12 months after application. Product concentrations as suspended solids (0.62-46.0 mg/L) stayed below lab EC50s (e.g. Daphnia 871 mg/L). This is a safety/exposure paper with no algal-response data.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: The record left out that FLa exceeded the C. dubia EC50 (0.08 mg/L) in two lakes and did not return to baseline in at least two lakes.

reasons.reproducibility: Monitoring data from 16 whole-lake Phoslock applications.
reasons.effectiveness: Reports lanthanum concentrations only; no algae outcome is given.
reasons.cost: Whole-lake dosing exceeds $5,000.
reasons.time: Up to 60 months of monitoring.
reasons.environment: Filterable La exceeded the C. dubia EC50 (0.08 mg/L) in two lakes, and in at least two lakes never returned to the <0.001 mg/L baseline.

papers.title: Humic substances interfere with phosphate removal by lanthanum modified clay in controlling eutrophication
papers.authors: Miquel Lürling, Guido Waajen, Frank Van Oosterhout
papers.scale: Controlled lab experiments
papers.dose: Phoslock 50 mg/L (4.37% La measured by ICP-MS) with ~0.6 mg/L FRP and humic substances 0-14 mg/L DOC
papers.result: Humic substances lowered Phoslock's FRP removal in both the 1-d and 42-d experiments, matching equilibrium modelling; even without DOC, 24-h FRP removal was only 46% and 42-d residual FRP was ~34% higher than predicted. Filterable La rose above 270 µg/L within a week with humics, vs the Dutch standard of 10.1 µg/L.
papers.env_effects: Filterable lanthanum exceeded 270 µg/L in the presence of humic substances, far above the Dutch surface-water La standard of 10.1 µg/L.
papers.key_details: Controlled lab experiments plus CHEAQS/WHAM chemical equilibrium modelling of La-humic complexation at pH 7 and 8. Short-term (24 h) series compared FRP solutions with and without 50 mg/L Phoslock across eight DOC levels (0-14 mg/L); a 42-day experiment followed. Modelling predicted only 81.7% of P could bind as LaPO4 at the dose used, and DOC reduced this further. Authors conclude the recommended Phoslock dose seems too low and DOC-rich waters need site-specific testing. No algae were measured; FRP of 600 µg/L is higher than typical field values.

reasons.reproducibility: Lab jars with Phoslock and humic substances are simple, but phosphorus and lanthanum analyses need a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: No algae measured; even without humics Phoslock removed only 46% of FRP in 24 h, and humics cut removal further.
reasons.cost: Phoslock, humics and P/La analyses are roughly $150-500.
reasons.time: Runs were 1 d and 42 d; the long-term result needs 6 weeks.
reasons.environment: Filterable La exceeded 270 ug/L within a week, over the 10.1 ug/L Dutch standard.

papers.title: Effects of alum treatment on water quality and sediment in the Minneapolis Chain of Lakes, Minnesota, USA
papers.authors: Brian Huser, Patrick L. Brezonik, Raymond M. Newman
papers.scale: 4 lakes, Minneapolis Chain of Lakes (MN, USA)
papers.dose: Alum (aluminium sulfate), 1996 and 2001
papers.result: Growing-season chl-a fell from 12.2 to 3.7 µg/L (Calhoun), 7.2 to 4.1 (Harriet), 15.5 to 4.9 (Cedar, 5 yr post) and 35.3 to 17.4 (Isles, 5 yr post); Lake of the Isles (lowest dose) returned to pretreatment levels by 2002-2005, while internal P release still stayed suppressed in all four lakes.
papers.env_effects: Alum floc drifted to deeper sediments; adds aluminium.
papers.key_details: Before-after field evaluation of alum treatments in four Minneapolis lakes (Cedar and Isles 1996; Harriet, littoral-only, and Calhoun 2001) using biweekly monitoring since 1991, with no untreated reference lake. Secchi depth rose significantly in all lakes (e.g. Calhoun 2.7 to 4.7 m). Internal P release fell from 9.7 to 1.3 mg/m²/d in Cedar (rising to 4.8 in 2002-2003), from 10.6 to 1.6 mg/m²/d in Harriet (85%), was nearly eliminated in Calhoun, and fell from 5.9 to 1.7 mg/m²/d in Isles. In Harriet the floc drifted to deeper sediments, giving unexpected improvement. Isles' TP and chl-a in 2002-2005 were not significantly different from pretreatment despite lower sediment release, pointing to external loading.

reasons.reproducibility: Whole-lake alum treatments of four Minneapolis lakes.
reasons.effectiveness: Chl a fell in all four lakes (e.g. Calhoun 12.2 to 3.7, Cedar 15.5 to 4.9 ug/L), but Lake of the Isles returned to pretreatment levels by 2002-2005 and there was no reference lake.
reasons.cost: Whole-lake alum exceeds $5,000.
reasons.time: Evaluated over ~4-9 years.
reasons.environment: Alum floc adds aluminium and drifted to deeper sediments.

papers.title: Impact of iron addition on phosphorus dynamics in sediments of a shallow peat lake 10 years after treatment
papers.authors: Melanie Münch, Rianne van Kaam, Karel As, Stefan Peiffer, Gerard ter Heerdt, Caroline P. Slomp et al.
papers.scale: Whole shallow peat lake Terra Nova (NL)
papers.dose: 40% FeCl3 solution applied continuously at low doses over 1.5 years from 2010; total 0.5-1 mol Fe/m² (1 mol Fe/m² in the test area)
papers.duration: Treatment 1.5 years (2010-2011); sediment study ~10 years later (2021)
papers.result: Surface-water TP stayed below 0.5 µmol/L for ~1.5 years after treatment. Afterwards summer internal P loading returned stronger (whole-lake anoxic flux ~505 µmol P m⁻² d⁻¹; in situ ~420), producing the highest surface-water P since monitoring began in 1986.
papers.env_effects: Organic-rich sediment released P in excess of Fe under summer low oxygen; the treatment backfired long-term.
papers.key_details: Single-lake case study (Terra Nova, NL; shallow peat lake with filamentous cyanobacteria blooms 1987-2004) about 10 years after FeCl3 dosing. There was no control lake; the design is long-term monitoring plus sediment cores from 3 stations incubated oxic and anoxic for 26 days. Sediment released 10-84× more P under anoxic than oxic conditions. The added Fe still redox-cycles in the top 10 cm and binds up to 70% of sedimentary P, but organic matter keeps Fe²⁺ in the solid phase and limits re-capture. The authors could not fully explain why suppression lasted only 1.5 years.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: The treatment was a continuous low-dose application over 1.5 years, not a single dose, and P suppression lasted ~1.5 years; the record's 'two years' follows the abstract. The post-treatment P peak was the highest since 1986.
papers.study_note: sediment P dynamics after iron; no algal endpoint

reasons.reproducibility: Whole-lake FeCl3 dosing (0.5-1 mol Fe/m^2) of a peat lake.
reasons.effectiveness: P stayed low for only ~1.5 years after 1.5 years of FeCl3 dosing, then internal loading produced the highest surface P since 1986.
reasons.cost: Whole-lake dosing exceeds $5,000.
reasons.time: Evaluated ~10 years after treatment.
reasons.environment: Added iron persists in organic sediment that released 10-84x more P under anoxia; the treatment backfired.

papers.title: The effect of alum coagulation for in-lake treatment of toxic Microcystis and other cyanobacteria related organisms in microcosm experiments
papers.authors: Jisun Han, Bong-Seok Jeon, Noriko Futatsugi, Ho-Dong Park
papers.organism: Microcystis ichthyoblabe strain TAC95 (produces only microcystin-LR); sediment bacteria
papers.scale: 3 acrylic microcosm chambers (5 L Microcystis suspension each; +sediment, +alum, +alum+sediment) plus bottle experiments
papers.dose: Alum at the maximum dose keeping pH 6.0: 48 mg/L as Al (microcosm) and 35 mg/L as Al (bottles)
papers.result: Alum co-precipitated the cells so chlorophyll-a and intracellular MC-LR in the water fell sharply within 1 day, but in the +alum microcosm >95% of intracellular MC-LR was released to the water by day 7. With sediment present, extracellular MC-LR rose for 3 days and then fell.
papers.env_effects: Harmed cyanobacteria-lysing organisms and microcystin-degrading bacteria; authors conclude alum at this dose is unsuitable for bloom removal without toxin release.
papers.key_details: Lab microcosms (320 x 180 x 150 mm chambers) with washed M. ichthyoblabe in dechlorinated tap water; one chamber per treatment (+sediment control, +alum, +alum+sediment), with sediment from a eutrophic pond. Alum was dosed at the jar-test maximum that keeps pH at 6.0. No Microcystis-lysing bacterial plaques appeared in the +alum microcosm, and plaque counts in +alum+sediment were far lower than in +sediment alone; alum also reduced microcystin-degrading bacterial activity. Chlorophyll-a and phycocyanin fell in the precipitated cells. The authors conclude alum is not suitable for removing toxic blooms because floc remains in sediment for a long time. Caveat: very high dose and apparently a single chamber per treatment.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: The organism is Microcystis ichthyoblabe (TAC95), not M. aeruginosa; the setting is indoor lab microcosms (5 L chambers), not a mesocosm. The record omits that alum first removed chlorophyll-a from the water column by co-precipitation within 1 day.

reasons.reproducibility: Bottle and microcosm alum tests with Microcystis are bench-feasible, but microcystin analysis needs a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: Alum (48 mg Al/L) co-precipitated cells so water-column chl a fell sharply within 1 day, but with one chamber per treatment and cells simply moved to the floc.
reasons.cost: Microcystin ELISA kits and cultures are $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Chlorophyll dropped within 1 day.
reasons.environment: >95% of intracellular MC-LR leaked into the water by day 7, and Microcystis-lysing and toxin-degrading bacteria were suppressed.

papers.title: Trophic state decrease after lanthanum-modified bentonite (Phoslock) application to a hyper-eutrophic polymictic urban lake frequented by Canada geese (Branta canadensis)
papers.authors: Gertrud K. Nürnberg, Bruce D. LaZerte
papers.scale: Whole lake, Swan Lake (Greater Toronto), 5.5 ha, max depth 4.4 m, polymictic former gravel pit, terminal lake with limited flushing
papers.dose: Phoslock (La-modified bentonite) 25.2 metric tonnes, 4.6 t/ha, applied 29 April-1 May 2013
papers.duration: Pre-treatment monitoring from August 2011; 2 years post-treatment (2013-2014)
papers.result: Mean TP fell from 0.247 to 0.099 mg/L (year 1) and 0.060 mg/L (year 2); phytoplankton biomass fell only in year 2, when growing-season Secchi rose to 1.4 m from 0.5 m, moving the lake from hyper-eutrophic to eutrophic. Canada geese then supplied ~75% of nutrient input.
papers.env_effects: Waterfowl (geese) supplied ~75% of nutrients; repeated treatment or waterfowl management recommended.
papers.key_details: Before-after study of a single hyper-eutrophic urban lake without a control lake; phytoplankton tracked as chlorophyll a (uncorrected) and Secchi depth. First-year TP and TN fell 60% and 40% but trophic state did not change, attributed to late application after winter sediment P had already been taken up by phytoplankton. Mixing regime (Schmidt stability 1-6 J/m²) was similar before and after, so changes were not due to mixing. Pre-treatment internal load was estimated at 650-1100 mg/m²/yr; hypoxia remained widespread. Authors recommend goose management or repeat treatment.

reasons.reproducibility: Whole-lake Phoslock treatment of a 5.5 ha urban lake.
reasons.effectiveness: TP fell from 0.247 to 0.060 mg/L, but phytoplankton biomass fell only in year 2 and no percent is given.
reasons.cost: Whole-lake dosing exceeds $5,000.
reasons.time: Two years of follow-up.
reasons.environment: Lanthanum clay persists, and goose nutrient inputs mean repeat dosing may be needed.

papers.title: In situ evaluation of options for chemical treatment of hepatotoxic cyanobacterial blooms
papers.authors: Angeline K.-Y. Lam, Ellie E. Prepas
papers.venue: Canadian Journal of Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences
papers.scale: Closed-bottom limnocorrals in a hardwater Alberta lake
papers.dose: Lime-alum vs Reglone A algicide vs lime alone
papers.result: Lime-alum and Reglone A both removed phytoplankton, but exo-microcystin in lime-alum enclosures peaked 32-fold lower than with the lytic algicide.
papers.env_effects: Lime alone raised pH above 10 and increased dissolved microcystin (pH shock); lime-alum precipitated intact cells without toxin release.

reasons.reproducibility: In-lake limnocorrals with lime-alum and the herbicide Reglone A need field access and permits.
reasons.effectiveness: Both lime-alum and Reglone A removed phytoplankton, and lime-alum kept toxin release 32-fold lower, though no percent is given.
reasons.cost: Limnocorrals and chemicals are $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Removal seen over >5 days.
reasons.environment: Aluminium floc persists, and lime alone raised pH above 10 and released microcystin.

papers.title: Controlling Eutrophication along the Freshwater–Marine Continuum: Dual Nutrient (N and P) Reductions are Essential
papers.organism: Phytoplankton / HABs along the freshwater-marine continuum
papers.scale: Watershed to coast
papers.dose: N and P load reductions
papers.result: Argues that P-only controls upstream have worsened N-limited eutrophication downstream; both N and P reductions are needed along the continuum.
papers.env_effects: Treats the cause; nothing added to the water.
papers.key_details: Perspective essay by H.W. Paerl, not a new study. Main evidence is in situ nutrient-addition bioassays along the Neuse River Estuary, NC (N forms at 140 ug N/L, phosphate at 40 ug P/L, at 10, 25 and 50 km downstream) showing N limitation strengthening downstream of the chlorophyll maximum while P was sufficient. Argues against the Schindler et al. (2008) P-only view for estuarine and coastal systems and calls for dual N and P reductions. No treatment effect sizes.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: None; record should note it is an opinion/perspective piece supported mainly by bioassays from one estuary.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Phytoplankton / HABs along the freshwater-marine continuum

reasons.reproducibility: Review of watershed-to-coast N and P load policy; typical experiment is watershed management, not repeatable by a student.
reasons.effectiveness: Perspective essay; its evidence is nutrient-addition bioassays in one estuary (Neuse) showing N limitation downstream, with no measured bloom reduction.
reasons.cost: Watershed load reduction costs millions.
reasons.time: Load reductions act over years to decades.
reasons.environment: Nothing added to the water; treats the cause.

papers.title: Determining Critical Nutrient Thresholds Needed to Control Harmful Cyanobacterial Blooms in Eutrophic Lake Taihu, China
papers.authors: Xu Hui, Hans W. Paerl, Boqiang Qin, Guangwei Zhu, Nathan S. Hall, Yuchen Wu
papers.scale: Six in-situ 1 L Cubitainer dilution bioassays (triplicate, 30-70% dilution, 2-day incubations; spring 2009-2012, August 2009, October 2010) plus an August 2013 N and P gradient bioassay in 100 L buckets (up to 10 days), Lake Taihu; mass-balance load model
papers.dose: Dilution with N- and P-free major-ion solution, then N and/or P added back; August 2013: P 0-0.08 mg/L at fixed N 2.00 mg/L and N 0-1.00 mg/L at fixed P 0.20 mg/L, pulsed daily for 5 days
papers.result: P limited phytoplankton in spring (DIN could be diluted 70% without reducing growth) and N limited it during the summer bloom. Recommended bloom-free targets (Chl a <20 µg/L) are 1.26 mg/L TN and 0.082 mg/L TP, which by mass balance require cutting external loads by 61-71% for TN and 20-46% for TP.
papers.env_effects: None directly; informs load targets.
papers.key_details: Nutrient-threshold study, not a test of an actual load reduction: short in-situ bioassays with natural phytoplankton, triplicate treatments, then a mass-balance model to convert in-lake targets into load targets (TN 15,707 and TP 1,640 x10^3 kg/yr vs current means of 46,000 and 2,170 x10^3 kg/yr). Microcystis made up 60-90% of bloom biomass. Internal sediment loading was estimated at 13-20% (TN) and 12-19% (TP) of external loads, and legacy sediment P is expected to delay recovery. Bottle/bucket incubations may not reflect continuous field nutrient supply, which the authors address with daily nutrient pulses.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record's thresholds (TN <0.80, TP <0.05 mg/L) are not the recommended management targets; the paper recommends 1.26 mg/L TN and 0.082 mg/L TP to keep Chl a below 20 µg/L. Setting is bioassays plus modelling, not mesocosm treatment of the lake.

reasons.reproducibility: Nutrient dilution/enrichment bioassays in microcosms are bench-doable with a sponsor, though mesocosms were in Lake Taihu.
reasons.effectiveness: A threshold study, not a load cut: 2-day dilution bioassays and a 10-day bucket gradient show P limits in spring and N in summer, and recommend TN 1.26 / TP 0.082 mg/L via 61-71% TN load cuts.
reasons.cost: 1 L cubitainers, 100 L buckets and nutrient/chlorophyll analyses are roughly $150-500.
reasons.time: Bioassays ran 2 days (up to 10 days for the gradient test).
reasons.environment: Dilution adds nothing harmful; informs targets.

papers.title: Solving Problems Resulting from Solutions: Evolution of a Dual Nutrient Management Strategy for the Eutrophying Neuse River Estuary, North Carolina
papers.authors: Hans W. Paerl, Lexia M. Valdes, Alan R. Joyner, Michael F. Piehler, Martin E. Lebo
papers.scale: Neuse River Estuary, NC (watershed scale)
papers.dose: P-detergent ban (January 1988) and wastewater P-discharge limits in the late 1980s; later N reductions mandated by the Neuse River Basin TMDL
papers.result: After the late-1980s P controls, upstream freshwater Chl a and nuisance cyanobacterial blooms dropped (very low mean annual Chl a in 1989) and upstream blooms stayed absent, with cyanobacteria giving way to chlorophytes and diatoms. But TN/TP rose most in the mid-estuary, where Chl a and blooms of dinoflagellates and cryptomonads grew larger in 1989-1992, 1994-1996 and 2000-2003, so the bloom zone moved downstream.
papers.env_effects: Single-nutrient control moved the problem downstream; supports a dual N+P strategy.
papers.key_details: Long-term monitoring analysis (1978-2003) of the Neuse River Estuary, not a controlled experiment. Upstream P-only control succeeded locally against cyanobacteria but the eutrophication gradient and Chl a maximum migrated downstream to N-limited mesohaline waters. Hurricanes and floods added large variability but, the authors argue, did not change the long-term pattern. Similar downstream shifts are cited for the Potomac/Chesapeake and Swedish Baltic fjords. Authors recommend dual N and P reductions starting upstream.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record frames the P-only outcome as 'likely shifted'; the paper documents a clear upstream success against cyanobacterial blooms plus larger mid-estuary blooms of dinoflagellates and cryptomonads (not cyanobacteria) afterwards.

reasons.reproducibility: Neuse River Estuary watershed-scale P ban and wastewater upgrades.
reasons.effectiveness: P-only control removed upstream cyanobacterial blooms, but mid-estuary dinoflagellate and cryptomonad blooms grew larger in 1989-2003; monitoring only, no control.
reasons.cost: Wastewater upgrades cost millions.
reasons.time: Decades.
reasons.environment: Nothing added, but single-nutrient control moved the problem downstream.

papers.title: Lake responses to reduced nutrient loading – an analysis of contemporary long‐term data from 35 case studies
papers.authors: Erik Jeppesen, Martin Søndergaard, Jens Peder Jensen, Karl E. Havens, Orlane Anneville, Laurence Carvalho et al.
papers.scale: 35 shallow and deep lakes in North America and Europe (latitude 28-65 deg), recovery periods 5-35 years
papers.dose: External TP load reduction
papers.result: Summer chl a declined as TP fell in 71% of shallow and 69% of deep lakes; lake TP stayed above Vollenweider predictions for 5-10 years (internal loading) and reached a new equilibrium after 10-15 years. Cyanobacteria share declined in 80% of deep lakes, with no significant pattern in shallow lakes, where they stayed important down to ~50 ug TP/L.
papers.env_effects: Internal loading delayed recovery; TN load cuts were smaller than TP cuts.
papers.key_details: Synthesis of 35 case studies built on a questionnaire plus loading and lake data at maximum loading and every 5 years afterwards (3-year averages). All lakes had P-loading reductions, mostly beginning in the 1970s-1980s; three also had fish removal (Balaton, Veluwemeer, Apopka). Summer TP fell in 76% of shallow lakes and all deep lakes; phytoplankton biomass declined in 71% of shallow and 70% of deep lakes (not significant in sign tests). N response time was typically <5 years versus 10-15 years for P. There were no untreated control lakes, and some lakes (Peipsi, Vortsjarv) saw chl a rise despite load cuts, attributed to warming.

reasons.reproducibility: Analysis of 35 lakes' long-term TP-load reductions; field management, not repeatable.
reasons.effectiveness: Chl a fell in 71% of shallow and 69-70% of deep lakes and cyanobacteria share fell in 80% of deep lakes, but not in shallow ones; no control lakes and some lakes worsened.
reasons.cost: Catchment load reduction costs far over $5,000.
reasons.time: New equilibrium after 10-15 years (mean 16 years of data).
reasons.environment: Nothing added; internal loading delayed recovery but no harm.

papers.title: Eutrophication of lakes cannot be controlled by reducing nitrogen input: Results of a 37-year whole-ecosystem experiment
papers.authors: David W. Schindler, Robert E. Hecky, D. L. Findlay, Michael P. Stainton, Brian R. Parker, Michael J. Paterson et al.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.scale: Whole-lake experiment, Lake 227, Experimental Lakes Area
papers.dose: Lake 227 fertilizer P held near 20-32 kg/yr throughout; N cut from 308 kg/yr (1970-74, N:P 12.4) to 110 kg/yr (1975-89, N:P ~4.7) to 0 (1990-2005)
papers.result: After N fertilizer was cut and then stopped, N-fixing cyanobacteria (Aphanizomenon schindlerii) dominated and made up the N deficit; mean phytoplankton biomass (9,306 mg/m3) did not differ significantly among N:P periods, and annual chlorophyll a stayed 17-59 ug/L.
papers.env_effects: Shows N reduction alone fails in this lake; P control needed (contested by dual-nutrient advocates).
papers.key_details: Single whole-lake experiment (Lake 227, ELA, Ontario) fertilized 1969-2005 with nearly constant P while N input was reduced stepwise to zero; no replicate lake. N fixation (from heterocyst counts) was negligible before 1975 and rose after N:P was lowered. Biomass ranged 1,502-39,000 mg/m3 with no significant difference among periods; chlorophyll per unit biomass fell when N was scarce, so chlorophyll alone can mislead. Pike were added in 1993-1994 (food-web manipulation superimposed).
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: None material; record lacked the load figures and the finding that biomass did not differ among N:P periods.

reasons.reproducibility: 37-year whole-lake fertilization experiment in the Experimental Lakes Area.
reasons.effectiveness: Cutting N from 308 to 0 kg/yr let N-fixers take over; mean biomass (9,306 mg/m3) did not differ among N:P periods in this single unreplicated lake.
reasons.cost: Whole-lake decades-long experiment far exceeds $5,000.
reasons.time: 37 years.
reasons.environment: N reduction adds nothing; no non-target harm reported.

papers.title: Toward Reversal of Eutrophic Conditions in a Subtropical Estuary: Water Quality and Seagrass Response to Nitrogen Loading Reductions in Tampa Bay, Florida, USA
papers.authors: Holly S. Greening, Anthony J. Janicki
papers.scale: Tampa Bay estuary, Florida
papers.dose: Advanced wastewater treatment (TN <=3 mg/L, cutting that source's TN load by 90%), 1980s stormwater rules and port-facility BMPs; estimated total N load fell 60% (1985-2003 vs mid-1970s); later 'hold the line' at 1992-1994 load levels
papers.result: Estimated N loading fell 60% from the mid-1970s to 1985-2003; Chl a declined significantly from 1985, most in Hillsborough Bay (25-35 µg/L in the mid-1970s to typically <15 µg/L), and Secchi depth there rose from <0.6 m to 1.0-1.4 m. Seagrass grew by 2127 ha from 1982 to 1996, lost 839 ha in 1996-1999 (El Niño) and regained 883 ha by 2004, the highest cover since 1950 but still 5512 ha below the 1950 extent.
papers.env_effects: Reduced extent and duration of hypoxia; seagrass recovery. Projected 20% population growth and 7% higher N loading by 2010 require ~15.4 metric tons TN/yr of further reductions to hold the line.
papers.key_details: Case study of Tampa Bay management using monthly sampling at >50 fixed sites since 1974 and biennial seagrass mapping since 1988. Point sources had made up 55% of N load before advanced wastewater treatment. Water-quality gains followed load cuts with no control estuary, so attribution is observational. Seagrass targets are set by the depth receiving 20.5% of surface light for Thalassia testudinum. Phytoplankton here is general Chl a, not a specific HAB taxon.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record lacks the 60% N-load reduction and the Chl a drop (25-35 to <15 µg/L in Hillsborough Bay); '25% seagrass increase since 1982' was not found as such, the text gives +2127 ha (1982-1996), -839 ha, +883 ha (to 2004), still 5512 ha below 1950.

reasons.reproducibility: Tampa Bay estuary program with multi-entity N load reduction.
reasons.effectiveness: After ~60% N-load cuts, Hillsborough Bay chl a fell from 25-35 to typically <15 ug/L, but attribution is observational (no control estuary) and it is general chl a, not a HAB taxon.
reasons.cost: Estuary-wide management costs millions.
reasons.environment: Nothing added; seagrass recovered.

papers.title: Long-term nutrient reductions lead to the unprecedented recovery of a temperate coastal region
papers.authors: Jonathan S. Lefcheck, Robert J. Orth, William C. Dennison, David J. Wilcox, Rebecca R. Murphy, Jennifer Keisman et al.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.scale: Chesapeake Bay, 30 years of data
papers.dose: Management-driven nitrogen reductions
papers.result: Water-column N fell on average 23% and P 8% since 1984; SAV cover rose 316%, from 7,878 ha (1984) to 24,874 ha (2015). Structural equation models link lower nutrients to SAV recovery, with P acting via phytoplankton chlorophyll-a and N acting directly (about 3x stronger than the chlorophyll/clarity path).
papers.env_effects: Positive habitat recovery; nothing added to the water.
papers.key_details: Observational analysis of 30 years of Chesapeake Bay aerial SAV surveys and water-quality monitoring using structural equation models (120 subestuaries coupled to watershed loads, plus a bay-wide model). No experimental control; attribution to management is by model. Outcome is seagrass cover, not phytoplankton or HAB abundance; chlorophyll-a appears only as an intermediate path from phosphorus.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record implies phytoplankton outcomes; the paper reports none directly (target is SAV). Adds that P fell only 8% and that the direct N effect outweighed the chlorophyll path.
papers.study_note: N and seagrass recovery only; no phytoplankton endpoint

reasons.reproducibility: Chesapeake Bay management-driven N reductions over 30 years.
reasons.effectiveness: Outcome is seagrass (+316%), not phytoplankton; chl a appears only as a modelled path, and water-column P fell just 8%.
reasons.cost: Bay-wide program costs billions.
reasons.environment: Nothing added; habitat recovery.

papers.title: Recovery of Danish Coastal Ecosystems After Reductions in Nutrient Loading: A Holistic Ecosystem Approach
papers.authors: Bo Riemann, Jacob Carstensen, Karsten Dahl, Henrik Fossing, Jens Würgler Hansen, Hans Henrik Jakobsen et al.
papers.scale: Danish coastal waters
papers.dose: N loads cut ~50% and P 56% since 1990
papers.result: Land-based N inputs fell ~50% and P 56% since 1990; annual mean chlorophyll a fell from a peak of 7 ug/L (1985) to ~2.5 ug/L, and Secchi depth rose only from ~4.2 m (early 1980s) to 5.1 m (2013). Bottom-water oxygen did not improve.
papers.env_effects: Stratification and warming offset oxygen gains; filter-feeding benthos declined; Secchi gains modest.
papers.key_details: Observational 25-year synthesis of Danish national monitoring data (nutrient loads, concentrations, chlorophyll a, Secchi, macroalgae, eelgrass, benthos, oxygen); no control area. Chlorophyll decline in spring followed P reductions; the continued decline since the mid-1990s mainly followed N reductions (May-October N limitation). Macroalgal cover rose 0.69%/yr and eelgrass spread deeper only in the last 5 years. Oxygen gains were offset by more frequent stratification and warming. effect_pct 64 is computed from the 7 to ~2.5 ug/L chlorophyll decline, not stated by the authors.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record had no phytoplankton magnitude; full text gives chlorophyll a 7 to ~2.5 ug/L. Secchi did not improve after 1990 despite the chlorophyll decline.

reasons.reproducibility: Danish national coastal N (~50%) and P (56%) load cuts.
reasons.effectiveness: Annual chl a fell from 7 to ~2.5 ug/L (~64%) after ~50% N and 56% P cuts, but it is observational with no control area and Secchi barely rose.
reasons.cost: National program costs far over $5,000.
reasons.time: 25 years.
reasons.environment: Nothing added; filter-feeding benthos declined, cause uncertain.

papers.title: Inadequacy of best management practices for restoring eutrophic lakes in the United States: guidance for policy and practice
papers.scale: US lakes; BMP performance literature
papers.dose: Watershed best management practices
papers.result: Restoring most eutrophic lakes needs >80% external P reduction, but watershed BMPs achieve at most ~50% and in practice <25%, explaining the few positive outcomes.
papers.env_effects: Recommends supplementing with P inactivation or engineered treatment.

reasons.reproducibility: Review of US watershed BMP performance; not repeatable by a student.
reasons.effectiveness: Negative: BMPs achieve <=50% (in practice <25%) P reduction when >80% is needed, explaining few successes.
reasons.cost: Watershed BMPs cost far over $5,000.
reasons.time: Years to decades.
reasons.environment: BMPs add nothing to water.

papers.title: Phosphorus and nitrogen loading restraints are essential for successful eutrophication control of Lake Rotorua, New Zealand
papers.authors: Val H. Smith, Susanna A. Wood, Chris G. McBride, Javier Atalah, David P. Hamilton
papers.scale: Lake Rotorua, New Zealand; >10 yr data plus a global lake dataset
papers.dose: Catchment N and P load targets (target TLI 4.2 needs TN and TP loads well below current); 496 t Al added as alum to 2 tributaries June 2006-June 2015
papers.result: GAMs showed highly significant (p<0.001) declines in TP, TN and Chl-a in 2001-2015, and the target TLI of 4.2 was reached in 2012. Much of the improvement tracks tributary alum dosing: modelled TP fell from ~35 to 15 mg/m3 as dosing rose to 0.2 t Al/d, and Chl-a fell nearly 4-fold at the maximum 0.3 t Al/d.
papers.env_effects: Includes alum dosing (aluminium addition) alongside catchment controls.
papers.key_details: Case study of Lake Rotorua (New Zealand) using two >10-year water-quality datasets with generalised additive models, plus comparison with a global lake dataset, to argue for dual N and P control. Alum dosing entered the models as an 18-month rolling mean and had a highly significant negative effect on TP and Chl-a (p<0.001). Agriculture covers ~45% of the catchment and supplies an estimated 75% of the N load and 45% of the P load. The authors do not advocate alum dosing in perpetuity; success means removing alum while holding TLI <=4.2. Observational, with no control lake.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record credits catchment nutrient-load reduction; the paper attributes much of the 2001-2015 Chl-a decline to in-stream alum dosing (a chemical P-inactivation measure), with catchment load targets not yet met.

reasons.reproducibility: Lake Rotorua catchment load targets plus alum dosing of two tributaries.
reasons.effectiveness: Chl a and TP declined significantly (p<0.001) and target TLI was reached in 2012, but much of the gain tracks tributary alum dosing rather than load cuts, with no control lake.
reasons.cost: Catchment program and alum dosing cost far over $5,000.
reasons.environment: About 496 t of aluminium as alum was dosed into two tributaries over 9 years; catchment load targets were not yet met.

papers.title: Eutrophication and harmful algal blooms: A scientific consensus
papers.authors: J. Heisler, Patricia M. Glibert, JoAnn M. Burkholder, Donald Mark Anderson, William P. Cochlan, William C. Dennison et al.
papers.scale: US EPA expert consensus roundtable
papers.dose: n/a
papers.result: Seven consensus statements, including that nutrient pollution promotes many HABs and that managing watershed nutrient inputs can lead to significant reductions in HABs.
papers.env_effects: Treats the cause; nothing added.
papers.key_details: Consensus paper from a 2003 US EPA-sponsored roundtable; review, no new data. Case examples: Seto Inland Sea red tides rose sevenfold (1965-1976), then fell to less than 30% of the peak frequency (>300 blooms/yr) after the 1973 law halving loads; phosphate removal from sewage on a Chesapeake Bay tributary reduced Microcystis blooms; Long Island brown tides nearly disappeared in the mid-2000s alongside N reductions. Correlational evidence only.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: None; record could add the Seto Inland Sea example (red tides fell to <30% of a >300/yr peak after loads were halved).

reasons.reproducibility: EPA consensus statements; the typical intervention is watershed nutrient management.
reasons.effectiveness: Consensus review with correlational cases, e.g. Seto Inland Sea red tides fell to <30% of a >300/yr peak after loads were halved; no controlled data.
reasons.cost: Watershed programs far exceed $5,000.
reasons.time: Years.
reasons.environment: Nothing added; treats the cause.

papers.title: Contributions of external nutrient loading and internal cycling to cyanobacterial bloom dynamics in Lake Taihu, China: Implications for nutrient management
papers.authors: Hai Yan Xu, Mark J. McCarthy, Hans W. Paerl, Justin D. Brookes, Guangwei Zhu, Nathan S. Hall et al.
papers.scale: Lake Taihu, China; mass balance 2005-2018
papers.dose: External loading 2005-2018: tributaries 16.6-24.1 g TN/m2/yr (mean 19.3) and 0.73-1.20 g TP/m2/yr (mean 0.89), plus atmospheric 3.8 g TN and 0.09 g TP/m2/yr; loads rose after 2007 to 2010, fell to 2013 and rose again to 2016, tracking inflow
papers.result: Over 2005-2018, lake TN concentration fell 40% (p < 0.01) but TP did not decline, and annual mean Chl a rose slightly, peaking at 44 µg/L in 2017; annual TN and TP loading showed no relationship with Chl a. Internal P release supplied 23-90% of bloom P demand and water-column regeneration 38-58% of summer-fall demand.
papers.env_effects: Denitrification removed 54% of external N; parallel N and P cuts recommended.
papers.key_details: Whole-lake nutrient mass balance for Lake Taihu (2005-2018) from monitoring data, with estimates of burial, denitrification, water-column regeneration and internal P loading; observational, no control. Tributaries supplied 83% of TN and 91% of TP inputs, atmospheric deposition 16% and 9%, N2 fixation only 0.38% of TN. Authors expect a lag between load cuts and bloom decline because of legacy internal N and P, and argue that cutting N along with P gives faster recovery since denitrification removes N. Warming is expected to lower bloom nutrient thresholds.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record implies steady external load reductions; the paper shows external loads fluctuated with inflow (up 2007-2010, down to 2013, up to 2016) rather than declining steadily, TN concentration fell 40% while TP did not decline, and Chl a slightly increased.

reasons.reproducibility: 14-year mass balance of Lake Taihu.
reasons.effectiveness: External loads fluctuated rather than fell; TN fell 40% but TP did not and chl a rose slightly (peak 44 ug/L in 2017), with internal P supplying 23-90% of demand.
reasons.cost: Lake-scale program and monitoring far exceed $5,000.
reasons.time: 14 years.
reasons.environment: Nothing added; no harm reported.

papers.title: Recent advances in ultrasonic treatment: Challenges and field applications for controlling harmful algal blooms (HABs)
papers.authors: Park J, Church J, Son Y, Kim K, Lee WH
papers.scale: Literature review of lab, pilot and field studies
papers.dose: Various frequencies, intensities and exposure times (reviewed)
papers.result: Review concluding that field efficacy of ultrasound for HAB control 'is still debatable', with only a few full-scale field tests. The authors' own tests: a commercial LG Sonic e-tank reduced Microcystis 43% vs 5% in the control after 4.8 days in 50 L reservoir water, but both fell similarly after 11 days; sound pressure dropped 85.6% within 1 m in a lab tank and 91.3-95.8% within 1 m in Daechung reservoir.
papers.env_effects: Authors describe ultrasound as leaving no chemical residues; toxin release from lysed cells is discussed as a concern.
papers.key_details: Narrative review of mechanisms (cavitation, gas-vesicle collapse), influencing factors (frequency, intensity, duration, cell morphology), toxin removal, pilot studies and scale-up challenges (flow, turbidity, HRT, light, nutrient loading). It adds original case studies. In the lab test, two 50 L containers of Daecheung reservoir water were inoculated with Microcystis (~300,000 cells/mL) with one control and no replication, run July 7-21, 2016; ultrasound improved reduction by 30-55.2% over control between 4.8 and 7.8 days, and the difference was gone by day 11. Hydrophone surveys showed stable frequencies but steep pressure attenuation (e.g. 53.73 Pa at the device to 6.79 Pa at 0.5 m and ~0.3 Pa at 10 m in the reservoir). The authors recommend multiple devices for large reservoirs.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record omits the paper's own unreplicated experiments: a transient 30-55% Microcystis reduction vs control that vanished by day 11, and >85% sound-pressure attenuation within 1 m.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Cyanobacteria and HAB algae (review)

reasons.reproducibility: Review plus 50 L container tests with a commercial ultrasound unit; doable with a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: The authors' own unreplicated test gave a transient 30-55% Microcystis cut that vanished by day 11; field efficacy 'still debatable'.
reasons.cost: A commercial LG Sonic unit costs $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Largest difference seen at 4.8-7.8 days.
reasons.environment: No chemical residue, but toxin release from lysed cells is a concern.

papers.title: Beating the blues: Is there any music in fighting cyanobacteria with ultrasound?
papers.organism: Anabaena sp., Cylindrospermopsis raciborskii, Microcystis aeruginosa, Scenedesmus obliquus, Daphnia magna
papers.scale: Laboratory cultures
papers.dose: Four commercial Flexidal AL-10 pond transducers (square waves at ~20, 28 and 44 kHz; acoustic power 0.7 +/- 0.2 W) in 800 mL cultures
papers.duration: 5-19 days (Anabaena 19 d, Cylindrospermopsis 10 d, Microcystis 7 d, Scenedesmus/Daphnia 5 d)
papers.result: Ultrasound did not kill Anabaena (biovolume growth rate cut from 0.28 to 0.02 /d, but filaments fragmented and chlorophyll kept rising) and had little effect on Cylindrospermopsis. Microcystis chlorophyll growth rate was actually higher under ultrasound (0.74 vs 0.59 /d), and all Daphnia died within 15 min of exposure.
papers.env_effects: All Daphnia magna exposed to ultrasound died within 15 min (all controls survived), removing grazing control of Scenedesmus.
papers.key_details: Lab jar experiments (1 L jars, 800 mL, 25 C, 14:10 light-dark) run in 2007, with four transducer jars vs four untreated controls (n=4; Scenedesmus/Daphnia in duplicates). Endpoints were chlorophyll-a, biovolume, particle counts, particle volume and PSII efficiency, with t-tests on growth rates. Anabaena filaments shrank from 331 to 28 um (56 to 7 cells per filament), so particle counts rose. Scenedesmus biomass was lowered only by Daphnia alone; with ultrasound plus Daphnia it matched controls because the Daphnia died. The authors conclude the tested commercial devices are not a solution for cyanobacterial blooms.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record says Microcystis growth was unchanged; its chlorophyll-based growth rate was significantly higher under ultrasound (0.74 vs 0.59 /d). The record also omits the 100% Daphnia mortality within 15 min.

reasons.reproducibility: 800 mL jar cultures with commercial pond transducers; bench scale but needs purchased strains and devices.
reasons.effectiveness: No kill: Anabaena fragmented and Microcystis grew faster under ultrasound (0.74 vs 0.59 /d).
reasons.cost: Four commercial pond transducers plus cultures cost $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Growth compared over 5-19 days; Microcystis 7 days.
reasons.environment: All Daphnia died within 15 min of exposure.

papers.title: Effects of Hydrogen Peroxide and Ultrasound on Biomass Reduction and Toxin Release in the Cyanobacterium, Microcystis aeruginosa
papers.authors: Lürling M, Meng D, Faassen EJ
papers.scale: Laboratory suspensions
papers.dose: Commercial Flexidal AL-05 and AL-10 transducers, ~20/28/44 kHz block waves, acoustic power ~0.63-0.68 W
papers.result: Chlorophyll-a rose as strongly under ultrasound as in the control; particle counts rose 1.2x vs 2.3x in controls and PSII efficiency fell only slightly (0.56 to 0.52-0.53). Dissolved microcystin share after 5 d was 19% vs 5% in controls; authors conclude commercial transducers are ineffective.
papers.env_effects: Increased the dissolved (released) microcystin fraction.

reasons.reproducibility: Bench suspensions of purchased Microcystis PCC 7820 with commercial Flexidal transducers; feasible with a sponsor but needs a toxic strain and specific gear.
reasons.effectiveness: Chlorophyll-a rose as much as in controls and PSII efficiency fell only 0.56 to 0.52-0.53; authors call the transducers ineffective.
reasons.cost: Commercial Flexidal AL-05/AL-10 units plus a culture-collection strain likely cost $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Result visible after the 5-day exposure.
reasons.environment: Dissolved microcystin share rose to 19% vs 5% in controls, i.e. toxin release.

papers.title: Evaluation of several end-of-pipe measures proposed to control cyanobacteria
papers.authors: Lürling M, Waajen G, de Senerpont Domis LN
papers.scale: Critical review of end-of-pipe measures incl. ultrasound
papers.dose: n/a
papers.result: Field evidence for ultrasound is weak: in a 365,000 m3 reservoir with 10 x 2 x 100 W (200 kHz) units, chl-a was 81 (+/-56) ug/L before vs 74 (+/-42) ug/L during treatment, and a 9,000 m3 pond study (630 W, 22 kHz) showed no difference by the end. Field intensities (~5.5e-9 to 7e-8 W/mL) are orders of magnitude below lab intensities, and commercial 20-200 kHz units cannot resonate 60-70 nm gas vesicles.
papers.env_effects: Targets symptoms rather than nutrient enrichment.
papers.key_details: Critical review (Lurling et al., Aquatic Ecology 2016) of effective microorganisms, golden algae, plant extracts, ultrasound and mixing of non-stratifying waters. For ultrasound it re-analyses published field studies (data digitized from figures) and applies resonance physics to gas vesicle sizes. Cites controlled lab tests where commercial transducers (20, 28, 44 kHz, 0.7 W) failed to control Anabaena, Cylindrospermopsis, Microcystis or Scenedesmus even in 800 mL. Concludes these end-of-pipe measures treat symptoms and none is a widely applicable solution.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: None; record lacked the specific field re-analysis numbers.

reasons.reproducibility: Critical review; the typical test is a jar culture with a commercial transducer.
reasons.effectiveness: Field chl-a 81 vs 74 ug/L before/during treatment and no pond difference; commercial frequencies cannot resonate gas vesicles.
reasons.cost: A typical jar test with a small transducer costs about $150-500.
reasons.time: Typical tests run one to three weeks.
reasons.environment: No chemicals, but treats symptoms without addressing nutrients.

papers.title: Ultrasonic frequency effects on the removal of Microcystis aeruginosa
papers.authors: Zhang G, Zhang P, Wang B, Liu H
papers.scale: Bench sonication reactor
papers.duration: minutes (sampling every 2 min; 90% removal took 100 min at 80 W and 328 min at 32 W, 80 kHz)
papers.result: Removal (OD684) followed first-order kinetics; k rose from 0.007 to 0.023 /min as power went from 32 to 80 W at 80 kHz, and was 0.114 /min at 1320 kHz vs 0.0224 /min at 20 kHz. Reaching 90% removal needed 100 min at 80 W (0.134 kWh) vs 328 min at 32 W (0.175 kWh).
papers.env_effects: No microcystin release at 32 W for 5 min and little at 15 min (safe below 48 W); at 80 kHz, 80 W, 5 min raised extracellular microcystins from 0.87 to 3.1 ug/L (MC-LR 0 to 2.11 ug/L).
papers.key_details: Bench study with lab-cultured M. aeruginosa in BG11 (near 10^9 cells/L at 14 days), sonicated in two home-made multi-frequency cells. Removal was tracked as OD684 decrease, so it reflects cell removal/decolorization rather than verified kill. Exponential- and stationary-phase cells responded similarly. Higher frequencies (410-1320 kHz) worked much better than 20-150 kHz, explained by resonance with gas-vesicle size. The authors recommend low power for drinking-water use to avoid toxin release; no replication statistics were reported in the extracted text.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: effect_pct was null; the paper reports times to 90% removal (100 min at 80 W, 80 kHz). The microcystin rise was 0.87 to 3.1 ug/L total extracellular microcystins, not 3.11.

reasons.reproducibility: Custom multi-frequency sonication reactors up to 1,320 kHz; specialist equipment.
reasons.effectiveness: 90% OD684 removal in 100 min at 80 W, but OD is not verified kill and no replication statistics were reported.
reasons.cost: Multi-frequency ultrasonic generators cost $500-5,000.
reasons.time: 90% removal within 100-328 minutes.
reasons.environment: At 80 W extracellular microcystin rose from 0.87 to 3.1 ug/L in 5 min.

papers.title: Neglected methane production and toxicity risk in low-frequency ultrasound for controlling harmful algal blooms
papers.authors: Xu H, Tang Z, Liang Z, Chen H, Dai X
papers.scale: Lab microcosm glass bottles (18.5 cm tall, 7.2 cm diameter; 200 mL lake sediment + 300 mL water), 27 bottles (3 treatments x 3 sampling batches x triplicate)
papers.dose: 29.4 kHz at 0.059 W/mL for 15 min, applied once before incubation
papers.result: Sonication cut M. aeruginosa from 6.19 x 10^8 to 4.12 x 10^8 cells/L (33.49%), but microcystin was 20.54 ug/L right after treatment (5.70-fold higher than unsonicated) and peaked at 41.18 ug/L on day 6. Cumulative CH4 by day 40 was 531.40 vs 371.67 umol/dm2 (1.43-fold).
papers.env_effects: Sonicated treatments went anaerobic immediately (DO 0.07 mg/L, ORP -360.03 mV on day 0, DO <0.1 mg/L until day 20); DOC and microcystin significantly higher than unsonicated throughout (p < 0.05); CH4 flux peaked at 41.43 vs 32.06 umol/dm2/d on day 17; shift in methanogen community.
papers.key_details: Lab microcosms with sediment and filtered water from a campus landscape lake (Tongji University) during a bloom. Three treatments: sediment + water control, unsonicated M. aeruginosa, and pre-sonicated M. aeruginosa, each in triplicate with destructive sampling, incubated 40 days at 25 C. The design simulates bloom collapse after one sonication rather than ongoing field treatment. Both algae treatments became anoxic, but the sonicated one did so from day 0 while the unsonicated one did so by day 9-12.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: The setting is a lab bottle microcosm (500 mL per bottle), not a mesocosm. The record omits the 5.70-fold higher microcystin right after sonication (20.54 ug/L) and the 41.18 ug/L peak.

reasons.reproducibility: Bottle microcosms with lake sediment and a lab sonicator; doable with a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: One 15 min sonication cut M. aeruginosa by only 33.5%.
reasons.cost: Sonicator access, bottles and cell counts cost about $150-500.
reasons.time: Cell reduction was immediate after 15 min sonication (harm tracked over 40 days).
reasons.environment: Microcystin rose 5.7x at once (peak 41 ug/L), water went anoxic and methane rose 1.43x.

papers.title: Variation of efficiencies and limits of ultrasonication for practical algal bloom control in fields
papers.authors: Park J, Son Y, Lee WH
papers.organism: Natural Microcystis sp.-dominated (>99%) reservoir water (Chungju Dam), South Korea
papers.scale: Field test at Baekje weir, Geum River; 100 L pilot batch reactor; 4 m3 algal raceway pond with circulation
papers.dose: 36, 108 and 175 kHz at 300-650 W; pilot power density 0.0030-0.0065 W/mL; raceway 7.5 x 10^-5 to 1.63 x 10^-4 W/mL
papers.duration: 10-20 min in pilot tests; 60 min circulation (30 min cumulative exposure) in raceway
papers.result: In the 100 L pilot, 10 min of sonication cut Chl-a and Microcystis cells by about 80% at all frequencies, and 20 min gave 80-90% reduction out to 1.0 m; within 5 min, reduction fell from ~80% at 0.1 m to 15% (Chl-a) at 1.0 m. In the 4 m3 raceway, 108 kHz-450 W and 175 kHz-650 W gave >40% Chl-a and >60% cell reduction after 10 min, with efficiency falling after 60 min.
papers.env_effects: Extracellular microcystin rose as Chl-a fell, more at 36 kHz and at higher power (650 vs 300 W at 175 kHz).
papers.key_details: Staged tests with a customized ultrasound system in natural Microcystis bloom water (initial pilot Chl-a 1,135 mg/m3, 4.89 x 10^6 cells/mL, microcystin 8.8 ug/L). Algal reduction was measured in the supernatant after 1 h of settling, so it counts damaged or sunk cells rather than confirmed kills. The pilot used gentle manual stirring; the distance test used no mixing; the raceway had 5.8 cm/s flow and initial densities varied between runs (222-1,016 mg/m3 Chl-a). Ultrasonication efficiencies were 0.8-15.2 m3/kWh. No untreated controls are described in the text read, and there is no long-term regrowth follow-up.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record's '50-90% in the 4 m3 pond' should be >40% (Chl-a) and >60% (cells) after 10 min in the raceway; the 80-90% figures come from the 100 L pilot within 1 m. Reductions are measured after 1 h settling, and microcystin release increased.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Natural algae / cyanobacteria (Microcystis measured via

reasons.reproducibility: Customized 300-650 W ultrasound system with 100 L and 4 m3 reactors; industrial gear.
reasons.effectiveness: ~80% Chl a/cell cut in the 100 L pilot but >40-60% in the raceway, measured after 1 h settling with no untreated controls or regrowth follow-up.
reasons.cost: A custom 650 W multi-frequency system costs over $5,000.
reasons.time: Reductions appeared after 10-20 min.
reasons.environment: Extracellular microcystin rose as Chl a fell, more at 36 kHz and higher power.

papers.title: Selective Control of Cyanobacteria in Eutrophic Pond by a Combined Device of Ultrasonication and Water Pumps
papers.authors: Ahn C-Y, Joung S-H, Choi A, Kim H-S, Jang K-Y, Oh H-M
papers.scale: 9,000 m3 eutrophic pond vs untreated neighbouring pond
papers.dose: Ultrasonic apparatus plus water pumps to spread sonicated water
papers.result: Chlorophyll-a and total algae in the treated pond were 61% and 53% of the control pond; cyanobacterial growth was selectively inhibited. Cyanobacteria share rose again within days when the device was stopped.
papers.env_effects: Green algae proportion increased; effect not persistent after switch-off; unreplicated pond comparison.

reasons.reproducibility: Field trial in a 9,000 m3 eutrophic pond with an ultrasonic apparatus plus water pumps.
reasons.effectiveness: Chlorophyll-a 61% of control (39% reduction) in one unreplicated pond, and cyanobacteria rebounded within days after switch-off.
reasons.cost: Pond-scale ultrasonic device and pumps run a full season, well over $5,000.
reasons.time: Evaluated over one season (2003).
reasons.environment: Nothing added; only a shift toward green algae was reported.

papers.title: In Situ Algal Bloom Control by the Integration of Ultrasonic Radiation and Jet Circulation to Flushing
papers.authors: Nakano K, Lee TJ, Matsumura M
papers.scale: Lake Senba, Mito, Japan (33 ha, 365,000 m3, mean depth 1.0 m); 10 USRS units (12 calculated as needed), each with two 100 W, 200 kHz transducers plus a water-jet circulator
papers.dose: Ultrasonic radiation + jet circulation combined with river-water flushing at a target 75,600 m3/day (residence time 4.8 days)
papers.result: Before the test, chlorophyll-a peaked at 200 ug/L and SS at 100 mg/L with transparency <10 cm; in 1998, with the target flushing volume, SS stayed low and transparency improved, though a chlorophyll-a peak still occurred in June. In 1999 flushing fell below target and chlorophyll-a and SS rose again in summer.
papers.env_effects: Summer COD peaks fell from 30 mg/L to 12 (1998) and 18 mg/L (1999); the summer T-P peak (0.35 mg/L) disappeared, with T-P around 0.1 mg/L; the jet circulator also aerates the bottom.
papers.key_details: Whole-lake before/after trial with no control lake, sampled at three stations. Ultrasound was used only to slow cyanobacterial growth (M. aeruginosa) below the flushing dilution rate of 0.207/day; flushing was the main removal mechanism. Only 10 of the 12 calculated units were installed because of budget, positioned by computer simulation. Correlation analysis before and after the test was used to separate the effects; results depended strongly on inflow volume. Each unit drew about 1.9 kW in total (0.2 kW for sonication).

reasons.reproducibility: Whole 33 ha lake with 10 ultrasound-plus-jet units and river flushing; not school-repeatable.
reasons.effectiveness: No control lake; flushing was the main mechanism, a June Chl a peak still occurred and 1999 relapsed when flushing fell.
reasons.cost: Ten 1.9 kW units plus flushing works cost far over $5,000.
reasons.time: Judged over two years against 1996-1997.
reasons.environment: No chemicals; jets aerate the bottom and summer COD and TP peaks fell.

papers.title: Ultrasonic Treatment of Algae in a New Jersey Reservoir
papers.authors: Schneider OD, Weinrich LA, Brezinski S
papers.scale: Canoe Brook Reservoir 1, Short Hills NJ; 4 ultrasonic buoys
papers.dose: 4 LG Sonic MPC buoys (1 master, 3 slaves); programs changed during the season (Anabaena, then general cyanobacteria on Aug 25, then Aphanizomenon on Sep 9)
papers.duration: May 13 to (mid) November 12, 2014; master buoy lost communication Sep 24
papers.result: Algae stayed <2,000/mL until Aug 13, when opening the Reservoir 2 inlet seeded Aphanizomenon, which the Anabaena and general-cyanobacteria programs did not control (counts >20,000/mL). After the Aphanizomenon-specific program, Sep 17-24 showed ~93% removal by cell counts and ~63% by phycocyanin/chlorophyll fluorescence; counts rose again weeks after the master buoy failed.
papers.env_effects: Not assessed for non-target organisms; geosmin generally lower in Reservoir 1 than Reservoir 2.
papers.key_details: Utility field study at Canoe Brook Reservoir 1 (Short Hills, NJ) with weekly sampling for algal counts (including dynamic particle imaging), TOC, fluorescence EEM, geosmin/MIB and plant operating data. Comparisons were against earlier years (copper-treated before 2012; DAF plant from 2012) and against untreated Reservoir 2, whose cyanobacteria counts were up to an order of magnitude higher through early August. 2014 weather was within the 2008-2013 range but slightly drier. Unreplicated single reservoir; the effect depended on picking the right program for the dominant taxon, and the 93% figure covers one week.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: The record gives no algal effect size; the full text shows the device failed against Aphanizomenon for several weeks (counts >20,000/mL) until the program was changed, then ~93% cell-count removal over Sep 17-24. Reservoir 2 served as an untreated comparison, so 'no control reservoir' is not quite right.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Algae and cyanobacteria (taste-and-odour producers)

reasons.reproducibility: Four commercial ultrasonic buoys on a utility reservoir; not school-repeatable.
reasons.effectiveness: Failed against Aphanizomenon for weeks (>20,000/mL), then ~93% cell (63% fluorescence) removal for one week after a program change; single reservoir.
reasons.cost: Four LG Sonic buoys cost far over $5,000.
reasons.time: After the right program was set, removal showed within about 1-2 weeks.
reasons.environment: Non-target effects not assessed; geosmin generally lower than in the untreated reservoir.

papers.title: Sound field and water quality in reservoirs using ultrasound as a management strategy to control cyanobacteria blooms
papers.authors: Tischer MA, Murphy KA, Weaver CR, Crafton-Nelson E, Weavers LK
papers.scale: Five Ohio drinking-water reservoirs (3.8 x 10^5 to 5.4 x 10^6 m3) with 1-4 commercial ultrasound units from three manufacturers; at Del-Co, treated reservoir 3 vs untreated reservoirs 2 (upstream) and 4 (downstream)
papers.dose: Commercial units; measured field sound pressures and frequencies
papers.duration: Two field seasons (2022-2023); e.g. five sampling dates at Wilmington in 2022
papers.result: Sound pressure decayed exponentially from each unit, and turbidity, chlorophyll-a, phycocyanin and temperature showed no significant change with distance from the source (least-squares test, p=0.05). Chl-a and phycocyanin fell sequentially from upstream to downstream reservoirs regardless of treatment, which the authors attribute to settling; they conclude ultrasound had no effect.
papers.env_effects: None detected; no water-quality difference.
papers.key_details: Field survey combining hydrophone sound-field mapping (plus anechoic-tank tests of unit directionality) with EXO2 sonde water-quality transects. Maximum transducer pressure was 11 kPa, two orders of magnitude below that needed to collapse gas vesicles, and kHz frequencies are three orders below the MHz needed for resonance; the units operate below the cavitation threshold. Attenuation coefficients varied within a water body by a factor of 2 (low frequency) and 7 (high frequency). Only one location had control reservoirs, and the others were sampled intensively at two sites and once at three.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record's claim that attenuation was '~10x faster than in pure water' was not found in the text read; the paper cites pure water alpha = 0.0022 dB/cm/MHz and reports within-reservoir variation of 2-7x.

reasons.reproducibility: Five drinking-water reservoirs with commercial units and hydrophone mapping; not school-repeatable.
reasons.effectiveness: No change in chlorophyll, phycocyanin or turbidity with distance from units; pressures far below gas-vesicle collapse.
reasons.cost: Commercial units and hydrophone surveys cost far over $5,000.
reasons.time: Studied over two field seasons.
reasons.environment: No water-quality change detected.

papers.title: Effects of ultrasonic algal control devices on fish
papers.authors: Getchell RG, George E, Rice AN, Malatos JM, Chambers BM, Griefen A, Nieder C, Rudstam LG
papers.scale: Oneida Lake nearshore surveys (on/off) plus hydroacoustics; lab: 700 L tanks, 20 fish per tank, device on in 2 of 3 tanks per species trial
papers.dose: One Quattro-DB ultrasonic unit (Hydro BioScience): 468 ms pulses every second, energy 2-250 kHz (to 500 kHz), mean SPL 199.9 dB and max 212.3 dB re 1 uPa; estimated source level 215.5 dB
papers.result: Nearshore fish density (excluding round goby, 88% of observations) was 0.12 fish/m2 with the unit off and 0.13 with it on, with no significant difference. In 14-day tank exposures, no effects were detected on behaviour, feeding or tissues of fish or tadpoles.
papers.env_effects: No detected harm to fish or tadpoles (algal efficacy not measured).
papers.key_details: Non-target safety study, not an algal efficacy test. The authors first measured the device's actual acoustic output with calibrated hydrophones in the field and lab, finding energy well outside the manufacturer's stated bands (down to ~9.8 kHz and up to 500 kHz). Field work at Oneida Lake compared fish communities with the device on and off; lab trials used resident New York species and wild tadpoles (Lithobates spp., American toad), 20 animals per tank, 2 exposed tanks and 1 control per trial. Tank replication per species is small (2 vs 1).
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: One device model (Quattro-DB) was tested, not several devices.
papers.study_note: fish and tadpole effects of ultrasonic devices
