reasons.reproducibility: Nearshore lake surveys plus 700 L fish tanks with a commercial ultrasonic unit; needs fish permits.
reasons.effectiveness: Algal efficacy was not measured; this is a non-target safety study.
reasons.cost: One Quattro-DB unit and tanks cost $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Lab exposures lasted 14 days.
reasons.environment: No effect on fish density (0.12 vs 0.13 fish/m2) or on fish and tadpole behaviour or tissues.

papers.title: Biomanipulation as a Restoration Tool to Combat Eutrophication: Recent Advances and Future Challenges
papers.authors: Jeppesen E, Søndergaard M, Lauridsen TL, Davidson TA, Liu Z, Mazzeo N, et al.
papers.organism: Lake phytoplankton incl. cyanobacteria; planktivorous/benthivorous fish (roach, bream), piscivores, Daphnia
papers.scale: Whole lakes, temperate and warm (e.g. 27 Danish shallow lakes with >200 kg fish/ha removed)
papers.dose: Fish removal; figure shows target catch rising with lake TP (up to ~250 kg/ha/yr); single cases 213 t (226 kg/ha)
papers.duration: Short-term (1-several years) vs long-term (decades) effects reviewed
papers.result: Short-term effects of fish removal 'have often been successful, provided that they have been sufficiently strong', but long-term perspectives 'less positive'; repeated removals may be needed. External nutrient reduction remains the key measure; in-lake restoration only reinforces recovery.
papers.env_effects: Changes the whole food web; clear-water lakes retain more P in sediment, raising internal loading if they revert to turbid; effects on biodiversity and lake metabolism discussed.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Lake phytoplankton incl. cyanobacteria

reasons.reproducibility: Review of whole-lake fish removal (>200 kg/ha, up to 213 t); needs permits and fishing gear.
reasons.effectiveness: Short-term effects 'often successful' if strong enough, but long-term 'less positive' and repeats needed.
reasons.cost: Removing hundreds of kg/ha of fish far exceeds $5,000.
reasons.time: Effects judged over 1 to several years.
reasons.environment: Restructures the food web; clear-water lakes store P that can be released if they revert.

papers.title: Lake Restoration by Fish Removal: Short- and Long-Term Effects in 36 Danish Lakes
papers.authors: Søndergaard M, Liboriussen L, Pedersen AR, Jeppesen E
papers.organism: Roach (Rutilus rutilus), bream (Abramis brama); phytoplankton incl. cyanobacteria
papers.scale: 36 mainly shallow eutrophic Danish lakes (whole-lake)
papers.dose: 41-1360 kg fish/ha removed over 1-19 years (mostly within 2-4 years); 27 lakes >~200 kg/ha within 3 years (mean 410, range 190-706 kg/ha), 9 lakes <200 kg/ha (mean 91, range 41-160 kg/ha)
papers.duration: Monitored up to ~10+ years after removal
papers.result: In the 27 lakes with >200 kg/ha removed in 3 years, Chl a and suspended solids fell to 50-70% of pre-removal and Secchi depth nearly doubled over the first 8-10 years, with an effect in >75% of lakes; total algal biovolume fell 30-50% and cyanobacteria by >50% after 3-7 years (significant only in years 2-5). Chl a 'survival' was only ~10% after 5 years, and most variables drifted back toward pre-removal after ~10 years.
papers.env_effects: Cryptophytes increased substantially (significant in years 3-4); submerged macrophytes increased; Secchi depth and SS changes were the most durable (mean survival >90% after 10 years). Lakes with <200 kg/ha removal showed no clear effects on nutrients or turbidity.
papers.key_details: Before-after analysis of 36 mainly small, shallow, eutrophic Danish lakes (median 32 ha, median mean depth 1.8 m, pre-removal TP 0.061-0.437 mg/L) where planktivorous and benthivorous fish were removed; no untreated control lakes. Phytoplankton composition data came from only 10 lakes. Survival analysis showed Chl a and TP improvements were short-lived (mean survival ~10% after 5 years, wide confidence intervals), while Secchi depth and SS changes lasted longer. Long-term (>10-14 year) conclusions rest on 1-3 lakes. Pike fingerling stocking in some lakes was judged to have no significant effect.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record says Chl a, TP, TN and SS all fell to 50-70%; the paper gives 50-70% for Chl a and SS only (TP and TN 'substantial' but lower). Phytoplankton and cyanobacteria results are from 10 lakes, not 36, and Chl a gains were short-lived (~10% survival at 5 years) rather than lasting 6-10 years.

reasons.reproducibility: Whole-lake fish removal of 41-1,360 kg/ha across 36 lakes; needs permits and commercial fishing gear.
reasons.effectiveness: Chl a fell to 50-70% of pre-removal and cyanobacteria >50% (10 lakes only), but no control lakes and Chl a gains had ~10% survival after 5 years.
reasons.cost: Multi-year netting of hundreds of kg of fish per ha costs far over $5,000.
reasons.time: Effects emerged over 2-5 years of removal.
reasons.environment: Macrophytes returned and no chemicals were added, though cryptophytes increased.

papers.title: Repeated Fish Removal to Restore Lakes: Case Study of Lake Væng, Denmark—Two Biomanipulations during 30 Years of Monitoring
papers.authors: Søndergaard M, Lauridsen TL, Johansson LS, Jeppesen E
papers.organism: Roach and bream; phytoplankton; Elodea canadensis
papers.scale: 16 ha shallow lake (whole-lake)
papers.dose: First removal 1986-1988: 4 tons fish (201,000 individuals; roach 98% by number, bream 62% by weight), ~50-70% of planktivorous/benthivorous biomass; second removal Oct 2007-May 2009: 2.8 tons
papers.result: After each removal summer Chl a fell from 60-80 to 10-30 ug/L and Secchi rose from 0.6 m to 1.3-1.6 m (and >1.5 m after 2010), but the first clear-water state lasted only about a decade: Chl a climbed from 9.4 ug/L (1991) to 85 ug/L (2006) before the second removal.
papers.env_effects: Macrophyte recovery; summer TP 0.12 -> 0.07 mg/L and TN 1.0 -> 0.4 mg/L; nutrient maxima shifted from summer to winter.
papers.key_details: Whole-lake case study in shallow Lake Vaeng, Denmark (catchment 9 km2, retention 15-25 days, ~70% groundwater inflow), no control lake; 30 years of summer monitoring. Wastewater was diverted in 1981 but the lake stayed turbid (Chl a 76 ug/L in 1986). Fish removed with gill nets, traps, trawling and electrofishing. Clear periods 1989-1998 and 2009-2015 had significantly higher Secchi and lower Chl a than turbid years (t-tests, Bonferroni p<0.0025); summer TP 0.036-0.072 mg/L at high macrophyte cover vs 0.084-0.170 mg/L at low cover. After macrophytes returned, Chl a peaks shifted to winter/spring (up to 96 ug/L).
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record's framing is correct; add that the first biomanipulation's benefit decayed after ~10 years (return to turbid 1999-2008), which is why a second removal was needed.

reasons.reproducibility: Whole-lake removal of 4 and 2.8 tons of fish with gill nets, trawls and electrofishing; not school-repeatable.
reasons.effectiveness: Summer Chl a fell from 60-80 to 10-30 ug/L after each removal, but one lake with no control and the first benefit decayed within ~10 years.
reasons.cost: Two multi-year fish removal campaigns cost far over $5,000.
reasons.time: Clear water came after 2-3 year removal campaigns and was tracked over 30 years.
reasons.environment: Macrophytes recovered and TP/TN fell; no chemicals added.

papers.title: Freshwater food web biomanipulation: A powerful tool for water quality improvement, but maintenance is required
papers.organism: Planktivorous and piscivorous fish, zooplankton, algae
papers.scale: Deep stratified lakes vs shallow lakes/ponds; six manipulation categories
papers.dose: Planktivore additions, complete planktivore removals, piscivore additions
papers.result: Planktivore removals in deep lakes often reduce algae at first, but ungrazable algae take over and biomass returns to pre-manipulation levels; shallow-lake removals are more stable. Piscivore additions to deep lakes 'seldom result in more than short periods of algal control'. The consensus is that 'maintenance is required'.
papers.env_effects: Restructures food webs; species substitutions (invertebrate predators, macrophytes, ungrazable algae); reinvasion by planktivores.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Planktivorous and piscivorous fish

reasons.reproducibility: Review of whole-lake planktivore removals and piscivore stocking.
reasons.effectiveness: Deep-lake removals often revert to pre-manipulation biomass; piscivore additions 'seldom' give more than short control.
reasons.cost: Whole-lake manipulation exceeds $5,000.
reasons.time: Multi-year.
reasons.environment: Species substitutions, ungrazable algae and planktivore reinvasion.

papers.title: Possibilities and Limits for Controlling Eutrophication by Biomanipulation
papers.organism: Piscivorous and zooplanktivorous fish, Daphnia, phytoplankton
papers.scale: Long-term whole-lake experiments: Bautzen reservoir and Lake Gräfenhain
papers.dose: Strong to extremely strong enhancement of piscivorous fish stock
papers.result: Top-down effects were strong at the top of the food web, but at the phytoplankton level only composition changed and 'mean biomass is not reduced'. Sustained reduction of phytoplankton biomass is expected only below a P-loading threshold.
papers.env_effects: Hard to control 0+ fish of the stocked piscivores; invertebrate predators can compensate for fish predation.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Piscivorous and zooplanktivorous fish

reasons.reproducibility: Long-term whole-lake piscivore stocking in Bautzen reservoir and Lake Grafenhain.
reasons.effectiveness: Negative: phytoplankton 'mean biomass is not reduced', only composition changed.
reasons.cost: Reservoir-scale stocking exceeds $5,000.
reasons.time: Multi-year.
reasons.environment: Stocked piscivore young hard to control; invertebrate predators compensated.

papers.title: Do high concentrations of microcystin prevent Daphnia control of phytoplankton?
papers.authors: Chislock MF, Sarnelle O, Jernigan LM, Wilson AE
papers.organism: Daphnia pulicaria vs toxic Microcystis and Anabaena
papers.scale: Exp. 1: 4200 L enclosures in MSU Lake 2, Michigan (2 Daphnia vs 4 control enclosures after two Daphnia enclosures were invaded by fish); Exp. 2: 160 L enclosures in two hypereutrophic Auburn, Alabama catfish ponds (F19, F20), 2 Daphnia vs 2 control per pond
papers.dose: Daphnia pulicaria stocked at ~0.3 animals/L (Exp. 1) or ~0.15 animals/L as an equal mix of three clones (Exp. 2); all four clones came from southern Michigan lakes; Exp. 2 enclosures fertilized biweekly with N and P
papers.duration: Exp. 1: 2 July-6 August 2007 (~5 weeks); Exp. 2: 22 September-24 November 2010 (~50 days after stocking)
papers.result: In Michigan (initial Chl a 130 µg/L, microcystin >3 rising to ~6 µg/L), Daphnia cut total phytoplankton 74% vs controls by week 3 (P = 0.010), and Microcystis 4-fold, Oscillatoria 56-fold, Anabaena 20-fold by day 28. In Alabama (microcystin 40 and 180 µg/L), mean effect sizes were 4.5 and 7.4 (about 78% and 86% less phytoplankton) and Microcystis fell 3.8- and 19.6-fold, but cyanobacteria still dominated all enclosures.
papers.env_effects: Daphnia marginally reduced microcystin in Michigan (P = 0.063) and significantly reduced it in both Alabama ponds; microcystin rose in the Michigan enclosures overall. Community stayed cyanobacteria-dominated (no shift in relative composition).
papers.key_details: Two enclosure experiments testing whether very high microcystin prevents Daphnia pulicaria grazing control. Replication was low: Exp. 1 had only 2 Daphnia enclosures (fish invaded two others), Exp. 2 had 2 per treatment per pond. Daphnia grew exponentially (r = 0.24/day) despite microcystin and reduced absolute biomass of all cyanobacteria, but relative dominance by cyanobacteria (Microcystis) was unchanged. Microcystis colonies were of edible size (ESD 28 and 70 µm). The Alabama experiment was in autumn and fertilized to maintain the bloom.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record says 'mixture of three cyanobacteria-adapted clones (Alabama)'; the clones came from Michigan lakes and were stocked into Alabama ponds. Record implies Daphnia raised microcystin; it rose in the Michigan enclosures but Daphnia marginally lowered it vs controls and significantly lowered it in Alabama. Only 2 Daphnia enclosures in Exp. 1.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Daphnia pulicaria vs toxic Microcystis and Anabaena

reasons.reproducibility: Daphnia culturing is simple, but the trials used 4,200 L lake enclosures and 160 L enclosures in catfish ponds.
reasons.effectiveness: Daphnia cut phytoplankton 74-86% vs controls in three settings despite microcystin up to 180 ug/L, but only 2 enclosures per treatment and cyanobacteria stayed dominant.
reasons.cost: Building and stocking field enclosures costs roughly $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Total phytoplankton was significantly lower by week 3.
reasons.environment: Native grazer with no chemical residue; Daphnia also lowered microcystin vs controls.

papers.title: Controlling Harmful Cyanobacteria: Taxa-Specific Responses of Cyanobacteria to Grazing by Large-Bodied Daphnia in a Biomanipulation Scenario
papers.authors: Urrutia-Cordero P, Ekvall MK, Hansson L-A
papers.organism: Daphnia magna vs natural cyanobacteria (Aphanizomenon, Dolichospermum, Microcystis, Planktothrix)
papers.scale: Six 10 L containers (9 L filtered lake water) incubated in eutrophic Lake Ringsjön, Sweden (40 km2), plus 19-yr lake monitoring
papers.dose: Gradient of Daphnia magna biomass
papers.duration: 3-day incubations, three times in one summer; monitoring 1996-2014 (biomanipulation since 2005)
papers.result: Daphnia grazing reduced total cyanobacteria and phytoplankton and suppressed about 66% of tested bloom-forming taxa, but Dolichospermum crassum grew faster under grazing when it dominated. Lake fish reduction raised Daphnia abundance 50% and body size 20%.
papers.env_effects: Taxa-specific: grazing can favour ungrazed filamentous cyanobacteria; authors say grazer control alone may not be sufficient and nutrient reduction is preferable.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Daphnia magna vs natural cyanobacteria (Aphanizomenon

reasons.reproducibility: Six 10 L containers of filtered lake water with a Daphnia magna gradient is a school-doable bench setup.
reasons.effectiveness: Grazing suppressed ~66% of bloom taxa, but Dolichospermum grew faster under grazing: mixed.
reasons.cost: Containers and Daphnia magna ~$50-150.
reasons.time: 3-day incubations.
reasons.environment: Daphnia native and retrievable, but grazing can favour ungrazed filamentous cyanobacteria.

papers.title: Short-term fish predation destroys resilience of zooplankton communities and prevents recovery of phytoplankton control by zooplankton grazing
papers.authors: Ersoy Z, Brucet S, Bartrons M, Mehner T
papers.organism: Juvenile perch (Perca fluviatilis), lake zooplankton and phytoplankton
papers.scale: 10 enclosures (~1000 L; 6 with fish, 4 without) with natural lake plankton
papers.dose: ~20 g wet mass/m3 juvenile perch for 4 days, then removed by electrofishing
papers.result: Four days of fish predation removed large zooplankton (calanoids) permanently; total zooplankton biomass recovered and even exceeded pre-fish levels, but small cladocerans and rotifers dominated and phytoplankton escaped grazer control. Only fish-free enclosures kept phytoplankton controlled.
papers.env_effects: Shows fragility of grazer control: brief planktivore pulses (e.g. young-of-year fish) can undo biomanipulation.

reasons.reproducibility: Ten ~1000 L enclosures with juvenile perch and electrofishing need field gear and animal permits.
reasons.effectiveness: Negative: 4 days of fish predation removed large zooplankton and phytoplankton escaped grazer control.
reasons.cost: Enclosures, fish and electrofishing ~$500-5,000.
reasons.time: 4 d predation + 4 weeks recovery.
reasons.environment: Shows fragile grazer control; community shift to small cladocerans and rotifers.

papers.title: Nontraditional biomanipulation: A powerful ecotechnology to combat cyanobacterial blooms in eutrophic freshwaters
papers.authors: Chen J, Liu J, Han S, Su H, Xia W, Wang H, et al. (Xie P)
papers.organism: Silver and bighead carp vs Microcystis and other cyanobacteria
papers.scale: 42 experiments reviewed plus a whole-lake case (Lake Donghu, China)
papers.dose: Silver and bighead carp stocking; enclosure trials used roughly 8-480 g/m3; in Lake Donghu the 2022 release was doubled vs 2021 (silver:bighead 2:1), raising standing stock to 82 g/m3 (March 2022) and 192 g/m3 (September 2022)
papers.result: Filter-feeding carp substantially reduced cyanobacteria in 88% of 42 experiments; in Lake Donghu Microcystis bloom coverage fell from 87% (2021) to 0% (2022). Carp graze colonial Microcystis better than filamentous forms.
papers.env_effects: Several enclosure and pond studies were negative (e.g. Villerest Reservoir: cyanobacteria increased at 8-32 g/m3 silver carp; bighead carp in Polish ponds raised filamentous Anabaena 4-fold to 70-fold). Carp handle colonial Microcystis better than filamentous cyanobacteria; in Donghu TN, TP and NH4+ fell (1.04 to 0.75, 0.13 to 0.10, 0.15 to 0.12 mg/L) despite over 4x more fish.
papers.key_details: Review by the Lake Donghu (Institute of Hydrobiology) group of 42 enclosure, pond and whole-lake experiments; 88% showed substantial cyanobacteria reductions by filter-feeding carp. Most enclosure trials had only 2-3 replicates per treatment in small enclosures (e.g. 6-100 m2); examples include 91% reduction of M. aeruginosa in Dongzhou Reservoir enclosures and 60-93% Microcystis reduction within 3-7 days in an Indian lake. The Donghu whole-lake case is a single before/after comparison (bloom in 2021 after fish stock declined since 2004; no bloom in 2022 after doubling the fish release and limiting fishing to winter) with no control lake. Authors also report commercial fishing profit from the stock.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record does not mention that the review itself lists negative trials (fish raising cyanobacteria, especially filamentous forms and at low stocking), or that the Donghu result is an uncontrolled one-year before/after comparison by the proponents' own group.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Silver and bighead carp vs Microcystis and

reasons.reproducibility: Review; the typical trial stocks live silver/bighead carp in 6-100 m2 enclosures or whole lakes, needing permits.
reasons.effectiveness: Carp cut cyanobacteria in 88% of 42 trials, but enclosures had 2-3 replicates, several trials raised filamentous cyanobacteria, and Donghu is an uncontrolled one-year comparison.
reasons.cost: Typical enclosure carp trials cost $500-5,000; whole-lake stocking far more.
reasons.time: Enclosure effects show over weeks to months; the Donghu result took a season.
reasons.environment: Carp are non-native in many regions and low stocking or bighead carp raised Anabaena 4-70-fold in some trials.

papers.title: Role of Microcystins in Poisoning and Food Ingestion Inhibition of Daphnia galeata Caused by the Cyanobacterium Microcystis aeruginosa
papers.authors: Rohrlack T, Dittmann E, Henning M, Börner T, Kohl J-G
papers.organism: Daphnia galeata vs Microcystis aeruginosa PCC7806 (wild type and mcy- mutant)
papers.scale: Laboratory feeding and survival tests
papers.dose: M. aeruginosa PCC7806 wild type vs mcy- knockout mutant at 20 mm3/L biovolume (reference strain HUB 5-3 for ingestion); 14C-labelled cells for ingestion
papers.duration: Ingestion assays (repeated 7-9 times); 5-day life-table survival tests (4 replicates) at 20 C
papers.result: Wild-type PCC7806 killed D. galeata with a time to 50% mortality of 1.2-2.0 days, while no animals died on the microcystin-free mutant. Both variants were ingested at the same low rate, 75% below the harmless reference strain HUB 5-3.
papers.env_effects: Grazer mortality and feeding inhibition by toxic cyanobacteria.
papers.key_details: Lab test separating toxicity from feeding inhibition using a microcystin-synthetase knockout of the same strain. Ingestion measured by 14C-labelled cells (n = 7 for PCC7806 variants, n = 9 for HUB 5-3). Survival compared against a no-food control in four repeat experiments; wild type differed from starvation (log rank P < 0.001) and mutant animals survived better than starved controls (P < 0.025). Daphnia on wild type became inactive after about 5 h. Single strain and single Daphnia clone.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: None material; adds the LT50 of 1.2-2.0 days and the 75% ingestion reduction.
papers.study_note: Daphnia ingestion and poisoning by Microcystis; no bloom reduction

reasons.reproducibility: Lab feeding and survival tests with Daphnia, but needs a purchased Microcystis strain and a knockout mutant plus 14C labelling.
reasons.effectiveness: Negative for grazing control: wild-type Microcystis killed Daphnia (LT50 1.2-2.0 days) and ingestion was 75% below a harmless strain.
reasons.cost: Cultures, mutant strain and radiolabel assays cost about $150-500.
reasons.time: Daphnia mortality appeared within 1-2 days.
reasons.environment: No chemical added, but the grazer itself is poisoned by the toxic cyanobacteria.

papers.result: In natural bloom water, Artemia nauplii cut C. polykrikoides by an average 57 +/- 19% (max 78%) in 48 h, A. fundyense by 48 +/- 9%, and A. anophagefferens by 24-73% in five of six experiments. Artemia mortality was 47 +/- 2.4% in A. fundyense blooms versus 13-18% in the other blooms.
papers.env_effects: Artemia is non-native to NY estuaries (introduction risk); grazers suffer high mortality on toxic Alexandrium.

Mortality on A. fundyense was 43% (Artemia) and 72% (Acartia), significantly above other diets. papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record's '25 field experiments... six New York estuaries' was not verified in the text read; field results give mean reductions of 57% (C. polykrikoides), 48% (A. fundyense) and 24-73% (A. anophagefferens), so effect_pct can be filled.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Artemia salina (non-native) and Acartia tonsa (native

reasons.reproducibility: 50 mL flask grazing tests with brine shrimp are simple, but need purchased HAB cultures (one toxic Alexandrium).
reasons.effectiveness: Artemia cut bloom cells by a mean 48-57% (24-73% for Aureococcus) and less at high densities; moderate and variable.

reasons.time: Reductions measured in 24-48 h incubations.
reasons.environment: Artemia is non-native to NY estuaries and suffered 43-47% mortality on Alexandrium.

papers.title: Algicidal Bacteria: A Review of Current Knowledge and Applications to Control Harmful Algal Blooms
papers.authors: Coyne KJ, Wang Y, Johnson G
papers.organism: Algicidal bacteria vs marine and freshwater HAB species
papers.scale: Literature review
papers.dose: n/a
papers.result: Reviews specificity, mechanisms and applications of algicidal bacteria and bacterial algicides. Notes that 'our understanding of these interactions is largely based on laboratory culture experiments', with only some field evidence.
papers.env_effects: Review stresses that 'environmentally neutral' claims are untested; direct dispersal of live bacteria raises biosafety concerns, so immobilized or product-based deployment is proposed. Field evidence is limited to Pseudomonas fluorescens SK09 in river enclosures, with inconsistent results.
papers.key_details: Narrative review of algicidal bacteria (specificity, algicidal compounds, mechanisms, application strategies). Its table of application studies is almost entirely laboratory work. The only field applications to date all used Pseudomonas fluorescens HYK0210-SK09 in river enclosures against the diatom Stephanodiscus hantzschii; strong lab and indoor-mesocosm effects gave inconsistent results in the field. Authors cite temperature, the high bacterial densities required, grazing by protists, pH and nutrients as reasons for field failure. No new quantitative data.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record is broadly right; it understates how thin the field evidence is (a single bacterial strain in river enclosures, with inconsistent results).
papers.study_note: review of efficacy: Algicidal bacteria vs marine and freshwater HAB

reasons.reproducibility: Review; the typical application study is a sterile lab co-culture needing purchased algicidal strains and microbiology gear.
reasons.effectiveness: Evidence is almost all lab culture; the only field trials (P. fluorescens SK09 in river enclosures) gave inconsistent results.
reasons.cost: Typical lab co-culture needs purchased bacterial and algal strains plus media, roughly $150-500.
reasons.time: Lab algicidal effects in the summarized studies typically show over one to three weeks of co-culture.
reasons.environment: Authors say 'environmentally neutral' claims are untested and live-bacteria dispersal raises biosafety concerns.

papers.title: Algicidal Bacteria in the Sea and their Impact on Algal Blooms
papers.organism: Marine algicidal bacteria vs eukaryotic microalgae
papers.scale: Literature review
papers.dose: n/a
papers.result: Concludes that, because of method limitations, 'the evidence for algicidal bacteria causing algal bloom decline is circumstantial'. Calls for ecosystem-level tests rather than a focus on HAB-control utility.
papers.env_effects: Frames algicidy as part of bacterial regulation of algal community structure (i.e. community-wide, not target-only, effects).
papers.key_details: Narrative review (Mayali & Azam) with sections on definition, taxonomy, mode of action, algicidal compounds, prey specificity and ecosystem considerations; no new data. Evidence that algicidal bacteria end blooms rests on MPN counts showing algicidal bacteria increase during bloom decline (e.g. Cytophaga during a Chattonella bloom), which the authors call 'no conclusive causal evidence'. In co-culture, algal lysis was seen only after the algicidal bacterium exceeded 10^6 cells/mL, about the abundance of the whole bacterial assemblage in seawater, raising doubt that a single species reaches that level in the ocean. Other bacteria in algal cultures can partly or fully block algicidal activity (e.g. against Karenia brevis). The authors suggest bloom decline may start from nutrient limitation, viruses or other pathogens, with algicidal bacteria as secondary colonizers.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Marine algicidal bacteria vs eukaryotic microalgae

reasons.reproducibility: Review; repeating a typical co-culture needs sterile technique and purchased marine algicidal bacteria and algae.
reasons.effectiveness: Authors call the evidence that bacteria end blooms circumstantial; lysis needed >10^6 bacteria/mL and other bacteria blocked it.
reasons.cost: Typical co-culture needs purchased strains and culture media, about $150-500.
reasons.time: Co-culture lysis in the reviewed work typically takes one to three weeks to appear.
reasons.environment: Algicidy is framed as community-wide regulation, so non-target effects on other algae are uncertain.

papers.result: Alginate retained >99% of Shewanella cells after 12 days, and bead-immobilized bacteria controlled K. veneficum and P. minimum as effectively as free bacteria. No harm to the non-target cryptophyte Rhodomonas.

papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Shewanella sp. IRI-160 vs Karlodinium veneficum and

reasons.environment: Beads retained >99% of bacteria after 12 days and spared Rhodomonas.

papers.title: Evaluation of a virus-based control method to protect cultured oysters from the harmful dinoflagellate Heterocapsa circularisquama
papers.authors: Nakayama N, Hamaguchi M, Yamaguchi H, Masuda K, Fujiwara M
papers.organism: RNA virus HcRNAV vs Heterocapsa circularisquama
papers.scale: One treatment and one control 15,000 L floating 'cage' mesocosm in Lake Kamo (saltwater lake connected to the sea), Sado Island, Japan, plus lab tests; n = 3 refers to replicate samples, not replicate mesocosms
papers.dose: 1.4 kg of local surface sediment containing HcRNAV (frozen at -20 °C for one day) sprayed into 15,000 L, i.e. ~0.093-0.1 g sediment/L, at a bloom density of ~3800 cells/mL (October 2016)
papers.result: H. circularisquama in the sediment-treated mesocosm fell to ~1% of the initial density after five days, while the untreated control also fell, to 20-30%; the treatment was significantly lower than control from day 3 onward (GLM, p < .01), and HcRNAV in water rose significantly by day 2.
papers.env_effects: Sediment addition (0.093 g/L) judged negligible for bacteria, nutrients and turbidity; temperature, salinity and nutrients did not differ between treatment and control. Unpublished tests: sediment (1-10 g/L) and HcRNAV did not affect survival of juvenile oysters, pearl oysters or clams, and HcRNAV strains did not infect Karenia mikimotoi, Chattonella or Heterosigma strains. Freezing inactivated cysts in the sediment so no other HAB species emerged.
papers.key_details: Paired floating mesocosms (one treatment, one control, 15,000 L each) during a natural H. circularisquama bloom (~3800 cells/mL) in Lake Kamo, October 2016, plus lab dose tests. Treatment received 1.4 kg of HcRNAV-bearing lake sediment (~0.1 g/L). Density fell to ~1% of initial after five days versus 20-30% in the untreated control, so much of the decline also happened without treatment; treatment-control difference significant from day 3 (GLM, p < .01). The design has no mesocosm replication (one of each), and the bloom was already declining in the control. Environmental safety claims rest partly on unpublished results.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: The record's 'n = 3' implies replicated mesocosms; there was one treatment and one control mesocosm (n = 3 was sample replication). The record omits that the control bloom also dropped to 20-30% of initial in five days, so the ~99% headline overstates the treatment effect relative to control. The site is a saltwater lake (Lake Kamo), not an oyster farm as such.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: RNA virus HcRNAV vs Heterocapsa circularisquama

reasons.reproducibility: Two 15,000 L floating mesocosms in a saltwater lake with a native algal virus; field-scale and not school-repeatable.
reasons.effectiveness: Cells fell to ~1% vs 20-30% in the untreated control, significant from day 3, but only one treatment and one control mesocosm on an already-declining bloom.
reasons.cost: Floating 15,000 L mesocosms, boat work and virus assays cost well over $5,000.
reasons.time: Treatment differed from control by day 3 (GLM p<.01) and reached ~1% by day 5.
reasons.environment: 0.1 g/L sediment had no measured effect on water chemistry and HcRNAV is host-specific, but shellfish safety rests partly on unpublished tests.

papers.title: Viral Impacts on Total Abundance and Clonal Composition of the Harmful Bloom-Forming Phytoplankton Heterosigma akashiwo
papers.authors: Tarutani K, Nagasaki K, Yamaguchi M
papers.organism: HaV (Heterosigma akashiwo virus) vs Heterosigma akashiwo
papers.scale: Field time series at surface and bottom in northern Hiroshima Bay (May-July 1998) plus cross-infection tests of H. akashiwo isolates against co-occurring HaV clones
papers.dose: Natural virus populations (no addition)
papers.result: H. akashiwo reached 6.5 x 10^3 to 1.4 x 10^5 cells/mL (up to 90% of phytoplankton) and crashed as HaV rose, but persisted at 10^1-10^2 cells/mL; mean susceptibility of isolates fell from 59% (bloom) to 18% (post-bloom) of HaV clones, then recovered to 61% as resistant cells were displaced.
papers.env_effects: Host resistance emerges after viral termination, limiting repeated use of one virus strain.
papers.key_details: Observational field study of a natural bloom, not a control treatment; no virus was added and there is no untreated control. Host isolates from three periods were each challenged with the co-occurring HaV clones (lysis checked for 10-14 days). Isolate susceptibility during the post-bloom period II (18% +/- 23%) was significantly lower than in periods I and III (59% +/- 40%, 61% +/- 37%; Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.001). The bloom collapse coincided with HaV increase, but a resistant residual population of 10^1-10^2 cells/mL survived. Causation of the crash by virus is inferred from correlation.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: None material; record lacked the densities and the susceptibility percentages, and should note that virus causation is correlational (no manipulation).
papers.study_note: natural virus dynamics during bloom crash; host abundance outcome

reasons.reproducibility: Observational field time series of a natural bloom in Hiroshima Bay with virus isolation; not school-repeatable.
reasons.effectiveness: No virus was added and there is no control; the crash is only correlated with HaV and a resistant 10^1-10^2 cells/mL population survived.
reasons.cost: Ship sampling, virus isolation and cross-infection assays cost far over $5,000.
reasons.time: The bloom-to-crash sequence played out over the May-July season, i.e. weeks to months.
reasons.environment: Natural virus is host-specific with no added material, though resistance emerges (susceptibility fell 59% to 18%).

papers.title: Resistance of the fish-killing dinoflagellate Cochlodinium polykrikoides against algicidal bacteria isolated from the coastal sea of Japan

papers.title: A Review of Cyanophage–Host Relationships: Highlighting Cyanophages as a Potential Cyanobacteria Control Strategy
papers.authors: Grasso CR, Pokrzywinski KL, Waechter C, Rycroft T, Zhang Y, Aligata A, Kramer M, Lamsal A
papers.organism: Cyanophages vs Synechococcus, Microcystis, Dolichospermum, Aphanizomenon, Cylindrospermopsis, Planktothrix, Lyngbya
papers.scale: Literature review (mostly to 2020)
papers.dose: n/a
papers.result: Reviews cyanophage life cycles, diversity and infectivity for seven North American cyanoHAB genera and discusses efficacy, optimization and scalability. Highlights high specificity and self-propagation as advantages.
papers.env_effects: High host specificity (many phages infect only one strain), so mixed blooms and resistant strains limit control; dosing is not standardized (many studies add an undefined 'cyanophage concentrate' at 10% v/v); propagation in the field depends on nutrients, light and temperature and is untested.
papers.key_details: Literature review of cyanophage biology and cyanophage-host relationships for seven cyanoHAB genera; no new experiments. It reports no field or mesocosm cyanophage control trials; the evidence base is lab infection assays. Authors note that 'cyanophage concentrate' added at 10% v/v has become an accepted but imprecise dosing standard and call for standardized dose-response work before field use. Examples: Ma-LMM01 infects only one M. aeruginosa strain; PaV-LD from Lake Donghu infected only P. agardhii isolates from the same lake.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record implies minimal non-target impacts as an advantage; the full text frames extreme specificity and lack of dosing standards as major barriers, with no field evidence at all.
papers.study_note: review of efficacy: Cyanophages vs Synechococcus

reasons.reproducibility: Review; typical cyanophage infection assays need purchased host strains and phage isolation skills.

reasons.cost: Typical lab infection assay needs purchased cyanobacterial strains and culture supplies, about $150-500.
reasons.time: Lab phage lysis assays typically show results over one to three weeks.
reasons.environment: High specificity limits non-target harm, but field propagation and resistance are untested.

papers.title: The potential of prodigiosin for control of Prorocentrum donghaiense blooms: Algicidal properties and acute toxicity to other marine organisms at various trophic levels
papers.authors: Chen Y, Luo G, Chen S, Zhang D, Xie W, Wang Z, Zheng W, Xu H
papers.organism: Bacterial pigment prodigiosin vs Prorocentrum donghaiense; non-targets Chlorella vulgaris, Photobacterium phosphoreum, Artemia salina, Lateolabrax japonicus
papers.scale: Lab cultures and acute toxicity tests
papers.dose: Prodigiosin (from Zooshikella sp. SZ14) 0.01-0.2 ug/mL; 0.05 ug/mL = inhibitory dose, 0.1 ug/mL = algicidal dose
papers.duration: 12-72 h algicidal assays; 96 h fish test
papers.result: Prodigiosin 24 h LC50 was 0.046 ug/mL for P. donghaiense; >=0.08 ug/mL killed 97% of cells by 48 h with no recovery by 72 h, while 0.03-0.05 ug/mL cells recovered to initial density by 72 h. The 0.1 ug/mL control dose was toxic to Artemia (24 h LC50 0.123 ug/mL) and sea bass juveniles (24 h LC50 0.125 ug/mL; 19.6% killed at 0.1 ug/mL in 24 h).
papers.env_effects: At the algicidal dose (0.1 ug/mL) prodigiosin killed 49.3% of Artemia salina nauplii in 24 h and 19.6% of Lateolabrax japonicus juveniles in 24 h; fish 96 h NOEC 0.05 ug/mL. Chlorella vulgaris unaffected up to 1 ug/mL (24 h LC50 31.8 ug/mL); Photobacterium growth slowed to ~74-76% of control at 0.05-0.1 ug/mL.
papers.key_details: Lab flask assays, at least triplicate, with cell counts every 12 h after prodigiosin dosing of P. donghaiense cultures. 0.03 and 0.05 ug/mL killed 29% and 53% of cells at 24 h, but survivors regrew to initial density by 72 h (attributed to photodegradation); 0.08-0.2 ug/mL gave >80% kill at 24 h and 97% at 48 h. Fv/Fm fell 20.6% and 93.4% below control after 3 h at 0.05 and 0.1 ug/mL. Non-target tests: Artemia 24/48 h LC50 0.123/0.088 ug/mL, sea bass juveniles 24/48 h LC50 0.125/0.116 ug/mL, Chlorella 24 h LC50 31.8 ug/mL, Photobacterium 15 min EC50 0.505 ug/mL. The safety margin between the algicidal dose and animal LC50s is only about 1.2x.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record implies non-targets are safe ('less sensitive than the HAB'); in fact the 0.1 ug/mL algicidal dose killed 49.3% of Artemia nauplii and 19.6% of juvenile sea bass within 24 h, and LC50s for both are only ~1.2x the control dose. Dose was missing from the record.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Bacterial pigment prodigiosin vs Prorocentrum donghaiense

reasons.reproducibility: Bench flask assays, but needs a purchased marine dinoflagellate culture and purified prodigiosin.
reasons.effectiveness: Triplicate flasks: >=0.08 ug/mL killed 97% by 48 h with no recovery, though 0.03-0.05 ug/mL let cells regrow by 72 h; one species only.
reasons.cost: Purified prodigiosin and a purchased P. donghaiense culture run roughly $150-500.
reasons.time: Kill was >80% at 24 h and 97% at 48 h.
reasons.environment: The algicidal 0.1 ug/mL dose killed 49% of Artemia and 20% of juvenile sea bass in 24 h; the safety margin is only ~1.2x.

papers.title: The Algicidal Fungus Trametes versicolor F21a Eliminating Blue Algae via Genes Encoding Degradation Enzymes and Metabolic Pathways Revealed by Transcriptomic Analysis
papers.authors: Dai W, Chen X, Wang X, Xu Z, Gao X, Jiang C, Deng R, Han G
papers.organism: White-rot fungus Trametes versicolor F21a vs Microcystis aeruginosa PCC7806
papers.scale: Lab co-culture with transcriptomics
papers.dose: Fungal mycelia pre-grown 5 days (from a 7 mm plug in 15 mL potato medium) transferred into 100 mL of algal culture
papers.result: About 85% of M. aeruginosa cells were eliminated within 30 h and chlorophyll-a fell to one sixth of the initial content; fungal DEGs rose from 193 to 742 over 0-30 h. Commercial decomposition enzymes alone only partially inhibited algal growth.
papers.env_effects: Not assessed.
papers.key_details: Lab co-culture of T. versicolor F21a mycelia with M. aeruginosa PCC7806 in 250 mL flasks (25 C, 90 umol photons m-2 s-1, 120 rpm). Chl-a declined gradually over the first 12 h to one sixth of initial after 30 h; about 85% of algal cells eliminated; fungal biomass rose about 12% (p < 0.05). RNA-Seq with two biological replicates per time point; qPCR validation with three. Main purpose is transcriptomic mechanism, not control efficacy; a single lab strain at flask scale with no environmental tests.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record said the target was generic 'blue algae' and gave no efficacy number; full text gives M. aeruginosa PCC7806 and 85% cell removal in 30 h.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: White-rot fungus Trametes versicolor F21a vs cyanobacteria

reasons.reproducibility: Flask co-culture is bench-scale but needs a purchased Microcystis strain and T. versicolor culture with sterile technique.
reasons.effectiveness: About 85% of M. aeruginosa removed in 30 h, but one strain at flask scale with two biological replicates and efficacy not the main aim.
reasons.cost: Purchased fungal and algal cultures plus media cost about $150-500.
reasons.time: Chl a fell to one sixth of initial within 30 h.
reasons.environment: Live fungus added; non-target and environmental effects were not assessed.

papers.title: Barley straw as an inhibitor of algal growth I: studies in the Chesterfield Canal
papers.authors: Welch IM, Barrett PRF, Gibson MT, Ridge I
papers.scale: Disused canal, UK
papers.dose: Rotting barley straw (dose not seen)
papers.result: Per Semantic Scholar summary, rotting barley straw reduced filamentous algae in the canal and 'shows promise as a long-term method of controlling algae'. No numbers seen.
papers.env_effects: Not reported in the summary seen.

reasons.reproducibility: Field trial in a disused UK canal with rotting straw; needs site access.
reasons.effectiveness: Summary says straw reduced filamentous algae but no numbers or controls seen.
reasons.cost: Canal-scale straw and monitoring ~$500-5,000.
reasons.time: Duration not reported; rotting-straw effects take months.
reasons.environment: Not reported; straw is biodegradable and retrievable.

papers.title: The use of barley-straw to control general and blue-green algal growth in a Derbyshire reservoir
papers.scale: Disused UK supply reservoir
papers.dose: ~25-50 g straw/m3
papers.result: Per the project's snowball notes (from an abstract summary), phytoplankton productivity and cyanobacterial dominance were both significantly reduced without nutrient removal. Numbers not seen by this collector.
papers.env_effects: Reported 'no short term deleterious environmental impact' in receiving streams; more grazers present.

reasons.reproducibility: Treatment of a whole UK supply reservoir at 25-50 g/m3 straw.
reasons.effectiveness: Productivity and cyanobacterial dominance 'significantly reduced', but numbers not seen.
reasons.cost: Reservoir-scale straw and monitoring ~$500-5,000.
reasons.time: Duration not reported; reservoir effects take months.
reasons.environment: 'No short-term deleterious impact' reported; more grazers.

papers.title: An Assessment of the Effectiveness of Straw as an Algal Inhibitor in an Upland Scottish Loch
papers.authors: Harriman R, Adamson E, Shelton R, Moffett G
papers.organism: Algal blooms driven by a black-headed gull colony
papers.scale: Upland loch, central Scotland; moored bales
papers.dose: Moored barley straw bales (dose not in abstract)
papers.result: Release of the inhibitory substance began 6-10 months after bale placement and lasted at least 18 months; cell numbers of the main species were affected but algal diversity was not.
papers.env_effects: Bales became substrate/shelter and detritus trap for benthic invertebrates.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Algal blooms driven by a black-headed gull

reasons.reproducibility: Moored bales in an upland Scottish loch.
reasons.effectiveness: Cell numbers of main species affected but diversity not; no percentage.
reasons.cost: Bales and monitoring ~$500-5,000.
reasons.time: Release started 6-10 months after placement.
reasons.environment: Bales served as invertebrate habitat; natural material.

papers.title: Limited Effects of Barley Straw on Algae and Zooplankton in a Midwestern Pond
papers.scale: Replicated limnocorrals inside a 1 ha Iowa pond
papers.dose: Three levels of barley straw
papers.result: No consistent algal growth inhibition for either filamentous or planktonic algae, and zooplankton community structure was unaffected. Authors attribute failure to low oxygen inside decomposing straw in stagnant ponds.
papers.env_effects: No effect on zooplankton community structure.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Filamentous and planktonic algae

reasons.reproducibility: Replicated limnocorrals inside a 1 ha pond need field access.
reasons.effectiveness: Negative: no consistent inhibition of filamentous or planktonic algae over 14 weeks.
reasons.cost: Limnocorrals and straw ~$150-500.
reasons.time: 14 weeks.
reasons.environment: Decomposing straw caused low oxygen inside bales; zooplankton unaffected.

papers.title: The effects of barley straw (Hordeum vulgare) on the growth of freshwater algae
papers.authors: Ferrier MD, Butler BR, Terlizzi DE, Lacouture RV
papers.organism: 12 freshwater algae incl. Microcystis aeruginosa, Anabaena flos-aquae, Synura, Oscillatoria
papers.scale: Lab bioassays of 12 unialgal cultures (nutrient media vs unfiltered or sterile-filtered barley straw liquor, replicate cultures) plus 6 central-Maryland ponds (0.2-1.6 ha, 1.8-4.3 m deep): 4 randomly assigned to straw, 2 untreated controls
papers.dose: Ponds: 112 kg straw/ha in loosened, netted bales near the surface; lab: barley straw liquor
papers.duration: Lab: two-week incubations; ponds: 21 May to 10 September 1998, sampled biweekly
papers.result: Straw liquor significantly inhibited Microcystis aeruginosa, Dinobryon and Synura petersenii (Synura undetectable after two weeks) but stimulated Selenastrum, Spirogyra, Oscillatoria and Navicula. In ponds, biomass declined in both treated and control ponds after application and did not differ significantly between them on any date.
papers.env_effects: Species-specific; some nuisance algae stimulated.
papers.key_details: Lab: two-week bioassays with replicate cultures; initial Chl a was not measured, so algistatic vs algicidal action could not be separated except for Synura (disappeared). Anabaena flos-aquae, Chlorella, Ulothrix, Synedra and Scenedesmus were not significantly affected. Field: four treated (112 kg/ha) vs two control ponds in 1998, Chl a from pooled samples biweekly. Variation among ponds was very large (coefficients of variation 36-157% treated, 33-141% control), so the field test had low power; biomass fell in all ponds right after the first sampling.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record lists Anabaena flos-aquae among target species without noting it was unaffected; field dose (112 kg/ha) and low statistical power (4 treated vs 2 control ponds, CVs up to 157%) were missing. Spirogyra was stimulated by unfiltered liquor but inhibited by sterile-filtered liquor.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: 12 freshwater algae incl. Microcystis aeruginosa

reasons.reproducibility: Lab bioassays are doable, but the reported field test used six 0.2-1.6 ha ponds.
reasons.effectiveness: Pond biomass did not differ between 4 treated and 2 control ponds on any date; lab response was species-specific (Anabaena unaffected, several algae stimulated).
reasons.cost: Straw is cheap, but repeating a six-pond season of sampling and Chl a work costs $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Pond trial ran May-September 1998, a full season.
reasons.environment: Straw is biodegradable, but liquor stimulated Selenastrum, Oscillatoria and Navicula.

papers.title: A series of experiments aimed at clarifying the mode of action of barley straw in cyanobacterial growth control
papers.authors: Iredale RS, McDonald AT, Adams DG
papers.organism: Microcystis PCC 7806 (Pasteur collection) and Microcystis SD053 (Yorkshire reservoir isolate, not axenic)
papers.scale: Lab decomposition and bioassay experiments
papers.dose: Lab doses far above field rates: 40 g wet (~4 g dry) straw/L in the activation time course; fresh finely chopped straw 0.1-5 g dry/L; whole straw up to 40 g dry/L; catalase 5 mg/mL
papers.duration: Three or more weeks of decomposition
papers.result: Whole fresh straw (~4 g dry/L) did not inhibit Microcystis at first; inhibition rose as straw decomposed, peaking at ~1000 h, then declined, and liquor alone only cut growth to ~80% of control. Finely chopped fresh straw inhibited at 5 g dry/L at 20 °C and down to 1 g/L (PCC 7806) or above 0.1 g/L (SD053) at 27 °C, while whole fresh straw gave no inhibition even at 20 g dry/L.
papers.env_effects: Not assessed.
papers.key_details: Series of flask bioassays (triplicate, three no-straw controls each, 7-14 days, Chl a daily) on two Microcystis strains. Autoclaved straw in sterile dialysis packages had no effect on Microcystis SD053 over two weeks, showing microbial decomposition is needed to activate whole straw. Straw decomposed under UV-supplemented light was more inhibitory than under visible light, and daily catalase reduced inhibition, consistent with a hydrogen peroxide role. Outcome depended on temperature (stronger at 27 than 20 °C) and strain (PCC 7806 more resistant, partly recovered after ~200 h). In some bioassays only two of three replicates were inhibited.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record gives no doses; the effective lab doses (grams of straw per litre) are roughly 20-100 times the ~25-50 g/m3 used in the field, which matters for any field inference.

reasons.reproducibility: Flask bioassays with straw and two Microcystis strains; bench scale with a sponsor for cultures.
reasons.effectiveness: Inhibition only after decomposition, only at 1-5 g/L (20-100x field rates), varied by strain and temperature, and sometimes in 2 of 3 replicates.
reasons.cost: Straw, flasks and a purchased Microcystis culture cost roughly $50-150.
reasons.time: Straw inhibition peaked only after ~1000 h (~6 weeks) of decomposition.
reasons.environment: Plant material that degrades; effect appears to work via H2O2, with no persistent residue.

papers.title: Laboratory tests of ammonium and barley straw extract as agents to suppress abundance of the harmful alga Prymnesium parvum and its toxicity to fish
papers.authors: Grover JP, Baker JW, Ureña-Boeck F, Brooks BW, Errera RM, Roelke DL, Kiesling RL
papers.scale: Lab batch cultures, complete 5 x 3 factorial (control, low/high ammonium, low/high BSE x 10, 20, 30 °C), each combination in duplicate, plus fathead minnow (P. promelas) toxicity tests
papers.dose: Weekly on days 0, 7, 14, 21: barley straw extract 0.015 mL/L (manufacturer's highest recommended pond dose) or 0.75 mL/L (50x); ammonium +0.4 or +40 µmol/L
papers.result: No barley straw extract dose significantly reduced P. parvum growth, endpoint density or fish toxicity; low BSE at 30 °C raised growth rate ~10%. High ammonium (40 µmol/L weekly) cut endpoint density by about 50% and abolished fish toxicity, although it raised early exponential growth rate by 0.065 per day.
papers.env_effects: No reduction of fish toxicity.
papers.key_details: Factorial lab test (duplicates) of a commercial barley straw extract and ammonium against Prymnesium parvum at three temperatures for 23 days. Fish toxicity at day 23 appeared only in 20 °C cultures without high ammonium (LC50 4-17% culture dilution over 48 h); toxic cultures all had >6x10^5 cells/mL and pH >9.0. BSE contained phenolics but negligible nutrients. BSE also raised day-23 pH by about 0.5 units at 30 °C. Replication was only duplicate per treatment-temperature cell.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record's ammonium note is incomplete: high ammonium reduced endpoint density by ~50% but increased early exponential growth rate. BSE was not just ineffective; the low dose slightly increased growth (~10%) at 30 °C.

reasons.reproducibility: Lab factorial culture test, but needs a purchased Prymnesium parvum culture and fish toxicity bioassays.
reasons.effectiveness: No barley straw extract dose (even 50x label) reduced P. parvum growth, density or fish toxicity; low dose raised growth ~10% at 30 C.
reasons.cost: Algal culture, commercial extract and fathead minnow tests cost about $150-500.
reasons.time: Endpoints were read after 23 days of culture.
reasons.environment: Extract is plant-derived with negligible nutrients, but it did nothing to lower fish toxicity.

papers.title: Efficiency evaluation of an algistatic treatment based on barley straw in a hypertrophic pond
papers.authors: Prygiel E, Charriau A, Descamps R, Prygiel J, Ouddane B, Billon G
papers.venue: Journal of Environmental Engineering and Landscape Management
papers.scale: Whole hypertrophic pond, Northern France (240,000 m3, mean depth 1.92 m, ~39 d flushing), five sampling stations, single treated pond with no untreated control
papers.dose: 3 tons barley straw (50 g/m2, CEH 2004 guidance) in 150 loose rolls on five floating anchored structures with 50 buoys to keep it aerobic; added early May 2010
papers.result: Barley straw did not prevent cyanobacteria: Aphanizomenon dominated the phytoplankton on 4 June, 17 July and 22 July 2010 (with an A. flos-aquae scum on 4 June), and Chl a ranged 8-83 ug/L. Authors judged it not appropriate for this pond type.
papers.env_effects: Pond remained well oxygenated; no community shift observed.
papers.key_details: Before/during monitoring of one treated pond from February to November 2010 with water and sediment chemistry at five stations; no control pond, so the design cannot separate treatment from seasonal succession. Straw dose followed the UK CEH recommendation (50 g/m2, 3 t total) and was kept floating and aerobic. Cyanobacteria (Aphanizomenon, later Aphanocapsa, Anabaena) still dominated in summer; nitrate limitation and sediment P release are discussed as drivers. Pond was well oxygenated through all seasons.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Dose was missing in the record (it is the standard 50 g/m2); record should state the design lacks any untreated control.

reasons.reproducibility: Whole 240,000 m3 pond with 3 tons of straw on floating structures; not school-repeatable.
reasons.effectiveness: Aphanizomenon still dominated in June-July despite the standard 50 g/m2 dose; single pond with no control.
reasons.cost: 3 tons of straw, 150 rolls and anchored floating rafts cost $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Monitored February-November 2010, a full season.
reasons.environment: Pond stayed well oxygenated and straw is biodegradable.

papers.title: The influence of active metabolites from the decomposition of camelina and barley straw on the development of phytoplankton from eutrophic freshwater ecosystem
papers.authors: Świerk D, Celewicz-Gołdyn S, Krzyżaniak M, Antoszewski P, Stuper-Szablewska K, Szablewski T, et al.
papers.organism: Mixed phytoplankton from a eutrophic reservoir (chrysophytes, cyanobacteria, dinoflagellates, green algae)
papers.scale: 15 glass aquaria (5 control, 5 barley, 5 camelina) with reservoir water and sediment
papers.dose: 20 g barley or camelina straw per aquarium
papers.result: Camelina straw had the strongest inhibitory effect on chrysophytes, potentially toxic cyanobacteria and dinoflagellates, via polyphenols (mainly gallic and caffeic acids, flavonoids); barley straw was the comparison. Polyphenols simultaneously promoted filamentous green algae.
papers.env_effects: Filamentous green algae stimulated; lower total molds and bacteria with straw vs control.
papers.study_note: camelina straw is the tested agent; barley only comparison

reasons.reproducibility: 15 aquaria with reservoir water, sediment and 20 g straw each is a classic school setup.
reasons.effectiveness: Barley was only the comparison; camelina inhibited cyanobacteria more, and green algae were stimulated.
reasons.cost: Aquaria and straw ~$50-150.
reasons.time: 8 weeks.
reasons.environment: Polyphenols stimulated filamentous green algae.

papers.title: Algal growth control by a barley straw extract
papers.authors: Ball AS, Williams M, Vincent D, Robinson JI
papers.organism: Lake-water algae; Microcystis sp. and Scenedesmus
papers.scale: Lab flasks with lake water
papers.dose: Chopped straw 1% w/v (1 g in 200 mL lake water); extracts 1% down to 0.005% v/v (Microcystis) and 0.01% or 0.001% (Scenedesmus)
papers.result: In lake water, controls rose ~10-fold to ~400 µg/L Chl a and wheat straw to 1160 µg/L, while no algal growth was detected with barley straw over 28 days. Decomposed-barley extract held Microcystis at 226-457 µg/L vs 3710 µg/L in controls (about 10-fold lower at every dose down to 0.005%), whereas fresh-barley extract slightly increased growth; Scenedesmus was fully inhibited at 0.01% but not at 0.001%.
papers.env_effects: Not assessed; lignin content of straw rose from 10 to 33% during decomposition.
papers.key_details: Flask experiments, triplicate, 20 °C, continuous light (375 µmol/m2/s), up to 28 days. Lake water (initial Chl a ~40 µg/L) with 1% chopped barley or wheat straw vs control; then Microcystis and Scenedesmus cultures in Bold's basal medium with fresh vs decomposed-barley extract. Decomposed straw had 33% lignin. Decomposed-barley extract at 1% gave 351 vs 3710 µg/L Chl a (about 91% lower); at 0.005% it gave 386 µg/L. Wheat straw stimulated algae, presumably by nutrient leaching; fresh-barley extract gave no inhibition. No field test.

reasons.reproducibility: Flasks of lake water with 1% chopped barley straw; common materials and a clear bench protocol.
reasons.effectiveness: Triplicate flasks: no algal growth with barley straw vs ~10x rise in controls, and decomposed-straw extract cut Microcystis Chl a ~91% at every dose.
reasons.cost: Straw, lake water and flasks cost under $50.
reasons.time: Effects were tracked over 28 days, and the straw must be decomposed first.
reasons.environment: Biodegradable plant material, though wheat straw stimulated algae via nutrient leaching.

papers.title: Use of barley straw to control nuisance freshwater algae
papers.organism: Microcystis aeruginosa, Anabaena flos-aquae, Scenedesmus, Spirogyra, Cladophora, Hydrodictyon, Oscillatoria
papers.scale: Lab bioassays (triplicate tubes, 14 days) of seven algae plus field trial in nine 300 m2 earthen ponds (20 x 15 x 1 m) in Iran: 3 ponds at 400 kg/ha, 3 at 800 kg/ha, 3 untreated controls
papers.dose: Lab: straw liquor from 360 g chopped straw in 18 L water rotted 60 days, 10 mL per 30 mL tube; field: 400 and 800 kg/ha straw bales
papers.duration: Lab 14 days; ponds April-August 2008 (about four months)
papers.result: In ponds, control Chl a rose to 1,180 µg/L after four months while both straw treatments peaked at ~460 µg/L after one month and fell to 223 (400 kg/ha) and 106 µg/L (800 kg/ha); mean total phytoplankton density was 76.51 vs 32.08 and 30.26 x10^4 units/mL, and cyanobacteria 40.99 vs 7.16 and 6.47 x10^4 units/mL. In the lab, M. aeruginosa Chl a was almost undetectable after two weeks, and Scenedesmus and Anabaena were eight and five times lower than controls.
papers.env_effects: Nitrate-N significantly higher in treated ponds (1.65-1.72 vs 0.83 mg/L); reactive P slightly lower and dissolved oxygen not significantly different. Diatoms became dominant (>56% by August) in treated ponds while cyanobacteria stayed dominant (69%) in controls; Chrysophyceae significantly reduced. Hydrodictyon (and non-significantly Oscillatoria) stimulated in the lab.
papers.key_details: Replicated pond trial (three ponds per treatment, randomly assigned) in problem ponds in Iran, April-August 2008, with lab bioassays of seven species in triplicate. Final Chl a was 81% (400 kg/ha) and 91% (800 kg/ha) below controls; total phytoplankton density was about 58-60% lower and cyanobacteria about 83-84% lower. The 800 kg/ha dose was not significantly better than 400 kg/ha for density. Both treatments reached ~460 µg/L Chl a after one month, so the effect built up after a lag. effect_pct 81 = final Chl a reduction at 400 kg/ha vs control.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record had no numbers or duration; full text gives a replicated pond trial (n = 3 per arm) with 81-91% lower final Chl a and a rise in nitrate in treated ponds.

reasons.reproducibility: Lab tubes are simple, but the headline trial used nine 300 m2 earthen ponds.
reasons.effectiveness: Randomized pond trial (n=3 per arm): final Chl a 81-91% and cyanobacteria ~83% below controls, backed by lab bioassays.
reasons.cost: Straw is cheap, but nine ponds over four months of sampling cost $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Effect built up after a ~1-month lag and was clearest after 2-4 months.
reasons.environment: Treated ponds had doubled nitrate and a community shift to diatoms; Hydrodictyon was stimulated in the lab.

papers.title: Growth inhibition of bloom-forming cyanobacterium Microcystis aeruginosa by rice straw extract
papers.authors: Park M-H, Han M, Ahn C-Y, Kim H-S, Yoon B-D, Oh H-M
papers.scale: Lab flasks of M. aeruginosa in natural water from Daechung Reservoir and two field ponds (Korea), duplicate experiments
papers.dose: Rice straw extract 0.01-10 mg/L; salicylic acid 0.1 mg/L
papers.result: All rice straw extract doses (0.01-10 mg/L) significantly reduced M. aeruginosa cells over 8 days, and 10 mg/L gave 98% inhibition on day 8. Singly, salicylic acid at 0.1 mg/L was the best allelochemical (26%), while a mixture of p-coumaric, salicylic and benzoic acids at 0.01 mg/L gave 66% inhibition.
papers.env_effects: Not assessed; proposed as environment-friendly biomaterial.
papers.key_details: M. aeruginosa grown in natural waters and treated with 0.01, 0.1, 1 and 10 mg/L rice straw extract; cells counted by haemacytometer every 2 days for 8 days; experiments in duplicate. Autoclaved and filtered extracts behaved alike, and inhibition was weaker in the more nutrient-rich pond water (pond I: 630 µg/L NO3-N, 120 µg/L PO4-P) and stronger by day 7 than day 3. Several single phenolics slightly stimulated growth at one of the two doses. No field application.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record omits the headline 98% inhibition at 10 mg/L and the 66% inhibition of the three-phenolic mixture; replication was only duplicate.
papers.study_note: rice straw extract, close variant; Microcystis cell counts

reasons.reproducibility: Flasks of Microcystis in natural water dosed with straw extract, counted by haemacytometer; bench scale.
reasons.effectiveness: All doses significantly cut cells and 10 mg/L gave 98% inhibition by day 8, but only duplicate runs and weaker effect in nutrient-rich water.
reasons.cost: Purchased Microcystis culture plus haemacytometer and flasks cost about $150-500.
reasons.time: Inhibition was clear by day 7-8.
reasons.environment: Plant extract with no persistent residue; non-target effects not assessed.

papers.title: Barley (Hordeum vulgare)-induced growth inhibition of algae: a review
papers.scale: Literature review
papers.dose: n/a
papers.result: Narrative review: early barley field studies lacked controls and replication and relied on visual assessment, lab results are species-dependent (inhibition, stimulation or no change) and not comparable because liquor preparation methods vary; lignin-derived phenolics are proposed as the driver. Cites field rates of 50 and later 25 g/m3 (Everall and Lees) and lab inhibition down to 1 g/m3 and 0.005% liquor.
papers.env_effects: Cites other mechanisms: straw supplying carbon to bacteria that compete for P, and bales trapping sediment, improving clarity and allowing Elodea canadensis to replace algae.
papers.key_details: Review in sections on early work, further research, and lignin as the driving force, with an updated table of species responses and a table of liquor preparation methods. The authors stress that early field work had no controls or replication and was based on visual assessment prone to sampler bias. They recommend documenting barley variety, lignin content through rotting, liquor preparation, and testing multiple liquor ages and extraction methods. No quantitative synthesis of effect sizes.
papers.study_note: review of efficacy: Freshwater algae and cyanobacteria

reasons.reproducibility: Review; the typical straw-liquor flask test uses common materials at bench scale.
reasons.effectiveness: Responses are species-dependent (inhibition, stimulation or none) and early field studies lacked controls and replication.
reasons.cost: Straw and jars for a typical liquor test cost under $50.
reasons.time: Straw must rot for weeks before inhibition, so results take one to three months.
reasons.environment: Biodegradable straw; may also help via bacteria competing for P and improved clarity.

papers.title: Evaluating the effectiveness of copper sulphate, chlorine, potassium permanganate, hydrogen peroxide and ozone on cyanobacterial cell integrity
papers.authors: Fan J, Ho L, Hobson P, Brookes J
papers.scale: bench cultures of toxic M. aeruginosa strain 338 in ASM-1, initial 7.0 x 10^5 cells/mL, triplicate
papers.dose: CuSO4 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 mg/L as Cu; chlorine 3, 4, 5 mg/L; KMnO4 1, 3, 5, 10 mg/L; H2O2 10.2, 51, 102 mg/L; ozone 2, 4, 6 mg/L
papers.result: All five treatments compromised membranes (flow cytometry, SYTOX Green): chlorine >=88% of cells within 1 min, ozone 6 mg/L 90% in 5 min, KMnO4 10 mg/L no intact cells after 6 h. Cell densities fell much less: about 22% after 3 days with 1.0-1.5 mg/L Cu, about 15% with 10 mg/L KMnO4, and no significant change with ozone or H2O2.
papers.env_effects: All oxidants compromise cell membranes, so intracellular metabolites (toxins, taste and odour compounds) are released; fast lysers release them at once.
papers.key_details: Lab time-course experiments on a toxic Microcystis aeruginosa strain (7.0 x 10^5 cells/mL, 20 C, pH 7.5) with untreated controls; triplicate analyses. The endpoint is membrane integrity by flow cytometry, not cell removal. CuSO4 1.5 mg/L gave >95% compromised cells; with 1.0 mg/L 98% were impaired at day 2 but intact cells rose again after day 3. H2O2 left 16%, 31% and 7% intact on day 2 at 10.2, 51 and 102 mg/L, yet 82% were viable again by day 7 at 51 mg/L and densities did not differ significantly from controls. Ozone 2, 4, 6 mg/L compromised about 50%, 70% and 90% of cells in 5 min with no significant density change.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: effect_pct 90 was the ozone membrane-compromise percentage, not a reduction in algae; cell densities barely changed for ozone and H2O2 (at most ~22% drop with CuSO4). The H2O2 'algistatic' claim is weak: cells recovered integrity after day 3 and densities did not differ from controls.

reasons.reproducibility: Bench Microcystis with chlorine, ozone, KMnO4, CuSO4 and H2O2 needs an ozone generator and flow cytometry.
reasons.effectiveness: Oxidants compromised membranes (chlorine >=88% in 1 min, ozone 90% in 5 min), but cell densities fell only ~22% (Cu) and ~15% (KMnO4), not at all with ozone or H2O2, and cells recovered after day 3.
reasons.cost: Ozone generator and cell-integrity assays about $150-500.
reasons.time: Lysis within minutes.
reasons.environment: All oxidants lyse membranes and release toxins; CuSO4 arm adds metal.

papers.title: Comparison of permanganate preoxidation and preozonation on algae containing water: cell integrity, characteristics, and chlorinated disinfection byproduct formation
papers.authors: Xie P, Ma J, Fang J, Guan Y, Yue S, Li X, Chen L
papers.scale: bench suspensions of M. aeruginosa (1.01 x 10^6 cells/mL, TOC 5 mg/L) in simulated drinking water, duplicate tests
papers.dose: KMnO4 or ozone 0-2.0 mg/L preoxidation (10 min, pH 7.0), then coagulation-sedimentation or chlorination (Cl2:TOC 3:1, 3 days)
papers.result: Preozonation at 0.4-2.0 mg/L left <=1% intact cells, while permanganate 0.4-2.0 mg/L kept >97% live cells. Both preoxidants raised cell removal by coagulation-sedimentation from 56.7% to 78.0% (KMnO4 1.0 mg/L) and 80.2% (ozone 2.0 mg/L).
papers.env_effects: Preozonation released intracellular organic matter and dramatically increased chlorinated disinfection by-products (haloaldehydes, haloacetonitriles, halonitromethanes); permanganate had much less effect. Authors favour permanganate over ozone.
papers.key_details: Bench study in simulated drinking water (pH 7.0, 25 C) with M. aeruginosa washed free of extracellular organic matter; tests in duplicate with an unoxidized control. Endpoints were flow-cytometric cell integrity, coagulation removal, DOC and 3-day chlorination by-products. Ozone raised DOC after coagulation from 0.42 to 1.00 mg/L; permanganate left DOC unchanged. Common DBPs (TCM, DCAA, TCAA) rose >40% at 2.0 mg/L ozone, CH and TCNM by 262% and 471%; permanganate changed most DBPs only slightly. Removal gains levelled off above 1.0 mg/L oxidant.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: effect_pct 98 was the share of cells lysed by ozone (not removal); the actual removal endpoint is coagulation-sedimentation removal, 80.2% with ozone vs 56.7% without preoxidation.

reasons.reproducibility: Needs an ozone generator, flow cytometry and GC analysis of chlorinated by-products.
reasons.effectiveness: Preozonation at 0.4-2.0 mg/L left <=1% intact cells and raised coagulation removal from 56.7% to 80.2%, but tests were duplicates only and permanganate kept >97% of cells alive.
reasons.cost: Ozone and DBP analysis $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Immediate (bench preoxidation).
reasons.environment: Dramatically increased chlorinated disinfection by-products; releases intracellular matter.

papers.title: Effectiveness of ozone nanobubble treatments on high biomass cyanobacterial blooms: A mesocosm experiment and field trial
papers.authors: Chaffin JD, Berthold DE, Braig EC, Fuchs JD, Gabor RS, Jacquemin SJ, et al.
papers.organism: Planktothrix (cyanobacteria bloom), Grand Lake St Marys, Ohio
papers.scale: 2,000 L mesocosms plus two 4-week trials in a ~4.7e7 L lake embayment
papers.dose: Mesocosm applied ozone 4.8 +/- 0.6, 7.1 +/- 0.8 and 15 +/- 1 mg O3/L (O3:DOC 0.68, 1.21, 2.04; DOC ~7.2 mg C/L), plus oxygen-only nanobubble control; field: two NBOT units in a 3.2 x 10^4 m2, ~1.5 m deep embayment (4.8 x 10^4 m3) at lower O3:DOC
papers.result: In 2,000 L mesocosms (3 tanks per dose, 100% of water passed through the unit) medium and high doses cut chl-a and phycocyanin 98-99% and microcystins 62% and 92%; low dose cut chl-a >70%. In the embayment trials there was no effect: chl-a at the outlet and 3.3 m away was within +/-10% of the inlet except one sample (-34.3%).
papers.env_effects: DOC was more oxidized at the outlet; treatment reach minimal. Failure attributed to high biomass and DOC, low O3:DOC and small fraction of lake water treated.
papers.key_details: Replicated mesocosm (triplicate tanks per dose, untreated and oxygen-only controls, sampled 1-96 h) plus two 4-week field deployments in the Sunset Beach embayment of Grand Lake St Marys, Ohio. The mesocosm bloom was diluted with 60% filtered Lake Erie water, so starting biomass was lower than in the lake, flattering the mesocosm result. Oxygen-only nanobubbles had no effect. Field failure attributed to high biomass and DOC, O3:DOC below the lowest mesocosm dose, and only a small fraction of lake water treated at any time; SUVA254 showed ozone reacted only near the outlet.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record is accurate; it omits that the mesocosm water was diluted 60% with filtered Lake Erie water, and the absolute ozone doses (4.8-15 mg O3/L).

reasons.reproducibility: 2,000 L mesocosms plus a lake-embayment field trial with nanobubble ozone gear.
reasons.effectiveness: Triplicate 2,000 L mesocosms cut chl a 98-99% at 7-15 mg O3/L, but on water diluted 60%; two 4-week lake trials showed no effect (within +/-10% of inlet).
reasons.cost: Nanobubble ozone system and field trials well over $5,000.
reasons.time: 4-week field trials; mesocosm effect faster, scored 1-3 weeks.
reasons.environment: Oxidized DOC; minimal reach; no reported harm but uncertain.

papers.title: The relative effects of algaecides and nanobubble ozone treatment (NBOT) on nontarget zooplankton in a mesocosm study
papers.authors: Stanislawczyk K, Braig EC, Laughinghouse HD, Raymond HA, Syed HE, Fuchs JD, Weavers LK, Chaffin JD
papers.scale: 15 outdoor ~2,000 L mesocosm tanks at Stone Lab, Lake Erie; 5 treatments x 3 replicate tanks; Lake Erie plankton inoculum with added N and P
papers.dose: Untreated control; SeClear copper algaecide 1 mg Cu/L; GreenClean Liquid 5.0 at 10 mg H2O2/L; NBOT at 0.9 and 4.6 mg O3/L
papers.duration: Single treatment on day 8 after inoculation; zooplankton followed to 120 h
papers.result: At 120 h total zooplankton changed +120% in controls, +90% (low NBOT) and +10% (high NBOT), but -80% (copper) and -90% (peroxide); cladocerans fell 70-100% under both algaecides. Phytoplankton declined similarly in all treatments over the first 48 h.
papers.env_effects: Higher ozone dose reduced Bosmina, but less than the algaecides. Copper and H2O2 harmed zooplankton more than ozone nanobubbles.
papers.key_details: Replicated mesocosm (n = 3 tanks per treatment) testing non-target effects only; the phytoplankton was mostly green algae (72.7% of chl-a; cyanobacteria 15.4%) at 30 ug/L chl-a, so it is not a test of bloom control. Differences in zooplankton were attributed to direct toxicity because phytoplankton responses were similar; chl-a in the peroxide tanks rebounded to control levels by 120 h but zooplankton did not. Calanoids and Leptodora showed no significant effects owing to low densities. Tanks were shaded ~55% and mixed twice daily.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record said duration unknown; it is 120 h after one dose. The test community was green-algae dominated, not a cyanobacterial bloom.
papers.study_note: zooplankton effects of ozone vs algaecides

reasons.reproducibility: Replicated mesocosms with nanobubble ozone and label-rate algaecides.
reasons.effectiveness: Non-target study on a green-algae-dominated community; phytoplankton fell similarly in all treatments, so no bloom-control effect is shown.
reasons.cost: NBOT equipment and mesocosms over $5,000.
reasons.time: One dose, followed for 120 h.
reasons.environment: Zooplankton grew +120% in controls but only +10% under high-dose ozone (Bosmina reduced), versus -80% copper and -90% peroxide.

papers.title: UV-C irradiation for harmful algal blooms control: A literature review on effectiveness, mechanisms, influencing factors and facilities
papers.authors: Li S, Tao Y, Zhan XM, Dao GH, Hu HY
papers.scale: literature review
papers.dose: UV-C (dose-dependent)
papers.result: UV-C suppresses microalgal growth in proportion to dose, but sensitivity varies between species and cells can regrow through photoreactivation and dark repair. Field cases cited: a UV boat (48 mJ/cm2 killed all Peridinium bipes at <=5.0 x 10^3 cells/mL; 700 m3/h) and a boat killing 80% of Chattonella in 40 s in the Ariake Sea.
papers.env_effects: No chemical residue, but efficacy depends on UV transmittance, salinity and pH; flow-through reactors and ship-borne units proposed for field use.
papers.key_details: Literature review, no new experiments. Cited field tests: a 1991 Japanese mesocosm with a 30 W UV lamp removed almost all live Peridinium bipes within 2 days; a UV boat treated 2.0 x 10^4 m2 in 5 h, needing 120 mJ/cm2 for 90% kill at >1.0 x 10^4 cells/mL. The authors note most studies are static lab tests on M. aeruginosa in culture medium and call for larger field tests, multi-species work and repeated irradiation to counter regrowth. Efficacy depends on UV transmittance, salinity and pH.
papers.study_note: review of efficacy: microalgae and cyanobacteria (multiple species)

reasons.reproducibility: Typical reviewed experiment is UV-C on a bench culture, doable with a sponsor's UV lamp.
reasons.effectiveness: UV-C suppresses growth with dose (e.g. 80% Chattonella kill in 40 s from a boat), but species sensitivity varies and photoreactivation/dark repair cause regrowth; mostly static lab tests.
reasons.cost: UV-C lamp and cultures about $150-500.
reasons.time: UV effect seen within hours to days.
reasons.environment: No chemical residue; non-target effects on other plankton not assessed.

papers.title: Direct and indirect inactivation of Microcystis aeruginosa by UV-radiation
papers.authors: Alam ZB, Otaki M, Furumai H, Ohgaki S
papers.scale: 40 mL samples in petri dishes (0.67 cm deep), then incubated in 60 mL tubes; ~10^5 cells/mL; triplicate
papers.dose: UV-C 254 nm at 37, 75 and 150 mW s/cm2 (1-1.5 mW/cm2 for 30 s to 2 min)
papers.result: By day 3 all irradiated samples had <25% of the control cell density; 150 mW s/cm2 killed all cells by day 7, while 37 and 75 mW s/cm2 left cells alive but not dividing for 7 days. Over 90% of cells settled within 3 days at all doses (all settled at 75 mW s/cm2).
papers.env_effects: UV of algal extracellular products had a residual growth-control effect lasting up to 7 days; UV produced micromolar H2O2, judged too low to explain the residual effect. Framed as an alternative to non-specific copper sulfate.
papers.key_details: Lab study with axenic M. aeruginosa (NIES) in CT medium, pH 9.0, 25 C, irradiated with low-pressure mercury lamps and incubated with unirradiated controls; growth runs in triplicate, counting only undamaged cells. Control density rose from 54 x 10^3 to 1039 x 10^3 cells/mL over 7 days while 37 and 75 mW s/cm2 samples stayed flat. Separate tests showed UV-irradiated algal extracellular products had a residual growth-suppression effect and UV produced micromolar H2O2. Authors propose UV before the bloom season for small eutrophic lakes; no field test.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: The record says 75 mW s/cm2 was lethal; in the full text 150 mW s/cm2 was the lethal dose (all cells dead by day 7), while 37 and 75 mW s/cm2 both stopped division without killing cells. The 150 dose was missing from the record.

reasons.reproducibility: Petri-dish UV-C exposure of a Microcystis culture with a germicidal lamp for 30 s-2 min is bench work, needing a sponsor for UV safety.
reasons.effectiveness: All doses held cells below 25% of control by day 3 in triplicate; 150 mW s/cm2 killed all cells by day 7 while 37-75 stopped division (controls grew ~20x).
reasons.cost: UV lamp, radiometer and culture about $150-500.
reasons.time: Density fell below 25% of control by day 3.
reasons.environment: No chemical added; micromolar H2O2 formed; residual effect from treated exudates.

papers.title: Chlorination of Microcystis aeruginosa suspension: cell lysis, toxin release and degradation
papers.authors: Ma M, Liu R, Liu H, Qu J
papers.scale: bench suspensions
papers.dose: chlorine 0.8-2.0 mg/L
papers.result: Chlorine exposure as low as 0.8 mg/L min released 63% of intracellular K+; membrane damage outpaced toxin release, and extracellular MC-LR accumulated because release was faster than degradation, peaking at 60, 30 and 1 min for 1.2, 1.6 and 2.0 mg/L.
papers.env_effects: Low chlorine doses raise dissolved microcystin; release of intracellular organic matter (a by-product precursor).

reasons.reproducibility: Chlorinating Microcystis suspensions with microcystin analysis needs ELISA/LC-MS.
reasons.effectiveness: Low chlorine lysed cells (63% K+ release) but released toxin faster than it degraded.
reasons.cost: Chlorine is cheap but microcystin analysis is $150-500.
reasons.time: Minutes to hours.
reasons.environment: Low chlorine raised dissolved microcystin; by-product precursors released.

papers.title: The effect of electrode materials on the removal of red tide organisms by microelectrolysis
papers.authors: Wei Z, Zang X, Yu Z, Jiang K, Cao X, Song X
papers.scale: bench electrolyte treatment
papers.dose: electrolysed artificial seawater (DSA, Pt or BDD anode, Ti cathode; up to 0.75 A/cm2, 4 min) added as 250 or 500 uL aliquots to 50 mL algal suspension; 580 mg/L hypochlorite in electrolyte = 5.8 mg/L initial in the suspension
papers.result: Best removal was 81.69 +/- 2.27% (DSA), 69.89 +/- 3.07% (Pt) and 64.43 +/- 4.10% (BDD). Hypochlorite (>95% of total chlorine) was the main algicide; H2O2 at 0.025 mg/L gave only 15% removal.
