papers.env_effects: Active oxidant is hypochlorite from seawater electrolysis; authors note chlorine can rupture Heterosigma membranes and may release intracellular toxin, and call for trials on ecological impacts. DSA used 25% and 17% less power than BDD and Pt.
papers.key_details: Bench study with cultured Heterosigma akashiwo in L1 medium; electrolyte was produced separately and pipetted into 50 mL algal suspensions in cuvettes. Removal was estimated from in vivo fluorescence (linear with cell counts from 0.1 x 10^8 to 2.5 x 10^8 cells/L); results given as mean +/- SD. The authors cite 70-80% removal as the threshold needed in the field to stop recurrence. No field or ecological tests were done; the treatment is effectively electro-chlorination.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Minor: the device does not treat algae directly by electrolysis; electrolysed seawater is dosed into the suspension (initial hypochlorite ~5.8 mg/L for >80% inactivation).
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Heterosigma akashiwo (red tide raphidophyte)

reasons.reproducibility: Microelectrolysis with DSA, Pt and BDD anodes is specialist electrochemistry.
reasons.effectiveness: Electrolysed seawater (hypochlorite ~5.8 mg/L) removed 81.7 +/- 2.3% (DSA) of Heterosigma, 64-70% with Pt/BDD, measured by fluorescence.
reasons.cost: Pt and BDD anodes plus a high-current supply push it to $500-5,000.
reasons.time: 4-min treatment.
reasons.environment: Effectively electro-chlorination; hypochlorite can rupture cells and release toxin, and no ecological tests were done.

papers.title: Photocatalytic inactivation and destruction of harmful microalgae Karenia mikimotoi under visible-light irradiation: Insights into physiological response and toxicity assessment
papers.authors: Wang W, Liao P, Li G, Chen H, Cen J, Lu S, Wong PK, An T
papers.scale: bench photochemical reactor; K. mikimotoi (Daya Bay strain) ~3.78 x 10^4 cells/mL
papers.dose: 50 wt% g-C3N4/TiO2 film on FTO glass (7.065 cm2 coating) under visible light (>=420 nm)
papers.result: Inactivation reached 64% within 60 min (in vivo chlorophyll-a fluorescence); h+ and singlet oxygen were the main reactive species and cells ruptured.
papers.env_effects: About 71% of intracellular organic matter was released after 1 h of treatment (possible secondary pollution); acute toxicity tests showed cytotoxicity decreased significantly after treatment. Films are immobilized and reusable.
papers.key_details: Lab study with dark control (photocatalyst without light) and light control (light without photocatalyst). Chlorophyll-a fluorescence fell in all lit systems within 10 min, but in the light-only control it recovered to the starting level after 60 min of darkness, while with the photocatalyst it did not; net inactivation was 64% in 60 min. Cell density used (3.78 x 10^4 cells/mL) was higher than typical blooms. Mechanism: h+ and singlet oxygen causing oxidative damage, antioxidant enzyme collapse and cell lysis.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: The record says the released organic matter had no cytotoxicity; the full text says cytotoxicity decreased significantly, while 71% of intracellular organic matter was released.

reasons.reproducibility: Synthesizing g-C3N4/TiO2 films needs a materials lab.
reasons.effectiveness: 64% net inactivation of K. mikimotoi in 60 min vs dark and light-only controls (light-only fluorescence recovered).
reasons.cost: Photocatalyst synthesis and culture $150-500.
reasons.time: 60-min result.
reasons.environment: Film is immobilised and reusable and cytotoxicity fell, but ~71% of intracellular organic matter was released.

papers.title: Photocatalytic removal of the cyanobacterium Microcystis aeruginosa PCC7813 and four microcystins by TiO2 coated porous glass beads with UV-LED irradiation
papers.authors: Pestana CJ, Portela Noronha J, Hui J, Edwards C, Gunaratne HQN, Irvine JTS, Robertson PKJ, Capelo-Neto J, Lawton LA
papers.scale: Bench: 30 mL cell suspension in 40 mL bottles, triplicates, with UV-only and TiO2-without-UV controls
papers.dose: 700 mg TiO2 (P25)-coated foamed recycled-glass beads (0.2% w/v TiO2) in mesh pods; 90-LED 365 nm panel, 2.8 umol photons m-2 s-1 (67.5 mW total output) at 100 mm; air sparged
papers.result: Cell density fell from 15 to 10 x 10^6 cells/mL (35%) in 7 days while both controls grew to 32-34 x 10^6 cells/mL (+213-226%); intracellular microcystins fell 49% (0.69 to 0.35 ug/mL), total microcystin removal was 74%, and released microcystins were fully removed.
papers.env_effects: Toxins released by damaged cells were destroyed by the photocatalyst; low-cost LEDs and recycled glass proposed for in-reservoir use.
papers.key_details: Lab test with M. aeruginosa PCC7813 at a very high start density (15 x 10^6 cells/mL) in artificial freshwater. Three treatments in triplicate: TiO2 beads + UV, UV only, TiO2 beads under ambient light only; UV-only and TiO2-only controls did not differ (p > 0.05). Decline began after 48 h; biovolume was 66% of the TiO2 control. Low-energy UV-LEDs are not germicidal alone. No in-reservoir testing; the in-reservoir unit is a proposal.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record called the scale a 'prototype in-reservoir unit'; it was 30 mL bottles. The 35% is the drop from the starting density; relative to controls the treated density was about 70% lower (10 vs 32-34 x 10^6 cells/mL).

reasons.reproducibility: 30 mL bottles with TiO2-coated glass beads under a 365 nm LED panel and cell counts are a bench protocol a sponsor can support.
reasons.effectiveness: In triplicate, cells fell 35% from the start while both controls grew +213-226%, leaving treated density ~70% below controls; decline began only after 48 h.
reasons.cost: LEDs, TiO2 and beads about $150-500.
reasons.time: 7-day result.
reasons.environment: Immobilised catalyst is retrievable, and total microcystins fell 74% with released toxin fully destroyed.

papers.title: Control of the red tide dinoflagellate Cochlodinium polykrikoides by ozone in seawater
papers.authors: Shin M, Lee HJ, Kim MS, Park NB, Lee C
papers.scale: 10 mL cultures in 25 mL batch flasks with natural Busan seawater; 0.5-3.0 x 10^3 cells/mL
papers.dose: ozone <1 to 5 mg/L
papers.result: Ozone inactivated 40-95% of viable C. polykrikoides within 20 s; doses >1 mg/L removed all viable cells within 300 s, and 5 mg/L destroyed all cells within 100 s. Efficacy fell with higher cell density, humic acid, pH and temperature.
papers.env_effects: Ozonation of seawater forms HOBr and carcinogenic bromate: 0.75 ug/L BrO3- at 0.5 mg/L ozone but 278 ug/L at 5 mg/L (WHO drinking-water guideline 10 ug/L); negligible below 1 mg/L. Possible release of intracellular toxins was not tested.
papers.key_details: Bench batch experiments with cultured C. polykrikoides (NFRDI isolate) diluted in natural seawater, dosed with ozone at several concentrations; viable (motile) and total cells counted by microscope. Inactivation was two-stage: instant kill by molecular ozone, then slow kill by residual ozone and HOBr. Over 90% of the ozone decomposed within 20 s. Bicarbonate increased efficacy and humic acid reduced it. Bromate data came from Br- spiked DI water because the method failed in seawater. No field or aquaculture-scale test.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record omits the bromate byproduct risk (278 ug/L at 5 mg/L ozone).

reasons.reproducibility: Ozonation of toxic Cochlodinium in seawater needs an ozone generator and cultures.
reasons.effectiveness: Ozone >1 mg/L removed all viable C. polykrikoides within 300 s (5 mg/L in 100 s), but efficacy fell with cell density, humics, pH and temperature and replication is not stated.
reasons.cost: Ozone generator and bromate analysis $500-5,000.
reasons.time: 1-2 min kill.
reasons.environment: Ozonated seawater formed bromate at 278 ug/L at 5 mg/L ozone (WHO guideline 10 ug/L), negligible below 1 mg/L.

papers.title: Mote Marine's ozone experiment works, sort of, but it's not the silver bullet to kill Red Tide (with CBS News coverage of the same test)
papers.authors: Pittman C (Tampa Bay Times); CBS News
papers.venue: Tampa Bay Times; CBS News (press coverage)
papers.scale: dead-end canal (Damfino Street, Boca Grande, Florida); system processes 300 gallons/min
papers.dose: ozone treatment system (dose not reported)
papers.result: Press reports only: the canal system ran five days and was described as working 'sort of' but not a silver bullet; Pierce (Mote) said it removes red tide, toxins and decomposing organic matter. No cell or toxin numbers were published.
papers.env_effects: Researchers named the size of the treated area and performance in a natural ecosystem as the main challenges; not intended for open water. Ozonix (ozone + cavitation + electrochemical, Mote 2025) likewise has no published results.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Karenia brevis (Florida red tide)

reasons.reproducibility: Canal-scale ozone system processing 300 gal/min; industrial gear.
reasons.effectiveness: No cell or toxin numbers published; press says it worked 'sort of'.
reasons.cost: Industrial ozone system over $5,000.
reasons.time: Ran five days.
reasons.environment: Not reported beyond scale concerns; ozone by-products in seawater uncertain.

papers.title: Side effects of 58 years of copper sulfate treatment of the Fairmont Lakes, Minnesota
papers.venue: JAWRA Journal of the American Water Resources Association (Water Resources Bulletin)
papers.scale: five whole lakes, 58 years (1921-1979)
papers.dose: copper sulfate, cumulative up to 1,647 kg/ha; 1.5 million kg total
papers.result: Treatments killed algae temporarily, but populations recovered within 7-21 days; long-term, algae became more copper-tolerant and species shifted from green to blue-green algae.
papers.env_effects: Oxygen depletion, faster phosphorus recycling from sediment, occasional fish kills, copper accumulation in sediments, shift from game to rough fish, loss of macrophytes and fewer benthic invertebrates.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: phytoplankton (green algae and cyanobacteria)

reasons.reproducibility: 58 years of copper treatment of five whole lakes; impossible to repeat.
reasons.effectiveness: Algae recovered within 7-21 days and shifted toward blue-greens.
reasons.cost: 1.5 million kg CuSO4; far over $5,000.
reasons.time: Decades of treatment.
reasons.environment: Fish kills, copper-laden sediments, loss of macrophytes and invertebrates.

papers.title: Occurrence of copper resistant mutants in the toxic cyanobacteria Microcystis aeruginosa: characterisation and future implications in the use of copper sulphate as algaecide
papers.authors: Garcia-Villada L, Rico M, Altamirano MM, Sanchez-Martin L, Lopez-Rodas V, Costas E
papers.scale: Modified Luria-Delbrück fluctuation analysis: 198 set-1 and 198 set-2 replicate cultures of M. aeruginosa strain MaM1, plus fitness dose-response (n = 3)
papers.dose: 10 µM free Cu2+ for selection; fitness tested across 1-10.5 µM Cu2+
papers.duration: About 4 weeks to 1 month under copper for resistant cells to regrow
papers.result: 10 µM Cu2+ destroyed sensitive cells within days, but 32 of 198 set-1 cultures (and all 198 set-2 cultures) regrew from rare copper-resistant cells; the spontaneous mutation rate was 1.76x10^-6 mutants per cell division. Wild-type fitness fell to zero at 3.2-10.5 µM Cu2+, where resistant mutants grew best.
papers.env_effects: Resistant mutants were smaller and less fit without copper; authors warn repeated copper treatment of water supplies selects for resistance.
papers.key_details: Lab fluctuation analysis distinguishing pre-existing spontaneous mutations from induced adaptation: set-1 variance/mean was >50 (set 2 ~1), showing resistance arises randomly before copper exposure. Repeatability 96%, reproducibility 100%. Without copper, resistant mutants had 20% lower Malthusian fitness and were smaller (3.99 vs 4.54 µm diameter). Authors conclude repeated copper sulphate dosing of supply reservoirs can select persistent resistant toxic populations. Single strain, lab only.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record's 'above 5.8 µM' threshold was not found in the full text; the results give wild-type fitness zero and resistant fitness maximal at 3.2-10.5 µM Cu2+.
papers.study_note: copper resistance in Microcystis; growth under Cu

reasons.reproducibility: Lab fluctuation test with ~400 Microcystis cultures; bench scale but needs a purchased strain and a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: 10 uM Cu2+ destroyed sensitive cells within days, but resistant mutants regrew in 32 of 198 set-1 cultures.
reasons.cost: Culture, media and copper for hundreds of cultures cost about $150-500.
reasons.time: Resistant cells took about four weeks to regrow under copper.
reasons.environment: Copper persists and repeated dosing selects for resistant toxic Microcystis.

papers.title: Effect of copper sulphate treatment on natural phytoplanktonic communities
papers.authors: Le Jeune AH, Charpin M, Deluchat V, Briand JF, Lenain JF, Baudu M, Amblard C
papers.scale: Nine 85 L indoor glass aquaria filled with Lake Pontalage (France) water, 200 µm-screened; triplicate controls, 80 and 160 µg Cu/L; run separately in spring and summer 2004
papers.dose: 80 and 160 ug Cu/L (below and above complexation capacity)
papers.result: Biomass fell until day 5 (80 µg/L) or day 8 (160 µg/L), then regrew; in summer, biomass stayed significantly below controls from day 12 to 27 at 80 µg/L and until day 27 at 160 µg/L, while in spring the 80 µg/L treatment ended higher than controls (days 16-20). Cyanobacteria biomass was significantly lower than controls at both doses in both seasons (p < 0.001), but cyanobacteria were at low density (7.5% of summer biomass) with no bloom present.
papers.env_effects: 160 µg/L gave Chlorophyceae dominance (>85% of biomass) and nanophytoplankton >90% of biomass, with microphytoplankton significantly suppressed; diatoms, Chrysophyceae and Cryptophyceae (spring) also reduced. The lake had never been treated with algicide.
papers.key_details: Replicated (n = 3) indoor mesocosm test of copper sulphate on natural phytoplankton sampled before any bloom formed; no nutrients added, zooplankton >200 µm removed. In untreated controls cyanobacteria rose to 40% (spring) and 30% (summer) of biomass, while copper significantly suppressed them at both doses. Total biomass responses were season-dependent. Because the starting community had low cyanobacteria and no bloom, this tests preventive dosing rather than bloom control.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record says total biomass 'recovered within a few days'; it declined for 5-8 days, and in summer stayed significantly below controls for most of the 27 days. Record omits that no bloom was present (cyanobacteria ~7.5% of summer biomass) and the 85 L, n = 3 design.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: natural phytoplankton communities (spring and summer)

reasons.reproducibility: 85 L aquaria of lake water dosed with copper sulphate; doable with a sponsor for microscopy counts.
reasons.effectiveness: Cyanobacteria were significantly suppressed (n=3), but no bloom was present (7.5% of biomass) and total biomass regrew after 5-8 days in spring.
reasons.cost: Nine aquaria, copper sulphate and phytoplankton counting cost about $150-500.
reasons.time: Biomass declined for 5-8 days and was followed over 27 days.
reasons.environment: 160 ug/L shifted the community to >85% Chlorophyceae and suppressed diatoms and other groups; copper persists.

papers.title: Cellular and aqueous microcystin-LR following laboratory exposures of Microcystis aeruginosa to copper algaecides
papers.authors: Iwinski KJ, Calomeni AJ, Geer TD, Rodgers JH
papers.scale: bench exposures
papers.dose: CuSO4 and copper-ethanolamine, 0.07-1.0 mg Cu/L
papers.result: Cellular MC-LR and chlorophyll-a declined with copper (sigmoidal exposure-response) and total MC-LR fell below untreated controls, but aqueous MC-LR rose with copper concentration; CuSO4 gave 10-20% more aqueous and total MC-LR than copper-ethanolamine at 0.5-1.0 mg Cu/L.
papers.env_effects: Toxin moves from cells into the water; lower copper doses were as effective while releasing less toxin.

reasons.reproducibility: Bench Microcystis exposures with MC-LR analysis need ELISA.
reasons.effectiveness: Cellular MC-LR and chl-a declined sigmoidally, but aqueous toxin rose; no percent given.
reasons.cost: Culture, copper products, ELISA about $150-500.
reasons.time: Day-1 measurements.
reasons.environment: Copper added, and toxin moved into the water.

papers.title: Laboratory-scale evaluation of algaecide effectiveness for control of microcystin-producing cyanobacteria from Lake Okeechobee, Florida (USA)
papers.authors: Kinley-Baird C, Calomeni A, Berthold DE, Lefler FW, Barbosa M, Rodgers JH, Laughinghouse HD
papers.organism: Lake Okeechobee cyanobacterial assemblage (6.14 x 10^6 cells/mL; 71% Microcystis aeruginosa, 29% Pseudanabaena mucicola)
papers.scale: 200 mL site water in 400 mL beakers, n=3 per concentration, 4 label-range concentrations per product
papers.dose: Minimum effective measured exposures: SeClear (copper sulfate) 0.51 mg Cu/L; chelated Cu (Algimycin PWF, Argos, Captain XTR, Cutrine Ultra) 0.63-0.74 mg Cu/L; GreenClean Liquid 5.0 11.4 mg H2O2/L; GreenClean Liquid 5.0 11.8 mg H2O2/L + Hydrothol 191 0.198 mg endothall acid/L
papers.duration: responses 3 days after treatment; toxins at 1, 4, 9 days
papers.result: At minimum effective doses, chelated copper cut cell density 77-90% and SeClear and GreenClean Liquid 5.0 (alone or with Hydrothol 191) >90-95% versus untreated controls at 3 days; granular peroxides (GreenClean Pro, PAK 27, Phycomycin SCP) and Hydrothol 191 alone achieved only 34-48%. Chelated copper kept most microcystin cell-bound at day 1 (10-23% aqueous vs 79-99% for SeClear and peroxide), and total microcystin fell below 10 ug/L by day 9 in all copper treatments.
papers.env_effects: Short-term toxin release; authors call for larger-scale studies before use.
papers.key_details: Lab exposures of Lake Okeechobee water collected August 7, 2019, with 10 USEPA-registered algaecides plus one combination, each at 4 label-range concentrations (n=3), and untreated controls (n=3). Controls grew from 6.14 to 8.06 x 10^6 cells/mL over 3 days. Cell density, chlorophyll-a and phycocyanin were measured 3 days after treatment; microcystin (cellular vs aqueous) at 1, 4 and 9 days. Control total microcystin was 787 ug/L at day 1 and 547 ug/L at day 9; by day 4, Algimycin PWF, Argos and Captain XTR treatments were at 11-28 ug/L. Measured peroxide and endothall exposures were 38% and 41% off target, so results use measured concentrations. Bench scale only.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record lists SeClear as a non-copper product; it is copper sulfate-based (0.51 mg Cu/L) and released 91% of microcystin into water at day 1. Granular peroxide products and Hydrothol 191 alone were only 34-48% effective, which the record omits.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: microcystin-producing cyanobacteria (Lake Okeechobee water)

reasons.reproducibility: Beakers of lake water with retail algaecides at label doses; bench scale but needs toxic bloom water and cell counts.
reasons.effectiveness: Replicated (n=3) with controls: copper products cut cells 77-95% at 3 days (SeClear >90%).
reasons.cost: Several algaecides, beakers and microscopy/fluorometry cost about $150-500.
reasons.time: Reductions measured 3 days after treatment.
reasons.environment: Copper persists in sediment and copper sulphate (SeClear) released ~91% of microcystin into water at day 1.

papers.title: Treatment of the red tide dinoflagellate Karenia brevis and brevetoxins using USEPA-registered algaecides
papers.authors: Hu J, Berthold DE, Wang Y, Xiao X, Laughinghouse HD
papers.scale: bench, natural bloom density 1.79e7 cells/L
papers.dose: three copper algaecides (from 0.31-0.34 mg Cu/L) and three peroxide algaecides (4.89-7.08 mg H2O2/L)
papers.result: As little as 0.31-0.34 mg Cu/L significantly decreased K. brevis cells within 24 h; brevetoxin at 72 h fell most with 1.00 mg Cu/L Algimycin PWF and the higher peroxide doses.
papers.env_effects: Fate of copper and toxins and effects on marine non-target species not tested; authors say pilot studies on marine non-targets are needed before use.

reasons.reproducibility: Toxic K. brevis at bloom density; sponsor lab needed.
reasons.effectiveness: 0.31-0.34 mg Cu/L significantly decreased cells in 24 h; no percent given.
reasons.cost: Culture and six algaecides about $150-500.
reasons.environment: Copper persists; marine non-targets not tested.

papers.title: New is not always better: Toxicity of novel copper based algaecides to Daphnia magna
papers.authors: Kang L, Mucci M, Fang J, Lurling M
papers.scale: acute and chronic toxicity tests
papers.dose: Measured-stock dilutions of CuSO4.5H2O, Captain XTR, SeClear and Lake Guard Blue; chronic top doses set at the acute EC10 (about 0.4-0.5 mg Cu/L)
papers.result: Acute 48 h EC50s ranged 0.50 (Lake Guard Blue) to 0.60 (Captain XTR) mg Cu/L (CuSO4 0.521). In 21 d tests the top doses (0.4-0.5 mg Cu/L) cut population growth rate by 29% (CuSO4), 49% (Captain XTR), 48% (SeClear) and 37% (Lake Guard Blue), and SeClear's top dose left only 60% survival.
papers.env_effects: All four products cut Daphnia reproduction and growth at 0.4-0.5 mg Cu/L, below the USEPA-allowed 1 mg Cu/L (about twice the acute EC50). Test medium contained EDTA, which chelated most copper, so field toxicity could differ.
papers.key_details: Lab ecotoxicity on Daphnia magna only (no algae treated). Acute tests: triplicates of five neonates per concentration, 48 h immobility. Chronic tests: 10 single-animal replicates per concentration for 21 days, fed Scenedesmus; stock Cu verified by ICP-OES. First brood was delayed 1.8-3.2 days at the highest doses; reproduction EC50s 0.274 (SeClear) to 0.498 (Captain XTR) mg Cu/L. Authors still see copper as an emergency option where nutrient control is absent.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record is correct; adds that effects occur at about half the US label maximum (1 mg Cu/L) and the EDTA-medium caveat.
papers.study_note: Daphnia magna toxicity of copper algaecides

reasons.reproducibility: Standard Daphnia magna acute/chronic tests with retail copper algaecides; bench scale and well documented.
reasons.effectiveness: No algae were treated; this is a non-target toxicity study only.
reasons.cost: Daphnia cultures, algaecides and glassware cost about $50-150.
reasons.time: Chronic endpoints needed 21 days (acute 48 h).
reasons.environment: At 0.4-0.5 mg Cu/L, half the US label maximum, all products cut Daphnia population growth 29-49%.

papers.title: A critical review on operation and performance of source water control strategies for cyanobacterial blooms: Part I-chemical control methods
papers.authors: Kibuye FA, Zamyadi A, Wert EC
papers.scale: review of in-lake/reservoir case studies
papers.dose: algaecides (copper, peroxide) and nutrient-sequestering coagulants
papers.result: Review of in-lake chemical controls (Al, Fe, lanthanum-modified bentonite, Ca, H2O2, Cu, KMnO4) finds that algaecides act fast but blooms rebound; one site needed up to six monthly copper applications with an average rebound time of 14 days. The authors conclude no single chemical strategy is a complete solution and external nutrient reduction is fundamental.
papers.env_effects: Over 90% of applied copper transfers to sediments; high mortality of fish and other fauna after Cu treatment has been linked to oxygen depletion or high doses. A whole-creek 50 mg/L H2O2 treatment cut zooplankton by 99% after 50 h, raised NH4+ 97%, and caused some fish kills.
papers.key_details: Narrative critical review with tables of field and pilot-scale studies covering nutrient-inactivation agents and algaecides. Copper examples: >90% chlorophyll-a decline at 0.02-1 mg/L Cu at low/medium Microcystis densities but higher doses needed at 10^7 cells/mL; an Albay et al. (2003) Microcystis bloom rebounded despite daily Cu dosing under high nutrient inputs. H2O2 examples: 99% cell decline 10 days after whole-lake injection, with cells back to 2 x 10^5 cells/mL at 49 days; 99% A. ostenfeldii decline in 48 h with 50 mg/L H2O2. It also covers toxin release, dose timing and US regulations.

reasons.reproducibility: Review of in-lake and reservoir chemical treatments; field-scale with permits.
reasons.effectiveness: Copper gave >90% Chl a declines at low-medium densities, but blooms rebounded (mean 14 days, up to six monthly doses).
reasons.cost: Whole-lake algaecide applications cost far over $5,000.
reasons.time: Algaecide declines appear within days, though rebounds follow in ~2 weeks.
reasons.environment: Over 90% of copper ends up in sediment and fauna kills are reported after treatment.

papers.title: Occurrence of toxic cyanobacteria before and after copper sulphate treatment in a water reservoir, Istanbul, Turkey
papers.authors: Albay M, Akcaalan R, Aykulu G, Tufekci H, Beattie KA, Codd GA
papers.scale: Omerli drinking-water reservoir, Istanbul
papers.dose: CuSO4 to surface water: 1,600 kg (Apr 2000), 4,800 kg (May), 5,050 kg (Jun), 5,000 kg (Jul), then 800 kg in Sep
papers.result: M. aeruginosa bloomed again whenever treatment stopped (78.91 mg/L surface biomass on 20 Sep 2000); 800 kg of CuSO4 then cut surface biomass to 34.75 mg/L, a 3.1-fold decrease reported at the surface.
papers.env_effects: Tonnes of copper added to a drinking-water reservoir; total nitrogen increased slightly after treatment; microcystin was present in the bloom (2.1 ug/L in raw water in 1999).

reasons.reproducibility: Tonnes of CuSO4 into a drinking-water reservoir; impossible to repeat.
reasons.effectiveness: 56% surface biomass drop, but blooms returned whenever treatment stopped.
reasons.time: April-September season.
reasons.environment: Tonnes of copper added to a drinking-water reservoir.

papers.title: The effects of three chemical algaecides on cell numbers and toxin content of the cyanobacteria Microcystis aeruginosa and Anabaenopsis sp.
papers.authors: Greenfield DI, Duquette A, Goodson A, Keppler CJ, Williams SH, Brock LM, Stackley KD, White D, Wilde SB
papers.organism: Microcystis aeruginosa (culture, 5 psu) and Anabaenopsis sp. bloom water (21 psu) from a brackish stormwater pond
papers.scale: 1 L flasks in triplicate per algaecide x dose, starting at ~5x10^5 cells/mL
papers.dose: Captain (chelated copper carbonate; label 0.4 ppm), K-Tea (copper-triethanolamine; label 0.5 ppm) and Pak 27 (85% sodium percarbonate; label 6.5 lb/acre-ft), each at 0.5x, 1x and 2x label dose
papers.result: After 7 days, both copper algaecides left significantly fewer cells than Pak 27 or controls at 1x and 2x (and for Anabaenopsis at all doses); Captain at 0.5x did not differ from control, and 0.5x Pak 27 cells were slightly more than double. Total microcystin (initially 11-30 ppb) generally rose over the experiments, often ending 2-10x above initial, with toxin shifting to the dissolved phase.
papers.env_effects: Algaecides may visibly control a bloom without reducing toxin, a public-health concern.
papers.key_details: Lab flask exposures (n = 3) of three commercial algaecides at half, label and double doses, sampled at 4, 8, 24, 48, 72 h and 7 days. Toxin analysis was done only for the M. aeruginosa culture because the Anabaenopsis bloom had microcystin <0.1 ppb. The copper products controlled cell numbers but no product reduced overall toxin; particulate:dissolved microcystin ratios dropped, meaning toxin moved into the water. The percarbonate product was the least effective on cell numbers.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record omits that total microcystin often increased 2-10x above initial during the experiments, and that toxin results come from the culture only (bloom water had <0.1 ppb).

reasons.reproducibility: 1 L flasks with retail algaecides at label doses; bench scale but needs Microcystis culture and bloom water.
reasons.effectiveness: Copper products significantly cut cells at 1x and 2x label (n=3), but 0.5x Captain did not differ from control and no percent reduction is given.
reasons.cost: Algaecides, cultures and toxin analysis cost about $150-500.
reasons.time: Endpoints read at 7 days.
reasons.environment: Total microcystin often rose 2-10x and moved into the water; copper persists.

papers.title: Evaluation of algaecide effectiveness of five different oxidants applied on harmful phytoplankton
papers.authors: Moreno-Andres J, Romero-Martinez L, Seoane S, Acevedo-Merino A, Moreno-Garrido I, Nebot E
papers.scale: 14-day concentration-response in seawater (ballast-water context)
papers.dose: peracetic acid, peroxymonosulfate, peroxydisulfate, H2O2, chlorine
papers.result: Peracetic acid (EC50 0.32-2.70 mg/L) and peroxymonosulfate (EC50 0.40-1.99 mg/L) acted strongly but briefly, H2O2 (EC50 6.67-7.08 mg/L) gave a sustained effect, and peroxydisulfate was negligible.
papers.env_effects: Not assessed; PAA, PMS or H2O2 proposed as alternatives to chlorine-based reagents.
papers.study_note: oxidation/peroxide: five oxidants, no copper tested

reasons.reproducibility: Dose-response of five oxidants on two purchased seawater cultures; sponsor-doable.
reasons.effectiveness: PAA and PMS strong but brief; H2O2 sustained (EC50 6.67-7.08); peroxydisulfate negligible — mixed.
reasons.cost: Two cultures and five oxidants about $150-500.
reasons.time: 14-day test.
reasons.environment: Not assessed; oxidants short-lived (no copper used despite file).

papers.title: Oxidation of Microcystis aeruginosa and microcystins with peracetic acid
papers.authors: Alnahas M, Almuhtaram H, Hofmann R
papers.scale: bench, 1e6 cells/mL in buffered water
papers.dose: peracetic acid 10 mg/L (with ~10% H2O2 in the product)
papers.result: At acidic pH, 10 mg/L PAA damaged cells immediately and killed them in 15-60 min, but at neutral and alkaline pH death came only after a 3-6 h lag; toxin degradation rates were orders of magnitude below free chlorine. Authors judge PAA impractically slow for cell or microcystin control.
papers.env_effects: Slow lysis: <35% of intracellular MC-LR was in solution after 12 h at 10 mg/L, so low risk of sudden toxin release.
papers.study_note: oxidation: peracetic acid on Microcystis, no copper

reasons.reproducibility: Microcystis culture with 10 mg/L PAA and toxin analysis; sponsor-doable.
reasons.effectiveness: Authors judge PAA impractically slow at neutral/alkaline pH (3-6 h lag).
reasons.cost: Culture, PAA, microcystin analysis about $150-500.
reasons.time: Within 12 h.
reasons.environment: <35% of MC-LR released after 12 h; low sudden-release risk; PAA degrades.

papers.title: The water footprint of water conservation using shade balls in California
papers.authors: Haghighi E, Madani K, Hoekstra AY
papers.scale: Los Angeles reservoir (Sylmar, CA), surface area ~710,000 m2, >96 million 100 mm HDPE shade balls released August 2015
papers.dose: Full surface cover with plastic shade balls
papers.result: Saving an estimated 1.15 million m3/yr of evaporation with 96 million HDPE balls costs 0.25-2.9 million m3 of water to make them (ball thickness 1-5 mm, water footprint 0.05-0.19 m3/kg HDPE), so the balls must stay 0.2-2.5 years for net water savings. The paper reports no algae or water-quality data and calls shade-ball control of water quality an open question.
papers.env_effects: Large manufacturing water footprint; plastic production and waste.
papers.key_details: Short perspective-style analysis using water-footprint accounting (consumptive use only) for HDPE production. The total HDPE mass needed to cover a given area depends only on ball thickness, not diameter. The balls were deployed partly to prevent algal-bloom water-quality deterioration, but whether they worked for that is stated as unresolved; some experts hypothesised a thermal-blanket effect promoting bacterial growth. Thin, lightweight balls may drift and expose warmed water, increasing evaporation. The water saving figure is the Los Angeles officials' estimate, not a measurement.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record's figures are rounded: 96 million balls (not ~100 million), 1.15 million m3/yr saved (not ~1.2), footprint 0.25-2.9 million m3, and payback 0.2-2.5 years depending on thickness.
papers.study_note: water footprint of shade balls; no algae

reasons.reproducibility: Desk life-cycle calculation of water footprint; repeatable with published data.
reasons.effectiveness: Reports no algae or water-quality data; shade-ball algae control is called an open question.
reasons.cost: A desk analysis costs little beyond reference data.
reasons.time: Payback of 0.2-2.5 years is a calculation; no algae result.
reasons.environment: 96 million HDPE balls cost 0.25-2.9 million m3 of water to make and become plastic waste.

papers.title: Controversy over the Use of "Shade Covers" to Avoid Water Evaporation in Water Reservoirs
papers.scale: Review of suspended shade cloth covers and floating shade objects on agricultural reservoirs
papers.dose: n/a
papers.result: Review: studies of suspended shade-cloth covers report evaporation cuts close to 85% and a 'dramatic limitation of algal blooms', but the evidence base is scarce; the author's own unpublished pool test (one uncovered vs two shade-ball pools, June-September 2014) found clearer water and up to 90% less evaporation under shade balls.
papers.env_effects: Polyethylene shade objects: high energy and raw-material cost, recalcitrant residues, possible endocrine-disrupting leachates after long sun exposure (~10 years), unstudied microplastic release, visual pollution.
papers.key_details: Short single-author narrative review (Sustainability, 2021) of suspended shade-cloth covers and floating shade objects (balls, hexagons) on reservoirs. No quantitative algal data beyond citing Martinez-Alvarez et al. for 'dramatic limitation of algal blooms'. Includes an unpublished, unreplicated pool experiment (1 control, 2 covered pools) measured by turbidity and OD600 rather than algal counts. Main point is the unresolved cost and plastic-waste trade-off.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: None material; record should note the algae evidence is second-hand plus one small unpublished pool test.
papers.study_note: shade-cover review; cost and plastics, no algae data

reasons.reproducibility: Review; the cited pool test (covered vs uncovered pools) could be copied with a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: Algae evidence is second-hand plus one unreplicated unpublished pool test measured by turbidity, not algal counts.
reasons.cost: Shade balls or cloth for small pools cost about $150-500.
reasons.time: The pool test compared water over June-September, but differences show within weeks.
reasons.environment: Polyethylene objects leave recalcitrant residues, possible leachates and microplastics.

papers.title: Experimental assessment of shade-cloth covers on agricultural reservoirs for irrigation in south-eastern Spain
papers.authors: Martínez Álvarez V, Maestre-Valero JF, Martín-Górriz B, Gallego-Elvira B
papers.scale: One agricultural irrigation reservoir, Segura basin, SE Spain: 2,400 m2 surface, 5 m deep, 11,920 m3; uncovered year 1 (2007-08) vs covered year 2 (2008-09); no simultaneous control reservoir
papers.dose: Black polyethylene suspended shade-cloth cover (<1% solar transmission); cost EUR 7.80/m2 (EUR 5.30 structure + 2.50 cloth)
papers.result: Evaporation fell close to 85% (84% used in economics). Under the cover photosynthesis dropped massively and algal growth was highly limited (chlorophyll shown only in a figure, 0-30 ug/L axis); farmers reported a 90% cut in filter cleaning.
papers.env_effects: Near-total light removal suppresses all photosynthesis; cost/benefit analysed.
papers.key_details: Before/after design on a single reservoir: year 1 uncovered (used to validate an open-water evaporation model), year 2 covered; monthly samples at 1-4 m for algal cells (inverted microscope) plus YSI profiles of EC, chlorophyll and turbidity. No numerical chlorophyll values are given in text; the 90% filtration benefit is an anecdotal landholder report. Discounted cash-flow analysis found the cover not economically viable when saved water is valued at purchase price (EUR 0.15-0.50/m3), but viable where water shortage limits cropped area.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record right in substance; adds the unreplicated before/after design, the cost, and that algae reductions are shown only graphically.

reasons.reproducibility: Suspended shade-cloth cover over a 2,400 m2 irrigation reservoir; not school-repeatable.
reasons.effectiveness: Algal growth 'highly limited' under the cover, but one reservoir before/after with Chl a shown only in a figure and a farmer-reported 90% filter benefit.
reasons.cost: Cover costs EUR 7.80/m2, about EUR 19,000 for the reservoir.
reasons.time: Compared an uncovered year with a covered year.
reasons.environment: Near-total light removal stops all photosynthesis; cover material is durable but removable.

papers.title: The Pond Dye, Aquashade, Does Not Prevent Cyanobacterial Off-Flavors in Pond-Grown Channel Catfish
papers.organism: Planktothrix perornata and pond phytoplankton; channel catfish
papers.scale: 6 earthen ponds (~0.05 ha, ~0.7 m deep, ~325 m3), 3 treated vs 3 untreated, randomly assigned; Stoneville, Mississippi, 1988
papers.dose: Aquashade 1.0 uL/L on June 8, then monthly through September 8 (four treatments)
papers.result: Chlorophyll-a did not differ between dyed and undyed ponds (early season 152 vs 145 ug/L; late season 117 vs 208 ug/L, P = 0.140). Odorous cyanobacteria appeared in 15 of 42 samples across all six ponds, and at the end two ponds per treatment had off-flavored fish.
papers.env_effects: No difference in nitrite, ammonia or aeration hours. About half the dye was gone 10 days after each application, possibly through anaerobic degradation in sediment.
papers.key_details: Randomized pond trial with 3 treated and 3 control commercial-style catfish ponds, sampled biweekly for chlorophyll-a, nitrogen and dye concentration, with microscopic checks for odour-producing algae and flavor tests. Late-season chlorophyll-a looked lower in dyed ponds (117 vs 208 ug/L) but did not differ statistically because of large pond-to-pond variation. Nine of the 15 samples with odorous cyanobacteria came from dyed ponds and six from undyed ponds; three ponds had very strong off-flavors (two dyed, one control). The dye's major absorbance is 550-680 nm, peaking at 630 nm.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: The record says Planktothrix was present in two ponds of each treatment; the full text says odorous cyanobacteria (Planktothrix perornata or Microcystis) were found in all six ponds, and two ponds per treatment had unacceptable off-flavor fish at the end. The late-season chlorophyll-a was 44% lower in dyed ponds but not significantly so, so effect_pct 0 means no significant effect rather than an identical value.
papers.study_note: algal/bloom outcome: Planktothrix perornata and pond phytoplankton

reasons.reproducibility: Randomized trial in six 0.05 ha catfish ponds; needs aquaculture ponds.
reasons.effectiveness: Chl a did not differ significantly (late season 117 vs 208 ug/L, P=0.14) and odorous cyanobacteria occurred in all six ponds.
reasons.cost: Six production ponds with fish over a season cost far over $5,000.
reasons.time: Monthly dye doses June-September, judged at October harvest.
reasons.environment: Dye half-disappeared in ~10 days; no change in ammonia, nitrite or aeration.

papers.title: The Effect of the Dye Aquashade® on Water Quality, Phytoplankton, Zooplankton, and Sunshine Bass, Morone chrysops×M. saxatilis, Fingerling Production in Fertilized Culture Ponds
papers.authors: Ludwig GM, Perschbacher PW, Edziyie R
papers.venue: Journal of the World Aquaculture Society
papers.scale: 9 fertilized 0.04-ha ponds (~70 cm deep), Stuttgart, Arkansas, 2006; 3 early-dye, 3 late-dye, 3 control, randomly assigned
papers.dose: Aquashade 4.8 mg/L (label rate for macrophyte control is 2 mg/L), applied at filling (May 18) or at day 25 (June 12)
papers.duration: 47 days from stocking to fingerling harvest
papers.result: Mean chlorophyll-a over the whole study was significantly higher in dyed ponds (86.5 early, 75.5 late) than in controls (66.7 ug/L; P = 0.02); cyanobacteria densities did not differ among treatments. Respiration, gross and net primary productivity, fish size and condition did not differ.
papers.env_effects: Two control ponds had the lowest fish survival (4.4% and 1.8%) and the highest unionized ammonia (0.14 and 0.10 mg/L average, up to 0.48 mg/L) and pH up to 9.73; differences in pH and unionized ammonia among treatments were not statistically significant.
papers.key_details: Randomized pond trial with three treatments (dye at filling, dye at day 25, no dye), n = 3 ponds each, fertilized with rice bran and stocked with sunshine bass larvae at 15,000 per 0.04 ha. Water chemistry was sampled throughout, with phytoplankton identified to species. Secchi visibility did not differ overall (44.2, 52.3, 47.4 cm). Chlorophyll-a was higher, not lower, in dyed ponds; macrophytes (Najas sp.) were still present at draining. effect_pct -29.7 is computed from 86.5 vs 66.7 ug/L (early dye vs control).
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Dose was 4.8 mg/L, not 4 mg/L. The record says there were few differences in chlorophyll-a; in fact chlorophyll-a was significantly higher in dyed ponds than in controls (P = 0.02). The record's claim that undyed ponds reached harmful pH/ammonia is from two control ponds only and was not statistically significant.

reasons.reproducibility: Randomized trial in nine fertilized 0.04 ha fish ponds; needs aquaculture facilities.
reasons.effectiveness: Opposite effect: mean Chl a was significantly higher in dyed ponds (86.5 and 75.5 vs 66.7 ug/L, P=0.02) and cyanobacteria unchanged.
reasons.cost: Nine stocked production ponds cost far over $5,000.
reasons.time: Ran 47 days to fingerling harvest.
reasons.environment: Dye at 2.4x label rate showed no significant water-quality or fish harm; short-lived residue.

papers.title: Aquashade(R) Treatment of Channel Catfish Ponds
papers.venue: North American Journal of Fisheries Management
papers.organism: Pond phytoplankton, underwater weeds, channel catfish
papers.scale: 3 treated vs 3 control catfish ponds
papers.dose: Aquashade 4 mg/L
papers.result: Dye turned water blue but did not appreciably change Secchi depth; chlorophyll-a and weed cover did not differ from controls. Dye concentration fell ~0.75 mg/L per month through seepage.
papers.env_effects: Dusk dissolved oxygen lower in treated ponds; no water-quality improvement.

reasons.reproducibility: Six catfish ponds treated from April to August.
reasons.effectiveness: Chlorophyll-a and weed cover did not differ from controls and Secchi depth barely changed.
reasons.cost: Six production ponds, effectively unobtainable.
reasons.time: April-August season.
reasons.environment: Dusk dissolved oxygen was lower in treated ponds, and dye persisted, fading ~0.75 mg/L per month.

papers.title: Evaluation of Transparency and Light Attenuation by Aquashade™
papers.authors: Madsen JD, Getsinger KD, Stewart RM, Skogerboe JG, Honnell DR, Owens CS
papers.scale: 3-m deep outdoor tanks with reservoir water
papers.dose: Aquashade 0, 1 and 5 mg/L
papers.result: In filtered lake water, 1 and 5 mg/L cut transparency by ~10% and ~30%; with clay turbidity, 1 mg/L had no significant effect and 5 mg/L cut it 31%. Dye absorbs 550-650 nm (peak ~630 nm); at the allowed 1 mg/L the light effect is small.
papers.env_effects: Visibility stays above swimming standards at label rates.

reasons.reproducibility: 3-m deep outdoor tanks with reservoir water and light meters; a scaled-down version is possible but the tanks are specialist.
reasons.effectiveness: Algae were not measured; only transparency fell ~10-30%, and 1 mg/L had no significant effect with clay turbidity.
reasons.cost: Deep tanks and an underwater light sensor likely $500-5,000.
reasons.time: Short-term trials.
reasons.environment: Dye residue added; visibility stays above swimming standards at label rates.

papers.title: Illuminating the Impact of a Floating Photovoltaic System on a Shallow Drinking Water Reservoir: The Emergence of Benthic Cyanobacteria
papers.authors: Sandrini G, Wagenvoort AJ, van Asperen R, Hofs B, Mathijssen D, van der Wal A
papers.scale: Kralingen drinking-water storage reservoir, Rotterdam (shallow); sun-tracking FPV of 0.95 ha (24% of surface, 1.00 MWp) installed April 2020; under-array site compared with open water ~35 m away, diving surveys before (2019) and after
papers.dose: 24% surface shading by floating solar
papers.result: Direct light under the array peaked at 23% of open water in summer; benthic cyanobacterial mats (Gomphosphaeria, then Phormidium) developed under the FPV while Chara and other macrophytes disappeared there. Planktonic phytoplankton composition was generally very similar under the array and in open water.
papers.env_effects: Benthic mats produced geosmin up to 20 ng/L (odour threshold ~5 ng/L), 2-MIB, anatoxin-a (0.014 ug/g) and microcystins (8.8 ug/g wet weight in 2022), though not problematic for the treatment plant; loss of Chara; heavy Dreissena biofouling on floats; DO and temperature little affected.
papers.key_details: Field monitoring of one reservoir with a single FPV array (no replicate reservoirs); comparisons are before/after plus under-array vs open-water points. Light modelling explained the shift: bottom light under the array fell below the ~3% surface level assumed for Chara but stayed above the 1% level for cyanobacteria. No benthic cyanobacterial mats were found in July 2019 before installation. Overall phytoplankton biovolume decreased but cyanobacteria became relatively more abundant over time. Evides (the utility) authors.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: None material; record lacked the toxin and odour numbers and the fact that planktonic phytoplankton hardly changed.

reasons.reproducibility: A 0.95 ha, 1 MWp floating solar array on a drinking-water reservoir; industrial scale.
reasons.effectiveness: Plankton barely changed, and benthic cyanobacterial mats appeared under the array.
reasons.cost: Floating PV installation costs far over $5,000.
reasons.time: Changes were documented over 2.5 years.
reasons.environment: Benthic mats made geosmin up to 20 ng/L, anatoxin-a and microcystins; Chara disappeared under the array.

papers.title: Effects of floating photovoltaic systems on water quality of aquaculture ponds
papers.authors: Wang T-W, Chang P-H, Huang Y-S, Lin T-S, Yang S-D, Yeh S-L
papers.freshwater_or_marine: both (freshwater prawn and tilapia ponds; milkfish pond in diluted seawater, 23 ppt)
papers.scale: One FPV-covered and one control pond at each of 3 Taiwan Fisheries Research Institute sites (Chupei and Lukang ~800 m2, 1 m deep; Cigu ~3000 m2, 1.75 m deep)
papers.dose: Hydrelio HDPE floating PV buoys covering 40% of the pond surface
papers.result: Mean plankton biomass in control ponds was at least twice that in FPV ponds at all three sites (p<0.05; e.g. 12,923 vs 5052 units/L at Chupei, 19,597 vs 7683 at Lukang, 136 vs 43 at Cigu), and BOD was lower under FPV. Final production was 1.1x (prawn), 1.2x (tilapia) and 1.41x (milkfish) higher in FPV ponds.
papers.env_effects: FPV ponds had higher total ammonia nitrogen (significant at Chupei: 0.203 vs 0.037 ppm) and higher orthophosphate (significant at Chupei and Cigu), while total photosynthetic pigments were lower (significant at Lukang and Cigu).
papers.key_details: Paired-pond field comparison at three aquaculture sites: each site had one pond with 40% simulated floating-photovoltaic cover and one uncovered control, both aerated by paddle wheels and stocked identically (20,000 prawns, 5,000 tilapia or 3,700 milkfish). Water quality was sampled repeatedly (n=11, 12 and 6 sampling events), so replication is temporal only with one pond per treatment (pseudoreplication). Plankton biomass fell by about 61%, 61% and 68% (computed from Table 2 means) and total photosynthetic pigments by 35-88%. Survival was 30.9 vs 30.0% (prawn), 48 vs 40% (tilapia) and 66.4 vs 40.7% (milkfish).
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: effect_pct was null; Table 2 gives about a 61% lower plankton biomass under 40% FPV cover (computed from means). The record also omits the higher ammonia and orthophosphate in FPV ponds, and the design has only one pond per treatment per site.

reasons.reproducibility: 40% floating PV cover on 800-3,000 m2 aquaculture ponds at three institutes; not school-repeatable.
reasons.effectiveness: Plankton biomass ~61-68% lower under FPV, but one pond per treatment per site (pseudoreplicated sampling).
reasons.cost: Floating PV buoys on ponds cost far over $5,000.
reasons.time: Compared over a full culture season.
reasons.environment: FPV ponds had significantly higher ammonia and orthophosphate at some sites.

papers.title: Floating solar panels on reservoirs impact phytoplankton populations: A modelling experiment
papers.authors: Exley G, Page T, Thackeray SJ, Folkard AM, Couture R-M, Hernandez RR
papers.scale: MyLake-FPV 1-D model of a UK two-tank reservoir (existing 4.5% FPV array), 0-100% extra coverage in 10% steps, three siting scenarios (fast-flowing tank, central, slow-flowing tank), with uncertainty (GLUE-style) ensembles
papers.dose: FPV surface coverage
papers.result: Peak total chlorophyll-a declined roughly exponentially with coverage: in Scenario-Fast by 10.21 ug/L at 10% cover, 20.40 at 50% and 22.09 at 90% (negligible chl-a above 60% cover); Scenario-Central by 4.01, 19.69 and 22.01 ug/L. With the slow-tank siting, up to 30% cover gave anything from a 19% decrease to a 4% increase.
papers.env_effects: Altered thermal structure; species composition changes.
papers.key_details: Modelling only, no field validation of FPV effects (no published values existed for FPV effects on wind or light, so they were assumed). Phytoplankton simulated as three functional groups (diatoms, cyanobacteria, greens; grazed/ungrazed). FPV mostly cooled surface water (Tmax -0.55 C per 10% cover up to 70% in Scenario-Fast), with a few warmer days at low cover. Total cyanobacteria biomass fell with coverage, but authors warn functional-group aggregation could miss shade-tolerant species becoming dominant.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record gave no magnitudes; full text shows large chlorophyll cuts only at high coverage and possible increases at low coverage in one siting.

reasons.reproducibility: 1-D MyLake-FPV model runs; needs specialist modelling skills and reservoir data.
reasons.effectiveness: Modelled only, with assumed wind/light effects; big Chl a cuts only at high cover and slow-tank siting could raise Chl a up to 4%.
reasons.cost: Model software is free but site data and setup take specialist time.
reasons.time: A real FPV effect on peak chlorophyll would take a growing season to appear, not days.
reasons.environment: Modelled cooling and possible shade-tolerant species shifts.

papers.title: Impacts of a floating photovoltaic system on temperature and water quality in a shallow tropical reservoir
papers.authors: Yang P, Chua LHC, Irvine KN, Nguyen MT, Low E-W
papers.scale: Tengeh Reservoir, Singapore: field sampling at 6 sites (May 2015-May 2017), 6 m2 mock-up and 1 ha demonstration FPV (2017) for temperature, pH, DO and radiation; 3-D ELCD model predicting a hypothetical 30 MW (42 ha) array
papers.dose: ~30% surface coverage by FPV
papers.result: Model predicted chlorophyll-a under panels to decline by up to 30%, with water ~0.3 °C warmer and a more stable water column (Richardson number 2.3 to 3.3). Away from the panels, water quality was unaffected.
papers.env_effects: Model: DO under panels down up to 50%, TOC down 15%, TN +10% and TP +30%, mixing energy 9e-7 to 7e-7 W/kg. Measured under the 1 ha demo: DO 7.96 mg/L (105% sat.) vs 8.48 mg/L (111%) in open water, higher pH, surface water +0.32 C on average.
papers.key_details: The 30% chlorophyll-a decline is a model prediction for the hypothetical 42 ha installation, not a measurement; the field demo measured physical/chemical variables only (no chlorophyll comparison reported). Model was calibrated/validated against the 2015-2017 field sampling. Effects were confined to the area under the panels. Tropical reservoir setting.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: Record said the model was 'validated with a 1 ha demo'; the model was validated against 2015-2017 field sampling, and the demo supplied temperature, radiation, pH and DO only, so the 30% chlorophyll cut is purely modelled.

reasons.reproducibility: 3-D ELCD model plus field sensors on a reservoir demo; specialist tools.
reasons.effectiveness: The 30% Chl a cut under panels is purely modelled; the 1 ha demo measured no chlorophyll.
reasons.cost: Modelling and sonde data collection cost roughly $150-500 to repeat.
reasons.time: A real change under FPV would take a season to show.
reasons.environment: Model predicts DO down up to 50% and TP up 30% under panels.

papers.title: Viability of the cyanobacterium Planktothrix rubescens in the cold and dark, related to over-winter survival and summer recruitment in Lake Zürich
papers.scale: Single isolated filaments in tubes
papers.dose: Total darkness at 4 C
papers.result: After 58 days of cold darkness, filament viability ranged from 0% (strain 9307) to >50% (strains 9736 and 97112). In the hardiest strain viability was 93% at 34 days, 38% at 79 days and 0% at 111 days, with 50% mortality estimated at 70 days.
papers.env_effects: n/a (lab)
papers.key_details: Six P. rubescens strains isolated from Lake Zurich (1993-1997) were stored at 4 C in the dark, then single filaments were transferred to 20 C light and scored for regrowth. Population-culture tests (Method A) were abandoned because many filaments lysed and could not be picked. Single-filament tests used 36 filaments per strain at 58 days, and 72 filaments per time point in the time course for strain 9736. Integrated mean survival over 111 days was 61%. The study concerns over-winter survival, not a mitigation treatment, and relevance to shading-based control is indirect.
papers.fulltext_discrepancy: The record's '4-5 C' should be 4 C. Full loss of viability in the hardiest strain took 111 days (~16 weeks) of total darkness.

reasons.reproducibility: Needs purchased P. rubescens strains and single-filament picking under a microscope.
reasons.effectiveness: Darkness killed filaments slowly and unevenly: 0% to >50% viable at 58 days, and the hardiest strain needed 111 days.
reasons.cost: Strains, tubes and a cold incubator cost about $150-500.
reasons.time: Viability differences took about two months (50% mortality ~70 days).
reasons.environment: Darkness adds nothing to the water.

calibration.summary: 3 scorers each scored the same 6 papers. 26 of 30 criterion scores (87%) agreed within 1 point; 17 matched exactly; 4 differed by 2 or more.
